Correspondence respecting the Rights and Privileges of 
the Latin and Greek Churches in Turkey. 


No. 1. 


The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Received January 22.) 
(No. 23.) 


My Lord, Vienna, January 15, 1854. 
AT the Conference which took place on the 16th instant, Count Buol 
requested M. de Bourqueney, Count Arnim, and myself, to inquire of our 
respective Governments in what way they would propose that the answer which’ 
may be expected from the Cabinet of St. Petersbur h as to the proposals of 
negotiation should be transmitted to the Porte, He thought that an early 
decision upon this subject should be come to, in order that no time should be 
lost in forwarding the communication after it had been received. The answer of 
Count Nesselrode would naturally be addressed to himself, and he should com- 
municate it to the Conference before he took any further step with regard to it. 
I have, &c. 
(Signed) WESTMORLAND, 


No. 2. " 
Count Nesselrode to Baron Brunnow.—(Communicated to the Earlof Clurendon 
hy Baron Brunnow, January 23.) 


St. Peétersbourg, le yy Janvier, 1854. 

LES Représentants d’Angleterre et de France viennent de m annoncer 
verbalement la résolution prise ape leurs deux Gouvernements de faire entrer 
leurs flottes combinées dans la Mer Noire, dans le but de mettre les ports et les 
ebtes de la Turquie a Vabri d'une attaque de notre part. Le motif donné & cette 
détermination a été le coup porté a l'escadre Turque & Sinope, opération navale 
que les deux Cabinets représentent comme une agression gratuite. Ce n'est | 
sans une pénible surprise que je l'ai entendu qualifier ainsi, lorsqu'il est de notori¢té 
que Vescadre Turque, commandée par Osman Pasha, était partie du Bosphore 
chargée d'armes, cornet de munitions et de troupes de débarquement destinées 
pour nos cdtes de la Circassie; par conséquent dans un but agressif—dans le but 
de développer les opérations également agressives qui ont déji ensanglanté la terri- 
toire Russe en Asie, Cotte escadre n’avait pas sans doute quite son ancr du 
Bosphore pour venir s'établir 4 Sinope. Ce qu'elle y avait cherché a neat 
point ane station maritime, mais bien un refuge passager. _ Devions-nous 
souffrir patiemment qu'elle eft plue tard accompli sa destination hostile? 
Parceque, en Valachie, territoire Ture, nous avons déclaré vouloir attendre 
Vattaque des forces Ottomanes, sommes-nous tenus i lattendre également sur 
nos propres cétes? Devons-nous penser qu’aux yeux des Puissances, dans une

(Translation.) 


St. Petersburgh, January qq, 1854. 


THE Representatives of England and France have verbally announced to 
me the resolution adopted by ther two Governments to cause their combined 
fleets to enter the Black Sea with the view of securing the ports and coasts ot 
Turkey from an attack on our side, ‘The reason ussigned for this determination 
was the attack on the Turkish squadron at Sinope, a naval operation which 
the two Cabinets represent as a gratuitous aggression. It is not without painful 
surprise that | have heard tt thus characterized, when it is notorious that the 
Turkish squadron, commanded by Osman Pasha, left the Bosphorus freighted 
with arms, money, ammunition, and troops for disembarkation, destined for our 
Cireassian consts; consequently with the intention of giving greater extension, 
to the operations equally aggressive which have already stained with blood the 
Russian territory in Asia. ‘That squadron had doubtless not left its anchorage 
in the Bosphorus in order to station itself at Sinope. What it had sought there 
was not a maritime station, but a temporary shelter. Ought we patiently to 
allow it afterwards to execute its hostile purpose? Because, in Wallachia, which 


il 


3 


is Turkish territory, we have declared our intention of waiting for the attack of 
the Ottoman forces, are we obliged equally to wait for 1b on our own coasts ? 
Are we to suppose that, in the opinion of the Powers, in @ war which we have 
not wished for, and which has been declared against us, the privilege of acting 
offensively belongs to Turkey alone, and that when certam of being immediately 
and suddenly attacked we have precluded ourselves from the right of pre- 
venting it? 

If I have rightly understood the sense of the declarations which have been 
made to me, and specifically what was said to me by the English Represen- 
lative, it would be the intention of the two Powers to prevent the recurrence 
of a disaster resembling that at Sinope, and to establish henceforth a species ol 
naval armistice, preventing any attack on our part upon the Turkish ports or 
flag, but taking care, on the other hand, that the Turkish squadron should not 
commit any upon the Russian ships and territory, = 

It is essential, M. le Baron, that this point should be clearly established. 
Agsuredly it is the least that the two Cabinets can do in order to divest, at least in 
appearance, the cause of the entrance of their fleets into the Black Sea of the 
character of flagrant hostility against us; for to allow the Turks to attack, while 
assuming to prohibit us from doing 80, would be to take an active part im a war 
which they have not yet declared against us. 

It is only to be regretted that the two Powers, if they were desirous of pre- 
venting such collisions, had not, from the commencement of the contest, put a 
stop to the maritime expeditions directed by the Turks against our Asiatic 
coasts, expeditions of which the conflict at Sinope has been only a necessary 
consequence, or still more that they had not prevented the Turks from declaring 
war against us; for from the time that they allowed them to declare it and to 


wage it against us, in Asia as well as in Europe, the event which has occurred 
could not altogether be excluded from their anticipations. But if they con- 
sidered as contrary to the independence of the Porte the pretension entirely to 
interdict it from engaging in hostilities, we ask how that of allowing it 
henceforth to undertake hostilities only to a certain extent would be more con- 
sistent with the idea which they entertain of that same independence? As for 
ourselves, it is impossible for us to look upon such a resolution in any other 
light than as a violence offered to our belligerent rights. The Emperor, there- 
fore, finds himself obliged solemnly to protest against the declaration which has 
been addressed to him, and can in no wise admit its legality. 

He will await, in order to decide upon the course that he shall adopt, the 
manner in which that declaration shall have been carried into execution by the 
Admirals of the two fleets, and the attitude which their vessels shall take with 
regard to our own. 

He cannot but regret to see the peace with England and France, which he 
has never been desirous of interrupting, put in jeopardy by this freslt extension 
given to a system of pressure which the two maritime Powers have deemed tt 
their duty to adopt towards him, and which, advancing step by step, involving 
each time more and more his dignity as well as their own, at the same time that 
it encouraged the Porte to push matters to extremities, has ended by bringing 
affairs in the East to their actual state of tension. At the present moment a 
mere chance is sufficient to bring about a collision from which a general con- 
flagration would ensue, and the Emperor disclaims beforehand the responsibility 
of the first step which shall have given the signal for it. 

Your Excellency will read and give a copy of this despatch to the English 
Cabinet. 

Reecive, &c. 


(Signed) NESSELRODE,

(No. 49. Secret and Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, January 16, 1854. 

SINGE my despatches up to this number were written I have had a most 
interesting conversation with a person deep in the Emperor's confidence and 
master of many of his secrets, ‘ 

‘This person assures me, upon his word of honour, that he is convinced that 
the Emperor is sincerely desirous of peace, that the influence of Count Nessel- 
rode appears to be returning, and that His Majesty is evidently beginning to 
ask himself whether a heavy responsibility will not attach to him if he should 
neglect any means for preventing a general war, Upon my professing some 
incredulity the person in question entreated me to suspend iny belief, to defer

the departure of the messenger, and to see whether the events of the next two 
or three days confirmed my opinion or his assertions, 

I have accordingly determined that the messenger Blackwood should only 
set off'on the 18th or 19th instant, by which time I shall of course have received 
some answer Count Nesselrode to the notification made to him on the 12th 
instant. 

Learning that the Emperor was in a softened state of mind I have endea- 
voured to prevail on the person above alluded to, to represent or cause to. be 
represented to His Majesty what a splendid part he may.yet play if, after com- 
pleting his immense military and naval preparations, he should point to them 
and say, Precisely the means which I now possess of carrying on war on the 
most extensive seale enable me to give the world a convincing proof of my 
moderation. 

Some time since your Lordship was informed that a half-formed purpose 
existed here of despatching Count Orloff upon an extraordinary mission to 
London. 

Whether the idea has been resumed I am unable to say, but circumstances 
have come to my knowledge which induce me to believe that this may prove to 
be the case. 

I have, &c.

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received January 24.) 


(No. 71.) 
My Lord, Paris, January 23, 1804. 

THE Turkish Ambassador at this Court placed in M. Drouyn de Lhuys’ 
hands a few days ago a note on the part of his Government, intended to be 
supplementary to and explanatory of the note addressed by the Porte on the 
S\st ultimo to the Representatives of the Four Powers at Constantinople, 
stating on what terms the Porte would be willing to treat for peace with Russia. 
Your Lordship has no doubt received a similar note from M. Musurus, and you 
will have heard that it has been equally uddressed to the Courts of Vienna and 
Berlin, and that Count Buol returned it to the Turkish Envoy at Vienna with 
the remark that the Emperor of Austria refused to accept it. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys informed me yesterday that Count Buol had proposed 
to summon the Conference to take this note into their consideration, with a view 
of placing on record their disapproval and disayowal of its contents. M. Drouyn 
de Lhuys was averse to this proceeding, although he blamed the conduct of the 
Turkish Government. In the first place he did not see how Count Buol could 
bring before the Conference a document which he had himself repudiated and 
secondly, he thought that the interterence of the Conference would give greater 
importance to the note than it was desirable it should obtain. He had, he said, 
expressed himself in this sense to M, de Hiibner, He considered the observations 
now made by the Porte to be premature and to be matter for discussion here- 
after, should the present attempts at negotiation ever reach that point. In fact, 
the Conference could not entertain the note, whether for approbation or disap- 

robation, without informing the Russian Government that they had done so, 
icy could not Ignore it and discuss it in the same breath. 

I saw M, Drouyn de Lhuys again this morning, when he said that he 
had received advices from London and Berlin which showed that these two 
Governments coincided in opinion with him, and he did not doubt that when 
this was known, the Austrian Cabinet would agree to adopt their view. 

__ He proposed returning no answer to Vely Pacha, but aidressing an 
instruction to General Baraguay d’Hilliers, stating that the French Government 
considered thet they had discharged their task for the present in forwarding the 
Porte’s propositions to St. Petersburgh, with a recommendation that they should 
be accepted. Whatever more the Porte might have to say, must be left for the 
Conferences which would necessarily be established whenever the belligerent 
parties named Plenipotentiaries for the negotiation of a peace.

My Lord, Paris, January 23, 1854. 
M. DROUYN DE LHUYS has read to me a despatch dated the 19th 
instant, and addressed to Count Walewski, in which his Excellency calls the 
attention of Her Majesty's Government to the necessity under which the two 
Cabinets will be of asking the future intentions of Austria and Prussia, should 


the Russian answer be unfavourable to the entertainment of the propositions 
lately sent from the Porte. 


M. Drouyn de Lhuys recapitulated with his usual felicity of language the — 


different steps taken by the Austrian and Prussian Governments since the 
beginning of the Oriental question, and which all but bind them to more serious 
action should the present negotiations fail of success. 

Lasked whether it would riot be better to await the arrival of the answer 
from St. Petersburgh before deciding on the course which should then be taken. 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys replied, certainly, that was what he meant; but he thought 
that the two Governments might in the meantime interchange opinions as to 
the different eventualities they might have to consider,

No. 12. 
Lord Bloomfield to the Bart of Clarendon.—(Received January ud.) 


(No. 2. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, January 21, 1854. 

I CALLED this morning on Baron Manteuffel. We had some general 
conversation on the Oriental question, and I have much satisfaction in reporting 
that the opinions of the Prussian Minister appeared to me to be everything Her 
Majesty's Government could expect under existing circumstances. He spoke with 
great candour of the difficulties of his own position with the King, but he uttered 
not aword implying a doubt as to the success which he felt must attend his efforts 
to place Prussia in an independent position. I did not fail to state to him that 
Her Majesty's Government had been well pleased with the late mission of 
Count Pourtales, a8 giving 4 proof that the Prussian Government intend to act 
with us, and that I was able to convey to his Excellency the assurance that the 
desire of cordial cooperation existed in England as strongly as he could wish it ; 
that if war with Russia became ‘nevitable the union of Prussia with the maritime 
Powers would ensure an earlier termination of the differences than would 
otherwise be the case ; but that we till should devote all our energies to the 
maintenance of peace, which was the true interest of all. Baron Manteuffel 
then told me that the Russian Minister had received despatches from 5t. Peters- 
burgh this morning, and that the answers to the communication lately made to 
the Imperial Government by Sir Hamilton Seymour and General Castelbajac on 
the entrance of the fleets into the Black Sea had already passed through Berlin 
on their way to London and Paris, and that Baron Budberg was coming to him 
this evening. 

1 immediately asked his Excellency to permit me to call on him again, and 
Lam just returned from my second interview. 

Baron Manteutlel told me that the Russian Minister had left with him 
copies of two ‘netructiona of the #ath instant to Baron Brunnow and M. de 
Kisseleff, ‘The first contains some observations on the verbal communication 
made by Her Majesty's Minister at St. Petersburgh endeavouring to show the 
unreagonableness of our proceedings in this matter, and defending the attack at 
Sinope as essential to prevent the Turks from carrying supplies and troops to 
attack the Russian territory in Asia; a d the second instruction, which 1s con- 
fidential, directs Baron Brunnow to address an official note to your Lordship 
requiring a written explanation of the intentions of Her Majesty’s Government

Such, Baron Manteuffel said, was the nature of the communication to

I replied to his Excellency that the gravity of the case was euch that it

(Translation.) 


London, January +4, 1834. 


THE Undersigned, &e., has received orders to have an explanation, and to 
come to an understanding with his Excellency the Earl of Clarendon, &c., 
as to the precise meaning of a communication which the En lish Minister at 
St. Petersburgh has just made verbally to the Chancellor of the Empire. 

If it was caused by the wish to avert the contingency of a collision between 
the Russian and Ottoman naval forces, that result could only be effected by the 
observance of a principle of just reciprocity, 

For this purpose it would be requisite, in the first instance, that it should 
be expressly understood that the Ottoman squadron should refrain from all 

gression on the Russian flag and country on the coast of Europe and of Asia, 

Under this condition equal security would be obtained for the Ottoman flag 
and coast. 

In the second place, in case the Turkish ships should be allowed to continue 
without impediment to keep up communications between one Ottoman port and 
another for the transport of provisions, ammunition, and troops, it would be 
necessary that the same condition should be secured to the ships of the Imperial 
marine for freely keeping up communication between one Russian port and 
another on the coast of Europe and Asia. 

These arrangements, thus agreed upon and strictly executed, would have 

theeffect of suspending, in fact, hostilities at sea between the belligerent 
yarties. 
E The Undersigned has the honour to request his Excellency the Rarl of 
Clarendon to have the goodness to inform him, in reply to this note, if the 
‘ntentions of Her Britannic Majesty's Government are in accordance with those 
of the Imperial Cabinet as to the principles of pertect reciprocity established by 
the present communication. poe 

The Undersigned, &c. (Signed) BRUNNOW.

No. 19. 
Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received January 27.) 


(No. 48. Secret.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, January 16, 1854. 

[ FIND myself at this moment in such a maze of intrigue as to be utterly 
unable to follow its windings. Tecan but make out some of the objects whic 
are sought, and discover the features of certain of the persons engaged. Among 
them there are a few who from their position should have been restrained by & 
sense of dignity from engaging in these exercises of dexterity. 

The principal points to be attained appear to be these :—To induce Austria 
and Prussia to pursue a policy very different to that which their true interests 
should prompt them to carry through, and to put an end to that alliance 
ea England and France which the conduct of Russia herself has brought 
about, 

‘As ] am desirous to refrain as much as possible from mentioning names, I 
will only say that diplomatists and soldiers, courtiers of both sexes, and persons 
of still higher rank, are engaged in ecabals and negotiations of a kind happily 
unknown in England. 

Paramount to all other objects is that of putting an end to the Franco- 
Anglo alliance, to effect which all means, as 1 am bound to infer, are considered 
to be legitimate. 

Matters are pushed to such a point—the desire to establish a difference of 
bearing towards England and France is so manifest—that I can assure your 
Lordship very seriously that it would not surprise me if it should prove that a 
distinction were made between General Castelbajac and myself, and that T alone 
were to receive My passports. 

It is only by the disposition which might dictate guch an artful move, that 
I can account for the laboured attempt now making to vilify me, and to exalt 
the character and qualities of my French colleague. 

[had the honour of stating to your Lordship some time since, that it 
occurred to me, that in the course of a long and most unpleasant negotiation I 
might have been at times wanting in the energy which became a servant of the 
English Crown; but it appears that my failings have been of an opposite kind. 
My impetuosity and violence (as I now ascertain) have been of such a nature as 
render me unfit for the transaction of business of importance ! whilst the mode- 
ration of General Castelbajac has very much tempered the offence which other- 
wise might have been conveyed by the acts of his Government. 

I will not, at allevents at present, dwell upon this comparison, but proceed 
with my French colleague. 

As I have before stated he is a worthy and amiable man, but his weakness, 
and his blind and avowed admiration of the Court is such, that whilst this Court 
cajole him, make use of him, and then turn him into ridicule, the French 
Government must not be surprised if their policy is mistrusted, if their views 
are not carried out, and if illusions are preserved here, which even in the 
interests of peace should long ago have been dissipated. 

I can better exemplify than describe a constant system of courtiership 
pursued by General Castelbajac towards the Emperor Nicholas, which at all 
times vated be undignified, and which under existing circumstances is most 
mischievous. 

On the jyth January my unfortunate colleague wrote a complimentary 
letter to Count Nesselrode, with a second complimentary message for the 
Emperor, which of course was speedily conveyed to its destination. 

His Majesty replied by some flattering expressions which were written on 
the back of Ganeral Castelbujac’s letter, sent in original by the Chancellor, 
which portion of letter the General was allowed to detach, and to keep in recol- 
lection of the Emperor's feclings towards him. 

When it ig considered that these adulatory overtures fare made as often as 
oceasion offers, that they are accompanied by the warmest assurances of confi- 
dence in the Emperor's professions, by expressions of surprise at the mistrust of 
His Majesty exhibited by England, and even France, and when several very 
unguarded observations with regard to Sinope are current, your Lordship will 


21 


readily believe that it cannot he otherwise but that His Imperial Majesty is 
confirmed in his belief that the Emperor Napoleon is ready to answer as s00n as 
he shall be called in a friendly manner. 

To General Castelbajac that may be all very agreeable ; to me, with the duties 
imposed upon me, it is to the greatest degree embarrassing and perplexing. 

I entreat your Lordship’s attention to what follows, which is certainly very 
remarkable. {had written the preceding part of this despatch, down to the 
words “friendly manner,” when General Castelbajac entered my room, and at 
once began speaking of the intrigues set on foot to separate I'rance and England. 
We.” he said (the French), “are not s0 much abused; you and the English 
are dreadfully, and as that has an object, it has occurred to me whether it is 
possible that the Russians can meditate playing a trick (manuvais tour), 
whether they may not be capable of sending you your passports, and of 
leaving me quietly here. I can assure you it would place me ina very false 
position.” 

I told General Castelbajac that some suspicions of the same kind had passed 
across my mind, and T added this; “All that is passing 1s a miserable attempt 
ta break up our alliance; first England is abused, then France, then England 
again ; just now it happens to be our turn, to-morrow possibly it may be yours. 
Maintenant, Général, faites attention a ce que je vais avoir 'honneur de vous 
dire. Je n'ai point la prétention de vous dicter la conduite que vous avez a 
guivre, mais je vous dis cegi. Nous voila embarques dans une entreprise com- 
mune, Si par hazard cest & la France qu'on en voudra, si c'est vous qui alle 
recevoir vos passeports, je vous declare d’avance que sans hesitation et sans 
instruction je demanderai les miens aussi. Dailleurs le cas échéant, faites. comme 
vous lentendez.”’ 

I think it right to state a singular occurrence, but I am not sure of being 
able to offer your Lordship its explanation. It is not, however, improbable that 
it may be found in the fact of my having as a colleague a man who is utterly 
unfit to deal with the very difficult affairs into which his evil star has conducted 
him. 

T will only add, that as | am prepared for fresh foul play, so likewise I am 
wrepared to meet it. Ifthe Russian Government send me alone my passports 
1 all treat the matter as a personal question, and address a note to Count 
Nesselrode, stating that the resolution with regard to watching the Black Sea 
having been taken in comunon by the English and French Governments, I can 
only infer that I must have given unwillingly some offence, the natute of which 
T shall call upon the Emperor to explain. 

My French colleague now acquaints me that when he had his interview of 
the Chancellor he forgot to state that the Turkish ships were to be kept back 
from attacking the Russian coasts, and that he has now given that assurance to 
Count Nesselrode in a private letter | 

I do not doubt that it will prove that he has done so in terms that will 
make up for the delay and inadvertency, 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recetved January 27.) 


(No, 51. Secret and Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, January 18, 1854. 

IP ever there was a time when greater difficulty than at any other existed 
in arriving at the truth, and yet when its discovery wasessential for the conduct 
of affairs, it is the present moment. 

1 think it right accordingly to state to your Lordship that I have reason’ for 
believing that Count Reiset was the bearer of an autograph letter from the 
Emperor Napoleon to General Castelbajac, and that this letter has been shown 
to the Chancellor. 

What its contents may be I am wholly unable to state, and neither the 
French Minister nor his Secretary of Legation have alluded, in speaking to me, 
to the existence of such a letter. 

Princess Lieven, whose diplomatic functions are well known to your Lord- 
ship, writes word that having had the honour of an audience of the Empress 
Eugénie, the Emperor Napoleon came into the room and conversed with her for 
three-quarters of an hour ; his whole conversation, the Princess states (but with 
what correctness is at least doubtful), consisted of in uiries about the Ismperor, 
and in friendly messages to be conveyed to His Imperial Majesty. 

With reference to my despatch No, 48, I may take this opportunity of 
informing your Lordship that my conversation with General Castelbajac appears 
to have produced a good effect : on the 16th instant he wrote to his Government 
to say that he had some reason for believing that it was m contemplation to send 
Her Majesty’s Minister away and not to deliver him his passports. 

General Castelbajac added, that should this attempt nt establishing @ 
difference in the position of the two Missions be made, he should consider it to 
be his duty to demand his passports.

No. 22. 
Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received January 27.) 


(No, 52. Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, January 18, 1854. 
THE task of reporting favourably of one’s colleagues is as agreeable as it is 
painful to notice those who are wanting in their public duty. 
It is, then, with alacrity that I beg to state to your Lordship that the 
conduct of General de Rochow during the last anxious days has been highly 
conciliatory and very much to his credit, 
[ have not been able to obtain sight of a letter which he hag lately addressed 
to Count Nesselrode, but Iam assured that it contained a very judicious and 
pacific appeal to the calm judgment of the Emperor, and that, upon being laid 


23 


before His Majesty. it appeared to shake his warlike resolutions more than any 
representation which as yet has been made to him. | 

It is, however, but too probable that the voices of the many, whose only 
object is to recommend themselves to the Imperial opinion and prejudices, will 
drown those very few which are raised in the cause of good sense, moderation. 
and humanity. 

~ It is only by a sort of chance, and under a Pe of seeresy, that I have 
learned a very judicious suggestion which was made to the Emperor by the King 
of Prussia at the time His Imperial Majesty was at Olmiitz. | | 

The King of Prussia wrote to His Imperial Majesty to say that the Eastern 
uestion had given rise to too much writing, and had not been sufficiently 
diacdeeed by persons perfectly masters of the subject. Hep osed, accordingly, 
that Ee aat MeRAIFodS: a man well known and esteemed in England, should be

THE indications of that will to which all in Russia is subservient are 50 
contradictory, that it becomes extremely difficult to determine what are the views

my despatch No. 50, stated to a large number of his officers ‘qu'il avait éte 
entrainé par les évenements au-dela de ses intentions.” Tt was then to be inferred 
that at the time His Majesty, being sensible of having advanced too far, Was 
desirous of retracing his steps, and with this view that he would be eager to calm 
the excitement whieh his own acts had produced, 

Two or three days afterwards, however, His Majesty became very impatient 
for the representation of a new theatrical piece, which was to come out, ilhus- 
trative of the glories of Sinope—of the Russian Trafalgar—as the late wretched 
affair is termed by the more patriotic here, 

This piece was produced last night, and the theatre was thronged upon the 
vecasion. All the Imperial family (with the exception of the Emperor, who was 
kept away by business) were precent. The pit had been filled, by orders of the 
Grand Duke Constantine, with naval cadets, and fourteen of these boys, who 
were understood to be the children of officers serving in the Black Sea, were put 
in possession of the Emperor's box. 

Splendid scenes of Sevastopol and Sinope, with the destruction of the 
‘Turkish fleet, and the accompaniment of the National Anthem, made up a 
representation entirely deficient in dramatic interest, but very striking and well 
calculnted to work upon the feclings of a sensitive people, many of whom 
believe, in their ignorance, that their religion is in danger f the Emperor does 
not carry through victoriously the war which he has undertaken with the Turk.

My Lord, St, Petersburgh, January 19, 1854. 


WERE it not that the churacter of a public servant is in some degree 
public property, 1 should not trouble your Lordship with the following short 
detail of circumstances, of interest only to m self. 

I have been for some time past aware that feelings very unfavourable to me 
have been entertained in a high quarter, and that being expressed, they had the 
effect which they could not fail of producing in o gociety where every one follows 
the signal given by the lord and master. All this was a matter of comparative 
‘ndifference to me, and I should have readily borne the reproaches of ill-temper 
and ineapacity, my object in truth being to perform the duties assigned to me 
rather than to seck the approbation of those with whom I have nothing in 
common, 

Lately, however, 1 have ascertained that my misdoings ut this Court were 


25 


of a graver character, and that T have been charged not only with intemperance 
of conduct, but of such wilful misrepresentation of statements as had tended to 
bring about, or at least to complicate, the difficulties which are thickening 
around us, 

It may be susceptibility, my Lomi, oF it may be only the sense of dignity 
which is felt by every English gentleman, but so it is that this imputation, 
however high the quarter from which it may proceed, 1s to me intolerable. 

[ resolved accordingly to open myself to Count Nesselrode, and I did se 
yesterday. . 

Tt was with reluctance, | said, that I must speak to him, in the midst of 

ve affairs, of myself, but 1 had no option. 

I then alluded to the reports which had been circulated as to my uncon- 
ciliatory conduct, and the want of faithfulness in my reports of declarations 
which required peculiar fidelity in their transmission to my Government; and 
added that I was quite aware that, if such was the opinion entertained of me, 
my continued residence at this Court would be an obstacle to the renewal of 
those friendly relations between the two Governments which would, 1 hoped, 
follow as a matter of course if existing disagreements were once happily 
reconciled. | 

I begged, however, to assure his Excellency that no euch obstacle was to be 
apprehended, as nothing could be more settled than my purpose of requesting 
your Lordship to be pleased to take measures for my recall from St, Peters- 
burgh as soon as present difficulties should be removed, 

Gount Nesselrode was of opinion that I attached too much importance to 
flying reports and unauthorized statements. 

“This,” 1 said, “ M. le Comte, might be the case elsewhere; bat we know 
what Russia is. In this country, men, and men highly placed, do not pronounce 
strong judzments without having high authority on their side. In this injustice 
of which T have to complain I do not choose to aciulesce. 

“Now, M. le Comte,” | continued, “ you have heard what my conduct 
here has been represented ; you shall permit me to tell you what it has heen. 

«Towards the end of last May it began to be clear that the policy of the 
Russian Government was very different from that which Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment had been led to expect from declarations from yarious sources which had 
heen made to me. 

“1 immediately felt that, serious complications were likely to ensue, I felt 
that my removal might facilitate explanations and agreement, and 1 accordingly 
wrote to Eler Majesty’s Principal Secretary of State to say, that under these 
altered cireumstances my continuance here might prove an embarrassment 
which | thought the Government would do well to remove. What I offered 
then was my place and my professional reputation; and in thus acting T acted 
ag every English gentleman would haye done. I take no merit for my conduct, 
but I do say, that afterwards. to be reproached with wilful misrepresentation, 
and with having acted in a manner to embroil imternational relations, 18 an 
injustice which to me is wholly unbearable,” 

Count Nesgelrode in a few kind words expressed his satisfaction at the 
official relations which had always existed between us, saying that for his part 
he should be always ready to bear testimony to the temper which I had shown 
+n the discussion of affairs, often of a very trying nature. 

After a pause his Excellency added, ™ You have spoken frankly to me ; I 
will beg to be equally frank with you. May it not be said that in conversing 
with other persons upon penis affairs you have occasional departed from that 
calm and moderation which you have observed invariably when transacting 
business with me?” 

“Mle Comte,” I replied, “my answer shall be a very plain one; and it 
will be exactly what I should return to the Emperor if he were to do me the 
honour of addressing me the same question. It has been observed that a diplo- 
matic agent is a man who is sent abroad to lie for the good of his country. My 
principle is avery different one. [hold it that he is sent tos eak the truth in 
the service of his country, | haye the greatest respect for truth: 

Yon ask me whether I have not occasionally spoken warmly (avec vivacité) 
upon matters of public interest? I reply that 1 have done so often and often ; 
that I have constantly felt very keenly, and have in many instances expressed 
myself strongly. I will only beg leave to remark that this is nota matter al

Sir G. H, Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received January 27.) 


(No. 64.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, January 19, 1854. 

IF peace be the object and purpose of the Russian Government, certainly 
every effort is made to mislead the publie mind, for in every direction prepara- 
tions are making for wholesale war. | 

The forces in Asia being, as the Russian bulletins aint us, victorious ab 
all points, are about to be reinforced by 27,000 men, who are on their march 
through the southern Provinces of the Empire, and who appear to be received 
everywhere (thanks to the arrangements which are made) in a triumphal 
manner. 

Immense provisions of lead and sulphur are being made, and that without 
reference to expense, 

T have just heard of the purchase, on iblie account, of 30,000 poods 
(about 500 tons) of the latter material; whilst as respects lead, it has been 
purchased of the person who had the largest store, disregarding those forms 
which in general are rigidly observed in Russia with regard to contracts. 

In a word, all around betokens approaching war, and the distress which war 
brings in its train. ‘The prices of foreign produce rise from day to day, while 
home produce is very low; the price of stocks is not quoted, and Companies’ 
shares are almost unsaleable. 

L heard of a merchant having made yesterday an extensive sale of sugar, 
and of his ea it back immediately afterwards at an advanced price from the 
broker, and of his re-selling with great profit before the close of the market. 
The case is illustrative of the expectation which prevails among commercial men. 

lt need not, 1 think, be added, that these classes are very averse to the idea 
of war: but the feeling is so little confined to them that a gentleman who has 
been passing several days at Cronstadt assures me that war is equally unpopular 
with the officers of the fleet. They are brave men (my informant said), these 
Russian sailors; and let me tell you that you may yet find that they will fight 
much better than you have been led to believe; but while they declare their 
readiness to encounter death if such be the will of the Emperor, the mass of 
them will confess that the war which seems so imminent is wholly uncalled for 
and pernicious. 

‘As L have alluded to the rise in prices in foreign articles, it may be well to 

uote figures. I will state, then, that within the last month sugars have risen 
oth 94 to 13 roubles silver the pood; lead, from 81 to 38 roubles silver; and 
coals from 25 to 43 roubles silver. 

The only indications of individual confidence in the continuation of peace 
which have come to my knowledge are the discounting of long bills at 7 per cent. 
by the house of Gasser and Co. of St. Petersburgh, and the extensive purchases 
of hemp and tallow by a well-known London house, the name of which | am not 
at liberty to mention, | 

I would beg your Loniship’s attention to the experiments making by the 
house of Stieglitz, and by an English firm likewise of this town, The former 
has sent off a quantity of tallow by land for abipmen at Hamburgh ; the latter, 
a quantity of the same article for shipment at Memel, The object is to ascertain 
the exact cost of the exportation of Russian produce in the event of the Baltic 
being closed by war. 

I have, &e. 


(Signed) G. H, SEYMOUR.

Having given me this detailed account of his interview with M. de Kisseletf, 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys proceeded to say that he had had an interview with the 
Emperor this morning, and that he had submitted the following advice to His

M. Drouyn de Lhuys is of opinion that the answer returned by the two 
Governments to the Russian despatch should be short and reserved, but tem- 
perate; that the refutation of the assertions of the Russian Government should 
be left to facts; that all recrimination should be avoided ; and that the two 
Governments should rather restate their case than. attempt to explain what was 
already clear. While Russia alleged the extraordinary pressure exercised upon 
her by the two Governments ever since the commencement of this question as 
the cause of the present crisis, he would state the cause to be the occupation of 
the Danubian Provinces. Hewould show that when Russia abandoned negotia- 
tion to have recourse to violence, even then the Porte and her allies remained 
patient and unprovoked, and it was not until proof was given that negotiation 
could effect nothing, that the Porte appealed to the sword, and that the allied 
fleets proceeded step by ate from the Dardanelles to the Black Sea. The 
position now of England and France was this;—that whereas Russia had con- 
sidered it necessary to have a material guarantee for the fulfilment of her claims 
upon the Porte by the possession, both administrative and military, of the 
Danubian Provinces, England and France, to restore the equilibrium of the East, 
thus dangerously and, in their opinion, dishonestly disturbed, had thought it 
necessary to have a material muarantes aginst the encroachment of Russia, by 
the possession of the Black Sen, and as Russia would not allow a ‘Turk to 
appear in the Principalities, so England and France would not allow a Russian 
ship to navigate the Black Sea. The one was an equivalent for the other. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys proposes to introduce here some phrase which shall 
not amount to an engagement, but which shall show that it is the intention of 
the allies not to countenance any naval expedition from ‘Turkish ports on 
Russia, so long as the Russian flag is interdicted in the Black Sea; but he does 
not intend to apply the same rule in regard to sending soldiers, arms, &c., from one 
Turkish port to another, because he cannot admit that the two countries ought 
to be placed on the same footing, the one having committed an act of aggression 
which the other is only seeking to repel, 

Russia, said M, Drouyn de Lhuys, aske if we mean to institute a sort of 
naval armistice. 1 answer, Not exactly so, but 1 say that it depends on Russia 
to establish one. She says she means peace; so do we, Let her accept the 
bases of negotiation offered by Turkey, and recommended fram Vienna, Let 
her evacuate the Principalities, and give guarantees to the two Powers, to 
Turkey, and to Europe that the like acts of violence are not to be feared for the 
future, and the measures which England and France have taken will be no 
longer necessary. If she refuses this offer we ought to consider her refusal as a 
declaration of war. 

Such, said M, Drouyn de ra was the proposition which by the 
Emperor's orders he should instruct M. de Wulewski to-morrow to submit for 
your Lordship's consideration. He proposed drawing up in the course of the 
evening the draft of an answer in this sense. 

It is impossible to judge a proposition intended to be committed to writing 
until the pen has done its office, but M, Drouyn de Lhuys’ plan seemed to me 
on the whole to be temperate, firm, and judicious. His abject appears to be to 
present such a document to the world as must utterly condemn the Russian 
Government in the sight of every loyal and sensible mind, and as must make it 
exceedingly difficult for Austria and Prussta to withhold their sympathy and 
support trom Turkey, 

I asked M. Drouyn de Lhuys to whom he proposed transmitting this or 
any other answer that might be agreed upon between the two Governments. 
[t should, I thought, be conveyed to the knowledge of the Russian Government 
by the English and French Representatives at St. Petersburgh, and not by the 
Russian Representatives in London and Paris. In the first place, such a mode

that since 1 had seen him. yesterday, 1 had naturally been turning ever in My 
mind the different subjects which we had been treating, and that his project or 
« more definite understanding with Her Majesty’s Government appeared to me 
to require reconsideration; in fact, it bound the two Governments to nothing ; 
it recapitulated what we all knew to be the objects of the two Governments in 
the Eastern question, but it did not bind them to continue the war until those 
objects were attained. It stipulated that, if propositions were made to either 
of the two Governments singly, the Government ta which the propositions were 
made should inform the other, but it did not bind that Government not to 
accept them without the concurrence of the other; and finally, it inpawe 
obligations respecting the reinforcement of the two fleets, which had the 
appearance of a mutual jealousy instead of a cordial cooperation, wnd might 
prove exceedingly inconvenient, in case of any sudden emergency, It would be 
far better, in my opinion, to leave tt to each Power to bring all the force sey 
thought proper into the field, and to provide that, at the end of the war, the 
respective forces should be reduced to their usual complement. . 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys admitted the justice of some of my observations, euricl 
he expressed a willingness to abandon that part of his project which could be 
eovsidered as putting any limitation on the amount of force which either 
Government might think fit to display, but he objected to anything like an 
engagement between the two Powers, 1 regard to a continuation of the war. 
No doubt, he said, the present proposition was vague to a certain extent, but it 
ledged the two Governments to employ their naval resources, both in the 
Mediterranean and in the Baltie, in the prosecution of the objects they had in 
view; something must be left to the honour of the two Governments, Neither. 
it was to be hoped, would abandon the other unfairly; but still a slate al affairs 
might arise, which would induce the English Government ta think that France 
continued the war in the East in order to favour her projects in the West, or 
France might suppose that England wished to occupy & Russian army in a war 
with ‘Turkey, in order to turn Russian attention from India, anc the _two 
Governments ought not to be bound to continue a war under such oventualitics, 

I rejoined that such a case could hardly arrive ; because the object al the 
war was specified, and, that attained, both Goveriments would become free by 
the fact of the attainment. [remarked further that at all events same addition 
should be made to the last paragraph of the projected note, and that the two 
Governments should bind themselves not only to communicate any propositions 
that might be made to either singly, but should engage positively not to enter 
into any negotiation upon them without inviting its co-belligerent to take part in 
the negotiation,

No. 34. 
Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recewwed January 27.) 


(No. 87. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Paris, January 25, 1854. 

1 HAD the honour to inform your Lordship, in my despatch No. 74, that 
M. Drouyn de Limys had addressed a despatch to Count Walewsk, indicating 
ihe opinion of the French Goverment that the moment was approaching when 
‘t would behove France and England to take steps for ascertaining how far they 
could count on the cooperation of Austria and Prussia in the event of hostilities 
with Russia, 

Reverting to this subject this afternoon, M. Drouyn de Lhuys said that, 
judging from the information which had reached him from Germany and else- 
where, it would be imprudent, at the present moment, peremptorily to summon 
the Austrian and Prussian Governments to declare themselves ; that our tactics 
should be, to endeavour to bring these Governments to us by degrees ; that 
events would do more for us than exhortations; and that we might lead them 
on step by step until they could not escape from their own declarations 
and engagements. For this purpose he had imagined a Convention, which he 
should propose for the siznature of the Four Powers, and to Her Majesty's 
Government of course in the first instance: he read me the draft of this 
Convention. 

The preamble sets forth the objects which the Four Powers have in view, 
and which are to be found in the Protocols of the Conferences held at Vienna, 

Article 1 binds them to use all their efforts to obtain peace on the terms 
mentioned in the Protocol of the 13th of January, and on the assurance of equal 
protection to all the Christian subjects of the Porte. 

Article II stipulates for the evacuation of the Principalities. 

Article IIL stipulates for the revision of the Treaty of 1841, in such a 
manuer as to give greater security to Turkey for the future. 

Article iV obliges the Four Powers to name Plenipeotentiaries without loss 
of time, who are to meet in Conference for the purpose of discussing the measures 
to be adopted for carrying out the objects mentioned in the first three Articles, 

Ratifications to be exchanged within fifteen days. 

M. Dronyn de Lhuys appears to think that the two Northern Powers 
eunnot refuse to consecrate by a Convention principles and opinions to which 
they have already assented in the Protocol of a Conference ; and that, having 
signed a Convention, they will find themselves carried on in spite of themselves 
to defend vi ef armis the principles thus doubly accepted, Should he be mistaken 
in his provision, he should then think the moment arrived when a summary of a 
very different nature should be addressed to the recusant Governments, 

‘A dyntt of the proposed Convention will be sent to Count Walewski 
to-morrow. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) COWLEY.

My Lord, Berlin, January 24, 1854. 


BY the two telegraphic despatches which I have this day sent your Lord- 
ship you will have been inform of the mission of Count Orloff to jenna. It 
was supposed last night by Baron Manteuffel that the Count would have passed 
through Berlin on his way to his ultimate destination, but despatch which his 
Excellency received to-day from General Rochow dated St. Petersburgh, 19th 
instant, makes him believe that he will proceed direct to Vienna and be there 
about the 27th. He was to leave St. Petersburgh on the 20th. 


of which Count Orloff is the bearer, and he only knows that he is charged to 
explain to the Austrian Cabinet the concessions which Russia is prepared to 
make, and the terms on which she will conclude peace with Turkey. [sought 
in vain to learn some further particulars from his Excellency, and I believe that 
he possessed no information beyond the simple tact above reported. 

He, however, looked upon this migsion as offering some slight prospect of 
suecess, but his hopes were based chiefly on the well-known conciliatory character 
of Count Orloff; and of his, rhaps, darmg to take greater responsibility on 
himself than any other of the Fmperor’s servants, and not in any change which 
had come over the opinions of the Russian Government. 

The meeeoe who had left Vienna for St. Petersburgh on the 18th instant 
with the terms of arrangement agreed to by the Porte and recommended by the 
Conference does not appear to have arrived; and on my inquiring of Baron 
Manteuffel whether he thought the Emperor would consent to them, he gave me 
to understand that General Rochow’s impression was, that His Imperial Majesty 
would never be brought to treat collectively with the other Powers in a matter of 
this kind. ‘This, I should add, is only an impression which had been received, 
but General Rochow would doubtless not have reported it unless it was a well- 
founded conviction on his part ; still it must not be considered that any fixed 
decision has been taken to reject the last propositions, which had not yet even 
been formally communicated to the Imperial Government. 

I have, &e.

Inclosure | in No. 45. 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to Vice-Admiral Dundas. 


Sir, Constantinople, January 9, 1854, 

DESPATCHES, which arrived from London to-day, having put me in full 
possession of the views of Her Majesty's Government regarding recent occur- 
rences in the Black Sea, I lose no time in sending you such further instructions 
as on that account are necessary. 

You are already authorized to employ the squadron under your command 
for the protection of the territory and flag of Turkey. It is now my duty, while 
confirming that instruction, to add that wherever you meet any Russian ship-of- 
war in the Black Sea, you will require it to return to Sevastopol, or to the most 
neighbouring port; and that in every case of aggression on the Ottoman terri- 
tory or flag, you will repel force by force. 

It is obvious that a notification to this effect should be made to the proper 
authority at Sevastopol; and, consequently, I inclose herewith the draft of a 
letter, in French, to be addressed, under your signature, to the Admiral com- 
manding there in chief. The same letter is to he addressed by Vice-Admiral 
Hamelin to the same authority, in pursuance of instructions from the French 
Ambassador, who acts entirely in concert with me on this ocension. 

The transmission of the letter must, however, depend in some degree on 
the manner in which your preceding letter has been received or answered, and, 
being ignorant of the circumstances, I must of necessity contide this point to 
your discretion, 

You ave to understand the present instruction as extending to all parts of 
the Black Sea, and also the release of Turkish vessels captured ie any Russian 
force and met with at sea by your squadron. 

Her Majesty's Government and that of France being resolved to prevent 
the recurrence of any such event as that which took place at Sinope, you are 
requested to maintain an adequate force in the Black Sea so long as the flag 
and territory of the Porte are exposed to danger. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE,.

The Porte will of course understand that the existing agreement, namely, 
that no Turkish ships shall be sent into the Black Sea without the knowledge af 
the two Embassies, and the concurrence af the two Vice-Admirals, 15 expected 
to hold good. , 

It is also necessary that no room for misunderstanding should exist as to 
another point. Her Majesty's Government, in resolving to protect the Porte's 
just interests at every risk, are far from abandoning the wish for peace, an 
with that view they are deeply alive to the importance of keeping up the jot 
action of the Four Cabinets, ‘and reckon with confidence on the Porte for carry- 
ing into any negotiation which may take place that corresponding spirit of good 
faith and moderation whereon is founded the best hope of maintaining @ 
salutary union along them, and terminating the war with satisfaction an 
honour. 

Your faithful servant, &e. | 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

ships or vessels until I made the lighthouse of Kersenese on the morning of the 
6th instant, when | observed a brig-of-war cruizing,. 

I rounded the Heh ure about 9 a m. of the 6th instant, the weather thick 
and very hazy over the land: I stood straight in towards the harbour’s mouth, 
and owing to the fog, I was well in before a small steamer-of-war, the 
“ Bessarabia,” stood out and put herself across the entrance, hoisted a quarantine 
flag, and waved tome to stop. I continued on my course, and upon reaching 
the entrance between the two forts, three guns, blank cartridge, were fired from 
the principal fort. 1 anchored in ten fathoms water, and observed that men 
were running to man the several batteries. 

Immediately I had anchored, an officer came to inform me that I must 
proceed out of gun-shot of the forts, or otherwise that the batteries were pre- 
pared to fire. Istated that I had letters to deliver to the Admiral in command, 
and to the Governor of the Crimea; the officer repeated that I must remove 
from under the batteries before he would receive my letters, that coming from 
Constantinople I was subject to a quarantine of fourteen days. 1 then weighed 
and stood about one mile out, where 1 remained until the return of the officer, 
who came attended by a health officer, and took the letters entrusted to me for 
delivery, those in charge of Lieutenant Benie, and 2 letter from me addressed to 
the Russian Admiral in command, relative to the detention of the two engineers, 
British subjects, a copy of which I inclose, He then informed me that Prince 
Menchikoff was absent at Kherson; that Vice-Admiral Nachimolf was absent, 
and that the squadron, as per margin,” at anchor in the harbour, was under the 
command of Rear-Admiral Stoemen (promoted for the affair of Sinope). 

I saluted the Russian flag with twenty-one guns, and the flag of the Rear- 
Admiral with thirteen. 

Having stated that I required an answer to my letters, one hour lapsed 
before the officer returned to say, that in the absence of Prince Menchikoff no 
answer could be given; that the letters would be forwarded immediately to 
Kherson; that the Rear-Admiral was not authorized to open letters ;. and that 
answers should be sent to Constantinople. 

I replied that having been instructed to deliver the letters and to receive an 
answer, | must insist upon a document in writing to the effect that the letters 
had been received at Sevastopol. In about one hour and a half’s time, the 
officer returned with a letter from the commandant of the port, a copy of which 
I beg to inclose. 

Having received this answer, and finding that | could get nothing more, 
with a certainty of fourteen days’ quarantine if I remained, 1 proceeded at 3 p.m. 
of the 6th instant to join your flag at Sinope. 

I had sufficient time during my stay off Sevastopol, to observe that the 
harbour is very strongly fortified. The ships of the line were anchored with 
springs on their cables, broadside to the entrance of the harbour, 

shall forward to you my remarks upon the fortifications in a few days. 

A large portion of the Russian squadron was absent from Sevastopol, 
probably out under Vice-Admiral Nachimoff, either at sea or perhaps at anchor 
in Kaffa Bay, which from its position is a more convenient anchorage for the 
coast of Circassia at this season of the year. 

The harbour of Sevastopol, with westerly winds, is not easy for ships to 
move from without the assistance of steam.

My Lord, Paris, January 29, 1854. 

IN two conversations which I have held with M. Drouyn de Lhuys 
yesterday and to-day, his Excellency has made me acquainted with the views 
entertained by Her Majesty’s Government, as to the answer which should be 
returned to the note presented to your Lordship by Baron Brunnow on the 23rd 
instant, 

Yesterday he showed me the drafts of the note which your Lordship pro- 
posed to address to Baron Brunnow, and of the despatch which you destined for 
Sir Hamilton Seymour, He expressed his approbation of both, and he added 
that, having learnt from Count Walewski that some objections were entertained 
ta parts of the projects emanating from the French Government (referred to in 
my despatch No. 86), he should wait until he was made acquainted with them 
in detail before taking any further step, either with respect to your Lordship's 
drafts or his own, 

I saw M. Drouyn de Lhuys again this afternoon, when he stated to me that 
he had received this morning, from Count Walewski, the information he had 
been expecting: that Her Majesty's Government did not approve the idea’ of 
transmitting the answers to St Petersburgh (for which suggestion, as coming 
from me, | must express my regrets), but desired to have them placed in the 
hands of the Russian Representatives in London and Paris; that the project of 
his (M. Drouyn de Lhuys') despatch to General Serhannt ae was approved, with 
the exception of the last paragraph, which Her Majesty's Government desired to 
see suppressed, and that, in rendering due homage to the sentiments contained 
in the letter of the Emperor to the Emperor Nicholas, Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment suggested two alterations; Ist, the introduction of the word “ armistice,” 
as explanatory of or supplementary to the words “cessation of hostilities ;° 
Jndly, the suppression of the proposal for direct negotiation at Vienna between 
» Russian and a Turkish Plenipotentiary. Her Majesty’s Government desired to 
abide by the proposals transmitted from the Conference, M, Drouyn de Lhuys 
added that, for reasons which he appreciated, Her Majesty's Government declined 
advising the Queen to address a similar letter to the Emperor of Russia. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys said that he had been with the Emperor, and that 
His Majesty had agreed to adopt the modifications and the mode of transmission 
suggested, on the part of Her Majesty's Government, by your Lordship to Count 
Walewski; and he added, that the suppression of the last paragraph in his 
despatch to General Castelbajac would necessitate a similar moxlification of the 
corresponding paragraph of the Emperor's letter to the Emperor Nicholas. 

‘These points being settled, he proposed drawing ups draft of an answer to 
M. de Kisseletf, as nearly identic as possible with your Lordship’s note to M, de 
Brunnow; but as he had understood from Count Walewski that your Loree 
intended making some alteration in the latter, which alteration you had promi 
to communicate to Count Walewski to-morrow, he should wait to know what it 
was before putting the finishing stroke to his own note, The draft would then 
be sent to London for approval, and the note given to M. de Kisseleff, on the 
day on which your Contshin might state jt to be your intention to place your 
note in M. de Brunnow’s hands.

No. 57. 
Lord Bloomfield to the Earl af Clarendon,.—( Received January 31.) 


(No. 15. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, January 26, 1854. 

A PERSON usually well informed having mentioned to me last mght that 
General Rochow’s last despatch, to which I alluded in my No. 11 of the 24th 
instant, stated that one of the obec of Count Orloff’s mission to Vienna was 
to break up the Conference, I called to-day on Baron Manteuflel, and sought to 
discover whether this was stated in the above despatch. His Excellency assured 
me that it certainly did not contain any such expression, and he then repeated 
in nearly the same words as those which I have before reported, that Count 
Orloff was charged to explain the terms on which the Emperor of Russia would 
still continue to treat for peace with Turkey. 

I remarked that these words almost implied as much as, and were tantamount 
to a rejection of the Porte’s proposals, which were forwarded from Vienna on 
the 13th instant, the substance of which must certainly have been known at 
St. Petersburgh before Count Orloff’s departure, though the communication of 
them by the Austrian Chargé d'Affaires might not have taken place. 

To this Baron Manteuffel replied that he did not think it likely that the 
Russian Government would be in any hurry to send their answer, particularly 
after their late communication to London and Paris. 

We then conversed on the probability of Count Orloff being instructed 
to urge the Austrian Cabinet to enter into an alliance with Russia on the 
Eastern question, and if successful to invite Prussia to accede to it; and if 
Prussia should refuse to join in such an alliance, to call upon Austria to exert 
her influence with the small German States to declare themselves in favour of 
the desired arrangement ; and he readily admitted that he greatly feared this 
would turn out to be the main object of Count Orloff’s mission, but that he 
should be able to give me some details to-morrow, as he heard Baron Budberg 
was to receive a messenger in the course of the day. 

His Excellency then alluded to the great Hanae to which this country 
would be exposed by entertaining any questions which sayvoured so much of the 
Holy Alliance, the principles of which he seemed to consider opposed to the 
true interests of Prussia at the present conjuncture, and he said to me in the 
most positive manner that he would never be a party to any such policy ; 
that he knew that he should have the most serious difficulties to contend with, 
nay, dangers to encounter, but that he should not swerve from the line of inde- 
peas for Prussia which he thought the only one befitting her position in 
Europe and in Germany. He said further, that circumstances might change, 
and that it was useless for him to assure me with whom his sympathies 
would be. 

He finished by requesting that our conversation might be quite confi- 
dential, 
I have, &e. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD,

No. 58. 
Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.— (Received January 31.) 


(No. 16, Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, January 26, 1854, 


BARON MANTEUFFEL has just informed me, in the strictest confidence, 
that after he had communicated to the King the despatch from General Rochow 
relating to the mission of Count Orloff, he requested His Majesty's authority to 
direct Count Arnim, the Prussian Minister at Vienna, in the event of Count 
Orloff seeking to communicate with him and to exchange ideas on the object of 
his mission, to decline doing so, and further to take nothing from him for refer- 
ence to his Court, for his Excellency is determined to close the door at once 
against any false interpretation being given to the intentions of the Prussian 
Government. 

Baron Manteuffel observed to me that the King did not hesitate an instant 
in giving his orders to this effect, which were forthwith transmitted by telegraph, 
and that His Majesty shows no symptoms of wavering in his resolution to carry 
out the principles of an independent policy for this country. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

No, 59. 
Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon,—{ Received January 31.) 


(No. 17. Secret and Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, January 27, 1854- 


BARON MANTEUFFEL has told me, in the strictest confidence, that an 
important communication has been made to him by the Russian Minister. 
Baron Budberg has informed his Excellency that Count Orloff is not coming to 
Berlin as was reported, and that he, Baron Budberg, has been charged with a 
letter from the Emperor for the King of Prussia, which he desired to have an 
opportunity of delivering to His Majesty ata private audience, 

After Baron Budberg had communicated this part of his instructions, he 
read to Baron Manteuffel a despatch from Count Nesselrode Bp the present 
critical state of affairs, and the nature of the explanations w iich have been 
demanded in London and Paris as to the intended operations of the combined 
flects in the Black Sea, 

The probabilities of a rupture of amicable relations are then commented on, 
the position of Germany is discussed, and Prussia is informed that her refusal to 
agree to the Russian proposals, which are contained in a draft of Protocol that 
is forwarded, will be viewed in a hostilesense. By this Protocol Prussia is called 
upon to bind herself to be neutral in the event of war between Russia and the 
Western Powers, and she is invited further to unite with Austria and the States 
of the Confederation in one collective declaration of neutrality in a sense 
favourable to Russia, 

Having asked Baron Manteuffel whether he had communicated these docu- 
ments to the King, he said that he had done so, and that His Majesty will grant 
Baron Budberg an audience to-morrow at which he also is to be present; 
that these demands of Russia, the tone of which is peremptory, had been il 
received by the King, and that His Majest will not enter into any engage- 
ment whatever either with Russia or with Austria, but will maintain an 
entirely independent position. 

I asked Baron Manteufiel if he had inquired of the Russian Minister 
whether Count Orloff was to communicate with the Conference at Vienna, 
and he replied that Baron Budberg knew nothing about the Conference, and 
made some observations which implied that its recommendations and labours 


49 


were only so much waste paper, and that Russia would agree to nothing but 
direct negotiation with the Porte and to no collective act. ; 

Baron Manteuffel said further, that Baron pudbete. eave him to understand 
that there is every prospect of the proposals of whic Count Orloff was the 
bearer being favourably received at Vienna, adding some hints as to the isola- 
tion in which Prussia would be placed if she hesitated to agree to the proposal 
which he now communicated to him. : 

After telling me the foregoing, Baron 'Manteuffel said that he wished this 
conversation to be kept quite secret; that he knew Baron Budberg was watching 
for an opportunity of injuring him, and that anything that could be construed 
into a breach of confidence on his part might be attended with evil consequences 
at the present moment. ; ; : 

[ availed myself of this opportunity to ask his Excellency if any communi 
cation from Her Majesty's Government would be likely to fortify h's position, 
and he said he should like to have something to lay before the King; something, 
he added, which would be a contrast to the proposed Russian Protocol, and 
which would leave the King his independence, which he is resolved to main- 
tain, but which it is absolutely essential should be left to him for some time yet, 
at all events until the end of May. 


I have, &e. . 
(Signed) BLOOMETELD. 


No. 60. 


Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received January 31.) 


(No, 18. Secret and Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, January 27, 1854. 

_ WITH reference to the last part of my. preceding despatch No. 17, reporting 
the anxiety felt by Baron Manteuffel that Prussia should not be forced to com- 
promise her neutral position before the end of May next, I have the honour to 
explain to your Lordship the reasons for this anxiety. 

At the Conference of Olmiitz in 1850, Prince Schwarzenburg used every 
exertion to obtain the assent of Prussia to the admission of the whole of Austria, 
including her Italian possessions, into the Germanic Confederation, and had 
actually persuaded the King of Prussia to agree to a secret Treaty which should 
bind his hands for ever by guaranteeing to Austria the integrity of all her 
dominions, 

Baron Manteuffel said that he had always been opposed to this project, and, 
on learning how deeply the King had compromised himself in the matter, had 
proposed, with the object of saving the King’s dignity and Germany from a per- 
manent infliction of the kind, that the Treaty should be only for a term, which 
term expires, as his Excellency stated to me, on the 22nd of May next, 

Your Lordship will perceive from the foregoing that Prussia would be 
bound, in the event of a general war extending into Italy before the above date, 
to defend Austria from any attack that might be directed against her, but that 
after that day she is free and completely eliazed from her engagement. 

The above requires no further comment, and proves how difficult Baron 
Manteuffel’s position would be should he be suddenly called upon to act for the 
defence of the Austro-Italian States. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

Sir G. H. Seymour to the Eart of Clarendon.—(Received Janaary 31.) 


(No, 71.) 
My Lord, St. Petersimrgh, January 23, 1854. 

THE answer returned by the Porte to the last overtures was received here 
on the evening of the 20th instant in a despatel from Count Buol, which on the 
following day was communicated by Baron Lebzeltern to the Chancellor. 

Unfortunately, at a moment when activity is so much required, 1 am 
unable to leave my room; Baron Lebzeltern has, however, ealled upon me for 
the purpose of stating that his communication had been made on the 21st 
instant to Count Nesselrode, and that his Excellency undertook to bring it under 
the Emperor's consideration. 

I expressed my hope that everything which could be thought of to induce 
acceptance had been said by Baron Lebzeltern at his interview with the Chan- 
cellor; my colleague assured me that he had not been wanting in this respect, 
addine that the terms of Count Buol’s despatch were so urgent that it would be 
diffieult to render them more impressive. — 

L took the liberty of remarking to Baron Lebzeltern that, terms considered 
on all sides to be honourable being placed within the Emperor's reach, 1 was 
willing to hope that His Majesty would soon be made seneble that their refusal 
would expose him to the hostility of the whole of Europe; a system which 
recommended itself particularly to Austria, whose desire to maintain peace was 
so generally known. 

lagain reminded my Austrian colleague that a notable precedent for this 
line of conduct had been established in 1860, by the Emperor Nicholas himself, 
who had preserved peace between Austria and Prussia by declaring that the 
first of these Powera which moved against the other might count upon his 
hostility. 

I will not conclude my despatch without remarking that, considering the 
importance of the moment and of the interests at stake, it might have been 
expected that all possible cireumstance would have attended the communication 
to the Russian Cabinet of the Porte’s reply ; whereas adventitious aid has been 
so little called in, that Count Buol’s despatch, after being brought here by a 
Russian courier, was delivered by the agent to whom the temporary direction of 
the temporary direction of Austrian Mission is confided.

Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received January 31.) 


(No. 72.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, January 23, 1854. 

YOUR Lordship has been apprized that slow and reluctant as this Govern- 
ment is, and not unnaturally, in appealing to public opinion, writers have been 
employed to set forth in verse and in prose the atrocious conduct of those 
Powers which have come forward to the assistance of the infidel Turk, when 
attacked by an army fighting under the banuer of the Cross. 

It should appear that Russian statesmen must have very short memories, 
for the times are not far distant when they were professing warm interest in the 
preservation of the same infidel Power. 

Upon referring to my archives, | read in a despatch dated 26th January, 
1832: “The Emperor has sent agents to the Christian provinces of the Turkish 
Empire to prevent them from taking advantage of the present difficulties of the 
Sultan to throw off the Ottoman yoke, by assuring them that it is his intention 
to assist the Sultan, and that they must therefore look for anything but 
countenance from him.” 

In another despatch dated the 2nd of March of the same year, it appears 
that Count Nesselrode stated: “That a division of the Black Sea fleet had 
sailed on the 14th for Constantinople; that a fleet of transports escorted by two 
ships-of-the-line, and conveying 5,000 troops, would by this time have left 
Odessa for the same destination, and that the Emperor had dispatched orders for 
the advance into Turkey of 25,000 or 30,000 men ; and further that the Emperor 
had determined upon publishing in the ‘ St. Petersburgh Journal’ an exposition 
of the conduct of the Russian Government, and the motives which induced the 
Emperor to give that material suceour to the Sultan which his position enabled 
him to send more speedily than the other Powers of Europe, nee all appeared, 
ie himself, to be actuated bya desire to prevent the subversion of the Ottoman 

impure.” 

To these quotations, which might be mul liplied ad mine might be 
added the offer made last spring of putting the whole of the F mperor's forces at 
the disposal of the Sultan should they be required for resisting the encroach- 
ments of France ; from all of which it may be deduced that assistance to Turkey 
is perfectly compatible with the mterests of orthodoxy. 

Negotiations which are probably still carried on by the Russian Cabinet 
would lead to the same conclusion, and would establish the fact of the infidels of 
Persia being looked to with no slight anxiety as the allies of a war undertaken 
against the Crescent in the interests of the true orthodox faith. 

| T have, &c. 
(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

Sir G. H. Seymour to the Eurl of Clarendon.—(Received January 31.) 
(No. 77. Confidential.) 


My Lord, St. Petersburgh, January 24, 1854. 

A DISTINCT answer from the Russian Cabinet with regard to their 
intentions of coming to terms with the Porte seems to be the very “ ignis 
fatuus”’ of diplomacy; it occasionally flickers in the distance, but becomes 
invisible and impalpable when approached, and is probably destined to appear 
for the last time in a Wallachian marsh well filled with Russian recruits. 

For some time past the reception of the Porte’s reply to the overtures of 
the Four Powers has been looked forward to as the moment when the most 
important question of the last half century was to receive its solution, but 
hardly had this auxiously-expected despatch reached St. Petersburgh when Count 
Orloff’s travelling carriage, which had been prepared for the occasion, drove off 
carrying with it a negotiator whose precise destination is not known, and an 
answer the nature of which, if determined upon, is kept a secret from every one. 

lam to see the Chancellor to-day, and as he had heard that I was confined 
to the house, he has been kind enough to promise to call upon me; I feel 
confident, however, that 1 shall only learn from him what he stated yesterday to 
the French Minister, namely, that nothing could be said as to the Emperor's 
intentions until the result of Count Orloff’s mission should be known. 

It is reported to me upon excellent authority, that the Emperor has been 
heard to say within the last few days, “ Pourva seulement que les Autrichiens 
ne tiennent pas le méme langage aux autres qu’avee nous!" 

These words prove at once that very friendly assurances have been given 
here, and that, nevertheless, misgivings exist as to their not being corresponded 
to by acts—misgivings which tend to throw some light upon Count Orlotfs 
mission. 

Meanwhile, the Austrian Government can hardly fail of being sensible that 
not only their interests but their honour are engaged on the side of England 
and France, and that having led these Powers to believe that they were authorized 
to speak in the name of Russia, they must either find means to make good their 
words, or take part against the Cabinet by which a deception has been practised 
upon themselves. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR. 


P.S.—The French Minister, who has just left me, is more and more 
convinced that Count Orloff’s instructions are extensive and “elastic,” that, to 
use General Castelbajac’s expression, the question of peace or war is in some 
measure in his hands,
