Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received January 31.) 


(No. 78.) | 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, January 24, 1654. 


THE Chancellor, who has just left this room, was even less explicit with me 
than he had been with the French Minister, and had the appearance of entirely 
ignoring all the late proceedings at Vienna, ; 

‘The sum of his observations was this: that the Emperor seeing that there 
were difficulties and misconceptions in the way had determined upon sending off 
Count Orloff as a negotiator, and that he was actually setting off when the 
Turkish reply arrived here; that in this reply there was great vagueness; that 
the great fut had been committed of putting forward the evacuation of Turkish 
territory as a first condition, whereas it should have been only mentioned at last 
and as the necessary consequence of an arrangement; that difficulties were made 
without a cause which a little conciliation (bon vouloir) on the part of the 
Enolish and French Governments would immediately remove ; that if Turkey 
desired peace all that was requisite was to send a Plenipotentiary to St. Peters- 
burgh, where it might be obtained at once; finally, that the object in view was, 
he believed, a reconciliation between Russia and Turkey; that point ‘once 
obtained, the Sultan was of course at liberty to make any arrangements which 
he thought proper with other Christian Powers as to the treatment of the 
Christian subjects of the Porte. ' 

In this, which was the sum of Count Nesselrode’s conversation, there 18 
nothing, as your Lordship will perceive, but that which has been repeated over 
and over again by the Russian Cabinet during the last six or eight months. 

I took occasion to ask Count Nesselrode (begging him not to reply to my 
question if he had any hesitation), whether there were any truth in a report 
current here of the Emperor having said that he should leave things in their 
present state till the month of April, when, if no arrangement should have been 
made with Turkey, he should consider himself as freed from engagements and at 
liberty to march forward. | 

Count Nesselrode, with some slight uncertainty of manner, stated that the 
Emperor had not made this declaration, at all events had not made it in euch 
positive terms (aussi crfiment), but that if on the arrival of apring matters were 
still in their present unsettled state, His Imperial Majesty could not be expected 
to retain the attitude which he now maintained. 

I have, &c. 
(Siened) G. H, SEYMOUR.

Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to the Karl of Clarendon.—( Received January 31.) 


(No, 18. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, January 12, 1854. 

I HAVE long urged the Porte to adopt some striking measure of relief for 
the Rayahs of this Empire at the present criticul juncture, conceiving that their 
loyalty to the Sultan has need of some manifest proof of His Majesty's favour 
towards them in order to stand firm against their natural inclination to rely on 
the professions of Russia. No measure that I know of is better calculated to 
produce the desired effect, or more required hy justice, than the removal of that 
cruel and odious distinction which throughout this country is systematically 
established between Christian and Mussulman evidence in courts of criminal 
jurisdiction. My representations on this subject to Reshid Pasha have had the 
effect of inducing him to bring forward the question in Council; and it is not 
long since he assured me that the preparations for its detinitive adoption were

so far advanced as to promise an almost immediate completion of the firman 
destined to promulgate it. Finding, however, that his promises were not 
followed up with any visible symptoms of execution, I renewed my solicitations 
a few days ago, and have the mortification to learn that the Government was 
not disposed to incur the hazard of exciting discontent among their Mahometan 
subjects by placing the Christians on an equal footing with them in point of 
criminal justice. Reshid Pasha even implored me to be patient out of friendly 
consideration for him, the liberality of whose conduct had already marked him 
out as an object of popular indignation, and whose life, as he sent me word, 
might pay the price of an unseasonable demonstration in favour of the Rayahs. 
To this view of the matter [ could not in conscience assent. The ignorant 
and fanatical portion of the Mussulman people will, no doubt, be always opposed 
to any innovation upon @ system with ach their privileges and prejudices are 
habitually bound up; but the Government is strong enough to deal with them, 
and never so much so as now when the very existence of the Empire depends in 
xt measure on the assistance of those Powers who naturally sympathize with 
the Sultan’s Christian subjects, and whose juadrons are in a condition. to 
overawe as well as to protect his capital. therefore drew up a pressin 
instruction for M. Pisani, and directed him to read and explain it to Reshic 
Pasha with suitable earnestness. A copy of it is inclosed herewith, and it has so 
far produced the impression which I intended, that the Secretary of State no 
longer talks of indefinite postponement, but merely of delay, extending, perhaps, 
to a couple of weeks, He admits the truth of my arguments, advising at the 
same time that I should require him to communicate the instruction to his 
colleagues, and also rely on his management for engaging them to adopt the 
proposed measure. Willing to follow his advice in this respect for the present, 
{ am not sanguine enough to expect quite so early a solution as the report of his 
language warrants ; though I am satishied that a strong impression has been 
aie, and that the object of my exertions will in all probability be attained 
before long. 
I have, &c. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to M. E. Pisani. 


Dear Sir, Pera, January 10, 1894, 


| CANNOT conceal from you that I am greatly disappointed by the 
answer which Reshid Pasha has returned to my demands, again and again 
repeated, on the subject of Christian evidence. Sundry years have elapsed since 
this important question was first recommended by Her Majesty’s Embassy to the 
serious consideration of the Porte. The extreme injustice and cruel conse- 
quences of a law, which in eriininal and even in capital cases affords protection 
only to one class of subjects, and exposes anniek to false accusation and 
unpunished wrong, are too glaring to admit of uny reasonable excuse; and 
assurances have, therefore, been repeatedly given of the Porte’s disposition to 
remove the evil. 

When, after much exertion, 4 firman was obtained for the establishment of 
criminal tribunals in Egypt, on fair and impartial principles, although that 
firman was granted on the special demand of Her Majesty's Embassy, and for 
the immediate protection of British subjects, the regulations which it comprised 
were understood to be available for other foreigners also, and a promise was given 
that they should be extended, after a while, to the Sultan's subjects throughout his 
Empire. ‘This promise was founded no less on the Porte’s own interest than on 
views of justice and humanity, Year has, nevertheless, succeeded to year, and 
atill there 1s complaint without redress, and promise without execution, The 
Porte, meanwhile, has been drawn into serious difficulties by a neighbouring 
Power, and it has found in the necessities of a perilous situation cogent motives 
for satisfying its Christian subjects and concilinting its Christian allies, Nothing 
‘¢ better calculated to satisfy the one and to conciliate the other than the 


ag 


removal of a wrong, which is no less humiliating than oppressive, and which 
strikes at the very root of all confidence between the Porte and a very large 
proportion of its subjects. Stull, that fatality, which has long weighed on this 
enfeebled Empire, continues to preponderate, and more attention is paid to those 
who by ignorance and fanaticism have brought their country to the verge of 
ruin, than to those who by their faithful counsels and active support uphold and 
strengthen it in the hour of danger. 

1 am assured that the want of an improved system of justice is felt; 
that the utility of the bropaies change is undeniable; and that the long- 
promised firman is actually prepared. But when I press, after long delays, for 
the formal adoption of the measure and the promulgation of the firman, I am 
told that the fanatics would be irritated, and that the life of one or other of the 
Ministers would be required to appease their wrath. I reply to this excuse that 
the alleged danger, if not a pretext, is at least a fancy. No doubt in Turkey, as 
elsewhere, the ignorant, the prejudiced, and the corrupt are averse to all changes 
which tend to correct long established abuses, and to restrain certain privileged 
classes from gratifying their pride and cupidity at the expense of their fellow 
subjects. 

But the injury thus done to individuals, and to the societies of which they 
are part, is also a cause of weakness and dishonour to the State, and fortunate it 
is that the Sovereignand Government of the State have power enough to protect 
their own interests, and to enforce those measures of reform which can no longer be 
deterred with safety. Danger for danger, there ts far more to apprehend from a 
denial of justice than from a cry for privilege. ‘Che enemy with whom Turkey, 
though unable to maintain successfully a protracted and single-handed contest, 
is now at war, makes his strongest appeal to the unjust and oppressive manner 
‘1 which the Ottoman system of administration operates on the Rayahs ; and 
those Powers which have sent their fleets to protect the territory and flag of 
Turkey, cannot but sympathize with the sentiment, while they oppose the 
aggressions, of Russia. 

It is manifest, therefore, that the present juncture, so far from being an 
unseasonable time for abolishing the injustice, cruelty, and degradation which 
are inseparable from the criminal procedure now in practice, is emphatically the 
moment at which the corrective firman may be promulgated with the least 
amount of peril and the greatest amountof benefit to the Empire, If the Hodjas 
and Sottas are to rule over the Sultan and the Divan, it is time for the Christian 
ullies of the Porte to consider for whom and for what they are employing their 
squadrons and risking the peace of Europe. The best of causes may be lost for 
want of firmness and vigour. Let the Sultan's Ministers redeem the pledges 
which have been given, and exert their influence courageously on the side of 
justice and sound policy. All will then go well, and the fanatics themselves will 
ultimately feel grateful to the preservers of the Empire. 

You will read and explain the whole of this letter to Reshid Pasha. 

Yours sincerely, &c 


(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

instructions as to the course to be pursued under such circumstances.

THE combined detachments under Rear-Admirals Sir E. Lyons and De 
Tinan, together with the Turkish steam-vessels, returned to Sinope this morning ; 
and I inelose, for the information of your Excellency, a copy of Sir Edmund 
Lyon’s letter to me reporting his proceedings. 

The Turkish steam-vessels will sail again this evening for the Bosphorus, 
accompanied by two English and one French steam-frigate; the “ Fury” also 
will keep with them part of the way. 

Vice-Admiral Hamelin and [ have decided on not sending the second letter 
to the naval Commander-in-Chief at Sevastopol at present, as we have not 
received any answer, nor are we aware whether any has been sent to the first 
letter to Constantinople, Should a reply have been sent to the latter place by 
the Russian Admiral, your Excellency would have a knowledge of its tenour, 
and a8 you are now acquainted with the nature of Captain Drummond’s reception 
at Sevastopol, we have thought it advisable (their transmission having been left 
to our discretion) to send the second letters, signed by us, but open, to Constan- 
tinople, to enable your Excellency and the French Ambassador, should you deem 
it expedient, to send them forward without delay to Sevastopol by the “ Fury,” 
who has orders to proceed there on your expressing your wishes to that effect.

No. 77. 
Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received January 31.) 


(No. 21.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, January 16, 1854. 

IN continuation of my report respecting the operations of the Turkish army 
in Asia Minor and along the Danube, | have the honour to inform your Lord- 
ship that the advices which | continue to receive from Her Majesty's Consul at 
Erzeroum corroborate the accounts of the considerable reverses which the 
Sultan's troops in the former place appear to have suffered. The Ardahan 
division before Akhiska under the command of Ferik Ali Pasha was completely 
routed. The baggage, artillery, and stores all fell into the hands of the Russians. 
This division consisted of about 20,000 men with fourteen guns. 

‘The advanced guard appear to have borne the brunt of the attack, and to 
have been put to flight. Ali Pasha, who commanded the main body, showed 
great want of skill in placing his troops and seems to have been the first to run 
away when the attack was made. The defeated troops fled in every direction, 
but measures were in the course of adoption for collecting them. Four battalions 
had been gent to Kars, and six more are in quarters at Erzeroum. With the 
exception of the Irregulars, who had mostly all gone home, the greater part of the 
Ardahan division may, therefore, be said to be in quarters at Erzeroum and 
Kars, but in a state of complete demoralization, 

By another account from Mr, Consul Brant of the LOth December it would 
appear that a body of 25,000 Turkish regular troops with some irregulars was 
defeated near the Arpatchai on the Ist ultimo by a Russian division consisting 
principally of Georgian levies, and amounting to about 15,000 men, Part of 
the defeated troops had fled to Kars. 

The battle Eanes to have been lost in this instance also by the ineompe- 
tency of the Turkish General, who chose his own position, Ahmed Pasha 
formed his troops so unskilfully in an extended line at the bottom of a ravine 
that they were at the mercy of the Russian artillery, which made great slaughter 
among them. The Irregulars fled early, carrying a regiment of cavalry with 
them ; the officers from the Pashas to the lowest rank soon left the field, and 
the soldiers rushed on the enemy in a confused mass. A hand-to-hand contest 
ensued, which was very murderous on both sides, and was terminated by the 
approach of evening; the loss on each side appears to linve been about 
7,000 men. 

The campaign may now be considered closed, as the snow appears to be too 
deep to admit of further operations, and there is no fear of the Russians 
attempting to follow up these sucecsses. 

The Turkish army, which consisted of about 100,000 men, although 
capable of being collected Sopethes) may be said to be dispersed, and the greatest 
disaffection prevails among the troops against their eommanders. rhey loudly 
express their want of confidence in them, and their conviction that they can 
only be led successfully against the Russians under the direction of European 
officers, among whom General Guyon seems to have distinguished himself.

Brant’s correspondence, sent direct to the Foreign Office. ee

(No. 22.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, January 15, 1854. 


HAVING learnt from Mr. Fonblanque, as your Lordship will also have 
learnt, that according to general belief, M.de Moukhine had not only had a 
conference with the Prince of Servia and his foreign Minister, but that he had 
also announced the approaching arrival of Russian troops in Servia, I conveyed 
the intelligence to Reshid Pasha, and requested to be informed whether his

(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE, 


Inclosure in No. 79. 


Vice-Consul Guarracino to Lord Stratford de Redeliffe. 


(Extract.) Samsoon, December 12, 1853. 


UP to this date about 300 of the Turkish sailors, who escaped from the 
Sinope catastrophe, have arrived here, and I hear that many others are on the 
way hither, Among those already here there are upwards of thirty wounded, 
[ am told that many of these fugitive seamen have retired to their native villages, 
and others are on the roads to Trebizond and the interior, in order to escape 
further service if possible. Some of them have managed to arm themselves with 
muskets, which they procured at Sinope from their ships; the roads are, in 
consequence, insecure for travellers. 

All the natives have armed themselves, and appear to haye abandoned their 
usual occupations. 

I am of opinion that it will require some time, under any circumstances, to 
re-establish order in the country, and, if further reverses are sustained by the 
Government, it is impossible to predict what excesses the people may give 
themselves up to. 

The seamen who arrived here from Sinope are likely to remain here for 
some time, unless some man-of-war steamer come up from the capital to take 
them away.

My Lord, Constantinople, January 16, 1854. 

THE two Vice-Admirals at Sinope not having received from Sevastopol any 
answer to their first notification, have returned their second letters to the French 
Ambassador and myself, placing Her Majesty's steam-ship “Fury” at our 
disposal for the conveyance of those com munications to such point of the Russian 
territory as we may find reason to prefer. 

As the expected answer has not been received at Constantinople more than 
at Sinope, I have decided, after taking into consideration the reception expe- 
rienced by Captain Drummond, to transmit Admiral Dundas’s notification to 
Her Majesty’s Consul-General at Odessa, with an instruction to deliver it to the 
principal local authority for conveyance to Prince Menchikoff. I have reason to 
suppose that General Baraguay d'Hilliers will adopt a similar course of proceed- 
ing, which will afford us a safe opportunity of communicating on other subjects 
with our respective Consuls, an opportunity of which I shall be glad to avail 
myself at a juncture so full of interest to our trade in the Black Sea. 

The “ Fury,” after leaving Odessa, will proceed to Varna, in order to super- 
sede the French steam-frigate “ Promethée,” which has been stationed between 
that place and Bourgas during the last fortnight.

The Earl of Clarendon (o Baron Brunnow. 


Foreign Office, January 31, 1854, 

THE Undersigned, &c., has the honour to acknowledge the receipt of a 
note dated the 25th instant, from Baron Brunnow, &c., stating that he has been 
ordered to inquire of the Undersigned the precise meaning of a verbal communt- 
cation recently made by Her Majesty’s Minister at St, Petersburgh to the 
Chancellor of the Empire. 

Baron Brunnow adverts to certain arrangements which being agreed upon, 
and strictly executed, would suspend hostilities by sea between the belligerent 
parties; and he requests that the Undersigned will inform him whether the 
intentions of Her Majesty’s Government are in accordance with those of the 
Imperial Cabinet upon the principles of perfect reciprocity established in the 
note of Baron Brunnow. 

In replying to Baron Brunnow the Undersigned thinks it right to state that 
the communication made by Sir H. Seymour was to the following effect: that 
Her Majesty's fleet had been sent to Constantinople not for the purpose of 
attacking of Russia, but with the firm intention to defend Turkey, and Her 
Majesty’s Government would, therefore, have been well pleased if the necessity 
for thus employing the fleet had not arisen; but that the destruction of a 
Turkish fleet anchored peaceably in a ‘Turkish harbour proved that the concilia- 
tory dispositions of Her Majesty's Government, and the notice of their inten- 
tions given in an amicable spirit on the 27th October to Count Nesselrode, had 
been mistaken or disregarded, and that Her Majesty’s Government had 
determined to take measures to guard against the recurrence of disasters such as 
those of which Sinope had been the theatre. That Her Majesty's ships there- 
fore, and those of the Emperor of the French, would enter the Black Sea, and 
require every Russian ship-of-war which they might meet to return to a Russian 
port, and that if the summons were not attended to it would be enforced: but 
that Her Majesty's Government, being not less anxious than they were before to 
effect a peaceful settlement of difficulties, would take measures for preventing 
iny aggressive operation by sea on the part of the Turkish fleet against the 
Russian territory. 

The Undersigned has thus stated the terms of the communication verbally 
made by Her Majesty's Minister at St. Petershugh, in order to prevent misun- 
derstanding, and it can hardly be necessary for him to inform Baron Brunnow 
that they will he strictly adhered to. The Undersigned at the same time begs 
to add that the maintenance of friendly relations with Russia is earnestly desired 
by Her Majesty's Government, whose best efforts will continue to be exerted to 
secure a just and honourable solution of the differences between Russia and the 
Porte ; but a duty has been imposed upon Her Majesty's Government by Russia 
from the performance of which they will not shrink. Turkey is the aggrieved 
and the weaker Power; a portion of her territory has been forcibly occupied and 
retained, while military preparations upon a seale of the greatest magnitude are 
made by Russia: and in defending Turkey from the imminent danger that 
threatens her, Her Majesty's Government uphold that fundamental principle. of 
European policy involved in the maintenance of the Ottoman Empire that has 
been repeatedly proclaimed by the Five Great Powers of Europe. 

The extent to which this defence may be carried, and the nature of the 
operations it may entail, must depend on the course which may be pursued by 
Russia; but Her Majesty’s Government indulge a hope that peace may yet be 
negotiated upon the reasonable terms proposed by the Porte for the acceptance 
of Russia, and in the case of that acceptance an armistice both by sea and land 


71 


would stop the effusion of blood, and put an end to embarrassment regarding 
naval operations, and differences which now endanger the general peace of Europe 
might then be speedily terminated. 

: The Undemignet » &e. (Signed) CLARENDON.

No. 86. 


The Earl of Clarendon to Sir G. H. Seymour. 
(No. 27.) 
Sir, Foreign Office, January 31, 1854. 

| HEREWITH inelose the copy of a note addressed to me by Baron 
Brunnow, together with the copy of my answer.* 

I inclose also the copy of a despatch} from Count Nesselrode which Baron 
Brunnow, by orders of oe Government, placed in my hands, the purport of 
which is so extraordinary that 1 am compelled to desire you to communicate to 
the Chancellor the impression that it has produced on Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment. 

This despatch ends by saying; ‘‘ Un hasard suflit aujourd'hui pour produire 
ane collision d’ot naitrait une conflagration générale, et I'Hmpereur repousse 
@avance la responsabilité de Vinitiative qui en aura donné le signal.” Hence 
it would seem that the Russian Government has entirely forgotten the origin of 
this unhappy quarrel. They would seem to have forgotten that, so soon as the 
only cause of difference between Russia and the Porte had been satisfactorily 
terminated, Prince Menchikoff required, in peremptory terms, the assent of the 
Sultan to a certain large and new interpretation of the Treaty of Kainardji; that 
upon the offer of the Turkish Government to substitute other conciliatory 
assurances for those proposed by Prince Menchikoff, the Russian Ambassador 
at once quitted Constantinople ; that, immediately afterwards, Count Nesselrode 
required the Porte, within the space of eight days, to send back, signed, the 
note which the Sultan had ous declared it would be fatal to his independence 
to accept, under a threat that if His Highness did not com ly, Fuussian armies 
would oceupy the Principalities of Moldavia and Wallachia; that when the 
Sultan refused to submit, under compulsion, to so degrading a demand, the 
previous threat was at once carried into execution, and Provinces of the Sultan, 
containing 4,000,000 of his subjects, were invaded in time of profound peace by 
Russian ae that the territory of the Sultan has since been occupied asa 
conquered country, the Russian Government thus violating the status quo of 
Europe, contradicting the intentions proclaimed by the Great Powers of Hurope 
in 1840 and 1841, and stamping Russia as the disturber of the general peace. 

Not content with this aggression, which at first was announced as a tem- 
porary occupation and as a material pienes held only until the demands of 
Russia upon the Porte should be satisfied, the Emperor of Russia has prskered 
wreat armies at vast expense, apparently with the object of crossing the Danube, 
and attempting the conquest of Constantinople, 

Nor ig it to be overlooked, frequently as 1 have urged the topic, that no 
injury to the Christian subjects of the Porte afforded even a pretext for such 
acts, On the contrary, with the introduction of new laws for their protection, 
their own gradual progress in wealth and intelligence, and by meral advance in 
the arts of peace, the condition of the Christians was manifestly improving. 

All the serious events that have since arisen—the deplorable effusion of 
human blood, the oppression of the people of the Principalities, the aggression 
upon the Russian territory in Asia, the disaster at Sinope, and the entrance af 
the combined fleets into the Black Sea—are the direct consequences of the 
unprovoked conduct of the Russian Government; and if unhappily a chance 
encounter should produce a collision from which a general conflagration should 
arise, the Emperor of Russia will in vain attempt to throw off a responsibility 
which must attach to him who in time of profound peace first invaded the 
territory of his unoffending neighbour. 

You will read, and give a copy of this despatch to Count Nesselrode. 


Tam, &e. 
(Signed) CLARENDON,

both objected strongly to this document. 

I saw Count Buol after M. de Bourqueney had communicated to him this 
information, with which he was very much satisfied; he still, however, is of 
opinion that the best mode of dealing with this document is to allow the Con- 
ference to state their opinion with regard to it in a short Protocol, which would 
not otherwise be made use of than to prove, if reference should be made to it, 
that the Conference had not considered that document as interfering with the 
original despatch of Reshid Pasha which they had agreed to adopt. 

Count Buol adheres, therefore, to the recommendation of this Protocol as 
stated in my despatch to your Lordship No. 26 of yesterday's date, and he hopes 
for an early decision. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) WESTMORLAND. 


No, 89. 


Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.— (Received January 31.) 
(No. 105. Confidential.) 


My Lord, Paris, January 30, 1854. 
M. DROUYN DE LHUYS showed me this morning a despatch, dated 
the 26th instant, received yesterday from M. de Bourqueney, giving an account 
of a conversation which the latter had held with Count Buol, respecting the 
proposition lately made by the Austrian Cabinet to that of Berlin, to declare 
themselves, together with the whole of Germany, neutral in the struggle which 
was too likely to take place between the Western Powers and Russia. M. de 
Buol denied most emphatically and warmly that any such proposition had been 
made, and said that Prussin must either unwittingly or wilfully have misunder- 
stood the language of Austria, That language was to the effect that in the 
present state of affairs, which were looking blacker every day, it was of the 
utmost importance that the two great German Powers should understand each 
other, and the Austrion Cabinet wished to know how far the Prussian Cabinet 


id 


was willing to go. Count Buol insinuated that Prussia had given that version 
to the proposition which she thought would be most plone to Russia ; 
meaning, I presume, that Prussia would not declare herself neutral, supposing 
such a proposal to have been made, in order that she might hereafter assist 
Russia. - ; 

M. de Bourqueney adds that he took this opportunity of telling Count 
Buol that matters were assuming bag al which would necessitate a declara- 
ton from Austria as to what would be her future policy, and that Count Buol 
had rejoined that “when the proper moment arrived, Austria would be judged 
by her acts; but that, in the meantime, he trusted that she would not be called 
upon to do anything that might compromise the last chance of peace. 

Count Orloff’s mission had been announced, and it was surmised that he 
had been sent, in order that the Emperor of Russia might have the sppeamne 
of having spontaneously named a Plenipotentiary to treat for peace with Turkey, 
the Turkish propositions sent from Vienna not having reached St. Petersburgh 
before Count Orloff set out, though they were probably known through the 

ic telegraph. 

Se ae T have, &c. 
(Signed) COWLEY.

setting forth the terms on which those Powers engage themselves to employ all 
their efforts to bring about the re-establishment of peace between Russia and the 
Porte. 

Her Majesty's Government attach great importance to this Convention as 
the means of carrying out the object of the Protocols, and of preventing future 
embarrassments with respect to Turkey; and your Lordship is accordingly 
instructed to use your best efforts to procure its adoption by the Austrian 
Government, and you are authorized to sign it in conjunction with the Ministers 
of the other three Powers. 3 

There is not sufficient time to prepare a full power under the Great Seal

a day or two,

The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon—(Received February 2.) 


(Telegraphic.) Vienna, February 2, 1854. 

COUNT BUOL has communicated to the Conference the Russian counter 
propositions, expressly declaring that he did not support them. Having examined 
them, we declared by Protocol that the essential differences between these 
propositions and those of the 13th of January made it impossible for us [to send?) 
them to Constantinople. Nothing therefore remained but to transmit them to 
our Governments, and wait till they should have taken their ulterior decision. 

I send you by the post copy of the Protocol, with its Annex.* Nothing 
could have been more satisfactory than the unanimity with which the above- 
mentioned resolution was come to.

No. 98. 


Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received February 2.) 


(No. 110.) 
My Lord, Paris, February 1, 1854. 

M. DROUYN DE LHUYS received in the course of last night two tele- 
eraphie despatches from Vienna, the one dated in the afternoon, and the other 

ut half-past eight in the evening. 

M. de Bourquency informs the French Government in the first that the 
[uesian answer to the propositions of the 13th ultimo was arrived, and that as 
soon as he (Count Buol) was in possession of it, he intended to summon the 
Conference, and to lay it before them; that Count Orloff had made something 
in the shape of a counter-proposition to Count Buol, which the latter did not 
seem to approve, but which did not exelude all hope of an arrangement. 

In the second, M. de Bourqueney states that Count Buol is not at all 
satisfied with the Russian answer, which had been communicated to him, and 
that he requires time for reflection before laying it before the Conference. The 
Russian Government demands that a Turkish Plenipotentiary shall be sent to 
St. Petersburgh, and that negotiations shall be pursued there. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys’ opinion, founded on what reasons | am not able to 
say, is that Count Orloff’s mission was intended to pave the way to this propo- 
sition, and that failing in procuring its acceptance, he will endeavour to obtain 
of the Austrian Government terms favourable to Russia, such as the passage of 
Russian troops across Austrian territory, the provisioning of those troops from 
Austria, &c. ; and should he not succeed in either of these objects, that his last 
efforts will be made to a obtain a declaration of neutrality. 

When M. de Bourqueney wrote yesterday, he added that he had no reason 
to suppose that Count Orloff had met with any success, 

General Castelbajac, in announcing Count Orloff's mission, adds that he has 
reason to believe that the Count has full powers to terminate the Eastern 
question, and that he does not abandon all hope of an arrangement. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) COW LEY.

No. 100, 

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received February 2.) 
(No. 112.) 
My Lord, Paris, February 1, 1854. 


COUNT WALEWSKI has informed M. Drouyn de Lhuys that Her 
Majesty’s Government is desirous that the future action of the two Governments 
in the Eastern question should be regulated by a Convention rather than by an 
exchange of notes. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys in giving me this information, observed that the 
Emperor's Government has no positive objection to this alteration of their 
proposal, but that he thinks it would be inconvenient to have recourse to a 
Convention, if the Austrian and Prussian Governments accept the proposal 
which has been made to them of signing a quadruple instrument of the same 
kind. He appears to wish to let the question remain in abeyance until the 
suceess of the last scheme is ascertained. 

With regard to the extra stipulations proposed by your Lordship, he had no 
objection to them, and he had accordingly sent to London an amended draft of 
note embracing the two points suggested, namely, the abnegation of all direct 
benefit from the impending struggle, and a possible cooperation with the Turks 
by land as well as by sea.

No, 101. 
Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Received February 3.) 


(No. 115. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Paris, February 2, 1854. 
M. DROUYN DE LHUYS mentioned to me yesterday that he could 
not but look with suspicion at the conduct of the Austrian and Prussian 
Governments in the Eastern question, Each accused the other of duplicity and 
of playing a game of its own, while the language of their agents at foreign 
Courts, according to the reports received by the French Government, was antivery 
in a Russian sense. He instanced particularly the conduct of the Austrian and 
Prussian Consuls in the Principalities, which he described as imbued with 
spirit of partisanship in favour of Russia, though latterly the Prussian Consul 
appeared to have received hints to be more on his guard, He alluded with still 
vreater severity of tone to the behaviour of Count Lebzeltern, the Austrian 
Chargé d’Affuires at St. Petersburgh, who had not only assisted at a Te Deum 
for Russian victories, (though some excuse might be made for that, as it had 
been celebrated on the Emperor Nicholas’ féte-day,) but had been present in the 


78 


- Imperial box at a spectacle in the course of which the destruction of the Turkish 


flotilla at Sinope had been represented. 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys expressed his determination to address the French 
Ministers at Vienna and Berlin on this subject. 
I have, &c. 
(Signed) COWLEY. 


No. 102. 
Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received February 3.) 


(No, 119. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Paris, February 2, 1854. 


TWO telegraphic despatches of importance have reached the French 
Government since I had the honour of addressing your Lordship yesterday. 
The firet is dated Berlin, at 5 p.m. yesterday. It announces that a mes- 
senger was gone to St. Petersburgh with a refusal of Count Orloff’s propositions. 
The second is dated Vienna, 3°40 Pia. yesterday. It announces that Count 
Buol had summoned the Conference to meet at | o'clock this day, but without 
any idea that the Russian answer could be approved or accepted. M. de 
Bourqueney says that all the Conference ean do will be to put on record the 
divergence which exists between the propositions of the Porte and the Russian 
answer, and to ask for fresh instructions. No details are given. He considers 
Count Orloff’s mission, whatever may have been its object, to have failed. He 
states further, that both he and Lord Westmorland are of opinion that this is 
not the moment to put forward the project of Convention proposed by the 
French Government with any chance of suecess, and that it will be more 
prudent to wait. He promises to give his reasons by a messenger. In the 
meantime he solicits permission to leave the project in abeyance. He refers to 
the departure of Count Orloff as near, as if he connected the presence of 
the Count at Vienna with the difficulty of putting the Convention forward. 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys was about to reply by telegraph that he approved this 
reserve, not doubting that your Lordship would have the same. opinion. 
Besides these despatches, M. Drouyn de Lhuys has received another from 
M. de Bourqueney, conveyed in the usual way, and consequently antecedent to 
them in date. M, de Bourqueney relates in it that be had again spoken to 
Count Buol on the subject of the proposal of neutrality made at Berlin, that 
Count Buol had again denied the fact, and that this had led M. de Bourqueney 
to demand in a friendly but in a more eategorical manner, what would be the 
conduct of Austria if nothing came of the present negotiation, Count Buol had 
replied evasively at first; but urged to declare what he would do, for instance, if the 
Russians crossed the Danube, he had declared with warmth, that Austria would 
never permit it, and that if she did not permit it, Russia could not undertake it, 
From this and other circumstances which have come to his knowledge, and 
more particularly from intelligence which he has received of what transpired of 
Yount Orloff’s pas through Warsaw, M. Drouyn de Lhuys is inclined to 
think that when the Turkish propositions were sent to St, Petersburgh, Austria 
and Prussia declared that it the propositions were refused, they would not 
permit the passage of the Danube by the Russians, and that this declaration is 
the cause of Count Orloff’s mission to Vienna, 
I have, &e.

DURING a conversation which I had lately with M. Drouyn de Lhuys,

The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 
(No. 47.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, February 6, 1854. 

| HAVE to acquaint your Excellency that Her Majesty's Government 
entirely anneal the instruction which you gave to M. Pisani, and of which a 
copy is inclosed in your despatch No. 18 of the 12th ultimo, on the question of 
the admission of Christian evidence in the Turkish courts of law. ‘That instruc- 
tion explains, in clear and convincing language, the magnitude of the grievance 
complained of, and the absolute necessity of redress. 

It is perfectly monstrous thut a man should be exposed to the utinost 
wrong—should actually see those who are nearest and dearest to him suffering 
death, or worse than death—and yet that his evidence as to the facts shouldiba 
rejected, and the offenders escape with impunity, because he is a Christian. 

On the very first day of the meeting of Parliament, the people of England 
were reminded by a speech in the House of Lords that this unjustifiable abuse 
of power still existed in Turkey; and the Porte must clearly understand that if 
England and France are about to incur all the risks and dangers of an European

Christian Power, they have a right to demand that the brand of inferiority and 
degradation shall no longer be fixed upon the Christian subjects of the Sultan.

received from Reshid Pasha, your Excellency will give that Minister a copy 
of it.

No. 110. 
Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Receiwed February 6.) 


(No. 130.) 
My Lord, Paris, February 5, 1854, 

DURING a conversation which I had yesterday with M. Drouyn de Lhuys, 
he alluded again to the wish expressed by your Lordship that the future relations 
of Great Britain and France, in regard to the Eastern question, should be regu- 
lated by a Convention rather than an exchange of notes. 

He said that he had no objection to the principle of a Convention, but that 
he was unwilling to risk the chance of the quadruple Treaty, which the two 
Governments were desirous of signing with Austria and Prussia, by entering 
into a separate Convention of a more stringent nature with Her Majesty's 
Government. Such a proceeding, if divulged, might disincline Austria and 
Prussia to bind themselyes by any formal Act. He wished, therefore, to put 
aside your Lordship’s proposition for the moment, but he was ready to proceed 
at once to an exchange of notes, leaving it to the two Governments to sign a 
Convention in the same sense hereafter, if it were judged advisable. 

I venture to remark that, if your Lordship is anxious for a Convention, it 
will be more prudent to avoid at this moment an exchange of notes. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) COWLEY. 


No, 111. 
Lord Couley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received February 6.) 
(No. 131.) 
My Lord, Paris, February 5, 1854. 


THE French Government has received from Vienna a telegraphic despatch, 
dated the 3rd instant, of considerable importance. 

M. de Bourqueney states that Count Buol had informed him that the object 
of Count Orlofi’s mission was to obtain a declaration of neutrality on the part of 
Austria, in case of war being declared between Russia and the Western Powers. 

Count Buol, before replying, inquired of Count Orloff whether Russia was 
prepared to abide by the assurances already given to the Russian Cabinet, that 
she would not pass the Danube, that she would respect the integrity of the 
Ottoman Empire, and the present political condition (l'état politique actuel) of 
its provinces, and that her occupation of the Principalities was but a temporary 
measure. 

Count Orloff having deelared himself unable to reply affirmatively, Count 
Buol informed him, by order of the Emperor, that not only Austria would not 
give the desired assurance of neutrality, but that if the Russian troops crossed 
the Danube, the Emperor would be forced to consider what would be the line 


of conduct which the interests of his Empire and his subjects would require 
him to take.

Count Buol informed M. de Bourqueney at the same time, that the Austrian 
army on the Turkish frontier would be augmented immediately. 

Count Orloff, who it appears had intended leaving Vienna immediately, had 
put off his departure for some days. M. de Bourqueney could not explain the 
reason of this change of plan.

(ixtract.) Foreign Office, February 7, 1654. 

WITH reference to that part of my despatch No. 36 of this day's date, in 
which I state that Her Majesty's Government would approve of the archives and 
plate being left in charge of the chaplain of the British factory, T have to inform 
you that this direction is given in anticipation of the British Consul being 
obliged to leave St. Petersburgh simultaneously with yourself, and of its not 
being practicable at this season of the year to remove such bulky cases as those 
which might be required for the articles in question. 

If however the Consul should remain, the archives, sealed up, and the 
plate should both be left in his custody im the first instance, supposing the 
removal of the former cannot at once be effected. But it would certuinly be 
better, if it were possible, to provide for the extreme contingency referred to in 
my despatch, and send the archives home simultaneously with your own 
departure, giving the Consul directions, on his own withdrawal, to place the 
plate in the custody of the British chaplain, or of some respectable banking or 
mercantile establishment.

My Lord, Foreign Office, February 7, 1854. 
HER Majesty's Government have learned with the most sincere satisfaction 
the result of the audience given to the Russian Minister at Berlin by His 
Majesty the King of Prussia, a report of which is contained in your Lordship's 
despatch No. 22 of the 28th ultimo; and Her Majesty's Government a ain desire 
to congratulate Baron Manteuffel upon the firmness and decision his Excellency 
exhibits at a time when events of the most momentous gravity may turn upon 
the position assumed by Prussia. A bold course now, a fixed determination to, 
he neither intimidated nor cajoled by Russia, but to resist her aggressive policy, 
which, if successful, would render not alone the East but all Germany subservient 
to her will, cannot but have a salutary influence on Austria; and the united 
action of the two Great German Powers must render Russia comparatively 
impotent. : 
England and France can make war upon Russia, and are prepared, if 
necessary, to do so; but with Prussia and Austria it rests to prevent war, or to 
render it of short duration. Her Majesty’s Government accordingly look upon 
the complete independence of Prussia as a question of which it is impossible to

of Europe, and a guarantee for those mighty interests involved in the main-

No, 121. 
Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received February 7.) 


(No. 88. Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, January 30, 1854. 

AS it is my duty to report to your Lordship such facts of interest as come 
under my observation, so Tam desirous of submitting to you the opinions to 
which they give rise. 

IT have no hesitation, then, in stating to your Lordship my firm conviction 
that, under existing circumstances, one of the greatest misiortunes which could 
befall us would be that war with Russia should be averted by some hollow and 
insincere arrangement of difficulties. ; 

If I know anything of my feelings, no one more than myself appreciates the 
blessings of e, or more earnestly deprecates the horrors of war; but as [ 
noneae ously belisye the latter are only to be avoided for a short season, it 1s 
better that they should be encountered at the moment most favourable to 
England, than at the time and under the circumstances which would best surt 
the convenience of Mussa. 

Tam told constantly (the statement was repeated to me half-an-hour ago 
by a person in whose opinion | have great reliance) that Russia is very desirous 
of avoiding war, and I feel confident that the fact ia. so, but the wish applies only 
to the present juncture. | 

The Russian Government have had by degrees many unpalatable truths 
foreed upon them. They are at length convinced that England will strike as 
well ag remonstrate; that the alliance between England and France is not to be 
broken up by a few honied words and a little more activity of intrigue; above 
all, that the blows to which they are exposing their country will be of such a 
nature as will leave strong traces for the next half-century. All this is felt, and 
the folly and danger of having listened to supple diplomatists and cringing cour- 
tiers may possibly be at length appreciated. 

Meanwhile, hawever, whilst thie designs of Russia have been inade apparent, 
nothing has oceurred of a nature to modify them ; so fur trom this being the 
vase, ambitious plans, which were concealed in the Sovereign's breast, have been 
publicly identified with the religious wants of his people; engagements have 
been taken for their being attained, and during this boured process the public 
mind has been excited against the opponents of the Emperor (against England 
more especially) toa degree such as never prevailed in Russia with regard to 
foreigners since the campaign of 1812. 

My conviction, my firm conviction, then is, that the carrying out of these 
schemes and the gratification of the public feeling may he looked for as soon as 
England may chance to find herself engaged in war with France or with the 
United States. At this moment Russia has nearly the whole continent opposed 
to her: under the altered circumstances to which I advert, Russia may have 
resumed her favourite position of belonging to the majority of the Buropean 
Governments. 

In the Black Sea the naval men of Russia consider themselves already as 
nearly able to cope with the forces which ean be brought against them ; the con- 
fidence will be better founded if, at the end of two or three years, they have to 
try conclusions with the English fleet alone, and if, In the meantime, twelve or 
twenty-four first-class steamers be added to the fleet anchored at Sevastopol. 

{am told that the Emperor cannot extend his warlike resources to this 
amount without ruining the resources of his country ; that, my Lord, is very 
posi, but the hopes which are built upon the ussumption would nevertheless 

e perfectly fallacious; the Emperor looks to his army and his navy, and cares 
as little for other material interests when placed in competition with them as he 
does for those of his neighbours. 


1 


His pride is unbounded, and it has received a severe wound. He will 
attempt, when occasion serves, to avenge this imaginary affront ; of this 1 am 
aa convinced as if His Majesty had told me so. 1 may, indeed, say more sure, 
and, not having the slightest confidence in his pacific intentions, I will not con- 
ceal from your Lordship my anxiety that Her Majesty’s Government should 
obtain that security through the destruction of his means of offence. . 

If this judgment be severe and erroneous I can only say that it is that which 
is passed by many of His Majesty's own subjects. They understand perfectly 
that their master insists upon playing a leading part, they are aware that he can 
no longer hope to graduate in moderation or magnanimity, and they expect that 
the latter part of his reign will be directed to the acquirement of such pre-emi- 
nence as is to be obtained in the cause of orthodox encroachment, 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) G, H. SEYMOUR,

My Lord, St, Petersburgh, January 30, 1854. 

A CIRCUMSTANCE has come to my knowledge which from the evidence 
which it appears to give of the disposition of a person upon whose conduct so 
much may depend, I think it right to report to your Lordship. 

A letter was addressed some short time aga to Count Orloff by Prince 
Menchikoff, who took occasion to express his regret that the Count had not 
been charged with the Mission to Constantinople: “ Vous auriez montré,” he 
writes, “ plus d'eaprit, vous auriez eu, sans doute, plus de succes que mo.” 

No, Count Orloff replied, non, je n’aurais pas montré plus d’esprit, mais 
probablement j’aurais été plus heureux parceque jaurais été plus conciliant et 
que j’aurais pris plus sur mol.” 

It is to these latter words that I am desirous of calling your Lordship’s 
attention Count Orloff knows his master's inward thoughts better perhaps than 
any one ; he is not a man who is afraid of responsibility, and if he is convinced of 
the Emperor’s real desire to be freed from a position of great embarrassment and 
danger, it is not impossible that he may render him a service which none of the 
other Russian diplomatists would venture upon, 

I will only remark that Count Orloff’s observation to Prince Menchikoff 
was substantially the same as he had made to me two or three months since in 
speaking of the Prince's untoward mission to Constantinople.

St. Petersburgh, January 30, 1854. 

ALL that | hear, ag well of this place as of the interior, confirms what | 
have had the honour of stating to your Lordship as to the paralyzing effects 
already produced upon trade and industry by the preparations which are making 
iN ory direction of the country for an insane war. 

I learn that at Riga the merchants, both English and others, are availing 
themselves of the snow roads for the purpose of sending their goods to Memel. 
nee hope that it may be possible to make shipments from that port, when the 
ilockade which they are expecting shall be established higher a ‘coast. . 
Three days ago 1 saw a gentleman newly arrived from the interior who 
spoke to me.ol An {nglish manufactory established at some hundreds of versts 
from St. Petersburgh at which almost all the workmen had been just discharged. 

The proprietor manufactures sail cloth, of which he commonly sells

annually to the amount of about 300,000 roubles silver (48,000/.) to American 
houses; with the prospect of having these markets closed against him, he is 
preparing to suspend his business, 

The same thing will happen with the greater number of leading landed pro- 
prietors of Russia who will be, it may be observed, among the principal losers by 
the military operations in which the Government has engaged. 

These persons derive their incomes from the sale of their agricultural 
produce, which will shortly become unsaleable, and from the manufactories 
which they have very generally established upon their estates, and which will 
now in many instances be closed, whilst they will have to provide for the main- 
tenance of their serfs, whom they have made use of as workmen, besides having 
to provide their large quotas of the soldiers who will be called for in case of the 
continuance of war. 

I apprehend that a war of two years’ continuance would drive almost every 
landowner in Russia to seek the assistance of the Mortgage Bank, an institution 
which has already been the means of transferring a great part of the estates in 
the country from the gentry to the Crown. 

Colonial produce continues to rise in price, sugars more particularly ; ae 
regards this commodity the house of Stieglitz may command their own prices, for 
they have purchased all that was ‘n the market, and will realise an enormous 
profit upon the operation. 

Ou the other hand, native produce continues to fall in value; as, for instance, 
tallow, which fetched 140 and 160 roubles the 10 poods in the autumn is 
now to be purchased for 114 roubles, ——~—- 

Bristles, 1 believe, to. keep their price; but as regards this one article, 
lLussia appears to enjoy 2 natural monopoly, the bristles used by brushmakers 
and shoemakers being found of good quality only in the Southern Governments 
of this country. 

The brisile trade the Russians will therefore keep under all circumstances, 
whilst-awar is likely enough to cost them definitively their export trade in 
tallow. 

Tam not aware of having ever taken occasion to remark to your Lordship 
upon the beneficial effects, as regards commercial interests, of the delays which 
have oceurred between the offence committed against Europe by Russia, and 
that violent solution which appears now to be approaching. 

Independently of the vast amount of human food, so much wanted after a 
season of scarcity, which has been exported from Odessa durin the autumn and 
winter, British property not far short of the value of 1,000,000/. sterling has 
been got off during the same period from Riga, Archangel, and Cronstadt.

YOUR Lordship will have some difficulty in believing (although the fact 
admits, | apprehend, of no doubt), that the first resolution of the Emperor upon 
the arrival of the very honourable overtures which were received from Count 
Buol was to return no answer to the communication. 

Ata moment when the whole of Europe supposed the Imperial Cabinet to 
be engaged in weighing the enormous dangers of refusing against the advantage 
of closing with the conditions offered for an honourable peace, the Cabinet had 
almost if not altogether decided that such overtures were to be left unnoticed, 


93 


and that England and Franee, Austria and Prussia, speaking through the Con- 
ference, should be left to infer from silence that the terms which it had cost 


them so much labour to obtain from the Sultan were beneath the attention of 


the Sovereign by whom he had been so grossly insulted and so deeply injured. 

T will not indulge in the reflections which are suggested by the course 
which it was for a short time intended to follow, and will only say that wiser 
counsels prevailed, and that an answer of some kind will be returned to Count 
Buol as the mouthpiece of the Conference. 

The answer, | apprehend, will be of an evasive nature ; because, if I mistake 
not, it is determined that the resolution of the Government shail depend in 
creat measure upon the decision taken by Count Orloff, after he has had an 
opportunity of learning the state of affairs at Vienna, 

No efforts will, | am convinced, be spared to induce Austria and Prussia to 
cast in their lots with those of Russia. Fresh attempts will probably be made 
to disunite the Governments of England and France; but, supposing all this to 
fail, it may well be that Count Orloff will be the man who will take upon 
himself the responsibility of admitting a Turkish Plenipotentiary to the Council 
Board at which he and the Representatives of the Four Powers will take their 
places. 

‘All that I hear convinces me and more that Count Orloff’s powers are 
extensive and elastic. 

{ will only add, that | have some slight grounds for believing that the 
Russian Government would be found pre red to allow her Plenipotentiary to 
meet the other five for the arrangement ot @ basis of negotiation, provided that 
it were understood that the Treaty to be superposed should be negotiated by the 
Plenipotentiaries of Russia and T urkey alone.

THE language of the naval and military men here, as I hear from some of 
my diplomatic colleagues, confirms the observations which I have taken the 
liberty of submitting to your Lordship respecting the spirit of the sailors of the 
Sevastopol ships,

floets, and as being very sanguine as to the result, particularly if permitted to 
engage at close quarters. 

I am positively assured that the Emperor has taken the wise course of 
moderating this ardour, by causing it to be intimated to the naval officers at 
Sevastopol, that while he is gratified by the spirit which animates his navy, he 

peal.

1 AM still unable to state to your Lordship, with certainty, what has heen 
decided respecting the expected levy of fourteen men upon the thousand. 

Many persons assert that an order to this effect has been given, but the 
BEe by which it will be promulgated appears not to have been sent to the 

nate. 

Information worthy of confidence leaves me little or no doubt as to the 
attacks upon Kalafat having proceeded from the impatience manifested by the 
Emperor at any portion of the Turkish army being allowed to hold its ground 
on the left bank of the Danube. 

This impatience is still constantly expressed ; and, aa J expect daily to 
hear, will have led to a desperate attack upon a point which 1s likely to he 
defended with the same obstinacy. 

I only hope that those seductive means which were so Successfully employed 
by Peter the Great, and which were found equally efficacious in 1829, may not 
azain be brought to bear upon the cupidity of Turkish Generals. 

At St. Petersburgh, where the severe criticism of an active army 16 a 
favourite occupation of the military men who are unemployed, Prince Gortcha- 
kolf is now as much blamed for his rashness as he was two months ago for his 
inactivity. This present fault—if fault it be—is probably to be ascribed to the 
impatience to which I have above alluded. 

The want of success which hns attended Prince Gortchakofl’s operation ts, 
however, variously explained, and is stated to me by a retired officer of long 
standing to proceed from the fact of the Russian Commander-in-chief haying 
none but German lieutenants under him, General Dannenberg, General Liiders, 
General Fischback, and General Anrep, and Baron Sacken, are all Livonians and 
Fsthonians; and it is almost invariably observed that men of these races do not 
cooperate cordially with a Russian chiet. 

'The newspapers report General Anrep (whose name is improperly given as 
Aurep) as having been severely wounded in one of the late affairs. Nothing is 
known here upon the subject, and the report 18 not believed. 

T would here remark incidentally that some of the accounts which I have 
read lately in the English papers, and which protess to have been written by 
St. Petersburgh correspondents, must have been prepared in London, and by 
persons unacquainted with this country, 1 observe in them a series of 
statements for which there is no sort of foundation. 

I may take this opportunity for stating to your Lordship that General Cas- 
telbajae has read me a despatch which he has atldressed to his Government in 
which he gives an account of his last eonversation with Count Nesselrode, 

He represents himself as having laid before the Chaneellor the various dilh- 
culties of a military nature which will attend the prosecution of the war with 
Turkey, and of having particularly insisted upon the impossibility of the army im 
European Turkey being provisioned, and of the necessary communication being 
kept open with the army in Asin as long as the combined fleets have the 
superiority in the Black Sea. 

General Castelbajac states further, that some months or weeks ago he had 
taken an opportunity for submitting these Fi ec tie » the Emperor.

He was unwell, and stated that he should be unable, on the fclowE ey to

residing. ‘The next day, Monday, he waited upon the Emperor, and, after a long 
interview with His Majesty, he saw Count Buol for a few moments only, as the 
latter was called by the Emperor. Count Orloff on that day dined with the 
imperor, only a few persons, amongst them Count Buol, being present. 

In the course of the morning I had seen Count Buol, who stated, as he had 
done the previous evening, that he had not seen Count Orloff, who was firat to 
have his audience of the Emperor, whieh he was glad of, as he would learn from

with the allied Powers for the re-establishment of peace ; and Count Buol pro-

telegraph. 

On Tuesday, not having received any communication from Count Buol, | 
wrote to him begging that he would let me know whatever communication 
had been made to him by Count Orloff, and I received from him & reply which 
| transmitted to your Lordship in m) telegraphic despatch of yesterday dated 
valf-past twelve o'clock; according to which the first communications from Count 
Orloff had been unsatisfactory, but it was expected that, bya Russian messenger 
who had arrived in the morning, Count Orloff would have received instructions 
to reply to the proposals for negotiation which had been transmitted from 
Vienna on the 13th ultimo, and that Count Buol was appointed to see him in 
the course of the afternoon. 

1 met Count Buol at dinner, when he informed M, de Bourqueney and 
myself that he was very much dissatisfied with the communications he had 
veeeived: that he was to see Count Orloff later in the evening and discuss more 
fully these communications, after which he should better be able to appreciate 
them and to bring them before the Conference ; but he feared they were not ol 
character to forward the objects of peace, and that they contained a proposal 
that a ‘Turkish negotiator should repair to St. Petersburgh. 1 transmitted to 
your Lordship the substance of this information by telegraph last night.

No. 135. 
Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received February 7.) 
(No. 35.) 
My Lord, Berlin, February 4, 1854. 


THE French Minister at this Court received from his Government on the 
let instant the draft of a Convention to be aigned by the Representatives of 
Great Britain, France, Austria, and Prusaia at Vienna, setting forth the terms on 


oo 


which these Powers engage themselves to employ all their efforts to bring about 
the re-establishment of peace. The Marquis de Moustier immediately spoke to 
me on the subject, and as his Government appeared anxious that no time should 
be lost in making this communication, l accompanied my French colleague to 
Baron Manteuffel, where he delivered the draft in question to his Excellency, 
and we both urged him to advise the King to adopt it and to transmit instruc- 
tions accordingly to Count Arnim at Vienna. 

I received yesterday your Lordship’s despatch No. 10, and have spoken in 
a more formal manner to the Prussian Minister for Foren Affairs than I could 
do upon the previous instructions which I had received from your Lordship by 
telegraph. 

Baron Manteuffel made at the time but few observations on the proposed 
Convention, and said he should lay it before the King and take His Majesty's 
orders on the subject. 

I have just seen Baron Manteuffel, and he has informed me that he had 
embodied the remarks he wished to offer on this Convention in a memorandum, 
and forwarded a copy of this paper to Chevalier Bunsen, who would relate the 
substance of these objections to your Lordship. 

His Excellency added that this proceeding on his part must not be viewed 
in the light of a rejection of the Convention, for he felt that at a future time it 
could be again brought forward, but he thought the present moment inopportune 
for the negotiation. 

I replied that we had no desire to press this Treaty for his immediate 
acceptance, but that I hoped his Excellency would bear in mind the advantage 
of some such formal Act being completed by the Four Powers in the event of 
We Emperor of Russia's refusing to agree to the Vienna propositions of the 13th 
ultimo. 

I may add that Baron Manteuffel is not himself indisposed to agree to this 
Convention, and that the difficulties are raised elsewhere. 

M. de Moustier quite agrees with me that it will be advisable to wait for 
a while before taking a further step in the matter. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

No, 140. 
The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe, 
(No. 48.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, Vebruary 7, 1654. 


HER Majesty’s Government learn with much regret, but without surprise, 
the defeat of the Turks in Asia, reported im your Excellency’s despatch No. 21 
of the 15th of January, as the unfitness of Ali Pasha to command, and the want 
of confidence of the troops in such a commander, must long haye been known 
to the Porte. 

Although no mention of it is made in your Excellency’s despatch, [er 
Majesty's Government hope that the cowardice and incapacity of Ali Pasha will 
not be allowed to go unpunished, and that he will be replaced by an officer who 
understands and is prepared to do his duty. ‘The deficiency of good officers 
throughout the Turkish army 1s notorious; the troops are brave, enduring anc 
obedient, and there is reason to believe that they are willing to be commanded 
by Christians ; yet mumerous officers are at Constantinople anxious to engure ith 
the Sultan's service, and more would come if employment were riven to them, 
and confidence were placed in their knowledge and experience. 

If Her Majesty's Government are to give effectual aid to Turkey, and to 
engage in active operations, it 1s absolutely necessary that we should know upon 
what we can depend, and that we should not be spectators or sharers in defeats 
cused by imbecility and cowardice, 


1 am, &e. 
(Signed) CLARENDON,

No, 142. 
The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Cowley. 
(No, 80) | 
My Lord, Foreign Office, February 8, 1854. 


THE Vrench Ambassador has addressed to me a note, & copy of which 1s 
herewith incloged,* in which his Excellency states that it has ap neared to the 
French Government that, with reference to the eventualities which so justly 
engage the attention of the two Governments, the time has now come for defining 
the object of their alliance, and for denoting the means for carrying out that 
object. : See | 

To this end Count Walewskt proposts that Her Majesty's Government and 
that of the Emperor of the French should agree: ae | 

1. That the demonstiation already made by Great Britain and France, and 
the signature by their Re resentatives of the documents agreed to by the Confer- 
ence at Vienna on the 5th of December, 1853, and on the 13th of January, 1854, 
prove that the object of the two Governments 18 to maintain the territorial 
integrity of the Ottoman Empire and the sovereign independence of His Majesty 
the Sultan. 

a That this object would be attamed if peace could be re-established 
between Russia and the Sublime Porte on the ertectly honourable conditions 
which have been proposed to the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh. In the event, 
which may God avert, of war becoming necessary, its CAUse would naturally 
cease from the day on which peace should be re-established with Russia on the 
bases above mentioned, and when the Russian troops should have evacuated the 
Provinces of Moldavia and Wallachia, as well as every other part of the Ottoman 
dominions. - 

3. That until the end thus specified shall have been attained, the Govern- 
ment of the Emperor of the French engages to cooperate towards it by means of 
the fleet now acting in the Black Sea, by augmenting it in case of necessity ; 
and to give an ussurance that the Government of His Imperial Majesty would be 
disposed to unite a French squadron to that which Her Britannic Majesty may 


® No, 112. 


—— 


eee edo DieAd 


104 


send into the North Sea or the Baltic whenever the two Governments shall have 
agreed upon the necessity of making this further demonstration. 

4, ‘That if the proposed measures should not be held sufficient to cause 
Russia to evacuate the Ottoman territory and to conelude peace, the Government 
of His Imperial Majesty, in concert with that of Her Britannic Majesty, would 
consider the expediency of supporting their naval operations by means of a body 
of troops. 

5 That so long as war may continue, the Government of France would 
not receive any proposal or overture for a cessation of hostilities without 
instantly putting the Rritish Government in a position conjointly to discuss its 
expediency and opportuneness 5 and that the French Government, being solely 
animated with a desire to preserve the territorial integrity of Europe from scrigus 
danger, renounces beforehand the acquisition of any special advantage from 
events Which may Occur. 

To all the proposals thus stated Her Majesty's Government give their 
unqualified assent, and adopt the obligations which that assent imposes ; and to 
none of them do Her Majesty's Government agee with greater cordiality and 
satisfaction than to that in which the honourable and disinterested motives of 
the two Governments are clearly defined, 

Your Excellency will address a note to M. Drouyn de Lhuys in the exact 
words of this despatch. 

lam, &c.

find it difficult to form an opinion, while at the same time you might, under 
your existing instructions, feel called upon decidedly to point out to Vice-Admiral 
Dundas not only the course he ehould in any given circumstances Pursts, but 
also the manner in which he should give effect to your requisitions. 

To relieve your Excellency, therefore, from any doubt on this point I think 
‘t advisable to state that all that Her Majesty's Government expect of you is to 
‘aform the Admiral of the service which you require him to perform, leaving to 
the Admiral to determine, with reference to professional considerations alone, in 
what manner it may be moat advisable to give effect to your requisitions.

No, 145. 
Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recewed February 9.) 


(No. 27.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, January 18, 1854. 

IN the course of yesterday I received, not without surprise, a letter from 
Vice-Admiral Dundas intimating that he meant to return with the squadrons 
into the Bosphorus as soon as wind and weather would permit. | lost no time 
in communicating to the French Ambassador my opinion respecting this 
intended movement, and we agreed to write to the two Admirals in.the hope of 
preventing its execution. His Excellency having no stean-vessel conveniently 
at his disposal, I requested the commanding officer of Her Majesty's ships on 
the station to forward our despatches immediately by express. Captain Gold- 
smith having complied with this invitation, I am not without hopes that the 
despatches may reach the two Admirals in time. But the report of their 
intended return has already taken wind, and the impression produced by it 1s by 
no means such as I could wish. 

Inclosed herewith are copies of my correspondence with Admiral Dundas 
on this occasion. 

General Baraguay d'Hilliers informed me that he did not feel himself at 
liberty under his instructions to order the French squadron to remain in the 
Black Sea, as there might be nautical reasons for its return, In his reply to 
Admiral Hamelin he assumes the exclusive right of judging as to political 
reasons, and throws the responsibility upon that officer, In framing my 
despatch to Admiral Dundas I have endeavoured to prevent the return of the 
squadron at present, without diverging to any marked degree from the line taken 
by my colleague. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

“events that have occurred,” and * different letters received the last few days, 
think it my duty to remind you that the last instruction which I had the 
honour to address to you on the subject, terminated in these words, “ You arc 
expected to maintain an adequate force ‘n the Black Sea, so long as the flag and 
territory of the Porte are exposed to danger.” 

Now, as I am wholly ignorant of what is meant by the events and letters 
to which you have alluded, | remain of opinion that the territory and flag of 
‘Turkey are still exposed to danger from Russian aggression, beside that itis the 
declared resolution of Eler Majesty's Government to have the command of the 
Black Sea, and consequently to require, under compulsion if necessary, every 
Russian ship of war encountered on its waters to return’ into port. Such cir- 
cumstances as are known to me, tend to confirm that opinion, It appears both 
from Captain Drummond's report to you and from the latest commercial letters 
received here from Odessa, that a considerable portion of the Russian fleet may

necessary to send more troops and ammunition by set m aid of the defences ot 
‘ts Asiatic frontier, Moreover, it still remains for us to know the effect

Such being the state of the case | must beg to decline all share im the 
responsibility of your immediate return ; and I lose no time in requesting the 
senjor officer in command of Her Majesty’s ships on this station to forward my

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon —(Recetved February 9.) 


(No. 35.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, January 24, 1854. 


THE combined squadrons returned to their former anchorage in the 
Bosphorus on the 22nd instant. ‘he steamer which I sent out to prevent their 
return did not fall in with them till they were close to the entrance of the Strait. 

The French Ambassador is greatly dissatisfied with the return of Vice- 
Admiral Hamelin under existing circumstances, and in virtue of considerations 
which appear to him defective. My sentiments on the same subject are con- 
signed to a despatch, which I have thought it my duty to address to Admiral 
Dundas, and of which a copy is herewith inclosed. 

The general impression created by the return of the squadrons is by no 
means favourable, either to our credit or to our influence. 

The Admirals are at the same time ready to comply with any demand of 
convoy for vessels laden with troops or ammunition, and bound for Turkish 
ports in the Black Sea. 

What I understand from your Lordship’s No, 11 of this year, is that 
unnecessary exposure of the squadrons to loss or damage is to be avoided; but 
that whatever risks are unavoidable in carrying out the stated instructions of 
Her Majesty’s Government are to be frankly incurred without reference to the 
season. 

This was, in substance, the view of the question which I took when the 
affair of Sinope occurred ; and when, on the return of the “Retribution ” from 
that place, I called upon Admiral Dundas to go into the Black Sea with an 
adequate force, 

The remainder of my correspondence with Vice-Admiral Dundas is inclosed 
herewith in copy. 

I have, &c. . 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE,

Inclosure 3 in No. 146.

Vice-Admiral Dundas to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord, Britannia,” in the Bosphorus, January 22, 1854. 

IN reply to your Excellency’s letter of the 17th instant, received this day, 
| have the honour to acquaint you that Admiral Hamelin and I came into the 
Bosphorus because the experience we have had has convinced us that if the 
Emperor of Russia had to choose where the combined squadrons should pass the 
next two months, he would decidedly keep them “cruising in the Black Sea,” 80 
as to render them inefficient for operations in the spring, and thus giving the 
preponderance to his ships that are husbanding their resources in their own 
orts. : 

; The port of Sinope can never become the rendezvous of the squadrons from 
its many disadvantages arising from its leeward and distant position; for the 
necessary supplies for eighteen sail-of-the-line besides numerous steam-vessels 
cannot be safely obtained in the casual manner mentioned by your Excellency. 

We adhere to the opinion we have so clearly and often expressed, and 
which we hoped had been agreed to, that the command of the Black Sea and 
protection of the Turkish territory would be best maintained by the rapid move- 
ments of a steam-squadron as pointed out to your Excellency in my minute of 
the 29th of December, and which the late service, performed by Sir Edmund 
Lyons and Admiral de Tinan, fully proves. 

'The necessity of making the Rosphorus the chief rendezvous 1s clearly 
exemplified by the fact that, during the last eighteen days, accidents have 
occurred (which no foresight could have prevented) that would have obliged us 
to send two ships-of-the-line to the Bosphorus to refit, thus proving that we 
could not reasonably expect to continue operations in the Black Sea without 
gradually reducing our force. 60 88 ultimately to give up the command of the 
Black Sea to Russia. 

All these considerations make it desirable that the Bosphorus should be 
the main rendezvous of our squadrons, keeping our larger ships in reserve, and 
as many as possible together, and the screw and steam squadrons always moving 
about when the weather will permit. 

Among the events and letters alluded to in my letter of the 15th instant, | 
think it right to draw the attention of your eset yet a very important one— 
the letter that your Lordship recommended Admiral - amelin and myself to write 
to Sevastopol; and I beg to call to your notice that your Excellency has not 
done me the honour of informing me whether the letters signed by Admiral 
Hamelin and myself have been forwarded or not, a measure on which our opera- 
tions so materially depend, especially in the delicate and critical position in which 
we are at this moment placed with respect to Russia. 

T have, &c. 
(Signed) J. W. D. DUNDAS,
