My Lord, Britannia,” in the Bosphorus, January 23, 1854. 


WITH reference to the fourth paragraph of your Excellency’s letter of the 
Loth instant, I beg to acquaint you that M. Pisani has not been correctly 
informed ag to the diminished number of troops lately embarked in the Turkish 
steamers for the coast of Anatolia. In a conversation that took place between 
the Turkish Admirals and Rear-Admival Sir Edmund Lyons and myself, Vice- 
Admiral Mustapha Pasha said that he had orders to proceed to sea under convoy 
of the British flag, and that his steamers were so crowded with men (1000 cach) 
and stores, that the uns were not clear, and the vessels’ progress would be 
impeded, To which I replied that | had no instructions whatever on the 
subject, and that if his steamers were overloaded, he might remedy that evil by 
reducing the number of men in each vessel to about 800, 

Further than this conversation I gave no advice, nor did I receive any 
other intimation on the subject until I felt myself hound to interfere for the 
protection of the steam-vessels on their unexpectedly joining the combined 
squadrons on the morning of the Sth January, when more than a hundred miles 
to the eastward of the Bosphorus; and I must own that | was greatly surprised 
to find after all, that less than 1000 men were landed from the Turkish steam- 
vessels at Batoom.

Inclosure 5 in No. 146. 
Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to Vice- Admiral Dundas, 


Sir, Pera, January 24, 1854. 

THE vast importance of the service in which we are respectively engaged, 
imposes upon me the duty of expressing, without reserve or circumlocution, the 
opinion J entertain as to the return of the combined squadrons under present 
circumstances to the Bosphorus. 

1 have read with attention your statement of the motives which decided 
your conduct in that respect, and IT cannot conceal from you that the impression 
remaining on my mind is one of dissatisfaction and regret. 

It is not for me to determine the value of your reasons, in so far as they 
ure atrictly nautical; but as you wrote to me for transports to supply you with 
coal on the 13th instant, and announced your intention of returning to the 
Bosphorus on the 15th, 1 naturally expected to learn that your reasons for doing 
so were derived from the “events” and the ‘“‘letters’” to which you alluded in 
the latter despatch, and not from such nautical considerations as you liad already 
get forth in your memorandum of the 29th ultimo. ‘The only events of which 
| perecive any mention in your despatch are the operation condueted by Hear- 
Admiral Sir Edmund Lyons between Trebizond and Batoom, and the damage 
sustained by two ships belonging to one or other of the squadrons. 

On these I have to remark, that the detachment under Sir Edmund Lyons 
did not happen to fall in with any Russian squadron, and that the two vessels 
stated to ee been damaged might have returned without impairing the 
effective power of the combined squadrons. 

With respect to the second notification aldressed under your signature and 
that of Admiral Hamelin to the superior naval authority at Sevastopol, it never 
was understood that you were to suspend your operations until it had been 
delivered, and still less until an answer had been received, From any such 
necessity, had it ever existed, you would have been released by the delivery of 
the first notification, and the kind of reception given at Sevastopol to Her 
Majesty's steam-frigate ‘* Retribution.” 

Looking to the instructions under which, by order of Her Majesty's 
Government, you are called upon to act, | am at a loss to understand how 


115 


they can be effectively carried out by squadrons stationed in the Bosphorus, 
which, with the prevailing wind, is notoriously under the disadvantage of being 
more or less to leeward of almost every thing mm the Black Sea, 

After the declarations made by order of Her Majesty’s Government, both 
here and at St. Petersburgh, we are bound to maintain the command of the Black 
Sea, protecting therein the flag and territory of the Porte. 

You are the best judge of what amount of force is necessary for these pur- 
poses in the present forward condition of the Russian fleet, On this point the 
responsibility rests of necessity with you, But in the exercise of a paramount 
duty, | must adhere to my former instructions as to the above-mentioned objects 
being secured, if that be possible, by the employment of the forces under 
your command. 

At this moment 1 know but of two vessels in the Black Sea belonging to 
the combined squadrons, namely, the “ Prométhée” at Varna, and the “ Fury?’ 
despatched to Odessa. According also to such information as | have received, 
a considerable portion of the Russian fleet is absent from Sevastopol, either at 
sca, or in some other port or roadstead. Such being the ease, it is evident that 
the protection of the ‘Turkish flag and territory depends at present upon the 
diseretion of Russia, and not upon our command of the Black Sea. 

I perfectly understand what risk the service involves at this season to the 
shipping employed on it; and doubtless if the service can be efficiently per- 
formed without such risks the advantage is great. But 1 have no reason to 
suppose that Her Majesty’s Government contemplated the postponement of the 
service until a fair season und more settled weather shall set in, 

I have only therefore in conclusion to confirm my previous instructions on 
this subject. 

T have, &e, 


(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

No. 148. 


Lord Stratford de Redeliffe to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Received February 9.) 


(No. 37.) | 
My Lord, Constantinople, January 25, 1854. 

THE divisions which have long existed, with more or less inconvenience, 
in the Turkish Ministry, continue to produce delays and inconsistencies which 
threaten serious consequences in the end. Re: 

The individual who is chiefly responsible for this state of things 18 Mehemet 
Ali, the Seraskier, who, besides being at the head of the army, 1s the Sultan's 
brother-in-law. He is by no means deficient in energy; and in quiet times his 
administration of more than one department has done him credit. At present 
he acts with too much independence and obstinacy for a Minister who has more 
resolution than discernment, and more self-confidence than knowledge. His 
removal from office is greatly desired by more than one of his colleagues, and I 
have reason to know that the Sultan, aware of his intrigues with the war party 
and fanatics, is only restrained from dismissing him by an apprehension, not 
well grounded, of his influence with the ary: bik Averei) 

But Mehemet Ali is not the only member af the Cabinet whose retirement 
would be likely to prove advantageous to the conduct of public affairs... The 


Sheik-ul-Islam and the President of the Council might also be superseded with 


119 


an equal prospect of benefit to the State, In proportion as the likelihood of war 
assumes a stronger colouring, and we approach more nearly to the period of 
active operations, the importance of having a vigorous and united administration 
increases, If the present causes of weakness and vacillation continue, we must 
expect the reverse of everything which is necessary for bringing the contest to a 
prompt and satisfactory issue. 

nder this conviction | have made known my sentiments to the Sultan, and 
Iam warranted to hope that His Majesty, far from turning a deaf ear to my 
arguments, will endeavour seriously to overcome his objections, and to make 
before long the change which 1 have earnestly recommended. 

As soon as this first indispensable step towards improvement is taken, | 
hope to effect some understanding with the Ministry as to the future plan of 
proceeding, on the supposition that war, as Il fear is but too likely, shall 
continue on a larger scale and on a wider field. Reshid Pasha is well disposed 
in this respect, and he has already shown that his wishes extend to the formation 
of a conventional agreement between the Porte and its two maritime allies. It 
will be an object of my early solicitude to ascertain precisely the nature and. 
extent of his views, for the eventual consideration of Her Majesty's Government. 
In less than three months, if not sooner, it is reasonable to expect that the 
Emperor of Russia, supposing that he rejects the propositions accepted by the 
Porte, will cross the Danube with the view of striking a decisive blow before the 
Sultan's allies have matured their plans of auxiliary cooperation. I endeavour, 
without ceasing, to bring this danger so strongly before the Sultan and his 
Ministers, as to prevail on them to complete their measures of pre aration with 
the least possible waste of time. Hitherto they show no want of inclination to 
heed my counsels ; but the very foundation stone of successful progress is. still 
to be laid in a partial change of Ministry, and until that preliminary step be 
taken, I despair of obtaining any results more important than partial additions 
to the army, and, in less degree, to ne fortifications and military supplies. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received February 10.) 
(No. 148.) 


My Lord, Paris, February 9, 1854. 
'THE Earl of Westmorland will, without doubt, have made your Lord- 

ship a communication similar to that received here by telegraph last night 

from M. de Bourqueney ; but in a matter of so much importance I think it 

Beh that your Lordship should be made acquainted with the exact words of 
. de Bourqueney’s despatch. 

He says that M. de Buol had summoned the Conference to meet yester- 
day morning, and that he had communicated to them confidentially the sub- 
stance of a conversation which he had held the previous evening with Count 
Orloff, who had returned to St. Petersburgh on that morning, respecting the 
means of settling the Eastern question. 

The plan sketched out was this: ‘That Russia should send from 

St. Petersburgh the preliminaries of a peace, based on the propositions of the 
13th of January; that M. de Meyendorff should be authonzed to introduce 
into them any modifications thought necessary by the Conference, to whose 
consideration they would he submitted; that these preliminaries should be sent 
without delay to Constantinople, and their acceptance followed by an armis- 
tice. When accepted by the Porte, the Principalities to be evacuated and the 
fleets to be withdrawn. A place to be fixed upon for the signature of the 
Treaty of Peace.” 
M. de Buol, in making this communication toe the Conference, added, that 
it was not to be looked upon in the light of a Russian proposition, but as an 
idea that Count Orloff had promised to recommend to His Imperial Master to 
adopt. He wished the members of the Conference to submit it to the conside- 
ration of their respective Governments, in order that they might be prepared to 
coter upon the subject, should Count Ovloff succeed in his endeavours. 


120 


M. Drouyn de Ehuys did not appear to attach much importance to this 
communication, and as, when I saw him, he had just come from the Emperor, 
presume that His Majesty js not inclined either to hope much from it. His 
Excellency observed that, if Count Orlofi’s proposal was accepted by the Russian 


uence was guarded by the propositions of January 18; there was no longer 
any question or sending & Turkish Plenipotentiary to St. Petersburgh, and the 
evacuation of the Principalities would be effected before the signature of peace. 
But he could not help fearing, he said, that this was another attempt to gain 
time, and to detach Austria from her alliance with the Western Powers. He 
was of opinion that France and England should answer that if Count Orloff’s 
suggestions were adopted by the Russian Government and fairly carried out, the 
question might be considered as settled ; but that the two Governments should 
not desist in the meantime from any of their warlike prepartions, whether by 
sea or land, or from their diplomatie action upon the Governments of Austria 


and Prussia.

Inclosure in No. 156. 
Extract from the “ Wiener Zeitung” of February 6, 1854. 


Translation.) 


DURING the conflict which has been going on for some months past in 
Wallachia between Russia and Turkey, His Imperial and Royal Apostolic 
Majesty, in consideration of the terms of friendly alliance existing between 
Austria and both the belligerent Powers equally, has not hitherto felt himself 
called upon to increase the number of his troops in the Woivodina or the 
Temeswar Banat. | 

These unfortunate hostilities having however now extended into Lesser 
Wallachia, and consequently into the neighbourhood of our” frontiers, His 
Imperial Majesty, anxious for the peace of his dominions and subjects, and their 
preservation from even unintentional molestations, has commanded the con- 
centration of a corps d’armée of 25,000 men in the Government of the above- 
mentioned Provinces, in consequence of which a portion of the garrison of this 
city will shortly be removed hence and replaced by reinforcements to the 
regiments remaining here.

Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon —(Received February 11.) 


‘No. 102, Seeret and Confidential.) 


My Lord, St, Petersburgh, February 2, 1854. 

NOTHING can be more contradictory than the indications observable 
here as to the feelings of the Court with regard to the present alternative of 
peace or war. 

One of the chief persons about the Emperor, and one who has been 
remarkable for the moderation of his language, now says that he considers 
affairs to have advanced so far that the interests of the country, and even the 
dignity of the Crown, render war inevitable; an opinion to the same effect has 
been expressed by some other persons more closely belonging to the Court. I 
hear of more than one of these persons who express their opinions in the 
following language: That it is perhaps unfortunate that the Oriental question 
should have been prematurely raised; but that taking things as they are, con- 
sidering the immense outlay in preparations which has been made, and looking 
to the slight probability which would exist at the Emperor’s age of his being 
able, after the requisite interval, to recommence and carry through the great 
work, it is desirable that the apa ue not now be abandoned, 


——a 


124 


On the other hand, 1 am convinced that the more enlightened of the Russians 
feel that their position is a bad one, and that it 1s not likely to be improved hy 
an advance in the face of European fecling. 

These more moderate councils, chiefly advocated by the Chancellor here, if | 
not mistaken, led to the dispatch of Count Orloff to Vienna. 

Count Nesselrode feels that his powers of resistance to violent measures 
cannot be carried further. He is aware of the odium which attaches to his 
German name and his anti-Selavonie views, and he is desirous of putting upon 
another, and that other a favorite of the Emperor, a Greek as to faith and a 
Russian by birth, the responsibility of acceding, if needs must, to such terms as 
may be in some degree acceptable to Europe in the great question between her 
and Russia. | 

That every effort will be made by Count Orloff to bring back Austria to 
what is here regarded as her allegiance, and to confirm in a Russian sense the 
always somewhat uncertain policy of the Prussian Cabinet, | do not doubt; it 
may be, as well, that he will make a last effort to separate France and England : 
but supposing all this to be resisted, and only ordinary firmness and (which 1 
this ease is the same thing) prudence to be exhibited by the two German 
Powers, I fecl sanguine as to the event proving that Count Orloff will have some 
conciliatory proposal to make. 

[ will go further, and will venture to remark that if his first overtures shall 
not be found such as can be acceded to, a second or third examination of bis 
portfolio may not improbably bring fo light some proposition which is better 
calculated to meet the views of the Conference. 

L will not close my despatch without observing that the influence which the 
female portion of the Imperial family have exercised or endeavoured to exercise 
upon the policy of the Government has been anything but of a salutary kind. 
It seldom happens that Her Imperial Majesty or the Grand Duchesses interfere 
in State affairs: but by accident I have learned, and this upon undoubted 
authority, that before leaving Galetima the Empress, the Grand Duchess Mary, 
and the Grand Duchess Olga entreated the Emperor to come to a private 
understanding with the French Court, and to settle the business without the 
participation of England. 

OF this fact, which has surprised me considerably, | am certain. 

I have, &c.

(No. 104.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, February 2, 1854. 

PREPARATIONS for war upon the most extensive scale continue to be 
made in every direction by this Government, in profession so desirous of peace, 
go solicitous to maintain the independent rights of all other countries! 

For some days past, from 800 to 1000 recruits have arrived here daily by 
the Moscow railway; the greater number of them are intended for the Guards 
and Grenadiers, some however being drafted into regiments of the line. 

The want of rapid means of communication 1s sensibly felt at a moment 
when such extensive military operations are in contemplation ; and there is now 
question of establishing electric telegraphs between St, Petersburgh, Warsaw. 
Moscow, and even Odessa. 

The public papers, which bave been so constantly in errot lately with 
regard to what is passing in Russia, are correct in the motive which they assign 
to Marshal Paskewiteh's visit to St. Petersburgh. He has been sent for, as I 
know upon the best authority, for the purpose of expressing his opinion upon 
the plan of campaign which has been prepared here. 
| Some of the persons who have access to the Experor have been repre- 
senting to him that with the immense bodies of troops fo be provisioned, it will 

be desirable to prohibit the exportation of grain from Odessa and the other 
southern ports. I understand the uotion to have been resisted, and hitherto 


125 


successfully, by the Finance Minister and Baron Stieglitz, these gentlemen 
representing, what is indeed very notorious, that soldiers abound in Russia, but 
that money is likely to become soon very scarce.

of-battle shivs afford a ready conveyance for legions of invading troops to East 
Prussia and Pomerania. 

The same thing applies to Mecklenburgh, Denmark, and Sweden: they all 
are brought into dangerous proximity with Russia as soon as Cronstadt Harbour 
is filled with war steamers. 

But, my Lord, the security even of the English coasts will be toa degree 
siffected by the establishment of a force such as that I am speaking of, as by the 
help of steam they might at any time during the summer months be reached in 
the course of seven or eight days. 

An Englishman has some reluctance in admitting that danger can approach 
him on that which he considers his own peculiar element, but it is to be remem- 
bered that, although possessing ships in abundance, England, happily for her, 
does not keep on foot large standing armies, and that even if not obliged to 
‘nerease the number of her troops, the existence of a larger Baltic steam fleet 

will compel her to augment considerably her annual naval expenditure, 

To another possible contingency, that of a junction of the Russian and 
French navies in hostility to England, I will not do more than allude. 

hese considerations, which are too obvious to require being insisted upon, 
appear to me to lead to the conclusion, either that such precautions should be 
ndopted as may offer some security against the abuse of Russia’s extending 

means of offence; or (and this plan ts: more easily realized) that efforts should 
he made for crushing a Power which, if allowed to expand at: its ease, will 
become intolerable ta the rest of Kurope.

My Lord, St. Petersburgh, February 4, 1854. 


WHEN I waited upon Count Nesselrode on the 3rd instant, I read to his 
Excellency the inclosed extract of a letter which | had received from Mr. Consul 
Whitebead, remarking that my answer to Mr. Whitehead would depend ina 
great mensure upon the information which [ might receive from his Excellency. 

The Chancellor said that the wish of the Russian Government to press as 
lightly as possible upon foreign traders in the event of war was known to me. 
That in that ease so many days would be assigned, during which the merchant- 
vessels of the belligerent Powers would be at liberty to depart. 

L replied that the case was one which ought not to be left open to any 
doubt, and that it was clear that a measure which appeared at first sight fair 
and itnpartial, might in practice be unjust and one-sided. 

That, for instance, if England nesigned ten or twenty days for the free 
departure of Russian vessels, these ten or twenty deys were available all the year 
round, whereas in Russia the expiration of a like term might find English 
vessels blocked in the ice, ‘The proper course would be so many days to count 
from the opening of the navigation. 

Count Nesselrode’s answer was less explicit than I could have desired; he 
repeated, however, his assurance of the desire felt by the Government to deal 
liberally with English shipping, adding that everything would depend upon the 
treatment of Russian vessels in the ports of Great Britain. 

His Excellency then alluded to vessels belonging to Russia which were now 
building in England, and which in the event of war being declared would, he 
feared, be detained or confiscated. 

| replied that the cases were nowise similar, os the ships in question were 
chins of war: that I had no instructions by which to guide my answer, but 
although | could not for a moment believe that Her Majesty's Government 
would permit the completion or departure of vessels built for war purposes, that

My Lord, St. Petersburgh, February 6, 1854. 

A VERY strange circumstance has occurred to me; a stranger, an 
Englishman by birth, but a man who has been living entirely among Russians 
for the last twenty or thirty years, desired to ste me on business. 

I found 1 had to do with an intelligent man, and soon perceived that there 
were other subjects than that which formed the ostensible object of his visit, 
upon whieh he desired to converse. 

He proceeded to state that he 1s convineed that the seizure of Turkey 1s 
the object which the Emperor has in view, and that nothing will induce His 
Majesty to forego his purpose. ‘That as to armaments, I must be aware upon 
what stale they have been prepared: that as. to finance, from being intimately 
acquainted with a secret emplové of the Government, he is positive as to the 
metallic deposits in the fortress having been most extensively tampered with ; 
and equally positive that the enormous sum of 60,000,000 of silver rouble notes 
of 50 roubles each (about 60,000,001. sterling) have heen secretly ey and 
will be brought gradually into circulation, under cover of the ukases lately 
‘ssued authorising the fresh emission of paper. 

lam unable to contradict or affirm this startling intelligence, which, how- 
ever, is to adegree reconcileable with statements which T have already had the 
honour of making to your Lordship. I can only say that my informant 
abserved that he was stating not what he believed, but what he knew and was 
sure of: and that he asked for no reward or favour, present or future, beyond 
that of my employing such discretion with regard to his communications as 
should prevent the possibility of its uuthor being ever suspected. 

Refore leaving me, this person further acquainted me that he knows of 
three landed proprietors who are endeavouring to sell their estates, with the 
intention of vesting the proceeds i land in ‘Purkey.

' Tis to be regretted that Count Esterhazy’s recovery did not take place a 
few days sooner, and that he was not the bearer of the communication to the 
Court of St. Petersburgh made by Count Buol in the despatch which accom- 

‘al the Protocol of the 13th ultimo. 
ja Count Esterhazy's official rank, and the knowledge of the feelings of his 
Governmunt, might possibly have given an importance to a paper which it neither 
possesses in itself, nor by the influence of the diplomatic agent to whom it was 
addressed. 

The despatch will lave been communicated by Count Colloredo to your 
Lordship, and [ shall be much surprised if it has met with your approbation. 

From my knowledge of the feclings and prejudices of this Court I have no 
hesitation in stating my conviction that 1b was drawn up in language very ill 
calculated to attain its supposed object. ' 

Had Coun Buol informed the Russian Government that his Imperial 
master, being intent upon preserving the most friendly terms with Russia, and of 
remaining neutral in case of war, had obtained an unexceptionable basis of 
negotiation between the Emperor and the Sultan, but that the rejection of this 
basis mivht have the effect of affecting his ardent desire to keep clear of 
hostilities: the dignity of one Emperor would have been asserted, and the 


F ‘ : es et Sh. ett, | [Peete oa i ae

obstinacy of the other would probably have been overcome; whereas the 
deprecatory and almost humble tone of the Austrian despatch only serves to 
encourage the notions unhappily entertained here, of the Russian Government 
being the great centre round which such satellites as the German monarchies 


revolve; and of its being optional with the Czar to deal with unbelieving: 


Turkey as in his magnanimity it may seem fitting to him. . 

Your Lordship may be assured that appeals such as those contained in the 
despatch to Baron Lebzeltern are more than useless. 

In the pursuit of his own objects, and for the consolation of wounded 
vanity, the Emperor of Russia is utterly regardless of the interests of his own 
country; still less solicitude can he be expected, then, willingly to bestow upon 
the subjects of Governments whose existence he believes to depend upon the 
protection which they may meet with at his hands. 

It has been said that fear is apt to incur the precise danger which it secks 
to avoid; and the truth of the apothegm will very certainly be experienced by 
the Governments of Austria and Prussia if they fail to make the Emperor of 
Russia sensible that their much-desired neutrality must be contingent upon His 
[Imperial Majesty's disposition to keep within the limits which the Four Cabinets 
have laid down as being those of fairness and of moderation.

Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon —(Received February 13.) 


(No. 125,) 


My Lord, St. Petersburgh, Vebruary 6, 1854. 

AS your Lordship is aware, my incredulity with regard to the declarations 
so constantly repeated here has exposed me to some reproach and odium. 

I regret that it should be so; but a man is not master of his convictions, 
and it has not been and is not yet in my power to reconcile the warm interest 
taken by the Emperor in the preservation of Turkey with the acts of Russian 
violence which haye suceceded one another with such rapidity during the last 
eight months. 

My incredulity might possibly have been less intractable, if the war forced 
upon the Turk, besides having some sort of pretext, had not been undertaken 
in the name of religion; but when an attempt is made to resort to means: 
employed in the dark ages—when hermits exhort their tellow-believers to hasten 
ta the protection of the Cross, and the largest armies in the world march against 
infidels with sentences of Scripture as their battle-cry—it is difficult not to 
suspect that independently of hoping to gain by their spoil, there must be a very 
settled purpose of driving these followers of Mahomet far beyond the pale of 
Christendom, 

__ Aslight circumstanee which has lately oceurred tends to strengthen these 
misgivings, 

I had heard in vague terms of some celestial vision which had appeared in 
the East to encourage the orthodox forces, and to complete the dismay of the 
Turks; but had paid little attention to the tale. It appears, however, to have 
acquired considerable consistency; and I take the liberty of submitting to your 
Lordship the statement now current, as it will be found in the inclosed extract 
of a letter addressed by the Exarch of Georgia to the Metropolitan of Moscow 
one of the great promoters of the actual crusade. | 

The picture which this sd-called Eastern question offers is truly not a 
pleasing one for the nineteenth century; it is sunply ambition making use of 
fanaticism as its instrument, fanaticism again leaning upon imposture for its 
support. ‘ 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clurendon.— (Received February 13.) 


(No. 126. Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, February 6, 1854. 


THE accounts of the public feeling which prevails in Russia are so 
sauener contradictory, that it is with some reluctance that I advert to the 
subject. 

An English gentleman who arrived here on the 4th instant from a long 
journey in the interior, states that he found the peasantry in general greatly 
exasperated, and clamerous for war. 

These poor people are profoundly ignorant, have nothing to lose, and 
withal have been led to believe by the village priests and vagrant monks that 
their religion is in danger, and that the Turks are magsacring the Greeks in all 
directions. 

The merchants and traders in general this same gentleman regards as being 
much disinclined to war; while as respects the landed proprietors, many of 
them are represented as deeply regretting the appeal which has been made to 
folly and fanaticism, and as apprehensive that a spirit has been aroused among 
the lower orders which may lead very possibly to such scenes as those by which 
a few years ago Gallicia was desolated. 

‘This opinion, | may remark, is held by one of the principal persons af the 
Emperor's Court. 

In a general way, | would observe that it is much easier to state what is 
not to be believed with regard to Russia, than to point out what may be safely 
admitted. | 

As regards the Russian articles which appear in the English papers, they 
are very commonly suggestive of the idea of their being written by persons who 
have not the remotest nowledge of the country; #n observation which applies 
especially to occasional articles supposed to be written by private correspon ents 
at St. Petersburgh. 

The Russian papers are still more deceptive; they are filled with garbled 
articles from foreign papers, and with most incorrect statements of whut is 
passing in this country. 

I will take the case of the so-termed voluntar contributions. 

In a few days it will be announced that, with that patriotic feeling which 
animates the burghers of Moscow, they have come forward to offer GO0,000 


133 


silver roubles for the expenses of the war; and it is quite true that such a sum 
is coming in from Moscow. 

This subscription will make a certain sensation; the Governor of Moscow 
will probably receive a new decoration or an autogra h Imperial letter; and my 
French colleague will have afresh opportunity atlor ed him of descanting to me 
upon the folly of going to war with a people so devoted to their Sovereign. : 

Neither Gencral Castelbajac, however, nor the public of France and England 
will be aware of the means which have been employed to produce this patriotic 
movement. The operation isa very simple one: the Governor, Count Sagrewski 
has informed one merchant that he is expected to pay 400 roubles for ‘the holy 
war now waging; another, that being richer, he ought to contribute 600; and 
so on, until the sum considered sufficient is made up. The merchants repine

Inclosure 1 in No. 173. 
Viee-Consul Stevens to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord, Trebizond, January 12, 1854. 
A LETTER reached our Pasha to-day from the Commander-in-chief at 
Churuksoo, informing him that on Friday the 30th ultimo five Russian 
steamers appeared off Shefketil (St. Nicolai). One of these vessels remained in 
the offing, the other four approached a small battery situated midway between 
Shefketil and Churuksoo, and commenced bombarding same, Some thirty 
shots were fired from the steamers without much effect, The Turks returned 
the fire, and the result was, that one of the vessels got crippled and was com 
pelled to retire under canvas; the other three, more or less damaged, soon 
followed. Selim Pasha says the number of shots fired from his side amounted 
to sixty from heavy guns, 
I have, &e. 
(Signed) FRAS. J, STEVENS.

Inclosure | in No. 174. 
Despatch from Selim Pasha, 


(Translation.) 8) Rebi-ul-Akhir, 1270. (January 21, 1854.) 

ON Saturday, the 14th instant, at about 5 o'clock, four battalions of 
Russian infantry, accompanied 1000 Georgian levies and two pieces of 
artillery, marched upon Shekvetil from up the country. On their emerging 
from the woods, some battalions of the army of Arabia, under Colonel Ismael 
ae together with a sufficient portion of infantry and redif from the garrison 
at Shekvetil, charged them. After an engagement of more than an hour, the 
enemy, unable to support the fire of our artillery and musketry, or to reply 
with a counter-fire, and having lost many soldiers and Georgians, were com- 
pletely routed and put to flight, Praise he to God, on the side of the Mussulman 
soldiers, no accident occurred, while the enemy suffered great loss from the 
crowded state in which they came on, and were completely repulsed, taking 
away their dead upon litters and their wounded, This circumstance is another 
of the glorious events attending the fortunate destiny of the Sultan.

Despatch recently received from the Mudir of Surmeneh, in the Province 
of Trebizond. 


(Translation.) Ou Rebi-ul-Akhir, 1270, (January 22, 1854.) 

LAST Wednesday night, about 5 o'clock, two Russian steamers appeared 
off the port of Surmeneh, Though beacons and fire-signals were displayed three 
times from the batteries of the town, no regard was paid to them; and the 
steamers were preparing to enter the harbour when a shotted gun was fired at 
them; they then put off to sea again.

Lord Stratford de Receliffe to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Received February 13.) 


(No. 51. Confidential.) 
My Lore, Constantinople, February 2, 1854. 

AS it is but too probable that the Emperor of Russia will reject the 
proposals for peuce recommended to him by the Four Powers, I am naturally 
anxious, considering the probable consequences of such an event, that the 
remainder of the inactive season should be employed in providing strenuously 
against those dangers to which, on the resumption of hostilities, the Turkish 
Kinpire will be exposed, 

As nothing efficient can be expected from a disunited Cabinet, my first 
ubject has bean to procure a change in the Ministry sufficient to obviate that 
evil, Some little tine has elapsed since I first expressed my opinion on this 
subject to the Sultan. Tis Majesty acquiesced in my reason, but “ippeared to 
require time for consideration, I renewed my representations in private a few 
days ago; und Tam happy to state that, after consulting with Reshid Pasha, the 
Sultan has taken the first decisive step towards the object by dismissing the 
Soraskier, his brother-in-law. Riza Pasha is transferred from the command of 
the arsenal to that of the army, and his place is to be filled by Mehemet Pasha, 
formerly Ambassador in London, and now Mouchir at Admanople. Other 
Ministerial changes will probably ensue; and I entertain a sanguine hope that 
the completion of the new arrangement will greatly facilitate the nagption 
af sound measures; and a more complete understanding with Her Majesty's 
Embassy

Tnclosure 1 in No. 177. 
Vice- Admiral Dundas to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord, “ Britannia,” in the Bosphorus, January 26, 1854. 


1 HAD the honour to receive at 6 p.m. on the 25th instant, your Excel- 
leney’s letter dated the 24th, conveying to me without reserve or cit 
cumlocution the opinion you entertain, and the impression on your mind of 
dissatisfaction and regret at the return of the combined squadrons under present 
circumstances 1o the Bosphorus, 

I have cavefully perused the observations your Excellency has offered in 
support of the opinion you have thus been pleased to express, and I have no 
hesitation in saying that I see no reason to doubt the advantage of employing 
the combined squadrons in the Black Sea at this season, as proposed in the 
minute of the 29th ultimo to which your Excellency refers, and in which my 
colleague Viee-Admiral Hamelin so fully concurs, 

With reference to my letter to your Excellency of the 11th January, stating 
the necessity of four Turkish transports being attached to the squadrons as 
colliers, it was neither my intention that they should be sent to Sinope nor 
loaded with the country coals, which could only be used by our steam-vessels in 
case of absolute necessity ; but my wish was to have such vessels ready to be 
loaded to accompany the squadrons in the eyent of war rendering continuous 
operations in the Black Sea necessary. 

LT share equally with your Excellency in anxiety to maintain and promote 
the honour and welfare of our country, and to carry fully into. execution the 
wishes of Her Majesty's Government, but I feel obliged to observe to your 
Excellency that the performance of my duty is much impeded and rendered 
very dificult by the apparent want of concert between your Excellency and 
the Ambassador of France. This has been exemplified in several instances in the 
difference of the instructions received by Viee-Adimiral Hamelin and myself, and 
it was only yesterday that 1 was invited by Vice-Hamelin toa conference in conse- 
quence of a letter from the French Ambassador acquainting him that the Ottoman 
Government had called for an escort for six frigates and eleven other vessels 
loaded with troops and munitions for Trebizond and Batoom, and had also asked 
for 5000 or 6000 Turks to be embarked on board the French squadron for con- 
veyance to those ports. 

I need hardly tell your Excellency that Vice-Admiral Hamelin was deeply 
surprised that 1 had not received any communication on the subject, mor point 
out to your Excellency that this dissimilarity in our instructions renders it 
really impossible to carry out with success the combined operations of the two 
squndrons. 

As I do not think that the public service would be benefited by my 
replying at length to your Excelleney’s expression of “ dissatisfaction an 
regret,” I shall refrain from doing so and follow the course pursued by your 
Excellency on a former occasion with regard to one of my communications, and 
submit your Excellency’ letter to the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty 
with such observations as 1 may consider necessary. ; 

{ have, &e. 
(Signed) J. W. D. DUNDAS,

Inclosure 2 in No. 177, 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to Vice-Admiral Dundas, 


Sir, Pera. Janunry 27, 1854. 

IN the despatch dated yesterday, which I had the honour of receiving from 

ou this morning, there is a paragraph which I cannot possibly leave unnoticed. 
You complain of an * apparent want of concert” between me and the French 
Ambassador ; you state that “this has been exemplified in several instances ,” 
you specify a more recent one respecting certain Turkish vessels to be escorted 
with troops and ammunition, and “5000 or 6000 Turks to be embarked 
on board the French squadron ;"’ you tell me that ‘ Vice-Admiral Hamelin is 
deeply surprised” that you had not received any communication on the subject; 
and finally you point out that such ‘ dissimilarity in the instructions renders it 
nearly impossible to carry out with success the combined operations of the two 
squadrons,” 

: On these passages | have to remark that both the circumstances and the 
allegations stated therein would leave, if unchallenged and unanswered, a strong 
impression to the prejudice of the two Ambassadors from whom respectively 
you and Vice-Admiral Hamelin are directed by the two Governments to receive 
instructions, 

First as to the circumstances. Not having yet received any official appli- 
eation from the Porte for convoy or transport of troops and ammunition, | 
cannot address any instructions to you on the subject. Ihave been led to 
expect such an application, and 1 am still waiting for it. : This is the only 
instance of an ‘apparent want of concert’ between the French Ambassador 
and myself which you have specified; other instances are merely alluded to, and 
I have no time to waste in conjecture, Admiral Hamelin’s “deep surprise” 
concerns the French Ambassador more than myself, 

Now for the allezations. ‘They are common to both of us, charged by you 
with a want of concert shown by dissimilar instructions, and with making it 
“nearly impossible” for you ‘to carry out with suecess the combined opera- 
tions.” 

These are heavy charges, considering the object of the instructions and 
of the operations. To me they are unexpected. It remains with Her 
Majesty's Government to determine how far they are warranted by fact or by 
propriety. ey ~< 

The instructions, it is true, have not been identical, The dititrence of 
language alone creates a difficulty in that respect. But in meaning and spirit | 
am not aware of any real dissimilarity. 

How under these circumstances your operations can be impeded by us | 
am at a loss to imagine, : 

I huve, &c. / 
. (Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recetved February 1d.) 
\No. 158.) 
My Lord, Paris, February 10, 1854. 


M. DROUYN DE LHUYS informs me that the lust accounts received 
by the French Government from Greece represent so much excitement to 
prevail against the Turks—excitement which had already led to a collision in the 
neighbourhood of Arta—that he had at once written to the French Envoy at 
Athens, directing him to eall the immediate attention of the Greek Government 
to this state of things. The French Government, M. Drouyn de Lhuys 
observed, offered the Greek Government the choice between the advantages 
which must follow by the observation of a strict neutrality, throwing into her 
bands the commerce of the Levant, or the disasters which would be the conse- 

uence of uny acts of aggression on ‘Turkey; for France would not permit 
sreece to enjoy the advantages of neutrality and to be a belligerent at the same 
time, and she would employ the means at her disposal to prevent it, 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys added that he had reason to know that the Austrian 


Government had pronounced itself in the same sense at Athens. 
I have, &e. 


(Signed) COWLEY,

My Lori, Paris, February 11, 1854. 


_ M, DROUYN DE LHUYS read to me this afternoon an extract of a 
despatch from General Castelbajac, dated the Qnd instant. ‘The General speaks 
of the immense preparations making by Russia to carry on war, should war be 
the ultimate result of the present crisis; but he still asserts his conviction that 
the Einperor Nicholas, whatever may be said to the contrary, is sincerely 
anxious for peuce, and fully alive to the dangers which war must entail upon 
him, and he maintains that His Majesty will accept any solution which would 
not be dishonourable to himself and to his army. | 

General Castelbajac adds that he does nob think that it would be impossible 
to obtain the Czar's consent to the propositions transmitted from Vienna on the 
lath of January, with the exception of that which relates to sending a Plenipo- 
tentiary to: some neutral town, to attend a congress at which the Four Powers 
would assist ; and even here he is of opinion that Russia would not object to 
evttling the preliminaries of peace in a conference of the Six Powers, provided

Lord Cowley to the Burl of Clarendon.—(Received February 13.) 


No. 164.) 
= Lord, Paris, February 11, 1854. 


| HAVE addressed an official note to M. Drouyn de Lhuys, as desired h 
your Lordship’s despatch No. 80. Although I have employed the at ay 
of that despatch, the pon of the subject of which it treats induces me to 
inclose a copy of the note itself. 

a With er to the communication of this note, as of that addressed ae 
your Lordship by Count Walewski on the 6th instant, to the Austrian a 

Prussian Governments. as suggested by your Lordship, 1 have had more than 
one conversation with M, Drouyn de Lhuys. He quite agrees m the propriety 
of this step, and the following appeared to us an eligible manner of carrying out 
four Lordship’s proposition. 

ee ‘The Bavenimente of Great Britain and France may say that the answer of 
the Russian Government to the propositions of the 13th of January having been 
deemed such as the Conference could not transmit to Constantinople, while it 
appeured at the same time that Russia refused to give any explanation ot San 
tees respecting her future proceedings in regard to lurkey, it became the duty o 

the Four Powers to consider in what way they could give effect to their re- 
corded declaration not to permit any alteration of the territorial limits of the 
‘Turkish Empire. That the Governments of Great Britain and France had 
exchanged notes upon this subject, defining their future action as well as the 
objects which they had in view, and that feeling that, the Governments of Austria 
und Prussia had an equal interest with themselves in the settlement of this 
question, they at once communicated to them the correspondence which had 
passed between Paris and London, being desirous that, before any more binding 
engagement was concluded, the Cabinets of Vienna and of Berlin might ph = 
opportunity of considering whether and in what mesure they could adopt the 
views and language of the British and French Governments. ' 

With respect to any direct propositions either to the Austrian or Prussian 

Governments to sign a Convention, or to enter into any sort of engagement, 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys is of opinion that the utmost latitude must he left to the 
French and English Representatives at Vienna und at Berlin. They would be the 
best judges how far it may be prudent to urge so important a step, as also of rhe 
proper moment for so doing ; and too precise instructions would injure rather 
than promote the object at which the two Governments aimed. At all events 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys considered that the time was not yet arrived to ask the 
German Powers to engage themselves inan armed interference. Such a demand 
might alarm them, and our object would be to lead them insensibly on until they 
found themselves obliged to enforce their own deliberate declarations. 

Such had been the object of the Convention which he had proposed should 
be signed by the Four Powers ; but even the furtherance of this, at Vienna and 
Rerlin, had not been judged advisable at the present moment. 

L have, &c. 
(Signed) COWLEY.

Inclosure in No. 180, 
Lord Cowley to M. Drowyn de Lhuys. 


Paris, February 9, 1854. 

THE Undersigned, Her Britannic Majesty's Ambassador Extraordinary and 
Plenipotentiary to the Emperor of the French, has the honour to inform lis 
Excellency M. Drouyn de Lhuys, Secretary of State for the Department of 
Foreign Affairs, that the Earl of Clarendon has received the note which Count 
Walewski addressed to him under date of the 6th instant, and in which that 
Ambassador states that it has appeared to the French Government that, with 
reference to the eventualities which do justly engage the attention of the two 
Governments, the time has now come for defining the object of their alliance and 
for denoting the means for carrying out that object. 

To this end Count Walewski proposes that Her Majesty’s Government and 
that of the Emperor of the French should agree ; 

lst. That the demonstration already made by Great Britain and France, 
and the signature by their Representatives of the documents agreed to by the 
Conference at Vienna on the Sth of December, 1853, and on the 13th of 
January, 1854, prove that the object of the two Governments is to maintain the 
territorial integrity of the Ottoman Empire and the sovereign independence of 
His Majesty the Sultan. 

@ndly. That this object would be attained if peace could be re-established 
between Russia and the Sublime Porte on the perfectly honourable conditions 
which have been proposed to the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh. In the event, 
which may God avert, of war becoming necessary, its cause would naturally 
cease from the day on which peace should be re-established with Russia on the 
basis above-mentioned, and when the Russian troops shall have evacuated the 
Provinces of Moldavia and Wallachia as well as every other part of the Ottoman 
dominions. 

Srdly. That until the end thus specified shall have been attained the 
Government of the Emperor of the French engages to cooperate towards it by 
means of the flect now acting in the Black Sea, by augmenting it in case of 
necessity, and to give an assurance that the Government of His Imperial 
Majesty would be disposed to unite a French squadron to that which Her 
Britannic Majesty may send into the North Sea or the Baltic whenever the two 
Governments shall have agreed upon the necessity of making this further 
demonstration. 

4thly. ‘That if the proposed measures should not be held sufficient to cause 
Russia to evacuate the Ottoman territory, and to conclude peace, the Government 
of His Imperial Majesty, in concert with that of Her Britannic Majesty, would 
epusiies the expediency of supporting their naval operations by means of a body 
of troops. 

Sthly. That so long as war may continue, the Government of France would 
not receive any ee »osnl or overture for a cessation of hostilities without 
instantly putting the British Government in a position conjointly to discuss its 
expedicney and opportuneness ; and that the French Government being solely 
animated with a desire to preserve the territorial integrity of Europe from 
scrious danger, renounces beforehand the acquisition of any special aFeantias 
from events which may occur. 

_The Undersigned has received orders from Her Majesty's Principal Secretary 
of State for Foreign Affairs to declare that to all the proposals thus stated Her 
Majesty's Government give their unqualified asseut, and fully adopt the obliga: 
tions which that assent imposes ; and to none of them do Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment agree with greater cordiality and satisfaction than to that in which the 
ponpusanle and disinterested motives of the two Governments are clearly 

efined, 


The Undersigned, &c. (Signed) COWLEY.

No. 18. 


Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recewed February 13.) 
(No. 165.) 
My Lord, Paris, February 12, 1854. 


M. DE HUBNER had an interview yesterday with M. Drouyn de Lhuys, 
for the purpose of communicating to his Excellency the answer which the 
Austrian Government had returned to the proposition of which Count Orloff 
was the bearer. Count Colloredo will have made a similar communication to 
your Lordship, 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys did not conceal from M. de Hiibner the disappomt- 
ment, and toa certain extent the apprelensions, with which his answer inspired 
him, and he is about to write more fully to M. de Bourqueney upon the 
subject. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys informed me that the Austrian despatch implied 
that, provided the other assurances given by Russia were satisfactory, the 
continued occupation of the Danubian Provinces by that Power would not 
prevent a declaration of neutrality on the part of Austria, He intended to call 
the attention of the Austrian Government to the dangers which might arise from 
this temporizing policy, While Austria maintained the doctrine of the integrity 
of the Turkish Empire, she would hold one language for the right and another 
for the left bank of the Danube, and she would give Russia a fair pretext for 
drawing the same distinction. Moreover, if Russia gave the Austrian Govern- 
ment the promise required by the latter not to pass the Danube, she would never 
keep that promise, though the T urks might be deceived by it, and, thinking 
thomselves safe in thab quarter, might transfer the greater part of their army 
where it would apparently be more wanted in Asia. But in fact the Russian 
troops would soon be unable to maintain themselves in the Principalities: for 
want of provisions, and must return or cross the Danube, ‘The very presence 
of an Austrian army on the frontier, M. Drouyn de Lhuys observed further, 
would be an embarrassment instead of an nssistance, since it would tend to prove 
that. Austria permitted the continuance of an aggression against which the 
Western Powers. had protested, and on account of which they were im arms. 
Finally, 1 told M. de LHiibner,” said M. Drouyn de Lhuys, “to beware ; 
for if Austria shewed so: little care about. the fate of the Principalities, the 
day might come when France and England would say that they were not 
forced to defend a cause which Austria, who ought to tuke the greatest interest 
in it, abandoned ; and as their special interest was to be looked for in the pos- 
session of Cousanney: and the Black Sea, they would confine themselves to 
obtain guarantees for the future scourity of those important positions.”

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon,—( Received February 13.) 
(No. 166.) 
My Lord, Paris, February 12, 1854, 

THE publicity which is at length given to the Emperors intentions of 
aiding the "Turkish cause hy land as well as by sea, absolves me from the secrecy 
in which my correspondence with your Lordship on this subject has of necessity 
been enveloped, since 1 first placed before His Majesty the opinion entertained 
by Her Majesty's Government, that the cooperation of an army was heeessary 
if any decisive blow was to le struck at the aggressive action of Kussia in the 
Kast. 

The Emperor, while admitting that the fleets could do’ little more than 
prevent any further naval attack on the al of Russia, was unwilling to cal ea 
a small land expedition, and a large one he could not send, to the risks to which 
it would be unavoidably exposed. 

Putting aside the difliculty of transporting an army of 50,000 men, with 


— : i ry, - » b 4 
— = = : : = nae Ser* qT 


148a 


all their material, from France to Turkey, His Majesty could not, he said, risk 
the honour of his flag at such a distance from all his resources, when the army 
i case of a reverse could have no reserves on which to fall back, and no safety 
but in a hasty and perhaps an ignominious retreat, 

The uncertainty, moreover, of the attitude which Austria and Prussia 
would eventually assume, naturally ‘nfluenced the Emperor's intentions. For 
while defending the Turkish cause in the East he might find those Powers 
suddenly threatening him in the West. 

Another motive for caution, though not avowed, must be traced to the 
apprehensions of a Republican outbreak in France, should the employment of 
her armies abroad give the enemies of order a chance of success at home, 

Such, no doubt, were the reasons which caused the Emperor to discounte- 
nance the suggestions of Her Majesty's Government in favour of a land expe- 
dition, though I have since had reason to think that if Austria could have 
been brought to declare her readiness to act on the Russian flank, all hesita- 
tion on the part of His Majesty to cooperate in front would at once have 
disappeared. 

it was not until Sir John Burgoyne passed through Paris, and during an 
audience with which the Emperor Henoured him, showed the possibility of 
defending Constantinople and the Dardanelles with a comparatively small army, 
and with but little risk, that His Majesty appeared willing to cooperate in the 
manner suggested by Her Majesty’s Government. 

My more confidential communications have since made your Lordship 
aware that the Emperor is prepared to send an expedition of 20,000 men to the 
assistance of the Turks, leaving it to Her Majesty's Government to afford a like 
aid in whatever numbers they choose to contribute. 

Before, however, taking this decisive step, Mis Majesty will await the result 
of his last appeal to the Emperor of Russia. Should that appeal prove abortive, 
or even unsatisfactory, the Emperor will no longer hesitate, but will employ all 
the means at his disposal to render the war, provoked by Russian aggression, 4s 
ahort and decisive as possible. 

The troops that will be sent by France will be drawn chiefly, if not entirely, 
from the Zouaves of the army of Africa, the Emperor thinking that troops 
‘nured to the African sun and climate will be less likely to sufier when employed 
én the East than troops drawn from France. 

‘As soon as the engineer officers employed to examine the localities make 
their report, and the place of debarkation for the troops is settled, it is pro- 
posed to send the first detachment of about 10,000 men trom Africa. 

These will be followed by others, as the necessities of the service or the 
extent of operations may require, By the end of March 20,000 French soldiers 
ean be landed in Turkey. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys proposes sending a messenger to Constantinople at 
an early day, either by a special steamer or overland, with instructions to 
General Paetey to prepare the Porte for the arrival of these and English 
troops on Turkish territory, 

This notification, which might otherwise be a delicate one, is rendered 
comparatively easy in consequence of the Ottoman Ambassador at Paris having, 
on more than one occasion, made an official demand for the assistance of some 
French troops, a5 I had the honour to mention to your Lordship at the time; 
and M, Drouyn de Lhuys proposes instructing General Baraguay d’Hilhers 
to aay, that the French Government, after mature consideration, and after 
consultation with Her Majesty’s Government, have determined to accede to the 
request which has been made to them, and that an expedition of British and 
French troops will shortly sail for the Levant. General Saraeuey d'Hilliers will 
be directed to state further that the exact point of disembarkation will depend 
upon the Sia of the English and French officers sent to examine the 
localities, and that it is probable that it may be thought necessary to disembark 
the firat detachments in the neighbourhood of the Dardanelles, as a sure basis of 
operation, either to prevent a Russian army descending on Constantinople or to 
succour that city if a descent is operated, 

More private instructions will empower General Baraguay d’Hilliers to 
hold far more positive language if necessary, or even to assert the right of the 
two Governments to conduct a war in which they are engaged ont of friendship 
for Turkey, in such a manner as they mey judge advisable.

No. 182. 
The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon —(Received February 13.) 
(No. 44.) 
My Lord, Fienna, February 8, 1853. 


I HAVE just left the Conference to which Count Buol had this morning 
invited me, in conjunction with my colleagues, Upon our assembling, he 
stated that he had no proposal to make to us; but, in consideration of the 
perfect union existing amongst us upon the Eastern question, he thought he 
was forwarding our common objects by communicating the despatches he had 
addressed to Count Esterhazy, for the purpose of being submitted to Count 
Nesselrode, 

Count Buol then read to us these despatches. The first gave an account 
of the proposal brought forward by Count Orloff, that the Emperor of Austria 
should, in conjunction with Prussia, take an engagement with the Emperor of 
Russia for the maintenance of a strict neutrality in the war now existing with 
the Porte, and in which the Maritime Powers seemed likely to take part. Count 
Buol, in his despatch, developes in the clearest and most distinct language the 
impossibility of the adoption by the Emperor of any such engagement. He 
states, with all courtesy to the Emperor Nicholas, the obligations by which the 
‘Austrian Government is bound to watch over the strict maintenance of the 
principle of the independence and integrity of Turkey—a principle proclaimed 
by the Emperor Nicholas himself, but which the passage of the Danube by his 
troops might, by the encouragement of insurrections in the Turkish Provinces, 
endanger. Count Buol, therefore, states that he cannot take the engagement 
proposed to him. The second despatch to Count Esterhazy relates to the 
answer which has been returned to the proposals for negotiations transmitted 
by Count Buol with the sanction of the Conference on the 13th ultimo. 

In this despatch, Count Buol states with considerable force the disappoint- 
ment felt by the Emperor at the want of success which had attended his recom- 
mendation in favour of the Turkish propositions. He enters very fully into the 
subject, and renews the expression of the Emperor's most anxious desire that 
te Emperor Nicholas may still adopt the proposals which had been submitted 
to him. 

The last despatch is one in which Count Buol replies to the reproach which 
was addressed to the Imperial Government, that. by its present conduct it was 
abandoning the principles upon which the three Governments of Russia, Austria, 
and Prussia had hitherto acted for the maintenance of the established interests 
and independence of the different States of Europe, and that, by so doing, it 
was endangering the established order of things in Europe, and the security at 
present existing. | 

The answer of Count Buol to this reproach is very firmly and clearly stated, 

It is impossible for me to give your Lordship a more detailed account, 
before the departure of the messenger, of these despatches; but | must add, 
that they met with the entire approbation of the members of the Conference, 
that they were loaked upon as most ably drawn up, and that while using every 
courteous and friendly expression towards the Emperor Nicholas, they most 
clearly pointed out the present position which the Austrian Goycrament would 
maintain with the view of upholding the principles they had proclaimed, and the 
enzogements which they had taken for their support, , 


149 


After these communications, Count Buol stated that the Emperor, in 
speaking of the departure of Count Orloff, had inquired whether any suggestion 
could be made to him, in a confidential manner, by which the negotiations for 
peace might still be continued. Count Buol had consequently given this subject 
his best consideration. He had gone to Count Orloff before his departure, 
which had taken place this morming, and, as a private suggestion of his own, 
and only verbally, had stated that if the Emperor Nicholas would accept the 
Turkish proposals, and, upon their general import, send to Vienna the form of 
preliminaries for peace which he would agree to, and which might be discussed 
by the Conference with Baron Meyendorff, who should be instructed to that 
effect, these preliminaries, if approved by the Conference, might be sent to Con- 
stantinople with the recommendation of the Four Powers. In the meantime, 
Baron Meyendorff should be instructed to announce to Prince Gortchakotf that 
+f the Turkish Commander-in-chief proposed to him a suspension of hostilities, 
upon the ground of the acceptance by ‘Turkey of these preliminaries, he was to 
agree toit. ‘That when that acceptance arrived at Vienna, from that moment 
the war should be considered as at an end, and that the Russian troops should 
immediately receive orders to evacuate the Principalities, and the combined fleets 
to quit the Black Sea aad the Bosphorus. That the Emperor of Austria would 
then depute a Plenipotentiary of his own to return these preliminaries (approved 
by His Majesty) to the Emperor Nicholas, and to request him to appoimb a 
person to proceed to any place which might be fixed upon for the signature of 
the Peace. In stating this plan to the Conference, Count Buol repeated that 1t 
was a mere informal suggestion; that he had refused even to put pen to 
paper with regard to it; but that Count Orloff had taken down the heads of it, and 
had said that he should submit them to his Emperor. Count Buol stated, that 
under these circumstances he had thought it right to communicate tous what had 
passed, although it might be doubtful if it ever again would be brought under 
discussion. He thought, however, that we might make our Governments 
acquainted with the general outline of his idea. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) WESTMORLAND,

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon —( Received February 13.) 
(No. 50.) 
My Lord, Berlin, February 10, 1854. 

A PERSON lately arrived from Paris has mentioned to me the substance 
of a long and interesting conversation with Prince Adam Czartoryski relative to 
the military operations which his Highness conceives Thussia is likely to pursue 
against Turkey. The Prince expressed his belief that the Russians will not 
face the Balkan, but that they will attempt to turn the Turkish position at 
Widdin by crossing the Danube higher up, and that ey will then advance 
through the flat country by Sophia to Adrianople; and the Prince added his 
conviction that the Russian army is now much more formidable and better 
prepared for the campaign than it ever has been, and that the disasters expe- 
enced in the last war with Turkey are not liable to recur, for that their 
commissariat and all other arrangements have undergone immense improvement, 

Prince Czartoryski not only considers this plan to be feasible, but he 
seemed to have faith in its adoption, and further, that it would be attended 
with success; and he seems to fear that, should these operations be earried 
out, considerable danger for the Dardanelles would result, 08 he conceives that 
a corps d'armée might be easily detached to take possession of those forts, 
slnuitaneoualy with the advance of the main body of the army on the Turkish 
capital. 

Your Lordship will be enabled to form # mere correct opinion of the 
wacticability or probability of these designs than it is in my power to offer ; 

ut L have thought the opinions of Prince Czartoryski on this subject deserving 
of consideration, and have thus ventured to convey them to your Lordship’s 
knowledge, 


I have, &c. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recewed February 13.) 


(No. 51. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, February 10, 1854. 

THERE is perhaps no Court in Europe at the present moment where 
such a maze of intrigue is being carried on as at Berlin, 

The suecess which has lately attended the efforts made by the Government 
to establish an independent policy for this country, and to liberate it from all 
engagement with Russia in the approaching contest between that Empire and 
the maritime Powers, have rendered the Court party rabid. 

No means are left untried by them to thwart Baron Manteuffel’s manage- 
ment of the Foreign Department, and to support the attempts of the Russian 
Minister to get his case listened to by the King; and the following incident will 
serve to elucidate the nature of the influence against which Baron Manteuffel 
has to contend, and the difficulties which surround his position. 

Baron Budberg, having failed in drawing Prussia into the alliance with 
Russia which he was charged to propose, and finding the King’s confidence in 
General Gerlach so shaken that no communications made through that channel 
were likely to be favourably received, eneceeded in enlisting General Count 
Stolberg, the Master of the Royal Household, in his interest, and actually for- 
warded through that person a fresh proposal to His Majesty for an arrangement 
with Russia. Hitherto Count Stolberg, though belonging to the Kreuz Zeitung 
party has kept aloof from intrigues, but has been worked upon by his son and 
othera of the more violent partisans. | 

This attempt, however, of Baron Budberg has, | am happy to say, com- 
pletely failed, and his new propositions were at once rejected; but your Lordship 
inay judge of the position here when you are informed that the King made no 
observations to Baron Manteuffel on a communication which had reached hin in 
eo singular a manner, until his Excellency produced a copy of Baron Budberg’s 

roposal, which had been subsequently left with him by that Minister. The 
King, in fact, cares nothing for the feelings of his Ministers, and has been used 
to find them sa subservient to hiswill, that things are continually occurrring here 
which are happily almost unknown in any other country ; and His Majesty, instead 
of showing that confidence in Baron Manteuffel to which his position and services 
entitle him, persists in refusing, and has not the courage, to remove from his im- 
mediate entourage any of those persons who are working against his present avowed 
policy ; whereas there can be no doubt if, as an example, one or two of the leaders 
were to get honouruble appomtments elsewhere than at Berlin, the position of 
the Government would be completely changed, and its foreign policy receive an 
impulse which would tend to great cood ; but the King thinks, by not avowing 
his partiality for any particular party, by playing fast and loose with all, that he 
maintains his own independence and freedom of action, and though he pleases 
none he also quarrels with none. 
~ T have thought it right to send your Lordship this but too true account of 
the working of the Camarilla here. T must, however, also add, that a person 
who sees the King almost daily, and who is at the present moment playing an 
important part in directing the Oriental policy of this Government, has just 
‘aformed me that His Majesty continues firm, and that he sees no change or 
vacillation in his opinions on this question, | 
At the same time that he has received this assurance, an appointment hns 
been talked of at the Prussian Foreign Office which does not satisly those who 
are working for the independent policy of Prussia. It is believed that Baron 
Werther, at present ment Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary at 
Copenhagen, is to be the Under-Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, in the 
place of M. de le Coq. | 
Baron Werther is said to be imbued with Holy-Alliance Roel inherited 
fiom his father, who was formerly Minister at Paris, and for a short time 
Minister for Foreign Affiirs; but Baron Manteuffel, to whom I have spoken of 
the nomination, says that he is not so, and he evidently expects to mould him 
in the way that will suit him, and adyance his present policy. [, however, told 
his Excellency that Baron Werther was probably uninitiated in the Kastern

who was willing to continue to serve_in his present irresponsible position ; anil

Werther was decided on, that his Excellency would allow him at all events to

is therefore likely to remain liere for some months to come, when it is probable

Vienna. :

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Received February 15.) 


(No. 173.) 
My Lord, Paris, February 14, 1894, 


THE Austrian Minister had a long conversation yesterday with M. Drouyn 
de Lhuys on the subject of the confidential communication made to the Vienna 
Conference by Count Buol on the Sth instant, the apparent object of M. de 
Hiibner being to obtain from M. Drouyn de Lhuys an expression of opinion on 
the possibility of an arrangement of the Eastern question on the terms which 
Count Orloff had at the last moment undertaken to recommend to the favourable 
consideration of his Imperial master. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys, in telling me this conversation, said that he had 
stated to M. de Hiibner that the French Government had no official knowledge 
of any other propositions for the re-establishment of peace than those forwarded 
to St. Petersburgh on the 13th of January ; that these propositions, if must be 
recollected, had been suggested to the Porte by the Representatives ol the Four 
Powers, had been adopted by the Sultan and his Ministers, and recommended 
by the Vienna Conference to the Emperor of Russia as a fair and equitable 
settlement of his differences with the Porte. The Conference wis therefore 
bound in honour to abide by its declared opinions ; and Russia having refused 
the terms thus deliberately recommended, had, to say the least, rendered herself 
liable to the comminatory language whieh Count Buol had himself proposed 
should be employed against whichever party might refuse to enter into the 
conciliatory course proposed by the Conference. 

Such was the exact state of the ense; and the French Government could 
not be called upon to give an official opinion upon mny other scheme of arrange- 
ment, particularly on one which Count Buol himself announced to the Conference 
was not 2 formal proposition, but one which the Emperor of Russia might be 
induced to entertain. 

“Having said this,” continued M. Drouyn de Lhuys to M. de Hiibner, 
“officially, 1 have no objection to. discuss with you confidentially the means of 
converting the propositions of the Conference into a Treaty of Peace. If the 
terms suggested to us by Count Orloff, and communicated confidentially to the 
Conference by Count Buol, mean that preliminaries of peace based on, and con- 
sequently including, all the stipulations contained in the propositions of the 

19th January, are to be discussed in a Conference of the Four Powers, at which 
a Russian and ‘Turkish Plenipotentiary are to assist, the object being to settle 
the exact form of words in whieh the Treaty of Peace is to be drawn up, and 
that the preliminaries thus settled are to be sent. to Constantinaple for the 
aeceptaice of the Porte, and when accepted to be followed by an armistice, the 
evacuation of the Principalities, and the withdrawal of the combined fleets trom 
the Black Sea ; and that further a Treaty of Penee, thus discussed and settled, is 
to be signed in some neutral place by a Russian and a ‘Turkish Plenipotentiary 
alone—to such terms the French Government could have: no objection, for 
they have never required more, But if, on the other hand, it is intended to 
discuss the propositions of the 15th of January with a view ol modifying or 
altering them, to such a course ihe French Government would not lend them- 
solves, because they are bound in honour to support the propositions which they 
themselves, together with the other members of the Conference, sugested to the 
Porte and recommended to St. Petersburgh.” ots 
Neither, added MM, Drouyn de Liwys, would France (lesist from the prose- 
cution of such coercive measures 15 she may judge advisable, until mitters liad 
assumed a shape which would guarantee the Ottoman Kmpire from all further

one good effect, and which, if persevered in, would no doubt produce much

THE French Government has received intelligence that Russia is making 
great efforts to obtain the consent of the United States Government to the issue 
of Russian letters of marque to subjects of the United States; and M. Drouyn 
de Lhuys is about to address that Government, to state the prevalence of these 
reports, and to express his conviction that they will not countenance so inimical 
a proceeding towards France and England, with whom the United States are in 
relations of peace and amity. 

He hopes that your Lordship will take the same course.

Turkish territory could be in the contemplation of the two Governments, they 
will not hesitate distinetly to abjure any such intention. 

But it will be apparent to the Porte that the two Governments, having 
undertaken to assist Turkey, and having consequently staked their honour that 
their assistance shall be effectual, must be free to decide what means are best 
ealeulated to carry that object into effect; and Her Majesty’s Government do 
not doubt that the Porte will appreciate the great advantage which the proposed 
military expedition to the shores of Turkey is caleulated to afford by encou- 
raging its own troops, and discouraging those of its enemy, and will cordially 
accept the proffered aid, and give such orders to the Turkish Generals as may 
insure unity of action in combined operations which the British and French 
Commanders may propose to undertake. 

Her Majesty’s Government are the more confirmed in this conviction by 
the fact of the Turkish Ambassador at Paris having more than once officially 
demanded from the Government of France the assistance of French troops ; and 
they cannot doubt that the Porte will be glad to sce a British army associated 
with that of France, as the fleets of the two Powers already are, for the defence 
of the Turkish Empire against the aggressions of Tussia.

Sir, Foreign Office, February 16, 1854. 

M. TRICOUPI called here yesterday, for the purpose of giving me the 
most recent accounts he had received of the insurrectionary movements at Arta, 
and in the neighbourhood of that place. He read to me some extracts from 
the despatches of M. Paicos, who admitted that a lieutenant and some soldiers 
on the frontier had deserted from the Greek service, and had jomed the 
insurgents; but M. Tricoupi assured me that the efforts of his Government 
were unceasing to calm excitement, as they felt they had nothing to gain by 
promoting disaffection to the Porte, whereas, by perfect neutrality, they might 
earn for themselves the goodwill of the Great Powers. 

T told M. Tricoupi that although his Government might not openly promote 


insurrection, yet they in fact did nothing to sare it, nor even to make

eencies may grow out of the prosecution of active iostilities by Russia agamst 
‘Turkey, which may be looked for in the coming sping. se mos

tolerate that the Greek subjects of the Sultan should be excited to rebel against 
his authority, in consequence of measures sanctioned by the Greek Government.

M. Tricoupi expressed much alarm at the thought of a blockade, which,
