My Lords, Foreign Ojfice, February 17, 1554. 

HGR Majesty's Government have lad onder consideration the statements 
contained in Captain Peel's despatch of the 7th instant, of which a copy was 
transmitted to this office in your Secretary's letter of yesterday, in regard to an 
application made to him by the Lord High Commissioner in the Ionian Islands 
to assist the ‘Turkish authorities in Albania in putting down an insurrection by 
which the towns of Arta and Prevesn were threatened. Sir Henry Ward's 
application appears to have been founded on the policy which Her Majesty's 
Government are engaged in carrying out for the support of the Sultan against 
Russian aggression, and on the suspicions which he entertained that the 
insurrectionary movement to which he referred might be traced to foreign 
intrigue, having for its object to weaken or overthrow the authority of the 
Sultan, and thereby to counteract the views of Her Majesty's Government, 

The presence of the Russian squadron at Trieste, with which your Lordships 
are ulready acquainted, cannot be overlooked in considering the course which 
should be taken ithe matter in question. ‘That squadron, if not fomenting, 
cannot but be considered as in some degree influencing the insurrectionary move- 
ments; and the active intrigues, accompanied in some instances by overt acts, 
whieh are carried on against the peace of Turkey in the neighbouring kingdom 
of Greeee, must needs be taken into account when endeavouring: to form a just 
estimate of the character of the Albanian movement. 

Under all these circumstances Her Majesty's Government, although doing 
full justice to the prudence shown by Captain Peel in hesitating to act, in so 
delieate a matter, without specific instructions, are disposed to acertain extent to 
coincide in Sir Henry Ward’s views ; und 1 have therefore to suggest to your 
Lordships that Captain Peel should be instructed to visit the coasts of Albania 
and Epirus with the ships under his orders, and to. employ all the influence which 
the presence of his ships can give him to uphold the constituted authorities 
against insurrectionary movements originating with and carried on by the 
inhabitants of the disturbed districts. 

If Captain Peel should have good reason to suppose that the insurrection 
has its origin or is supported from without, the position of affairs would be 
changed. It might then become virtually a foreign aggression against the 
territory of the Sultan; and against any such aggression at the present time 
Her Majesty's Government are prepared to assist the Porte. Captain Peel 
would therefore be justified in declaring to the insurgents that the prosecution of 
their insurreetionary movements may bring them into collision with the British 
forces; but unless Captain Peel should be persuaded of the foreign character of 


163 


the insurrection, he would not be justified in employing Her Majesty’ i 
supporting the Turkish qathonties against the Christian beau oF te us is 

Of course if the Russian squadron should take any part with a view of 
supporting or encouraging insurrection, or should commit any act of aggression 
on the Turkish territory or flag, it will be the duty of Captain Peel to protect 
them both to the utmost of his power; and in any case Captain Peel, after 
explaining the duty with which he is charged, will warn any Russian ships of 
war which he may fall in with on lis station that they cannot be allowed to hover 
on the Turkish coasts, but must proceed in some other direction; and Captain 
Peel will see that the warning thus given is attended to by the Russian ships, by 
keeping sight of them until he shall consider the Ottoman coasts as secure from 
ageression on their part; or even by using force to compel them to bear away 
from those coasts if they refuse to attend to his warning.

_L CANNOT exaggerate to your Lordship the bad impression produced on 
all persons with whom I have conversed by the publication of the Emperors 
letter to the Emperor of Russia, 1 have met with no one who has attempted to 
ica it. Those, including the Ministers, who do not blame it, take refuge in 
silence. 


It is in vain to seek for the motives which have led to this atep. They are 


166 


locked up in the Emperor’s own breast. The official reason given is, a8 your 
Lordship will have seen by the few lines which accompanied the publication, 
that the sense and meaning of the letter had been perverted in foreign journals, 
and that it was necessary to rectify them. Explanations of another nature have 
been given from one source or another to some of my colleagues, the penors) 
being that the Emperor wished that a declaration of his policy should precede 
the debates which were about to take place in the British Parliament, and that 
His Majesty did not like the idea that if peace with Russia was preserved, the 
honour of it should be given to Count Orloff and to Count Buol rather than to 
himself, Finally, vour Lordship will find, in the inclosed article from the 
« Constitutionnel”’ of this morning, the semi-official defence of the Emperor. 

I should add that when the letter first appeared, people were so convinced 
that the answer to it must have been received and was unfavourable, ar that the 
letter could not have been published, that the funds fell 3 per cent. There are 
not wanting those who declare that the Emperor was persuaded to give his 
letter publicity by those who expected its appearance to have a very different 
effect upon the public securities, and who have suffered severe losses in conse- 
quence. ol en 

Your Lordship will recollect that when M. Drouyn de Lhuys first mentioned

(No. 70.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, February 18, 1854. 

COUNT COLLOREDO has read to me a despatch from Count Buol on 
the subject of Count Orloff’s mission to Vienna, | 

Count Buol says, in this despatch, that the identity of the objects pursued 
by Austria in common with the other three Powers which was established by the 
Protocol of December 5th, imposes upon the Austrian Government the duty of 
entire frankness lowards them with regard to this mission, 

He states that Count Orloff was instructed to urge in the strongest manner 
upon the Emperor of Austria to enter into un engagement, simultaneously with 
the Court of Berlin, to observe the strictest neutrality in the case of the 
maritime Powers taking an active part in the war between ‘Turkey and Russia ; 
and as a proof af the entire confidence subsisting between the Cabinets of Vienna 
and Lssidor the despatch to the Austrian Minister at St. Petershurgh, giving 
the reasons which have induced the Emperor of Austria to decline this proposal 
of Russia, is communicated to Her Majesty's Government. 

In this despatch to Count Esterhazy, Count Buol observes with reference 


169 


to the grave proportions which the war between Russia and ‘Turkey appears 
to be on the eve of assuming, the Court of Russia proposes to Austria and 
Prussia to enter into an agreement by which the position of the three Courts 
will be clearly defined, as well in their relations with each other as towards the 
Western Powers who are about to engage in the conflict, 

The Emperor of Russia aRpades the strictest neutrality as the attitude to 
be assumed by the two principal German Powers and their confederates, and an 
armed defence of this neutrality against any who might threaten to infringe it. 
Russia would engage to assist them, for this purpose, with all her forces, to an 
extent which should hereafter be determined by a joint arrangement to be con- 
cluded by military commissioners. She would further undertake, in case the 
events of the war should lead to» modification of the state of things existing in 
Turkey, not to adopt any resolution on this subject without a previous under- 
standing with the Courts of Vienna and Berlin, 

Such is in substance the plan of conduct traced out by the Court of 
st. Petersburgh, on which Count Buol, after mature examination, has arrived 
at the following conclusions. 

_ The King of Prussia, as is already known, has declined the Russian pro- 
positions; this fact alone would be sufficient to remove every chance of the 
practical application of the project, since it is founded on the agreement of the 
three Powers. . 

But setting aside this circumstance, which would in fact relieve Austria 
from any further action, the frankness which she has prescribed to herself in 
her confidential comnmnications with the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh, does not 
allow her to leave that Cubinet in ignorance of the grave objections which under 
all circumstances she would have entertained to this plan. 

With reference to events the consequences of which cannot be foreseen, the 
Emperor of Austria could not bind himself by an engagement of this nature, at 
any rate unless the Emperor of Russia would limit the field of his: action 
(l’étendue de son action). The results of a prolonged war between Russia and 
Turkey would be so uncertain, that Austria, so directly interested in the 
astern question, could not engzuge on her part to follow out a policy of absolute 
neutrality. 

The suceess of the Russian arms, joined with the wishes of the populations 
subjects of Turkey, might bring on a state of affairs so detrimental to. the 
interests of Austria, that the Emperor of Austria might find himself placed 
between the necessity of a military intervention, or an inaction incompatible with 
his dignity and the most vital interests of his Empire. 

Originally, the dispute might be considered as an affair between Russia and 
Turkey alone, and so long as Russia declared and maintained a defensive 
attitude Austria was able on her side to preserve an attitude of expectancy. 
But this question unfortunately has since assumed a European character, and 
has become of such intense importance that Austria could not do otherwise than 
reserve to herself entire freedom of action with respect to it, 

Ifthe Emperor Nicholas would engage not to extend further his military 
operations in aru p ea Turkey, to seek no territorial aggrandisement, no right 
of interference in the internal affairs of Turkey, nor any new rights not resulting 
from the ancient Treaties between Russia and Turkey—engagements which 
appear to Count Buol to be in conformity with Russian interests—Austria would 
he ready in return to give the assurances that have been demanded of her; but 
otherwise the Russian Cabinet must perceive the difficulties which Austria 
would encounter in tracing out, at present, the line of conduct which future 
circumstances may impose upon her. Moreover, the Russian Government must 
be aware that the inevitable effect of an engagement so positive as the one 
proposed would be to cripple Austria in her conciliatory eflorts; to cause a 
pressure adverse to her on the part of some of the contending parties. 

_,__ The prevailing idea of the plan proposed by Russia consists in maintaining 
intact during the present erisis the conservative alliance which has so lone 
arn between the three Courts, to the advantage of the purty of social 
Order. 

__ But is the question one of preservation, or, on the contrary, of entering 
Into new combinations, of which it would be impossible to define the nature 

or to foresee the consequences ? 


Tt is not on this ground that the question had been placed by the Pratocals 


aq) Eee 


170 


of Vienna, which have made so painful an impression at St. Petersburgh, Tie 
mutual agreement of the Four Powers as set forth in these Acts, rests on the 
importance which they attach to the integrity of the Ottoman Empire as an 
element of the balance of Europe, In this principle the special interest of 
Austria and that of Europe in general are united. Count Buol has therefore 
learnt, with deep regret, that the Emperor of Russia appears ready to renounce 
the firm intention he had previously declared, of maintaining a defensive position 
on this side the Danube: The graver the consequences which are connected 
with the passage of the Danube, the more Count Buol conceives that Austria 
fulfils a friendly duty in conjuring the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh in its wisdom 
once more to consider them before taking a decisive step. 

If Count Buol does not conceal from the Russian Cabinet the painful 
feelings caused to the Cabinet of Vienna by the differences of opinion existing 
between them as to the best course to be pursued at the present juncture, the 
latter harbour no thought which can be considered hostile to Russia. 

Count Buol has considered it a duty to state, with entire frankness, the 
attitude which Austria is compelled to reserve to herself for the eventuality, 
which she still hopes may be averted, of the conflict assuming Greater dimen- 
sions; he trusts, however, that these observations, which Count Esterhazy 1s 
directed to offer to Count Nesselrode, may contribute to put an end to a state 
of tension alarming to Europe and detrimental to'so many interests. Austria, 
he declares, has faithfully applied herself to trace out the path of peace, and 
her efforts will constantly be directed to the same end. 

Count Buol states that he has nothing to add to this despatch to Count 
Esterhazy, which clearly defines the attitude of Austria in the present situation 
of affairs. 

The Emperor of Austria will not tie his hands by a Convention of absolute 
neutrality as long as he is not in possession of satistactory guarantees that the 
interests of his Empire will not be compromised by a dissolution of European 
‘Turkey. These guarantees Count Orloff was not authorised to give ; besides, 
adds Count Buol, how could Russia reassure Austria as to the incalculable 
consequences of a rising of the Christian population from the moment that the 
Emperor of Russia should determine to push the war vigorously beyond the 
Danube ? on : 

Whilst, therefore, renewing its serious representations against the extension 
of the war beyond the Danube, the Austrian Government has not concealed 
from Russia, that in the presence of the dangers with which she is threatened 
by the continuance of the struggle, Austria must reserve to herself entire 
liberty of action. 

With this view a body of troops has been concentrated in the Austrian 
provinces which border on the theatre of war. and their numbers will be 
augmented as the course af events may require, 

~ ‘This measure, on the subject of which tranquillizing assurances have been 
wiven to the Porte, is not to be considered as of a hostile nature towards either 
of the belligerents; its object is solely to preserve the Austrian frontiers from 
insult, and, if necessary, from the contagion of insurrection in the adjoiming 
Turkish provinces, ind even if an armed intervention on the part of Austria 
should become indispensable, it would be with the firm intention of preserving 
intuct in all respects the status quo established by Treaties—an intention which 
Count Buol is eontident will be'shared by the other Powers who are represented 
at the Conference of Vienna. 

Tam, &c.

The Earl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland,

My Lord, Foreign Office, Mebruary 18, 1854, 

AS the answer of the Russian Government to the propositions which were 
submitted to that Government by the Representatives of the four Powers on the 
13th of January has been such as the Conference at Vienna could not transmit 
to Constantinople, and as the Cabinet of Russia has refused to offer any explana- 
tion, or to afford any guarantees with respect to the future proceedings of Russia 
towards Turkey, the time appears to have arrived for the Four Powers to con- 
sider in whiat tanner they can give effect to their recorded declaration not to 
permit any alteration of the territorial limits of the Turkish Empire. 

The Governments of Great Britain and France have already exchanged 
notes defining their future action, as well as the objects which they have in view; 
and feeling that the Governments of Austria and Prussia have an equal interest 
with them in the settlement of this question, Ner Majesty’s Government lo not 
hesitate to transmit to your Lordship, for communication to the Austrian 
Government, copies of the correspondence which has passed between Her 
Majesty's Government and the Government of France, in order that before any 
more binding engagement shall have been concluded the Cabinet of Vienna may 
have au opportunity of considering whether, and to what extent it can adopt 
the views and aid in carrying out the objects of the British and Freneh Govern- 
ments. 

Your Lordship will state to Count Buol that Her Majesty’s Government 
invite the Government of Austria to aceede to arrangements similar in their 
objects and their spirit to those agreed upon between Great Britain and France. 
The instrument might afterwards take the form of a Convention between the 
four Powers, framed with a view to put an end to a war which now disturbs and 
threatens to convulse Europe. 

Circumstances fully justify Her Majesty's Government in asking for this 
explanation ; proposals for peace, sanctioned by the four Powers ind assented 
to beforehand by Turkey, have been put aside without a serious reply from the 
Exnaperor of Russia, whose preparations mre ona vast seale; and noe one can 
doubt that, if victorious on the Danube, he will no longer think himself bound 
by his declarations of respecting the integrity and independence of Turkey. 
The expense of his armaments will serve as an excuse for demands of indemnity, 
to be secured by prolonged occupation of the Principalities, or for terms destruc- 
live of the sovereign rights of the Sultan as one of the independent Powers of 
lurope.

The Earl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland. 
(No. 76.) 


My Lord, Foreign Office, February 20, 1854. 

COUNT COLLOREDO has communicated to me a despatch from Count 
Buol referring to the previous communications he had made to Count Colloredo 
on the subject of Count Orloff’s mission, and the rejection by the Conference at 
Vienna of the counter-propositions made by the Cabinet at St. Petersburgh, and 
pointing out the gravity of the situation which this determination has created 
and the complications which rapidly approaching events appear to lead to. 

Count Orloif, although limited to his instructions, could not deceive 
himself as to the danger of the situation, and appeared to Count Buol to be 
animated with the desire of being enabled to carry to St. Petersburgh an 
expedient calculated to lead to an honourable issue. 

Perceiving this disposition on the part of Count Orloff, and impressed by 
the fact that the difference which exists between the bases of pacification pro- 
posed by cither party, scems to have reference rather to their form than to their 
substance, Count Buol turned his attention to some means of' restoring peace, 
Which might be suggested to the Court of St. Petersburgh ; and having received 
the authority of the Emperor of Austria, introduced such a plan in his con- 
versation with Count Orloff, on the understanding that Count Orloff’ must not 
attribute to Count Buol’s idea the character of an overture on the part of the 
Court of Austria, or of a desire on their part to assume an intermediate position 
between Russia and the maritime Powers, as it was simply an attempt made in 
goodwill towards conciliation. On this understanding Count Buol proceeded 
to develop his idea in the following manner, which was : . 

First. That, in answer to the last communications of Austria, inviting the 
Cabinet of St. Petersburgh to re-examine the propositions of the Porte, of which 
the Conference had been the organ, the Court of Russia should transmit to the 
Austrian Cabinet preliminaries of peace, drawn upin accordance with the above- 
mentioned propositions, and should leave it to Count Buol to arrange with 
he Conférenee to cause such preliminaries to be agreed upon and signed by the 

orte. 

Secondly, That the Russian Envoy at Vienna should be authorized to 
concert ina confidential manner with the members of the Conference on the 
alterations which might still be judged necessary to render them such as the 
Porte could accept, ‘ 

Thirdly. The preliminaries thus arranged would be sent to Constantinople 
by the Conference, which would undertake to insure their adoption by the Porte, 
and to obtain for them the signature of the Sultan's Minister for Foreign Attairs, 
und to arrange with the Porte a temporary suspension of hostilities. 

Fourthly. The preliminaries of peace thus signed should be sent to Vienna, 
and from thence transmitted to St. Petersburgh by an Envoy Extraordinary trom 
His Majesty the Emperor of Austria, who should, in the name of the Emperor 
and in that of the other Powers, obtain from the Emperor of Russia, in exchange 
for the Turkish document, one bearing the signature of the Chancellor of the 
Russian Empire to be sent to the Porte, 

Fifthly. After this formulity shall have been accomplished, the Emperor of 


| 


7 
4% 
| 
\ 


174 


Russia should give orders to his troops to evacuate the Turkish territory, and 
on their part the Cabinets of London and Paris would direct their fleets to leave 
the Black Sea, as well as the Bosphorus and the Dardanelles. 

Sixthly. ‘Che two measures being thus set on foot the Plenipotentiares named 
by the belligerent parties would mect in a place to be arranged between them, to 
negotiate and sign the definitive instrument in conformity with the preliminaries 
already signed. And, 

Seventhly. The six Powers would afterwards proceed to a renewal of the 
Treaty of 1841. 

‘Yount Buol left it Count Orloff to make use of these ideas if he judged 
proper. Count Orloff appeared disposed to submit them to the Emperor of 
Russia, and requested Count Buol at the same time to pave the way so as to 
insure for them a favourable reception by the three Courts in the event of the 
Cabinet of St. Petersburgh deciding to adopt them. 

With this object, Count Buol has instructed Count Colloredo to ascertain 
the feelings of Her Majesty's Government on this matter, and states that in these 
proceedings he has had in view, first, to secure to the Conference the participi- 
tion he wishes to have in the work of peace ; secondly, to conciliate the self-love 
which has been brought into play, by setting aside any questions of form likely 
to offend it: and thirdly, to obtain as soon as possible the evacuation of the 
Turkish territories and the cessation of hostilities. 1 told Count Colloredo 
that without analysing all the grave objections to which these propositions were 
liable, they would entail a most inconvenient delay, and that although they were 
said to have been made in an informal mauner, yet if they were accepted by the 
Cabinet of St. Petersburgh, Count Buol would find himself bound by them, and 
the great object of the Emperor of Russia, viz, that of creating disunion between 
the Four Powers, might thas be effectually attained. 

I added that Her Majesty's Government would recognize no propositions 
but those which were transmitted to St. Petersburgh on the 13th ultimo, and could 
consent to no modification of terms that had been declared by the Conference to 
he just and reasonable; and that in the meanwhile they would not relax in those 
preparations which were now actively making for bringing toa speedy conclusion 
the war in which Europe was about to be involved by the Emperor of Russia. 

lam, &e. 
(Signed) CLARENDON,

No, 221. 


The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe, 
(No. 78.) 


My Lord, Foreign Office, February 20, 1854, 

1 HAVE received from Mr, Consul James Brant copies of his despatches 
to your Excellency Nos. 89 and 90, of the 23rd and 24th of December, and 
other despatches addressed to myself of the 20th of December and 9th of 
January, giving an account of the reverses which had been sustained by the 
Sultan's forces in Asia, of the incapacity and misconduct of the Porte’s Mussul- 
man officers, of the diseraceful outrages committed by the irrezular troops, and 
of the efforts of Khoorshid Pasha (General Guyon) to reorganize, and infuse 
confidence into, the Turkish army in that quarter. 

___ Her Majesty’s Government have read the accounts given by Mr. Brant with 
indignation as regards the misconduct of the Turkish Pashas, and the revolting 
atrocities of the irregular troops, and with the deepest concern as regards the 
apathy exhibited by the Porte respecting its true interests at this crisis of the 
affairs of Turkey. M 

__ Abdi Pasha, it appears, has been recalled, and Her Majesty’s Government 
will expect to hear that his cowardice and incapacity have been punished as they 
deserve; but Her Majesty's Government learn with astonishment that he has 
been sueeceded by Ahmed Pasha, who has not only proved his unfitness for 
command, but who is justly detested by the soldiers for the eruel wrongs and 
ill-treatment which his rapacity has inflicted upon them; and this man’s oecu- 
pation will now probably be to thwart and undermine Khoorshid Pasha, the only 
goo officer in the Sultan's service in Asin. ; 

_ _ Great opportunities have been already lost, and Georgia might have been 
easily occupied ; but the army has been demoralized. and confiding friends have 
been converted into bitter enemies. Men like Abdi Pasha and Ahmed Pasha 
are far more formidable enemies to the Sultan's cause, than any number of 
Russians that liave yet been brought into the field; but the Turkish Govern- 
ment, which has so long tolerated their misdeeds, and now rewards and pro- 
motes one of them, is hardly less culpablo or less unfhithfal to the best interests 
of its Sovereign. 

Your Excellency, whose voice las been so influential in effecting beneficial 
changes in the Turkish Ministers, might render good service to the Porte hy 
directing the attention of the Government in the choice of their military com- 
manders to persons of honesty and capacity. ; 
___The English and French Governments are now about, at vast expense and 
inconvenienee, to protect the Sultan's territory from Russian aggression. ‘They 
are about to encounter the risks of an European war; and they have at least a 
right to insist that the Porte shall be true to itself, and thit not only suels 
eriminals as these Pashas should not be retained in command, but that their 
condign punishment should warn others from following their example, 

Your Excellency will communicate this despateh to Reshid Pasha. 

Lam, &e, 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

No, 228. 


Sir G. H, Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received February 21.) 


(No, 138.) 


My Lord, St, Petersburgh, February 10, 1854. 

THE messenger Townley arrived here at 10 o'clock yesterday night, 
placing me in possession of your Lordship’s despatches down to No. 29 
inclusive. 

I have lost no time in addressing a private note to Count Nesselrode to 
know on what day and at what hour I can have the honour of waiting upon his 
Excellency for the purpose of making a communication to him on the part of 
Her Majesty's Government. I shall upon this occasion read to him your 
Lordship's despatch No. 27, a copy of which has been prepared for the purpose 
of being placed in his hands. | 

It is very possible that this may prove the last interview which [may have 
of his Excellency, und I will not conceal from your Lordship that if public con- 
siderations were not such as infinitely to outweigh those of a personal nature, | 
should hail with unfeigned satisfaction the approach of the moment which will 
release me from one of the most ungrateful tasks which I believe to have been 
ever imposed upon a diplomatic servant of the Crown. 

[have long felt that Iwas struggling against a current which was too 
strong for me; while the pain of finding myself unable to give effect to the views 
of Her Majesty's Government has been heightened by the conviction which I 
shall ever entertain that very different results would have been obtained if those 
upon whose assistance I had in various degrees a right to count, had not been, I 
cannot say even the lukewarm supporters, but the secret opponents of my 
efforts. 

I have seen a most dangerous policy adopted by a Government which 
considered my timely warnings as exaggerated and absurd; 1 have witnessed the 
disruption of those relations which it had been my great object to render of the 
most friendly nature: in the attempts which I have made to stem a course of 
ambition and folly, [ have encountered odium and abuse, and I shall leave this 
country embarked in an undertaking which, while it can but insure great injury 
to itself, may be productive of extensive mischief to England and to Europe.

My Lord, St. Petersburgh, February 11, 1854. 
A GENTLEMAN whose extensive connection with business renders him 
well acquainted with what is passing here, informs me that he never remembers 
such activity as prevails at present in the public departments. He states that 
some considerable purchases of military stores have been made within the last 
three or four days upon public account; among which he notices those of 400 
tons of sulphur and 1200 tons of lead, Of this last one-half is to be delivered 
at St. Petersburgh, and the other half at some place or places on the Volga, 
One of my diplomatic colleagues states as a fact that the Russian Govern- 
ment have purchased three yessels—goelettes he terms them—in Holland, 
which will be sent as merchantmen, probably to Lisbon, either having on board 
or taking on board at that intermediate point, a considerable number of Russian 
sailors, who are to be sent on to reinforce the Lmperial squadron in the Japanese 
seas, My informant states further, that the vessels will sail from Lisbon under 


the fe (supposing war to have broken out) of some neutral country, 


his account seems to be a little improbable; the person, however, from 
whom it is received is confident as to its correctness, 


180 


I hear further, and this report appears to me to be at least as much worthy 
of belief, that several of the less seaworthy of the line-of-battle ships are to be 
employed as batteries, and to be moored off Cronstadt i the event of an attack 
from seaward appearing probable. 

A notion prevails, as | understand, among some of the naval men here that 
it would have been judicious to have posted the ships now at Helsingfors, in the 
Sound, where, as they imagine, position might have been taken up which would 
have prevented the entry of a fleet of very superior force.

Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received February 21.) 


(No. 140.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, February 11, 1854. 

I HAD the honour of submitting to your Lordship, some months since, 
that although no prospect of a rupture with Russia was sufficiently alarming, 
it might prove that one of the attendant dangers of such a war, notwithstanding 
the contrary opinion go generally entertained, would prove visionary. 

It had been supposed that a Russian war would be the signal for a 
revolutionary movement of an European character, 1 conjectured that if might 
prove, on the contrary, a cure for revolution, and such a duct for bad humours 
as would tend to bring about a more healthy state of public opinion than has 
prevailed for many years in Europe. 

My calculation was, that in the presence of common evils, the tendency 
of men’s minds is naturally to disregard those which are less; internal move- 
ments would probably not oceur if Christendom were again threatened by the 
Saracens, or if the Moors were now to be ejected from Europe: and I reflected 
that so it would be were the hour to arrive when the civilization of the West 
and the South should find it necessary to make o stand against the encroach- 
ments of Russia. 

lf a colossus of this magnitude, however, is to be assailed, the attack should 
be very general, and some very general motive must be provided. 

I would venture to remark that the motives already exist, and of the 
strongest order. ‘ 

If Russia be strong enough to measure her forces against those of Mngland 
and France, as she is prepared to do; if she is able to meet all Europe in arms, 
which she professes her intention of doing, rather than desist from an unjust 
demand upon an inoffensive neighbour, her strength must have become too 
aveat for the actual balance of power, whilst so far from the limits of her means 
of offence being exhausted, we know that she is preparing to make the most 
formidable additions to her fleets in the Black Sea and the Baltte. 

These motives are sufficiently strong; but there is another which will likely 
carry great weilght—the national feeling which must, exist in Poland, Germany, 
and Sweden, as well as in Turkey and Persia, the absorption and plunder of 
which have made Rugsia what she now is, 

It was but a few years ago that the cry of “ Germany for the Germans” 
fired the whole Confederation, and led a Prussian army into Schleswig, Tt might 
prove that the same feelings, if ealled forth, would induce Germany to reflect 
that her safety would be insured and her power extended by making Esthonia, 
Courlund, aud Livonia German by possession, as they are already in language, 
habits, and creed; whilst the attempt would probably be accompanied by 4 move 
on the part of Sweden upon those provinces of which she was despoiled but 
half a century since. 


18] 


__, 1 would venture then to submit to your Lordship, that, should Russia 
insist upon war, and should circumstances favour the undertaking to which 
Lallude, no nobler task could be proposed to the energies of Governments and 
eA than ran of averting the dangers of brute force and extended despotism 
Ly, f nipping t spas of her ill-gotten possessions, and restoring her to her former 
In the case of Italy, Germany, France, or England, any injurv infil 
upon these countries, as upon many of smaller extent, would be niece inflicted 
upon civilization and humanity: the curtailment of Russia, and the rolling back 
of a half civilized population would offer no disadvantage ; an enormous benefit 
would be conferred upon the rest of Europe, while the people whose vanit 
would suffer would be the only one, with the exception of their Turkish 
neighbours, of the whole European family which, never having made any 
contributions to science, arts, or literature, have established no claims upon the 
sympathy of the rest of the world. : 
_ Thave, &e. 
(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR,

Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received February 21.) 
(No. 143. Confidential.) 


My Lord, St. Petersburgh, Februury 11, 1864, 

I HAVE heard for some days past that it was likely that a Russian 
decoration would be sent to General Castelbajac, but felt tolerably sure that the 
report was to be ascribed to malevolence; it appeared to me much more certain 
that if what, under the circumstances of the case, is to be considered as an 
indignity, should be offered to my colleague, a sense of what is due to his 
official character would point out the course which he had to follow. 

_ I had formed an ineorrect judgment, as well of the man as of the 
circumstances of the case. 

On the 8th instant General Castelbajac received an autograph letter from 
the Emperor, who wrote that he had very great pleasure in sending him the 
Grand Cordon of’ the Order of St. Alexander Newsky as a mark of his regard, 
and of the great satisfaction felt by His Majesty at the manner in which his 
diplomatic duties had been performed at this Court. 

To this announcement my unfortunate colleague replied by a letter of 
grateful and humble aeceptance of the honour conferred upon’ him by His 
mperial Majesty. 

Not the least curious circumstance of this very remarkable transaction is 
that of the Chancellor having intimated to General Castelbajac that, had his 
opinion been taken, it would not have been advisable that a mark of Imperial 
favour should have been conferred upon him at a juncture like the present, 

It is only an act of justice to state to your Lordship that the gentlemen 
forming the French Mission feel most sensibly the humiliation to which they 
have been subjected, . 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) G. H, SEYMOUR. 


P.S.—Sinee my despatch was written General Castelbajac has shown me 
the letter or reseript addressed to him by the Emperor Nicholas, ‘The letter is 
not in His Majesty's own hand, as [ had stated,

a hoi ut: Pies the Emperor on the Sth instant, 
GENERAL DE ROCHOW waited) upon’the pare contoh {ram Bator 
and et | have reason to believe, besides reading to him a despatch from Baron 
Mantentlel explanutory of the views of Prussia with regard to the date Oversites 
of the Imperial Cabinet, delivered a letter from the King his master to the same 


185 


effect. | am assured that the King's letter contains these remarkable words : 
* Pour Dieu, faites que la Prusse ne soit pas forcée de tirer ’épée!”’ 

The extreme repugnance shown by General de Rochow to afford me any 
information as to what passed upon the occasion, or even to admit of any allusion 
to his interview, was, I thought, injudicious on his part, and the more so as it 
tended to strengthen my suspicion of his being not uncommonly rather the 
zealous friend of the Emperor of Russia than the devoted agent of his own 
Sovereign. 

I would here venture to observe that if it could in future be managed that 
the Ministers sent here from the Great Courts should be selected rather with 
reference to the steadiness of their opinions and the independence of their 
characters than for more brilliant qualifications, an immense advantage would be 
attained, and some chance would be afforded for the access of truth to quarters 
from which it is so habitually excluded. 

I have been told that extraordinary talent is required on the part of the 
diplomatic gladiator who is to enter the arena of St. Petersburgh, but this 
opinion I cannot share. Very little talent would be encountered here—deceit 
and falsehood, the arms the most successfully employed in Russia, and these 
being within the grasp of yery ordinary mediocrity. What I believe to be 
required here is good sense, great watchfulness, aud, above all, honest straight- 
forwardness. 

Russia is a country of courtiers, and T am convinced that foreign Govern- 
ments would render a real service to their own interests by not allowing the 
number to be swelled by the addition of their own Representatives; if this was 
not cet before, the fact has been well established by the events of the last few 
months. 

To return to the communication made by General de Rochow to the 
Emperor, It was extremely ill received by His Majesty, whose feelings, even if 
kept under during the audience (a point upon which i have no information), 
appear to have been very freely vented afterwards. If I am rightly informed, 
His Majesty's displeasure at the conduct of his Royal brother-in-law was 
expressed in terms the least ambiguous, and was probably accompanied by 
denunciations of Prussian perfidy and Austrian ingratitude. 

Had this not been the case similar expressions would not have been heard 
from those who are the faithful echoes of words pronounced in the Palace. 

The Emperor's state of excitement appears to have been of some duration, 
for, on the following day, he expressed his resolution of sending away Count 
Miinster, saying that he had no longer any oceasion for the service of a Prussian 
Aide-de-camp; there is, [ believe, however, no intention of acting upon a deter- 
mination taken ab irato. 

The plain truth is, that His Imperial Majesty has contrived to place himself 
in so deplorably bad a position that [I should even now feel hopeful as to his 
endeavouring to recover himself by timely retreat if truth and reason could 
but gain a hearing, and if it were possible to assign the bounds within which a 
will during long years freed from all contradiction and control could now be 
brought under restraint. 

it is yet just possible that the removal of two foreign Ministers from this 
Court may afford the means of deluding the Russian public into the belief of 
measures of great energy being commenced, and that a method may thus be 
devised for extrication from the difficulties which have been created by holding 
big language, by taking up over-forward positions, and by making appeal to 
dangerous passions. 

I have, &e.

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received February 21.) 


{No. 65. Most Confidential.) 


My Lord, . Berlin, February 18, 1854, 

A FEW days ago Baron Manteuffel received an order from the King to 
consult with the Minister of War as to the arrangement which should be made 
in the event of foreign ships of war appeating in the Baltic ports, Upon hearing 
this information | immediately spoke to Baron Manteuttel, and learnt from his 
Execllency that this instruction had not originated with the King, but had been 


187 


addressed to him at the suggestion of General Gerlach and M. Niebuhr, who 
are both interested in the cause of Russia; that he felt a great deal annoyed at 
it, but that he had no intention of sanctioning any arrangement which would 
close the Prussian harbours to our fleets; and that, as no regulations on the 
subject existed, he should endeavour to draw up an answer which would leave 
the matter much as it already stood. 

1 have, &e 


(Signed) BLOOMFIELD. 
No. 239. 
Lord Bloomfield to the Eurl of Clarendon.—(Received February 21.) 


(No. 66.) 
My Lord, Berlin, February 18, 1854. 

I READ this morning to Baron Manteuffel your Lordship’s despatch 
No. 24 of the 18th instant, in which you approve of the course I had pursued 
in communicating to the Prussian Minister for Foreign Affairs, in conjune- 
tion with my French colleazue, the draft of the proposed Convention to be 
signed by the Representatives of the Four Powers at Vienna ; and his Exeel- 
leney was much gratified with the assurance contained in that despatch, that 
there is no wish on the part of England and France unduly to press upon the 
Prussian Government, although in the present state of things the importance of 
coming to a clear understanding with reference to the future cannot be over- 
estimated. 

His Excellency observed further, that Prussia is most anxious not to be 
pressed at the present moment, for many reasons. ‘The greatest, perhaps, was 
the difficulties caused by the military organization; for though she had an army 
of 500,000 men, the calling out this force, and putting it on the war footing, 
would create financial requirements which it would be difficult to meet; and 
that he thought the prudent and best course was to reserve their strength with 
a view to striking a decisive blow hereafter. 

IT replied, that I thought this was scarcely fiir towards the maritime 
Powers, who would thus have to bear the brunt of the commencement of 
the war; but, L added, can we count on your cooperation hereafter 7? 

He answered, that he trusted we should find Prussia ready and disposed to 
do so; and he said, that he had no misgivings as to the King, for although he 
knew His Majesty might waver and be worked upon by Russia, still in the 
present state of the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh, he had less to fear, as its ill- 
humour would have less influence than its cajoleries. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD,

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received February 21.) 


(No. 188.) 
My Lord, Paris, February 19, 1854. 

I HAVE the honour to inclose herewith, for your Lordship’s information, 
the copy of a despatch which I addressed yesterday to Her Majesty's Ambas- 
sailor at Constantinople, informing his Excellency that the French Government 
had no objection to the draft of Convention which your Lordship proposed 
should be entered into by the Governments of Great Britain, and France, and 
Turkey, for the better regulation of the measures to be taken by the three 
Governments for the defence of the latter country. 

Your Lordship will see that General Baraguay d'Hilliers will be instructed 
to urge the Porte’s acceptance of that Convention. 

i have also read to M. Drouyn de Lhuys your Lordship’s despatch No. 60 
to Lord Stratford, informing that Ambassador that a considerable military force 
will shortly be sent by the English and French Governments to Turkey, and 
instructing him to insure a proper reception for the combined forces, and 
expressing a hope that orders will be given by the Porte to the Turkish com- 
manders to prevent any want of unity of action between them and the English 
and French Commanders-in-chief, 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys appor these instructions, and on my asking him 
whether it might not be as well to leave some latitude to the Ambassadors to 
introduce a stipulation of the kind into the proposed Convention, he replied that 
he had no objection, provided that care was taken not to press any conditions 
that might seem to trench upon the independent action of the Porte, or which 
would make the French Government appear to be responsible for every act of 
the Turkish Government. - 

My despatch to Lord Stratford will show your Lordship further that the 
idea of sending a messenger oyerland to Constantinople had been abandoned by 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys. Your Lordship’s despatches, therefore, which were 
destined to be transmitted by that messenger, were forwarded in the usual way 
by the extra messenger Purdie. 

L have, &c. 
(Signed) COWLEY,

NOUS avons annoncé hier que |'Empereur avait recu une réponse de St.

Dang sa lettre A l'Empereur, le Czar diseute les conditions d’arrangement 
qui lui avaient été proposées, et déclare qu'il ne peut entrer en négociation que 
sur les bases qu'il a fait connaitre. 

Cette réponse ne laisse plus de chance 4 une solution penn et la France 
doit se preparer 4 soutenir, par des moyens plus efficaces, la cause que n'ont pu 
faire prévaloir les efforts pers¢vérants de la diplomatie. 

En défendant plus énergiquement les doit de la Turquie, l'Empereur 
compte sur le patriotisme du pays, sur l’alliance intime de l’Angleterre et sur les 
sympathies des Gouvernements d’Allemagne. | 

Ces Gouvernements ont constamment déclaré qu’ils voulaient, aussi réso- 
liment que nous, maintenir l'équilibre Européen, faire respecter l'intégrité et 


Vindépendance de l’Empire Ottoman. Il n'y a pas d’autre question engagée 
dans le débat, 


Lattention se tourne vers |'Autriche, que sa position appelle 4 jouer un réle 
actif et important, L’Autriche s'est toujours prononeée, avec une grande 
fermeté, en faveur des points qui ont été établis dans le protocole de la Conférence 
de Vienne du 5 Décembre dernier. 

Nous avons toute confiance dans la loyauté et le caractére chevalresque du 
jeune Empereur d’Autriche; nous trouvons, en outre, une garantie des disposi- 
tions de son Gouvernement dans les. intdéréts de ses peuples, intéréts qui sont 
identiques aux nétres. 

Dans les circonstances générales de la politique Européenne, la France, forte 
de ses intentions loyale et désintéressées, n'a rien A redouter de la lutte qui se 
prépare. Elle sait d’ailleurs qu'elle peut compter sur énergie autant que sur la 
sagesse de [Empereur.

eee an Bond understanding By nlen they are influenced when combining

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received February 22.) 


(No. 203.) 
My Lord, Paris, February 2), 1854, 


A TELEGRAPHIC despatch, dated 6 o'clock this morning, has been 
received by M, Drouyn de Lhuys from M. de Bourqueney. ‘The latter recounts 
that at a ball last night at Prince Schwarzenberg’s, where he had met the 
Emperor of Austria, His Majesty had fully confirmed the language held by 
Count Buol, to which reference was made in my despatch No. 198, transmitted 
yesterday, His Majesty spoke of the proposed Convention with approbation, 
and any modications, M. de Bourqueney says, which may be asked for by 
Austria will only be to render it more effective, The Emperor said that he 
approved the policy of France, and would remain united with her; that the 
would come to an understanding about Italy, s0 that he might have all his

expiration of which would he the siznal for hostilities, the Cabinet of Vienna 
would support the summons. Tt will be refused, adds M. de Bourqueney, and 
we shall then have Austria on the ground with us. 

Count Buol is afraid of some resistance on the part of Prussia to the 
roject of Convention, and he thinks that a little pressure will be necessary at 
serlin. 

The Austrian Cabinet is about to advise the assembly of 30,000 Prussian 
troops on the Polish frontier. Their own military movements arc proceeding with 
activity.

THE Russian forces in the Principalities are supposed to consist of two 
corps d’armée and a part of a third, besides Cossacks. 

These corpsare the 3rd, or Osten-Sacken’s, the 4th, or Dannenberg’s, and a 

rt of the Sth, or Litders’, the remainder of which are supposed to be in 
“ircassia. 

The different corps are believed to be posted as follows: Dannenberg’s to 
the west of Bucharest as far as Kalafat, Osten-Sacken’s between Bucharest and 
Foktchani, and Liiders’ along the Danube from the Yalonitza eastwards, and as 
far as Ackerman; this latter corps being in greatest force about Ibraila, Galatz, 
Reni, and Ismail, between which places it 15 supposed that about 18,000 men 
are stationed, It will be seen, therefore, that these corps are en échelon, part 
of Osten-Sacken’s forming & second line in rear of Liiders’. 

The operations of the Russian army appear, therefore, to extend over a front 
from Kalafat to Galatz of about 280 miles in a direct line, the principal part of 
their troops being at Bucharest, in the front and to the eastward of it, 

The Turkish army is posted along the Danube and in the rear of it, there being 
in front of the Balkan probably about 120,000 men, of whom the main portion 
are at Schumla, und in front of that place between Rustehuk and the Black Sea, 
18,000 being in the Tartary Dobrudscha. _ 

From the best information respecting the Danube, it appears that there are 
numerous points at which it can be crossed by an army above Silistria, but that 
below Silistria, in consequence of the marshy nature of the banks and the 
numerous islands, it can only be crossed at Hirsova and between Matchin and 
Tultscha. 

Silistria being a fortified town, garrisoned by about 8,000 soldiers, and 
requiring regular siege operations to reduce it, appears, with the forces at Schumla 
and near it, to secure the Dobrudscha from being taken in reverse by any 
Russian force which might pass the Danube to the west of Silistria. Hirsova, 
therefore, being covered, the position of the Dobrudscha would appear to afford 
a means for taking the Russian forces ‘1 Wallachia in reverse, extending as it 
does about ninety miles north of Silistria. | 

It is not improbable that heimg aware of this defect in their position the 
Russians have already made such strenuous and repeated efforts to gain @ 
footing in the Dobrudscha. 

Other causes may also have operated to produce these efforts; the road 
through it is the shortest line towards the Balkan, and by a well-selected 
entrenched camp near Karasow, they would secure their position if obliged to 
retreat and assume the defensive. 

The position of the Dobrudscha might probably be used against the 

Russians, and afford a basis of operations for an offensive war in the Princi- 
salities. 
If the Turkish troops could be depended upon to secure the position of 
Silistria, and to occupy the Russian forces at Kalafat and in front of Bucharest, 
it would be worthy of consideration—for which a careful reconnaissance of the 
course of the Danube from Silistria to its embouchure would be necessary — 
whether a corps d’armée might not te thrown into the Dobrudscha, and if the 
materials for crossing the Danube were collected at some point in its course 
(Matchin and the creeks near it appear to afford some advantages for this 
purpose) ; whether it might not cross and take up a good position witha (éle de 
pont as a basis of operations on the left bank of the Danube, near the bend at 
Galatz, or ot [braila, and operate ‘a rear of the Russians, so as to threaten their 
line of operations and compel them to evacuate Wallachia, in which their position 
would, by a successful movement of this nature, become exceedingly critical. 
Their position would not only be critical on account of the distance of their 
advanced corps from their base of operations on the Russian frontier, but on 
account of the narrowness of the space, some fifty miles, left open to them 
between the Danube and the Carpathinns above Foktchani, to which by the 
nature of the country their operations would be confined,

Inclosure in No. 252. 
Memorandum. 


WHATEVER hopes of peace might reasonably be founded on the Porte'’s 
acceptance of terms recommended by the Four Powers, in virtue of the 
Emperor of Hussia’s declarations, it is difficult to read the correspondence’ 
from Petersburgh, or to observe the movements in Russia, without entertaining 
a strong persuasion that war will not only continue, but probably extend. On 
this supposition the Porte has little time to lose. ‘Three months are barely 
sufficient for repairing her losses, completing her preparations, and arranging her 
plans for another and far more serious campaign. 

If the Emperor of Russia were sure of having a single enemy to deal with, 
his policy might he directed rather to the exhaustion of Turkey by prolonge 
and overstrained exertions, than to its prompt submission under a violent and 
overwhelming attack, But having to apprehend the hostility of two other 
Powers at least, it is obviously his interest to strike home at once, and to gain a 
decisive advantage before England and France can mature and concentrate their 
efforts for the Sultan's defence. Appearances, and in some respects positive 
information, support the correctness o this presumption. There is much reason 
to expect a large increase of force in the Prineipalities, and a forward movement 
across the Danube on a proportionate seale, carly in the spring. It is natural 
to suppose that the main attack will be accompanied with every auxiliary 
measure calculated ta weaken the Porte's resistance. ‘The Asiatic frontier of 
Turkey will, no doubt, be threatened by a Russian army; and also, notwith- 
standing the late return to better counsels at Tehran, by a strong Persian 
demonstration, capable of ripening into downright hostility on the first tempting 
occasion. ‘The barbarous mountain tribes will naturally come in aid of an 
enemy advancing on that side, Long-prepared au he will be brought into play; 
and it is easy. to foresee that wherever Russian influence can o erate, from the 
Danube to the Morea, endeavours will be made to divide the subjects, to distract 
the counsels, and to cripple the energies of the Porte. 

If the success of such operations were to stop short of Constantinople, the 
prospect of its going 80 far as to throw the Porte into alarm and to disperse her 
means of resistance for the time, is a just subject of eet and precaution. 4A 
negotiation imposed in this manner on Turkey would hardly fail of proving fatal 
in its results to that earope liey for which so many notes have been framed, 

so many conferences held, and so many ‘nterests disturbed. Supposing even 
that the Turkish Empire could preserve its territorial integrity im such o case, 
ts virtual independence must necessarily give way t Russian ascendancy ; and 
the same act which confirmed the triumph of unjust aggression, would cast @ 
deep shade on every prospect now opening throughout the East to improved 
civilization, and a more beneficial intercourse with Christendom. England, in 
particular, would have to rue the eonsequences of such a disaster, Foremost 
among those Powers which derive their nutriment from commerce, their vigour 
from {vee institutions, and their glory from the triumphs of justice and truth, she 
of all others would have reason to deplore the subjection of so fair and wide a 
field to the blighting influence of Russia. 

Hence the duty, the importance, and the necessity of exploring and pre- 
varing, without loss of time, the most efficient means of proce Turkey in 
its weakest points, and of reducing its northern assailant to terms which would 
secure the Porte’s independence and the future tranquillity of Europe on that 
sore. 

The Turks may not be entitled, as such, to extraordinary sacrifices on the 
part of Europe, but they have at least one real and powerful claim to support. 


They are the only existing race now capable of keeping this extensive Empire 


201 


together, and averting the calamities of a struggle for its partition. We are not, 
therefore, at liberty to abandon them on account of their errors and deficiencies. 
True policy appears to dictate another course, namely, that of supplying their 
deficiencies, to the best of our means, by friendly suggestions where friendly 
suggestions may avail, and, in failure of their own resources, by adequate 
material assistance. en 

Taking the average testimony of observers, whether professional or not, we 
must lay out our aecount for much imperfection in the national defences of Turkey, 
With respect to the army, it appears that its best points are the artillery and the 
infantry; its worst the cavalry. Its regiments of the line exhibit, in general, 
those qualities which characterize the good soldier, Their officers, if still im 
the ranks, would probably not differ from the men; but in the requisites for 
command they appear to be wofully deficient. The partial successes hitherto 
obtained by the Sultan's troops, may be traced to the artillery and privates. In 
Asia, where more depended on the commanders, success was limited to the 
impulse and vigour of a first attack. Reverses soon followed; and an army 
rated at 100,000 men fell into disorder and was all but dispersed, “The soldiers 
have no reason to complain of their clothing and food. But they are scantily 
supplied with shoes—an essential article ; and the Commissariat is wretchedly, 
if at all organized. The cavalry are ill mounted, and worse armed. The Turks 
imagine that their artillery would make up for the weakness of their cavalry ; but 
the notion is a mistake which may cost them dear. 

‘Turning to the navy, the same causes of regret and apprehension are per- 
ceptible, The large ships may serve well enought at anchor, as floating batteries, 
and they might venture occasionally to sea during the summer months; but 
their fitness for braving a gale of wind, or an enemy of equal force, may well 
be doubted. ‘The Admirals of the combined squadrons gave their opinion 
against any such adventure, when there was lately an inclination at the Porte 
to hazard an nea The steamers are active in carrying troops and 
ammunition at the risk of being captured, and gun-boats for service on the 
Danube are only in a state of forward preparation. The seamen throughout the 
Purkish navy may appear to advantage when ranged for inspection, or engaged in 
exercising their guns; and they gave no doubtful proof of their gallantry and 
devotion m the late unequal combat, Yet so much practice is necessary for 
handling or fighting a ship at sea, that such appenrances in port, however 
pleasing to the spectator, require to be tested by active service before they can 
be telied on, 

Fortifications in Turkey are not more numerous than the defence of the 
country requires. The number, though already considerable, might, on the 
contrary, be extended with advantage. In those which exist, there is no lack 
of room for improvement ; and it may be added, that the tnoney and science 
wanted for their completion, ave still in great measure to be sought. The 
Bosphorus itself is thought to be inadequately defended ; and the Dardanelles, 
though, strange to say, an object of greater attention, is still susceptible of 
improvement. If Sinope hud been elliciently and seasonably fortified, the 
Russians might have found less reason to boast of their miserable exploit there. 
Batoom, to say nothing of ‘Trebizond and Heraclea, is still apen to attack; and 
on the European side of the Black Sea, the more important points, where troops 
might be disembarked, are insufficiently or not at all defended, while the 
seh works of Varna itself are far from affording a complete security to the 
: The supply of ordnance, though by no means small, is still unequal to the 

Fea The gunners are understood to be generally well-practised, “Those 
a the navy have derived much advantage from the instructions of Captain 
3orlase, The gun-carriages are often of a defective construction, and few of 
the puns are made to traverse.

‘at On this penSible it may justly be thought essential to establish: from the

allies: first, with respect to the plan of operations by sca and land; secondly, 


20a 


with respect to the means of execution, and the share to be contributed by each 
party ; thirdly, as to the material eecurities which it would be the settled deter- 
mination of the Contracting Parties to obtain from Russia. 

The form of a Convention would probably be found the most suitable for 
objects of so much delicacy and importance, 

On the supposition which forms the ground-work of this memorandum, 
there is no denying that Europe is in presence of that formidable Eastern ques- 
tion which has so long been an object of dread to all discerning statesmen, and. 
which it bas been the aim of so many diplomatic transactions to avoid or to 
ae i It is not too much to say, that such a question being now unavotdably 

rought forward for decision, it bchoves the Powers of Europe to settle it once 
for all on a basis of no temporizing character, and to grudge neither the means 
nor the exertions necessary for the accomplishment of so glorious and beneficent 
a purpose. 

The vulnerable points and defective means of the Porte, in so far as they 
are open to general observation, require no further notice here. Attention has 
been sufficiently called to them in the preceding parts of this paper, 

It remains with the Governments themselves to decide in what manner and 
deree the former are to be guarded, and the latter to be supplied. 

Looking to probabilities, it would seem that the object of immediate 
urgency is the defence of the Turkish Empire, from the Danube to Constanti- 
nople, The operations in Asia might reasonably be made subordinate to. the 
main object, A considerable portion of the regulars now stationed along the 
Asiatic frontier might he placed at the disposal of Omar Pasha, or held in 
reserve, ‘The remainder of that army might take up a defensive position, with- 
out fear of being seriously attacked, so long as Shamil agrees to threaten the 
rear of the Russian forces in Georgia; and that the present return of Persia 
to better and more friendly feeling towards the Porte shall be perpetuated by the 
fear of giving offence to England, ready, if required, to substantiate her advice 
by directing a force from India on Karrak or Bushire. 

The maintenance of a complete command in the Black Sea by means of the 
combined squadrons will obviously be still more requisite, even than now, when the 
military operations are actively resumed. It is to be hoped that the distribution 
of the squadrons for that purpose will be permanently settled in time. At 
present the difficult, if practicable, enterprise of taking Sevastopol, or destroying 
the Russian fleet, appears to be the surest, if not the only mode of permanently 
realising the views of Her Majesty’s Government in the Black Sea, 

If the allies entertained any idea of sending troops eventually to assist the 
Sultan's army in Hurope, it would be desirable to have them ready, and at no great 
distance from the scene of action; but the Porte itself would hardly desire that 
kind of cooperation so long as it can succeed in making head against Hussia by 
ineans of its own people alone. The need of it might, however, be felt or 
acknowledged too late: and on thisaceountit might be desirable to provide at once 
for the contingency. Officers would at all events be acceptable without delay, 
even, perhaps, those of the highest military rank, j 

A small naval foree under the two flags stationed in the Adriatic, and 
anotlier in the waters of Greece, might be conducive to the success of larger 
operations elsewhere. 

On the point of strengthening the coast and river defences, measures are 
already in progress, and it may be hoped that they will finally be carned out, 
though not by the unassisted energy 0 ‘Turkish officers. 

Looking, in conclusion, to the securities which the united interests of 
Turkey and Europe may imperiously require as the final results of the contest, it 
will be found that the principal and most obvious are, the revisal of the Treaties 
now suspended by the natural effect of war; the relief of the three Principalities 
from Russian protection, to be replaced by an improved political position, 
though still as privileged portions of the Turkish Empire; and a binding pro- 
vision for the practical free navigation of the Danube. Two other eventual 
stipulations are suggested by a sense of justice; one would provide for the 
tranquillity and just pretensions of the Caucasian tribes unsubdwed by Russia; the 
other would impose on Russia a fair indemnity for the expenses of the war, 


rai Russia herself has not unfrequently compelled a vanquished adversary to

These various and complicated matters demand a more extensive develop- 
ment than the present opportunity admits of. 

Impertectly as they are treated in this paper, they may, nevertheless, suffice 
to draw areasonable attention to those points which, in the case sup ged, will 
press for an early consideration, and whieh, to be dealt with effectually, require 
to be viewed in connection with each other, 

But in guarding the Ottoman Empire against the wiles and encroachments 
of its colossal neighbour, we must never forget that Turkey nurses in its own 
bosom a far more powerful and deadly foe—that vicious system of administration 
which has long neutralized its component forecs, and which spreads # corroding 
poison Ancien every part of its population. Tt should be carefully borne in 
mind that, owing to well-known causes, 4 state of security is exactly that con- 
dition in which the poison would acquire its most fatal virulence, and in which 
corruption and injustice, the one familiarized by habit, the other sanctioned by 
religion, would take the deepest root, and cast the most noxious shade. The 
Powers to whom Turkey is com ‘lied to look for safety will have done nothing 
efficient, nothing durable, for the substantive purposes of their union, unless, 
while fixing bounds to Russian aggression, they at the same time place ‘Turkey 
under a distinct obligation to carry out with vigour and good fiuth those prin- 
ciples and plans of improvement which the Sultan has so often proclaimed in 
favour of @ progressive intercourse with Europe, and of equal justice and 
benevolence to his subjects of every class, without exception, The Christians 
must henceforth be respected as well as tolerated throughout the Sultan's 
dominions, and Oriental Turkey must freely open its arms to the science, the 
ckill, the industry, the fertilizing capital, and the ennobling sympathies of Western 
urope. 

Constantinople, January 1854.

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received February 22.) 


(No. 55.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, February 5, 1854. 

1 AM happy to derive from the contents of your Lordships instruction 
No. 29 of the 17th ultimo, an additional confirmation of my fidelit in carrying 
cut the intentions of Her Majesty's Government, when, in spite of the difficu ties 
raised elsewhere, | pee in urging the immediate entrance of the combined 
squadrons into the lack Sea, first for the protection of the Sultan's territory, 
then for the protection of his flag and territory also; and thirdly, for obtaining 
the command of the Black Sea, and thereby preventing the recurrence of any 
affair like that of Sinope. | 

I learn, however, from the same snstruction, that Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment would have been well pleased, under all the circumstances, if the plan of 
operations proposed by Vice-Admiral Dundas’s draft of letter, dated the 29th of 
December, had been acted upon. 

With reference to this passage 1 beg to observe that I did not consider it 
as lying within my province to determine the exact amount or description of 
foree to be sent into the Black Sea, It necessarily required a professional judg- 
ment to decide that point. . 

In stating to panieal Dundas the object to be accomplished in calling upon 
him to send out his ships in sufficient force for that purpose, and in apprizing 
him of what was believed to be the strength of the Russian fleet at Sevastopol, 
I thought to provide for an efficient execution of the service without depriving 
the Admiral of that degree of margin which was desirable for secondary consi- 
derations. { am free at the same time to state my personal impression that, 
considering the nature of the service in question, it would have been far from 

wrudent to risk the honour of the combined flags with a force much inferior to 
that which Russia might have sent against them. 

I take the liberty of addin that the combined steam foree now in the 
Black Sea on the responsibility o the Admirals, would not be able to mive effect 


207 


to the instructions of Her Majesty's Government, if it fell in with that portion 
of the Russian flect which Captain Drummond reported to be absent from 
Sevastopol, and, if it returned to the Bosphorus in order to fetch out the 
squadrons, that, taking the chance of winds at this season, the Admirals would 
have little or no prospect of arriving in time to prevent an act of hostile aggres- 
sion on the territory or flag of Turkey. 

I have, £c. 

(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

Inclosure in No, 260. 
Vice-Admiral Dundas to Lord Stratford de Redcliffe. 


My Lord, Britannia, February 5, 1854. 

I HAVE the honour to acquaint your Excellency that the combines 
detachment of four steam-frigates, under Rear-Admiral de Tinan, which sailec 
on the 28th January, returned this morning. 

At anchor, close in shore, at Kaffa, they found three Rnssian steam-vessels 
of war, of about 600 or 700 tons each, and twenty-five merchant vessels, three 
of them having, however, something the appearance of store-ships. The steam 
squadron did not anchor nor approach nearer than two miles. No commu- 
nication took place. 

The weather prevented Sevastopol being closely reconnoitered ; and at Varna 
everything was tranquil, with no news from the Danube. 

The fortifications of the land and sea faces at Varna were progressing very 


slowly. 
The low land about Kaffa was covered with snow, and only one vessel, an 
Austrian trader, had been met with at sea.

(Signed) J. W, D. DUNDAS.

THE late Seraskier appears to have entertained the project of forming @ 
Polish Legion in the Sultan's service. How far his idea may have been 
sanctioned by the Stash I cn ‘ake aeor myself a re 
Zamoyski, invited by his Highness, arrived here ten days ago, and | 
the caaienld ed shavactet Be agent to Prince Adam Czartoryski. He called 
upon me, and stated his views with every appearance of eandour. : 

T have his assurance that he has no wish to outrun the progress of affairs, 
or to engage the Porte prematurely in plans which may compromise its interests, 
and expose his countrymen in Russia to unnecessary danger. | 

General Wysocki is also at Constantinople on a similar errand, and with 
similar professions of patience and discretion. He does not belong to Prince 
Czartoryski's party, and 1s more likely to embarrass Count Zamoyski than to 
promote his views. pe 

The Porte has already allowed a company of Cossacks, joined with a second 
company of Bulgarians and emigrants—Poles and others mingling together—

who embraced Islamism a few years ago, and assumed the appellation of Sadik 
Pasha. : eet 

Lord Dudley Stuart, who, after a short excursion to the Purkish camp and 
the passes of the Balkan, has returned to England, informed me that he had 
met Sadik Pasha and his corps of Lancers on their way to the camp. Lord 
Dudley himself, notwithstanding his well-known enthusiasm in favour of the 
Poles, though he waited, with my assistance, on some of the leading Ministers, 
and was presented to the Sultan, appears to have acted with becoming discretion, 
and to have abstained from language calculated to lead the Porte into any 

remature acceptance of the services offered so warmly by those who exercise 
a leading influence among the Polish emigrants.

ALL that is passing here is so strange that I think it desirable that some 
imperfect record should be preserved of transactions the exact account of which 
will never be given. a 

The French Minister has written this day to his Government to say that 
he had an audience yertersiny, of the Emperor, at which he delive the 

‘mperor Napoleon's autograph letter. 
‘ Two os three hours afterwards General Castelbajac acquainted me that, 
having been advised that in the excited state in which the Emperor Nicholas

has been for some days, he might possibly speak to him in a manner which 
would not be decorous, it would be advisable that he should send the Imperial 
letter to His Imperial Majesty, and wait upon him for the answer on the 
9th instant, he had acted in conformity to this suggestion. 

On this occasion, as | happen Pikio, it is the French Government that 
have been misled, while the truth has been spoken to me. 

General Castelbajac has not seen the Emperor, and has been recommended 
not to see him until the impression produced by the receipt of the French letter 
should have been softened by reflection.

My Lord, St. Petersburgh, February 12, 1854. 

IT is not in my power to offer your Lordship exact copies of the Imperial 
reseript which accompanied the Grand Cordon of St. Alexander Newsky sent to 
General Castelbajac, or of the letter which was addressed to him upon the 
occasion by Count Nesselrode; but the terms of the two papers which I inclose 
vary very sligaty from the originals which were read to me, not without very 
manifest confusion on his part, by my French colleague. 

If in preceding despatches I may have appeared to have taken a harsh view 
of General Castelbajac’s conduct, at least it must be admitted that my justifi- 
eation is provided in the faet of his having under existing circumstances accepted 
at Be be having sought as well) a mark of favour at the hands of the Emperor 

icholas. 

Before dismissing a subject which it is highly unpleasant to my feelings to 
dell upon, I will venture te observe, that as regards Russian interests the 
reward received by the French Envoy has been well deserved, With regard to 
French objects the case is widely different, and | have no scruple in saying that 
my recollection supplies me with no instanee of the interests of a Government 
having been betrayed by its own agent in the manner in which those of France 
have been sacrificed by General Castelbajac. 

____ From the present hesitating and uncertain attitude of the Russian Cabinet 
it becomes tolerably clear that their policy would have been decisively influenced 
by the united and strenuous action of the English and French Missions. 

Now the obstinacy of the Emperor has been principally occasioned by the 
conviction which even in very latter days he has sitetaiued as to the impossibility 
of an alliance between England and France being sincere; and the opinion can 
hardly be considered unreasonable when French policy is judged of by so 
melancholy a specimen of national feeling as the conduct of the French Envoy 
has exhibited in circumstances the most critical. 

_ ‘There is probably no country in Europe m which acts of baseness are 
viewed with the same indulgence as in Russia; and perhaps the severest con- 
demnation which can be passed upon General Castelbajac is the fact of his 
acceptance of one of their own decorations being, as I hear, very unfavourably 
judged by the Russians themselves, 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) G, H. SEYMOUR,

No. 267. 
Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarenilon—(Received February 23.) 


(No. 153, Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, February 14, 1854. 

GENERAL GRABBE, the officer commanding the gendarmes in the 
south, arrived here a few days since, after a very rapid journey from Odessa. 
The object of bis visit to St. Petersburgh is not known, and gives rise to some 
speculation. 

The version which appears to me the most acceptable, is that he has been 
sent here for the purpose of obtaining extended powers for the authorities upon 
whom, possibly, the defence of Odessa may devolve. 

Already, if | may trust the report made to me, great alarm prevails at that 
port; and, as 1 am further informed, the Russians feel that, pevine no longer 
the command of the Black Sea, the arrival of a few thousand English or French 
troops at Constantinople, added to the facilities of steam-conveyance, would 
place the whole of their southern coasts in danger of attack. 

It is gratifying to me to perceive that Russia, who, in the ill-founded con- 
sciousness in the assumption of superior strength, and of possessions out of reach 
of all aggressive measures, has wantonly plunged all Europe into expense and 
alarm, is herself full of apprehension. 

This feeling is brought home to the great author of the mischief himself; 
and, as 1 learn, measures are being taken, even in the Imperial domains of 
Peterhoff, to guard against attacks which are to be apprehended from the 
Baltic. 

On the opposite shore (at Cronstadt, that is) all bricklayer and masonry 
works are stopped or much impeded by the frost, which continues to be severe. 
For some days the thermometer has ranged from 15° to 18° of Réaumur. 

Mr. Vice-Gonsul Simpson writes as follows from Cronstadt ; 

“The sailors, who were on unlimited leave, are making their appearances, 
according to the orders issued some time back. 

“Phe work at the battery leading to the harbour is progressing. 

I have, &e 


(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.
