Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon —(Received February 23.) 


(No. 152. Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, February 14, 1854. 

IT may be that having been misrepresented and unfairly treated myself 1 
ain the more disposed to come to the aid of those who are suffering from 
injustice; but so it is, that I should be sorry to quit this Mission without 
entering 4 protest against the unfounded attacks directed against General Count 
Orloff by a portion of the public press. 

Ceneral Orloff is a Russian, and is consequently obliged to obey the orders 
of his master, be these orders what they may, but I have no hesitation in 
stating that very few men about the Emperor exhibit their attachment to him 
by endeavouring to resist his will when he is in error to the same degree as this 


213 


his supposed unhesitating mstrument. I will go further, and will again state 
my firm conviction that all the present entanglements would have been avoided 
had Count Orloff been dispatched to Constantinople in the place of Prince 
Menchikoff, or if, at a much later period, his advice had been more attended to. 
As regards Prince Menchikoff, I will remark that one of the few instances 10 
which T am aware of having misled your Lordship (though I may often have 
done so unconsciously), was in the character which I gave of that person upon 
his departure for Odessa and Constantinople. - | 

The explanation of my incorrect judgment is a simple one. I knew him to 
be opposed to the principle of an extension of territory being an increase of 
strength and power, and an appreciation of this perception made me insensible of 
other circumstances which, as I might and ought to have known, rendered 
Prince Menchikoff a very unfit negotiator m an affair which required great 
discretion, some frankness, and conciliatory habits, to which the Prince is an utter 
stranger.

(Signed) G. H, SEYMOUR.

ACCORDING to a popular myth which has prevailed here during the 
latter weeks, the consciousness of having made exagverated reports of various 
transactions in which 1 have been engaged, was so strong that it was certain 
that I should quit St, Petersburgh before tlie appearance of those Parliamentary

Here however I have remained, and the despatches which it had been my 
duty to address to your Poca having been published by the public papers

persons, produced a good effect. ; 

Of the nature of the rumours which have been in circulation with regard to 
my conduct, your Lordship will be able to judge by the circumstance that one of 
my diplomatic friends has called upon me to say, “Je viens de lire quelques 
unes e vos dépéches, mais je vous assure que je n’y ai trouvé aucune indice

My Lord, St. Petersburgh, February 14, 1854. 

I FIND that I have omitted to state to your Lordship that the French 
messenger who left St. Petersburgh on the 11th instant was the bearer of 
the Imperial answer to the letter addressed to His Majesty by the Emperor 
Napoleon. May 

General Castelbajac had the honour of being received yesterday at the 
Winter Palace, when the Emperor read to him the copy of this reply. It 
appears to have been long, and, although courteous In terms rather official than 
friendly in their expression, according to General Castelbajac’ phrase it may be 
regarded asa “ piéce de Chancellerie.” | 

The expression employed in the letter of the Emperor of the French, 
‘Interdire la sortie de yos vaisseaux de Cronstadt,” appeared to have given 
some slight offence,—a feeling which did not, however, prevent General 
Castelbajac from meeting with a very gracious reception, Upon his entering 
the room His Imperial Majesty said, “ Comprenez que ce nest point une visite 
dadieu,’ He alluded to the contents of the Emperor Napoleon’s letter, and 
alserved that the terms of arrangement which it suggested were less favourable 
than those agreed upon at Vienna. | 

The Emperor was looking ill, —indeed, I hear onall sides that he is much 

altered of late, and he appeared out of spirits; he was, however, calm and 
eollected, aud General Custelbajac inferred that he had made up his mind not to 
viVe WAY. 
j When he left the palace General Castelbajac waited upon the Chancellor. 
His Excellency intimated to him in terms the most courteous, and with manifest 
feelings of reluctance, that it was probable that in three or four days passports 
would be—not sent—but offered to him and to myself, 

It ia to be believed that the Government would be well pleased that we 
should demand our passports, but being aware that Baron Brunnow and M, de 
Kisseleff have quitted their respective posts, they feel naturally that our pro- 
longed residence here might argue a want of spirit on the part of the Russian 
Court. 

. I need not observe to your Lordship that I shall consider the offer of a 
passport in the light of a courteous intimation to leave St. Petersburgh as 
speedily as those arrangements can be made which, in the case of a numerous 
family, require a certain time in this country and in the dead of winter. 
1 have, &e.

THE Undersigned begs to acknowledge the receipt of the note of this date 
which Count Nesselrode has done him the honour of addressing to him, 
acquainting him that in consequence of the circumstances which have led to 
Baron Brunnow’'s departure from London, the diplomatic relations between the 
two countries are suspended; and desiring to be informed on what day and for

and the persons attached to Her Majesty’s Mission. 

As regards the one point, the Undersigned will request his Exeellency tu 
have the goodness to give directions that his passport and that of his family 
should be made out for London by Kinigsberg: with regard to the other point 
he would beg permission not to answer the inquiry at the present moment, 
The state of health of one of the members of his family is such at present as to 
render immediate departure impossible, and by waiting a little he may be 
enabled to ascertain whether he can accompany his family on their journey, or 
whether it will be necessary to make arrangements for their remaining here some 
days after their departure. 

(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR.

No, 273. 


Cirvular addressed (a Her Majesty's Diplomatic and Consular Agents abroud. 


Sir, Foreign Office, February 23, 1854. 

‘THE communication which has recently been made to you of the corres- 
poudence on Eastern affairs which has been laid before both Houses of Parlia- 
ment, will have shown you that there is every probability of an early commence- 
ment of hostilities between Great Britain and France on one side, and Russia on the 
other. ‘That correspondence will also have shown you that the British and French 
Governments, throughout the difficult and complicated negotiations which have 
preceded the existing state of affairs, have earnestly and cordially acted together, 
with a view to avert the calamity of war, and that they are equally prepared to 
net with the same carnestnesss and cordiality for the preservation of the Ottoman 
Empire, if the Emperor of Russia should still be unwilling to negotiate for peace 
on fair and reasonable terms. 

The time hus now arrived when it is incumbent on the two Governments to 
prepare for all the contingencies of war; and among those contingencies it has 
been impossible for them to overlook the danger to which their subjects and 
their commerce on the high seas may be exposed by the machinations of their 
enemy, who, though unable from his own resources materially to injure either, 
may seek to derive means of offence from eountries Whose Governments take 
no part in the contest which he has provoked, 

But it is a necessary consequence of the strict union and alliance which 
exists between Great Britain and France, that, in the event of war, their conjomt 
action should be felt by Russia in all parts of the world; that not only in the 
Baltic, und in the waters and territory of Turkey, their counsels, their armies, 
and their fleets, should be united either for offensive or defensive purposes 
nninst Russia, but that the same spirit of union should prevail in all quarters of 
the world, and that whether for offence or defence the civil and mulitary and 
naval resources of the British and French Empires should be directed to the 
common objcets of protecting the subjects and commerce of England and France 
from Russian aggression, and of depriving the Russian Government of the 
means of inflicting injury on either, 

For these reasons Her Majesty's Government have apres with that of His 
Majesty the Emperor of the French to instruct their civil and naval authorities 
in foreign parts to consider their respective subjects as having an equal claim to 
protection against Russian hostility ; and tor this purpose, cither singly or in 
conjunction with each other, to act mdifforently for the support and defence of 
Retish and Freneh interests, Tt may be that, ina given locality, one only of 
the Powers is represented by a civil functionary, or by a naval force ; but, in 


217 


auch a case, the influence and the power of that one must be exerted as zealous! 
and efficiently for the protection of the subjects and interests of the other as if 
those subjects and interests were its OWN. LAOS es 

1 have accordingly to instruct you, Sir, to act in conformity with this prin- 
ciple. You will consider it your duty to protect, as far as possible, against the 
consequence of the hostilities m which England and France may shortly be 
engaged with Russia, the subjects and interests of France equally with those of 
England; and you will make known without reserve to the French eivil and 
naval authorities with whom you may have means of communication, any dangers 
to which the interests of either country may be exposed, or any opportunities 
with which you may become acquainted of inflicting injury on the common 


ety fs 

me TieracOnS to the same effect will be sent by the Government of France to 
‘ts civil and naval authorities in foreign parts, and Her Majesty’s Government 
coneur with that of France in anticipating the most favourable results from 
this decided manifestation of the intimate union which prevails between them, 


and whieh it is their earnest desire should influence their agents in all parts of 


the world at a moment when they are about to engage in a contest with the 
Empire of Russia for an object of such paramount interest to Europe as the 
maintenance of the Turkish Empire. 

I am,

(Signed) CLARENDON. 


No, 274, 
The Earl of Clarendon to the Lords Commissioners of the Admiralty. 


My Lords, Foreign Office, February 23, 1854. 

I HAVE the honour to acquaint your Lordships that Her Majesty's 
Government and that of France have agreed that their civil authorities and 
naval forces in all parts of the world should cooperate, or if necessary act singly, 
for the protection of the interests of the subjects and commerce of the two 
nations, wherever the same may stand in need of assistance, against the hostile 
machinations of Russia. 

I have accordingly addressed to Her Majesty's Diplomatic and Consular 
Agents abroad the instruction of which I inclose a copy,* and I am to signify to 
your Lordships the Queen's commands that an instruction to the same effect be 
forthwith issued by your Lordships for the direction of Her Majesty's naval 
forees in all parts of the world. 

; Lam, &c. 
(Signed) CLARENDON.

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received February 23.) 


(No. 215. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Paris, February 22, 1854. 

YOUR Lordship will no doubt have remarked that during the conversation 
which M. de Bourqueney states ina telegraphic despatch, © which I had the 
honour to give your Lordship the details in my despatch No. 203, had taken 
pac’ between himself and the Emperor of Austria, His Majesty is reported to 
have said, “ that France and Austria could come to an understanding concerning 
Italy, so that the Emperor would be enabled to dispose of all his military 
reacurees at the other extremity of his Empire.” 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys, in the course o the conversation which ensued, after 
he had read me M, de Bourqueney’s despatch, said, that he wished to explain 
himself at onee frankly though confidentially on this point. He need not, he 
continued, assure me that neither the Emperor of the French nor his Govern- 
ment had any arriére pensde in regard to Italy, and there was no assurance of 
this kind that he was not. willing to give to the Austrian Government ; but he 
confessed that he should have great difficulty in entering into any positive 
engagements with the Cabinet of Vienna, im consequence of the reprehensible 
measures in whieh that Government persevered in all its dealings with Italy. 
If the French Government were to enter into any solemn engagement defining 
the course of action to be followed by the two Governments in their relations 
with Italy, while Austria persisted in her present policy, the people of Italy 
would believe that the Emperor of the French approved of that policy, and that 
belief would soon gain ground in Europe. This made the question of joint 
action with Austria one of extreme delicacy and difficulty. 

I suggested that the moment might be turned to account. What if the 
French Government were to say, in a way that should not give offence, that, 
while abjuring all intention of encouraging the enemies of Austria in Italy, they 
would enter into no engagement upon the subject, unless Austria would consent 
to adopt a policy in that country more im harmony with the feelings of 
Eu ae (?). 

{. Drouyn de Lhuys replied that such a course might, perhaps, succeed ; 
but that his object venta be rather to lead Austria to sce the error of her ways, 
than to make any demand upon her—in other words, to let Austria understand 
that, under altered circumstances, France would not be averse to entering into 
some distinct engagement respecting Italy, 

There were two ways, M. Drouyn de Lhuys said, in repetition of what he 
had often remarked before; there were two ways of carrying on the war with 
Russia. ‘Ihe one by fair and legal means, in efence of the public rights and 
in virtue of the public Treaties of Europe, Such would be the union of the Great 
Powers to oppose the lawiess ambition of Russia, and a war waged in that way 
and for such & purpose, must carry with it the evmpathy of all lovers of real 
ed . ‘There need then be no fear of revolutionary movements to be com- 
valted. 

The other would be the consequence of apathy on the part of the German, 
Powers. But they would not escape war, they would be forced into it in gpite 
of themselves, but not a war in which they would be gloriously fighting for the 
oppressed, but in which they would have to defend themselves as oppressors, 

He need hardly add that the former of these ways secured, a8 far 9s 
was possible to seeure in war, the present state of Europe ; the latter threatened 
a total annihilation of the present state of things, and a reconstruction of the 
territorial distribution of Iurope. He could add with truth that the Emperor 
and his Government would not cease to persevere in the former course. 1f the 
latter supervened it would not be their fault, though they would not shrink in 
consequence from the task in which they were engaged. 

In truth, my Lord, whatever may have been the hints given by the 
Kmperor and his Government in the course of last autumn to the Austrian 
Minister here, as to the consequences which a prolonged neutrality on the part 
of Austria might entail upon her, it can never be the policy of the French 


Government, although circumstances may compel them to it, to encourage 


223 


evolutionary movements in Italy. They ma like to keep the power in their 
hands but they will be loath to use it, for the liberty they supported in Italy 
would soon seek to establish ‘teolf in France. In saying this | mean to cast no 
reflection upon the Emperor 5 for much as the present state of things may be 

tted by those who are reat lovers of constitutional liberty, 1 doubt the 
elements necessary to such liberty to exist in France, and every day's experience 
tends to change this doubt into conviction. 

An artiale having reference to the policy to be pursued by the French 
Government in Italy, appeared in the “Moniteur” this morning. 1 do mysel 
he honour to inclose a copy. 
ee ss T have, &e. 

(Signed) COWLEY.

My Lord, Berlin, February 22, 1804. 

BARON MANTEUFFEL was 50 much engaged at the Second Chamber 
yesterday, that I have only just been able to execute the instructions conveyed 
to me in your Lordship's despatch No. 26 of the 18th instant. 

His fexcellency has been for some time past prepared for the communicn 
tion of which I was the bearer, and was anxiously waiting for it, I commenced 
our conversation by stating that Thad brought with me a copy of a note which 
had been delivered by Lord Cowley to M. Drouyn de Lhuys on the Oth instant, 
in exchange for one which had been addressed to your Lordship by Count 
Walewski; that these documents might be looked upon as a preliminary 
engagement into which the British and French Governments had entered, in 


consequence of the rejection by the Emperor of Russia of the proposals of the 


Vienna Conference of the 13th ultimo, and that they would probably become 
the groundwork of a Convention to be hereafter concluded; that, however, 
before taking any further steps and entering into more detailed engagements 
with France for commencing ® war which appeared inevitable, Her Majesty's 
Government wished me to bring this note to the consideration of the Prussian 
Government, and to invite them to examine its object, and to join in our efforts 
to maintain peace if still possible, and if not, to ‘form us how far they would 
unite with us in the adoption of other measures that may become necessary in 
order to restrict the war to the smallest possible compass. 

1 then read to his Excellency your Lordship's despatch No. 20; he 
listened to it with the greatest attention, and seemed generally to approve of it, 
but he expressed doubts as to whether the King would be persuaded to join in a 
Convention of the nature proposed, and consent to bind himself as to his future 
course of policy; nevertheless, he thought [lis Majesty would make fewer 
objections to the present proposal than to the Convention which had been 
submitted to him from England and France a fortnight ago; and Baron 
Manteuffel asked me what was to become of that project? 1 replied that L had 
reecived no further instructions from Her Majesty's Government respecting: it, 
but that if the present proposals were more as resable to the King, the first one 
need not, | imagine, be persisted in ; that | had now laid the whole question 
before hia Excellency without reserve, ‘and [ hoped it might be favourably 
received. He requested me to give him a memorandum of my instructions, and 
| have since sent his Excellency a copy of them, and hope your Lordship will 
approve of my having done so. 

Karon Manteufiel made but few remarks on the abject of my visit to linn ¢ 
he said that he scarcely expects the King will go to the extent we desired, fur 
His Majesty could not as yet bring himself to contemplate the inevitability of 
war, and that he thought it would be advisable for Her Majesty’s Government 
not to press Prussia too hard; that there were undoubted convictions us to the 
political errors which had been committed by the Emperor of Russia, but that 
there was a wide difference between moral support and joint action in the event 
of hostilities; that he had already told me (as reported in my despatch No, 06 
of the 18th instant), that Prussia could certainly bring « large army into the 
field, if necessity peremptorily called for such o course, but that she had not

COUNT NESSELRODE having allowed me to call upon him yesterday, 
we conversed very amicably upon the position of Her Majesty’s subjects now

by grave cireumstances.

engagement on the part of the Russian Government to receive the representa

written promise on the side of the English Government.

IT appears to me very clear not only that the position which the Emperor 
has made for himself is an extremely bad one, but that the truth is becoming 
apparent, if not to himself, at least to his advisers. I haye always observed that 
phere ‘ea, certain throwing aside of reserve both on the part of and towards a 
diplomatic employé upon the eve of final departure from his post. — 

‘This disposition to speak with more freedom was very observable yesterday 
in Count Nesselrode, whose language really struck me as a kind of appeal “ad 
misericordiam.”” I must, he said, be sensible of the position of Russia; it could 
not indeed have escaped the observation of Her ajesty’s Government, He 
did not wish to make reproaches, but he must say that considering the friendly 
feelings not professed, but proved, by the Emperor when the invasion of Belgium 
was apprehended, when even the English coasts were considered in danger, he 


harsh, but that ! must observe that there was no parity between the cases: that the 
Emperor at one period had shown himself an enemy to aggression, and that it was 
feeling of the same sort which now bow us into opposition with him; but if 
His Majesty had been unjustly attacke 

be as ready to come to his assistance as we now were to defend the Turks. 

We spoke of England, and Count Nesselrode intimated to me, in guarded 
language, that the favourable opinions which had been expressed by the English 
press of him, and of Baron Brunnow, had produced an unfavourable impression 
in a high quarter here. é; 

I will not close my despatch without stating to your Lordship that even 
now, after the letter addressed to the emperor by the Emperor of the French, 
after the suspension of diplomatic relations between}France and Russia, the same 
miserable deception which has so long been wactised is still carried on. This 
Court insists upon receiving favourable intelligence; and the devotion of some 
of their diplomatic agents of both sexes has been shown by assurances. received 
here from Paris within the last three or four days, as to the sentiments of the 
Emperor of the French towards Russia not being at all of the kind which may 
be inferred from late acts.

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received February 25.) 
(No, 229. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Paris, February 24, 1854. 
T HAD yesterday a conversation of considerable interest with M. Bourré, 
who was formerly French Consul-General in Syria, and who is lately returned 
from the European Provinces of Turkey, whither he had been sent by the 


ee es he 


ina ooo eee 


959 


French Government on a journey of inquiry. M. Bourré is come back pene- 
trated with the danger to which ‘Turkey 1s exposed from the sentiments prevail- 
ing in the Provinces through which he passed, unless some measures are 
immediately taken by the European Powers to counteract the poisou which is at 
work, It is unfortunately to be apprehended that this warning may have come 
too late, 

| will endeavour to follow M. Bourré through the information which he 
cave me. He began with Epirus, where he stated as much danger was to be 
apprehended from the ‘Turkish as from the Christian inhabitants. The Turks 
were all of the old school, imbued with the most inveterate hatred against 
Christians, and consequently ready to rise against any Government whuse policy 
was founded on concessions to the professors of Christianity. 

The Christians here are chiefly of the Greek faith, and having been sub- 
jected to a long series of tyrannical oppression, are among the most discontented 
and the most rebellious of the Sultan's Christian subjects. 

Thessaly and Macedonia are in much the same state as Epirus, but there 
are fewer Turkish inhabitants, 

The object. of the Christians in these Provinces is to be annexed to Greece. 
Linguired of M. Bourré whether he thought that they had been excited by Russian 
emissaries? He replied very positively in the negative. He said that the 
people were led by the priests and schoolmasters, who appeared to have a par- 
ticular and very simple policy of their own in favour of a union with Greece, 
and that they were merely profiting by gircumstances which Russia had pro- 
duced to follow out their own ends, 

Passing to Albania, M. Bourré caid that the worst spirit prevailed there 
against the Porte’s authority, but that it was counterbalanced by the certainty 
which he felt that the Albanians would not be induced to leave their own 
country to serve the insurrection. 

Montenegro M. Bourré looks upon as a Russian fortress, containing 
45,000 or 30,000 soldiers of the most ferocious description. Luckily, he adds, 
the hatred with which they have inspired all their neighbours, renders them 
comparatively harmless. ‘They would not, he thinks, be allowed to cross their 
frontier, Every man capable of bearing arms would fall upon them, Austria 
appears to be a particular object of antipathy to this race. 

Servia is the point from whence M. Bourré anticipates the greatest danger 
to the Porte, and he thinks that sufficient attention has not been paid to the 
‘mmense influence for good or for evil which this country must have upon the 
‘asue of the Oriental question. He blames in very strong language the late pro- 
cceding of the Porte in sending & Commissioner with a firman which, although 
‘ntended to advance the liberties of Servin, appeared nevertheless to make thase 
liberties depend on the will of the Sultan, Now the whole object of Servia has 
heen to establish a real, although nota declared independence. She has long 
refused to have anything to do with firmans, it having been too clearly proved 
to her that the firman of to-day might be revoked by the firman of the morrow. 
It is impossible, M. Bourré observes, that Russia, whose protection has done 
so much for, should not have immense influence in the country, and he sees no 
remedy to this but tovestablish the independence of Servia, under such limits as 
may be thought proper, but under the protectorate of the Four Powers, in which 
Russia might be permitted to participate, whenever the Eastern question is 
settled, ‘ 

Bulgaria, M. Bourré represents to be so completely held in check hy the 
weaence of the ‘Turkish army, that there is no expression of public opinion, 
Nat so in Roumelia, where, about Nessa, Sophia, and Philippoplis, and from 
thence down to the sea const, great disallection exists. 

This state of things is certainly not encouraging, and if it be accurately 
painted, the longer the struggle lasts the greater will be the complication of the 
whole question. But your | ont will understand that Tam inerely narrating 
the opinion of another individual, though of an intelligent man, and ene who 
had some previous knowledge of the affairs of the Kast. ; 

What appears to have struck M. Bourre considerably is the comparative 
amittiness of the Greek population in the countries through which he travelled. 

North of the town of Monastir (Macedonia) he says that the Greek language 1s 
no longer understood ; that the population is Slavonic, and that the inhubitunts 
of those districts call themselves Bulgarians. 


233 


M. Bourré paid a visit to Omar Pasha, whom he had known in Syria. It 
is ustless giving his opinion of a man who has already gained a European 
reputation, and whom M. Bourré only knew previously as a queller of revolt in 
disturbed districts; but I was glad to hear that Omar Pasha had expressed an 
intention of avoiding general actions. 

T asked M, Bourré whether he did not think that the insurreetion which we 
knew unfortunately was daily gaining cround in the European provinces might, 
with judicious treatment, be turned to account by the allies. For instance, if 
the Ambassadors at Constantinople were to send confidential agents to assure 
the insurgents that their interests would be cared for by France and England, 
and that no settlement of the Eastern question would be made which did not 
guarantee them equal privileges with the Turks, at the same time that it was 
‘roved to them that, by aiding Russia and looking to her for protection, they 
risked becoming greater claves than they had been under the Turks, * Would 
it not be possible,’ I asked, “to give the insurrection a different direction, and 
even to induce the insurgents to combat by the side of French and English 
troops in defence of their country? Could they be brought to do so, it would 
be impossible that the Porte should not recompense their fidelity by the most 
ample concessions in their favour He 

M. Bourré replied, that he did not think that such aplan as I had proposed 
would effect much; but that if France and England would send special Com- 
missioners, who should proceed through the different provinces with a certain 
degree of pomp, explaining as they went along the objects of their visit, such a 
demonstration might have the happiest effect. The vanity of the chiefs would 
be gratified by the notice taken of them, the people pleased with the show, and 
eveat benefit might result from it. 

{ will only remark upon this part of M. Bourré’s conversation, that I can 
answer from my own experience for the effect which a display of wealth and 
power invariably produces in the Bast. The arguments of the wisest man in 
the world would produce but little fruit 1f he were dressed in homely garments 
and travelling on foot; while a fool with a costly retinue and other attributes of 
power would find favour, or at least would enforce respect wherever he went.

(Signed) COWLEY.

My Lori, Paris, February 24, 1854. 

GENERAL CANROBERT, who will command one of the divisions of 
the French army about to be sent to Turkey, will set out with his staff in 
a few days for Constantinople to make arrangements for the reception of the 
troops. 

I cannot but congratulate Her Majesty s Government and the general 
officers who will command Fler Majesty's troops that the Emperor's choice 
should have fallen, among others, on General Canrobert. I feel sure that it 
will tend greatly to keep up a good feeling between the two armies. 

I had some conversation with the General yesterday. He told me that 
he had been inquiring a great deal lately about the Russian army, and that 
he did not think it would prove very formidable. ; 

From all he could learn the Russian soldier was a mere machine, without 
enthusiasm or intelligence, but brave from sheer stupidity. No troops could 
advance better under a heavy fire of artillery, They would stand to © man 
to be mowed down; but where quickness of movement or presence of mind 
was required, they were next to useless, “They were so ill fed and so ill 
taken care of that they perished by hundreds of a dysentery known by the 
name of the " Russian fever.” Lf he was to command against them he should 
avoid great uctions, but harass them continually by quick and unexpected 
movements, the fatigue of counteracting which would soon destroy them,

No, 302. 
Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Reeeived February 27.) 


(No. 245. Confidential. ) 


My Lord, 
IN the course of the conversations which 1 have had lately with M. 
de Lhuys on the Eastern question, he hag more than once let fall an opinion that 
advantage must be taken of the impending war with Russia, to put the relations 
of that Power with Turkey ona footing that should not give Europe cause for 
future disquietude. . ios 

The first time he spoke to me in this sense, I replied that 1 fully partict- 
pated his opinion, and that T had never understood the reason why @ declaration 
had been introduced into the notes which defined the future action of England 
and France, and which had been exchanged between the two Governments; 

ledging them to muke peace on the basis of the ‘Turkish propositions approved 
y the Conference of Vienna; for that, in fact, Russia would be no worse off as 
to terms aiter an unsuccessful war than she was at the present moment, when 
war had not commenced, The French Minister rejoined, that that Article had 
been introduced to prove the moderation of the two Governments, and in order 
that Austria and Prussia might not be scared from joining them by a declara- 
tion of great harshness towards Russia; but that it never was intended that that 
Article should be binding in case of active hostilities, and that he had every 
reason to believe that Austria would be the first to Insist upon more stringent 
conditions towards Russia, 

The points, M. Drouyn de Lhuys observed, which he considered should be 
insisted upon, in any ‘Treaty of Peace, were the following : 

1. Such a reconstruction of the Treaty of 1841, as should be a guarantee 
for the integrity and independence af Turkey. 

9. The Protectorate of Servia and of the Danubian Provinces to be 
European, instead of exclusively Russian. 

3 The Protectorate of Christians in general within the Turkish dominions, 
to be exercised in the same way. 

4. The Dardanelles to be no longer shut, so as to exclude foreign ships of 
war from the Black Sea, Such a provision had no other effect than to make the 
Black Sea a Russian lake, and to enable Russia to prepare all her resourees 
against ‘Turkey in secret. 

5. The opening of the Danube to the commerce of the world, which is now 
interdicted by the manoeuvres of Russia to keep the Sulina mouth closed. 

In a subsequent conversation, | asked the French Minister whether it 
might not be possible to introduce into the Convention, which Austria had 
stated herself to be ready to sign, & declaration of the nature he proposed, or, at 
all events, whether that Convention might not supersede the exchange of notes 
between England and France, care being taken that it contained no binding 
engagements in regard to terms of peace. He acquiesced in this idea. 

| had subsequently an opportunity of saying @ word upon the subject to 
the Emperor, who, without going into details, gave me to understand that [His 
Majesty entertained the opinion that, in any Treaty of Peace, guarantees must he 
obtained for the future. 

M, Drouyn de Lhuys has, ‘fT am not mistaken, already written in this 
sense to M. de Bourqueney; and ! understand it to be his intention, in the 
course of a day or two, to address o detailed despatch upon the subject to the 
French Representatives in London, Vienna, and Berlin. 

1 have, &e. 


(Signed) COWLEY.

Inclosure in No. 305. 
Extract from the Vienna‘ Gazette” of February 22, 1854. 


(Translation. } 

IN consequence of the continued hostilities on the south-eastern frontier of 
the Empire, which still present no hope of a specdy peaceful conclusion, His 
Imperial and Royal Apostolic Majesty has felt himself called upon for the com- 
plete protection of the south-eastern frontier of his dominions, to order, in 
addition to the corps d’armée of 25,000 men already stationed in the Servian 
and Banat Provinees, and to the further reserves in the interior of the country, 
a further corps of 25,000 men to be +n readiness to be employed as circum- 
stances may require, so as to be at all times completely enabled to meet all 
disturbances on the frontiers of his States in a manner befitting the events 
occurring. 

[tis Imperial and Royal Apostolic Majesty, whilst seeking in this manner 
fo sectire the independence of his Empire, and its dearest interests, does not 
nevertheless abandon all hope that his indefatigable and increasing efforts may 
prove unsuccessful in promoting by all the strength of his influence the 
re-establishment of that peace so necessary to Europe after the convulsions 
which have gone before, and the cessation of the miseries of a war which 
sess caloulated to loosen the bonds of unity between all States, and in its 
ultimate consequences to menace them all equally with evil.

Excellency on a matter of the deepest importance to our respective Governments 
and to Europe. 

The British Government has for many months anxiously laboured, in 
conjunction with its allies, to effect a reconciliation of differences between Russia 
and the Sublime Porte, and it is with the utmost pain that the British Govern- 
ment has come to the conclusion that one last hope alone remains of averting 
the calamity which has so long impended over Europe. 

Tt rests with the Government of Russia to determine whether that hope 
shall be realized or extinguished ; for the British Government, having exhausted 
all the efforts of negotiation, is compelled to declare to the Cabinet of St. Peters- 
burgh, that if Russia should decline to restrict within purely diplomatic limits 
the discussion in which she has for some time past been engaged with the 
Sublime Porte, and does not, by return of the messenger who is the bearer of 
my present letter, announce her intention of causing the Russian troops under 
the orders of Prince Gortchakoff to commence their march with a view to 
reeross the Pruth, so that the Provinces of Moldavia and Wallachia shall be 
completely evacuated on the 30th of April next, the British Government must 
consider the refusal or the silence of the Cabinet of St. Petersburgh as equivalent 
to a declaration of war, and will take its measures accordingly. 

The messenger who is the bearer of this letter to your Excellency 1s 
directed not to wait more than six days at St. Petersburgh for your re ily; and I 
earnestly trust that he may convey to me an announcement on the part of 
the Russian Government that by the 80th of April next the Principalities will 
cease to be occupied by Russian forces,

THE messenger, Captain Blackwood, will deliver to you a letter from me 
to Count Nesselrode, which you will immediately place in Count Nesselrode’s 
hands, acquainting his Excelleney at the same time that the messenger will be 
yeady to return to England with his reply as soon as his Excellency shall send it 
to you. 

But if, on the expiration of six days from the day on which you deliver my 
letter to Count Nesselrode, his Exeellenc ‘should not have sent to you any 
letter to my address; or if, previously to the expiration of that period, Count 
Nesselrade should inform you that the messenger need not remain at St. Peters- 
burgh, in either of those cases you will direct the messenger to return to England 
with the utmost speed. 

The messenger will deliver to you at the same time a packet from Lord 
Cowley, inclosing a despateh from the French Government to their Consul at 
St. Petersburgh, covering a letter to Count Nesselrode; and you will concert 
with your French colleague for the simultaneous delivery of the two letters to 
the Russian Minister. If the messenger should likewise deliver to you packets 
for the Austrian and Prussian Ministers, you will place any such packets in the 
hands of those Ministers as soon as possible after the messenger's arrival. 

On dispatching the messenger fo England, you will give your French 
colleague an opportunity of sending by him to Berlin or to Calnis, if he should 
wish it, any despatches which he may have for his Government; and you will 
afford the same facility, as far as Berlin, to the Austrian and Prussian Ministers, 
‘1 case the messenger should have brought any despatches for them. 

You will forward to Lord Bloomfield, at Berlin, by the messenger, 4 
statement of the cireumstances under which the messenger will have left 
St. Petersburgh; and as long as you continue at St. Petersburgh you will keep 
Lord Bloomfield as fully informed as possible in regard to all matters of political 
interest.

The Earl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland.

My Lord, Foreign Office, February Q7, 1854. 


| TRANSMIT to your Lordship herewith a copy of a letter* which I have 
addressed to Count Nesselrode requiring the evacuation of the Principalities ; 
and I have to instruct your Lordship to communicate it immediately to Count 
Buol, and to state that Her Majesty's Government having anxiously, but in vain, 
Jahoured for many months in conjunction with the Governments of Austria, 
France, and Prussia, to effect an amicable settlement of the differences between 
Russia and the Porte, must now eonsider that negotiation is at an end; that the 
inadmissible terms upon which the Emperor of Russia will alone negotiate: for 
peace, and the vast scale on which military and naval preparations are proceed- 
ing in Russia, leave no doubt as to the disastrous policy which His Imperial 
Majesty is determined to pursue: 

The dignity of the Powers concerned in these recent transactions, and the 
creat interests now suffering from suspense, forbid any further delay, and require 
that all doubt as to the future should be removed; and as the forcible occu- 
pation of the Principalities was an injury inflicted upon Turkey and an offence 
offered to Europe by Russia, it has appeared proper to Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment, and to that of the Emperor of the French, that the final issue should have 
reference to that act of aggression, and that the Government of Russia should 
he required within a given time to evacuate that portion of the Sultan's 
territory: 

Both Governments, however, are animated by the sincerest desire of 
co-operating with Austria. They acknowledge the paramount necessity of a 
cordial understanding between the Four Powers at this critical juncture of the 
affairs of Europe; and they are convinced that the all-important questions as to 
whether the war is to become general of be contined within narrow limits, and 
whether the contest is to be protracted or peace 5 yeedily restored, must depend 
on the policy of the Four Powers being deeided, vigorous, and united. 

They have consequently determined not to send forward the identic letters 
they have addressed to Count Nesselrode without previous communication to 
the Government of Austria, ‘in the conviction that that Government will 
appreciate the friendly confidence implied by this proceeding. Her Majesty's 
Government bave every reason to hope that the letter to Count Nesselrode will 
meet with the approval of the Austrian Cabinet, and should this fortunately be 
the case they trust that it will be made known by Count Buol to the Cabinet of 
St Petersburgh. It is impossible for your Lordship to overstate the importance 
which Her Majesty’s Government attach to a decision upon which the best 

interests of Europe may depend, 

Your Lordship will place the messenger Blackwood at the disposal of 
Count Buol, and may for that purpose detain him fora few hours; but it is 
desirable that he should eos on his journey to St. Petersburgh with the 
least possible delay. 

You will read this despatch to Count Buol, and you will give his Excellency 
a copy of it. 
Lam, &c. 


(Signed) CLARENDON,

No, 313. 


Lord Cowley to the Barl of Clarendon.—{ Received February 28.) 


(No. 251.) 
My Lord, Paris, February 27, 1854. 


IN a telegraphic despatch dated yesterday afternoon, M. de Bourqueney 
informs M, Drouyn de Lhuys that he had communicated to Count Buol the 
text of the Convention which it was proposed to sign with the Porte. M. de Buol 
had highly approved it, but had at the same time pressed for the signature at 
the Quadruple Convention which France and England had proposed for the 
acceptance of Austria and Prussia. 

Your Lordship will have been made acquainted with the alterations 
proposed by Austria, and which will do away with the objectionable engagement 
to be found in the notes exchanged between the French and English Govern- 
ments, to which more particular allusion was made in my despatch No. 245. 

Your Lordship will also have been told that Austria declines signing the 
summons to evacuate the Principalities which the two Western Powers are 
about to address to the Russian Government, but she will support the demand 
when made, 

M. de Bourqueney observes in the telegraphic despatch alluded to above 
that the Austrian Government will not commit any overt act of hostility against 
Russia until the Western Powers are actually engaged ; that this is a fact on 
which they may rely, for that Austria would not risk the loss of a battle without 
any allies in the field; but he maintains that the active cooperation of Austria 
may be relied on whenever France and England are themselves engaged. 

| asked M. Drouyn de Lhuys whether ‘t would not be worth while to ask 
Austria to explain herself with a little less reserve, Here we are, 1 observed, 
on the point of a war with Russia. Our plans are uncertain and undefined, It 
is obvious that the cooperation of Austria must have an immense influence 
upon them. For instance, if ‘Austria were to say, “ Carry on your operations in 
Europe, and 1 am with you, v et armis; but carry them on in Asia and in the 

Crimea, and I wait to see the result,” we could hardl hesitate which we 
should attempt. Or we might tell her that our plans would depend very much 
on what she did, and that as a friend she ought to explain herself more clearly 3 
that we would respect her confidence by observing the utmost secrecy, if she 
desired it; but that really before the Commanders-in-chief started, they ought to 
know whether they were to look for active cooperation, or merely for a 
favourable neutrality. | 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys will write immediately in this sense to M, de Bour- 
queney, telling him to profit by the time which must elapse before the answer 
from Russia to our summons can be received, to ascertuin distinctly the exact 
intentions of Austria. 

I have, &c- 
(Signed) COWLEY.

No. 314. 
Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received February 28.) 


(No. 74.) 
My Lord, Berlin, February 25, 1854. 

WHEN I called to-day on Baron Manteuffel, the Austrian Minister was 
with him. I was in hopes that Count Thun had been charged with some com- 
munication connected with the Eastern question, and an announcement perhaps 
of the intentions of Austria to act more energetically with England and France , 
but was surprised that he had not made any communication whatever on this all- 
absorbing subject, and that his conversation had turned on the internal affairs of 
Germany. 

Baron Manteuffel told me that he had inquired of Count Thun if he had 
not received instructions from Vienna bearing on the position which the two 
Maritime Powers might shortly assume towards Russia, and that the Austrian 
Minister appeared to be in total ignorance of the intentions of his Government, 
and quite scoffed at the idea of a” rapprochement ” between his Government 
and that of France and England; so much so, indeed, that Baron Manteuttel 
scarcely knew how to reconcile the language 1 had held on the subject with 
that of the Austrian Representative, for Count Thun stated his conviction that 
rumours which had reached the Exchange of Berlin from Vienna to the effect that 
Austria was about to participate actively with us on the Eastern question, and 
that an army was ordered into Transylvania for the purpose of checking the 
Russian forces, were completely false. 

In the meantime Baron Manteuffel has written by telegraph to Vienna arch 
requested Count Arnim to report instantly the result of his inquiries of Count 
Buol on this subject, and I incline to think that. the future conduct of the 
Prussian Government will be a good deal influenced by the news which must 
coon arrive from Vienna, though I fear it will lag far behind that of Austrin. 
Indeed, Baron Manteuffel can scarcely bring himself to believe the extent to 
which the Austrian Government seems disposed to carry its policy. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) BLOOMFTELD,

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received February 28.) 


(No. 83.) 
My Lord, Berlin, February 25, 1854. 

BARON MANTEUFFEL has informed me that he has written this evening 
to Count Arnim at Vienna, upon the subject of the more decided policy which 
it is supposed the Austrian Government is about to adopt in the affairs of the 
Fast, and that he has expressed the satisfaction of the Prussian Government at 
the interests of Germany on the Danube being likely to be so warmly espoused. 
His Excellency appeared gratified at the course which Austria was apparently 
about to follow, aud he gave me to understand that he had thought it necessary 
to make this communication to the Imperial Court for fear of its being spread 
abroad by Russian or other agents that, because Prussia was not disposed to 
take un active part in these supposed measures, she was either indifferent to 
them or that she disapproved of them. Prussia, he said, must take a deep 
interest in everything which so deeply concerned the welfare of Germany as the 
mouths of the Danube, and he was glad that this question was likely to be 
seriously considered and strenously supported,

reflection might bring about o modification of the opinions which he now

My Lord, Vienna, February 22, Bh. 

IN a recent conversation with Count Buol, his Excellency remarked to me 
that, during the whole of the discussions. upon the Eastern question, the truth 
had not been told to the Emperor Nicholas; for he had always been permitted 
to believe that the German Governments would side with him, Baron 
Meyendorff, who since the month of April had constantly been told that 
Austria never could permit the humiliation of ‘Turkey, had never reported the 
case ag it really stood, He said that the Emperor Nicholas had now treated 
the Emperor Francis Joseph without proper regard, considering all the friendly 
exertions His Majesty had made to place the Russian Sovereign in a position to 
repair the false policy he had pursued. If he had accepted the modifications ot 
the Vienna note, he would have had a Turkish Ambassador at St. Petersbur h, 
and would have received every satisfaction he could have required; but the 
time was now gone by. 

Count Buol looked upon the determination of the British and Vrench 
Governments to send a corps of troops to the assistance of ‘Turkey, 03 of the 
highest consequence 5 and never, he said, had he felt greater piesa than on 
learning that Lord Raglan was chosen to command the English force. Tt was 
very important that his name should be associated with this measure ; it would 
be a demonstration which the revolutionary party could not mistake if they 
looked forward with any hope for their own projects in the active hostilities 
which might arise. He hoped Lord Raglan would pass through Vienna on his 
way to the seat of his command, ‘The Emperor has expreased himself to me in 
thi: same sense. 

With regard to the insurrection ‘ the Turkish provinces bordering on 
Greeee, Count Buol expressed great alarm lest they should spread to the 
provinces adjoining them. He said that they were toa far from the Austnan 
fonticr to permit of the action of the Austrian troops, but the Turkish 
Government should forthwith send a force to occupy them,

to a passage in & despatch of M. Drouyn de Lhuys, which stated that Austria

and being now acquainted with the sentiments of his Government, he would, no

Count Buol said the same with regard to the Russian tendencies attributed

ever the Governments of England and France had determined upon the time 
they would take if the declared war, if this was done by announcing a term 
for’ the evacuation of the Prineipalities, he would support that measure at 
St, Petersburgh. 

Count Buol said, that when Austria took the engagements above referred to, 
France and the allies would be asked to take similar ones for the maintenance of 
tranquillity in Italy, He said he should not require any extensive engagements, 
as he felt confidence in the French Government, which having happily put 
down insurrection, would not suffer her ally to be menaced by revolution while 
engaged in concert with her; but some act of assurance would be asked for, su

The Earl of Clarendon to Lord Bloomfield. 


(No. 40.) 
Sir, Foreign Office, February 28, 1854. 

WITH reference ta your Lordship's despatch No. 74 of the 22nd instant, 
reporting the substance of your conversation with Baron Manteuffel in com- 
munieating to his Excellency the notes which have been exchanged between Her 
Majesty's Government and the Government of France, in consequence of the 
rejection by the Emperor of Russia of the proposals of the Vienna Conference, 
] jaws to inform you that Her Majesty’s Government approve your language on 
this occasion. I have only to repeat that Her Majesty's Government are not 
desirous to press unduly upon Prussia, and still less to recommend any course 
of action that would be prejudicial to her interests ; but as England 1s equally 
concerned with Prussia in restricting the theatre of war to the narrowest limits, 
and rendering its duration as short as possible, Her Majesty’s Government 
ihink it is of vital importance that the policy of the two countries should he 
identically the same. ‘The Four Powers have solemnly recorded their opinion 
that the terms offered by the Porte were just and reasonable, and such as should 
be aecepted by Russia; but the Emperor has not even noticed them, and has 
sent to Vienna proposals of his own, which the Conference declared to be inad- 
missible, and not of a character that would justify their being transmitted to 
Constantinople. 

Thus the Emperor of Russia, who might, without loss of honour or dignity, 
have preserved the general peace, has preferred to involve Europe in war; for 
that calamity must now be considered as mevitable. 

The Four Powers have exhausted every effort to maintain peace, and they 
should now use every effort to restore it. A firm and decided policy, prompt 
and vigorous action, may prevent war from becoming general, and may bring it 
to a speedy termination. Weakness and vacillation cannot but lead to the 
pecuniary exhaustion and the protracted contest that the Prussian Government 
apprehend. It is therefore with regret and disappointment that Her Majesty's 
Government learn that although we may hereafter count upon her cooperation, 
yet that at the present moment Prussia 1s not prepared to make common cause 
with us. 

Lam, &

(Signed) CLARENDON.

Inclosure $ in No. 322. 
Consul Michele to Sir G. H. Seymour. 
Sir, St. Petersburgh, February 20, 1854. 


| HAVE had the honour to receive your Excellency’s despatch, of the 
18th instant, apprizing me that your passports having been forwarded ta you 
from the Chancellerie d’Etat, you propose leaving St. Petersburgh with the 
other members of Her Majesty's Mission, in the course of a few days; that the 
interruption of diplomatic relations between the two Governments does not, 
however, bring with it that of commercial relations ; and that itis, your Excel- 
lency believes, the intention of Her Majesty's Government that for the present, 
at all events, I should remain at St. Petersburgh in the discharge of my habitual 
duties. And further, that in the event of any case arising in which the special 
intervention of any intermediate authority should become necessary on behalf of 
any of our fellow-subjects, instructing me to address myself to Baron de Plessen, 
His Majesty's (of Denmark) Envoy Extraordinary and Minister Plenipotentiary, 
Her Majesty's Government being desirous that any British subject in Russia 
should be placed under the protection of the Danish Minister, an arrangement 
that has met with the approbation of the Imperial Government. 

In acknowledging the receipt of your Excellency’s communication, [ think 
it right to state that I am without instructions from Her Majesty’s Government — 
as to the nature of the duties that may, possibly, devolve upon me after the 
departure of Her Majesty’s Mission, “duties” that your Excellency described 
to the British merchants on Thursday last, as “ of a more onerous and respon- 
sible character?’ than those I have already had the honour of fulfilling during 
my residence in this country. While, therefore, it seems that increased lnbour 
and responsibility are likely to devolve upon me, 1 may suddenly be deprived, 
by the commencement of hostilities between Russia and Great Britain, and the 
consequent closing of the port of Cronstadt to British merchant-vessels, of 
nearly two-thirds of my ordinary revenue! 

Under these circumstances | have to request that, in conveying to Her 
Majesty’s Government ny willingness to remain at my post, and to exert 
myself to the utmost to afford assistance and protection to our fellow-countrymen 
in Russia, your Excellency will do me the favour to represent my position to 
Her Majesty’s Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, who, I feel assured, would 
not desire me to remain in this country in the altered position in which | am 
placed—a position necessarily entailing upon me increased expense —without 
assigning me such an augmentation of income as will not only supply the 
deficiency caused by the cessation of British trade with this port, but also 
enable me to meet the heavier disbursements that a state of war cannot fail to 

necessitate. 
I have, &e. 


(Signed) Cc, EASTLAND DE MICHELE.

(No, 175. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Si. Petersburgh, February 21, 1894. 

COUNT NESSELRODE called upon me on the 18th instant for the 
purpose of taking leave of me and my family. 

A conversation took place in which, although to terms the least displeasing 
and aggressive, he defended the conduct of the Imperial Cabinet at the expense 
of that pursued by Her Majesty’s Government, 

I told Count Nesselrode that, not being prone to argue, it was not at the 
moment of leaving that | would recommence a discussion which was so little 
likely to bring our opinions into accordance ; but that, as he regarded the case 
from his * point-de vue,” 1 did not hesitate to follow his example. As | view 
the case, M. le Comte, I said, all the mischief which lias arisen has been pro- 
duced by false calculation and erroneous information, You undertook an affair 
the serious consequences of which you did not foresee; and whilst irom one 
quarter you were told that the feeling manifested in England was temporary 
and fictitious, yon were assured from another that a bond fide allianes between 
England and France was a matter of positive impossibility, ‘There is the whole 
ease in a few words. 

Count Nesselrade who, as is now habitual to him, appeared dejected, 
observed, us he has done several times, that he still cannot bring his mind to 
“realize” the idea of awar between England and Russia, and, connected with 
this idea, expressed his regret that Baron Brannow had not established himself in 
Brussels instead of Darmstadt. 

He took Jeave of me in the most friendly manner, and left me under the 
full conviction that his opinions, if they could be made known, agree much more 
closely with mine than with the official language which he 1s compelled to 


employ.

No. 325. 
Sir G. H. Seymour to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received February 28.) 


(No. 176, Secret and Confidential.) 
My Lord, St. Petersburgh, February 21, 1894. 


1SHOULD have unbounded satisfaction in making the following communi- 
eation to your Lordship, were I not compelled to request earnestly that it may 
be regarded as strictly confidential. 

Not having seen Count Orloff, the Grand Master of Police, since his return 
from Vienna, | waited on him yesterday, to recommend the English who 

urpose remaining at St. Petersburgh to his goodwill and protection. 

The application was taken in very good part, and a communication respecting 
the deplorable state of affairs having ensued, Count Orloff observed that he 
owed me an explanation. 

I might, he said, remember that at the commencement of Count Menchikofl's 
mission he had assured me positively that the demands to be made upon the 
Turks related solely to the holy places. Before you leave St. Petersburgh, 
accordingly, Count Orloff said, Lam anxious to declare to you upon my honour 
that 1 misled you unconsciously. 1 had been told the mission had one sole 
object, and having been misled myself, I misled you. 

To this somewhat remarkable confession I can add, and upon the most 
certain authority, another which is still more striking; viz., that a few days ago 
the Emperor himself stated to Count Orloff that he had been misled as to the 
rights which were secured to him by the Treaty of Kainardji, and that his 
conduct would have been different but for the error into which he had been led. 
The person whose opinion upon this point was overruled and put aside was, as 
your Lordship will recollect, myself; the persons, if I am correctly informed, by 
whose representations the Cabinet were misled are the Greeks, Catacazi and 
Zographio. 

I need not observe to your Lordship that these tardy confessions, which 
justify to the fullest extent the information which at the time I had the honour 
of stating to your Lordship, would be of inestimable value to me if they could 
be er to public know edge ; but I feel obliged to repeat my request as to 
their not being divulged, as they would materially affect the position of one of 
the most honest men among the few with whom I have been brought in contact 
in Russia. I shall not, I hope, be thought presumptuous if | remark that what 
I have just related confirms fully not only statements which | have made but 
opinions which I have expressed to Her Majesty's Government. Nothing 
certainly was required to reconcile me to departure from St. Petersburgh; had 
anything of the kind been required, the want has now been supplied. 

| have, &c. 


(Signed) G. H. SEYMOUR,

No. 348, 
Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recetved March 4.) 


(No. 93, Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, March 1, 1854. 


BARON MANTEUFFEL has related to me confidentially the substance 
of a conversation which ‘he had just had with the King on the attitude which 
the Emperor might adopt towards Prussia if war was shortly declared. His 
Majesty appears to have expressed his conviction that the character of the 
Emperor was that of vindietive navure that it was not impossible but that his 
attention might be immediately directed against this country ; that there was 
still a large disposable force near St. Petersburgh and in Poland, consisting of 
upwards of 200,000 men which might be employed in this way ; and further, 
that it might be found perhaps more convenient for Russia to fight her battles 
on the Eastern question in Germany than on the Danube, where the troops 
would die of fever.and starvation if not able to advance with rapidity. 

‘These impressions of the King, Baron Manteuffel suid, might work well for 
the great cause in which we had embarked ; for if His Majesty conceived that 
there was a possibility of Germany being exposed to immediate danger, he 
would be less inclined to keep out of the alliance about to be concluded between 
Austria, England, and France, and more disposed to take an active share in 
military operations. 

{ have, &e. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD,

My Lord, Berlin, March 1, 1854. 

THE Austrian Minister communicated yesterday to Baron Manteutiel the 
draft of a Convention which his Government is ready to sign with England, 
France, and Prussia, by which the Four Powers shall! bind themselves to unite 
their efforts for the pacification of the Mast. 

His Excellency told me that he had not this paper at hand at this moment, 
or he would show it to me, but that he believed the modifications prepared by 
‘Austria were known to your Lordship, and he was happy to be able to assure 
me that he had reason to hers that the King would shortly be brought to agree 
ta the Convention, if not entirely, at all events to the essential points contained 
in it. 

asked Baron Manteutfel whether he had not received from the Austrian 
Minister some communication of the ulterior intentions of the Cabinet of Vienna 
in the event of Russia attempting to cross the Danube, and also whether nothing 
had been said to him by Count Thun as to the summons to evacuate the 
Principalities, which France and England proposed to address to the Russian 
Government, and in which Austria had expressed a willingness to join? His 
Excellency said that Count Thun had not said one word on the subject, and that 
Count Arnim bad not written to him at all. 

It is right that I should inform your Lordship that the French Mimster has 
received from his Government reports of M. de Rourqueney’s late conversation 
with Count Buol, and he has also received direct from Baron de Bourquency a 
copy of the Convention which Austria is ready to sign. 

Not being, however, in possession of any instructions from Paris, he has not 
communicated further with Baron Manteutfel, and has been prompted to this 
course in order not to press the matter without me, but we have only delayed 
our co-operation in this matter until we are made acquainted with the wishes of 
our respective Governments. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD.

| HAVE the honour to inclose to your Lordship herewith in translation, 
copy. ofa manifesto issued by the Emperor of Russia, bearing date February 9, 
old style, 


[ have, &e. 
(Signed) BLOOMFIELD. 


——_ _—_—— 


Inclosure in No, 351. 


Manifesto. 


Translation.) 
by the grace of God, we, Nicholas I, Emperor and Autocrat, &c., make known 
publicly. 


WE have already informed our beloved and faithful subjects of the cause of 
our misunderstanding with the Ottoman Porte. 

Since then, notwithstanding the commencement of hostilities, it has not 
ceased to be our sincere desire, as it is also still our desire, to put a stop to the 
shedding of blood, We indulged the hope that time and reflection would con- 
vince the Turkish Government of its delusion, engendered by crafty instigations, 
in which our just demands founded on Treaties were represented as an attempt 
against her independence, concealing projects of agerandizement, But our 
expectations have hitherto been in vain. ‘The English and French Governments 
have taken up the cause of Turkey, and the appearance of the combined fleets 
at Constantinople served as a further encouragement to the stubbornness of the 
Porte. Finally, both the Western Powers, without an previous declaration of 
war, have taken their fleets into the Black Sea, dec aring their intention to 
protect the Turks, and to forbid our ships of war a free navigation for the 
defence of our coasts. 

After such an unheard-of proceeding on the part of civilized Governments, 
we have recalled our Embassies from England and France, and suspended all 
political relations with these Powers. 

And thus England and France have ranged themselves by the side of 
the enemies of Christianity against Russia fighting for the orthodox faith. 

But Russia will not alter its divine mission, and if enemies fall upon its 
frontier, we are ready to meet them with the firmness which our ancestors have 
bequeathed us. Are we not now the same Russian nation of whose deeds of 
valour the momorable events of the year 1812 bear witness? May the Almighty 
assist us to prove this by deeds! And in this trust, taking up arms for our 
persecuted brethren professing the Christian fuith, we will exclaim with the 
whole of Russia, with one heart, “ O Lord, our Saviour, whom have we to 
fear? May God arise, and His enemies be dispersed.” 

Given at St. Petersburgh, on the 9th day of February, in the year of our 
Lord 1854, and the 29th of our reign. 

Signed by the Emperor's own hand, 
(L.S.) NICHOLAS,

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received March 4.) 


(No. 100.) 
My Lord, Berlin, March 2, 1854. 


IN obedience to the instructions contained in your Lordship’s despatch 
No. 38 of the 27th ultimo, I have this day delivered to Baron Manteuffel copies 
of that despatch and of the letter which your Lordship has addressed to Count 
Nesselrode requiring the evacuation of the Danubian Principalities. 

I read both these papers to his Excellency, and he seemed to concur 
entirely in the reasons which have induced Her Majesty’s Government to take 
this step. He said he should communicate them to the King to-morrow, and 
submit to his Majesty, at the same time, the draft of a despatch to General 
Rochow, instructing that Minister to support in strong terms the summons 
which has been addressed to the Russian Government; but he was unable to 
say, until he received the King’s orders, what terms would be given to the 
communication, and I can, therefore, only add, that he assured me there should 
he no delay in the matter, and that the despatch would probably reach St. 
Petersburgh as soon as the English messenger. 

I placed Captain Blackwood at his Excellency's disposal according to your 
Lordship's instructions, but on finding that there would probably be a delay, 
if he waited for the Prussian despatches, which might be detrimental to Her 
Majesty’s service, 1 decided on directing the messenger to proceed on his 
journey this night, and he has just started for Vienna.

(No. 102. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, March 2, (854, 

WITH reference to your Lordship's instructions to urge the Prussian 
Government to sign the Convention relative to the Eastern question which has 
already been agreed to by the Governments of England, Franee, and Austria, | 
have the honour to inform your Lordship that Baron Manteutfel is unremitting 
in his endeavours to bring the King to authorize Count Arnim to concur in it, 
but that he has hitherto failed in his efforts to do so, His Excellency and Count 
Pourtales were for two hours this day arguing the question with His Majesty, 
who raised objection after objection to it, and seemed at one moment resolved 
not to bind himself to uny measure which would tie his hands hereafter and 
fetter his liberty of action. 

Baron Manteuffel, whom I saw just after his return from the Palace, told 
me that the King was quite unreasonable, and that his imagination had been so 
worked upon by reports which His Majesty had received of the forces which the 
Emperor of Russia might dispose of to attack the Prussian dominions, and more 
particularly by intelligence which had reached him that orders had been sent 
from St. Petersburgh to stop the march of some of the troops from Poland 
towards the Danube, that any one who did not know the King’s character as 
well as he did would consider it useless to continue discussing the subject 
further with His Majesty; but his Excellence added that there were, nevertheless, 
some indications which lead him to hope that he may yet obtain his assent to 
the greater part of the Convention, though he scarcely expects that he will agree 
to the whole of it, particularly to the Sth Article. Still he did not despair, and 
should resume his task to-morrow, in the hove that his next efforts would be 
more successful, for he himself ardently wished that the Four Powers should act 
together in this matter. Tt appears ve me quite evident that the Prussian

manders in Moldavia and Wallachia, who are openly forming a legion composed 
of the subjects of the Sultan, and now amounting to nearly 3,000 men, for the 
purposes of the war carried on against the Turkish Empire, and which Count 
Buol characterises as a most revolutionary measure, and which he has instructed 
Count Esterhazy to represent in that light to Count Nesselrode.

The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon —(Received March 5.) 


(Telegraphic.) Vienna, March 4, 1654. 


“BLACKWOOD arrived here only this morning. At the same time 
Baron Meyendorff received a Russian courier bearing the answer of the Russian 
Government to the proposals taken by Count Orloff from [here 2] Count 
Buol assembled the Conference. He said the Russian answer now arrived con- 
sisted of preliminaries to be sent to Constantinople. They accepted the evacu- 
ation of the Principalities after the acceptance of these preliminaries, but they 
differ from those set forth in the Protocol of the 13th of January. He begged 
that the preliminaries might be examined in Conference. In the meantime he 
entreated that the messenger might be delayed. He cannot write in support of 
the summons without having examined these new proposals with the Conference, 
and he is most anxious to learn your Lordship’s opinions and those of the French 
Cabinet under the present circumstances. Count Buol will write his despatch 
in support of the summons and be ready to send it in case you should decide 
that the messenger is to proceed at once, but he wishes to have your sanction in 


the question. To escape the reproach of acting with precipitation, the French 
Ambassador and I consented to delay the messenger till Monday; we consider 
it of such extreme importance to remain in perfect union with Count Buol, who 
evinces extreme anxiety for your Lordship’s opinion at this crisis. 

A copy of the preliminaries will be transmitted by the post to-morrow,

réuni la Conférence, et lui a lu la piéee contenant les dits préliminaires. “Je 
n’exprime aucune opinion sur ce document,” a dit M. de Buol, ‘mais avant 
d'expédier la sommation, les Cabinets de Londres et de Paris ne devraient-ils pas 
étre informés de son arrivée par le télégraphe? La rédaction de mo dépéche au 
Comte Esterhazy me place dans un extréme embarras, car je préjuge seul, en 
l'écrivant, opinion des autres Cours. Jai pus la parole pour faire ressortir les 
différens que je discernais, au premier coup d’ceil entre, le Protocole du 13 Janvier 
et les préliminaires Russes, Ces différens m'ont paru décider irrevocablement 
du rejet.” Le Comte Buol n'a fait aucune objection, mais en insistant pour que

My Lord, Paris, March 4, 1854. 


M. DROUYN DE LHUYS received the day before yesterday a telegraphic 
despatch from Berlin, stating that the great hesitation felt by the King of 
Prussia to sign the proposed Quadruple Convention arose from an apprehension 
that if he took so positive a step the Emperor of Russia would attack him at 
once, and that Prussia was not prepared for that attack. M.de Manteuffel 
did not share this apprehension, but hinted that if an English and French 
expeditionary corps were to be disembarked in the Baltic it might decide the 
King to take more energetic proceedings. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys answered M. de Moustier yesterday by telegraph that 
he could not understand these hesitations, and that he thought it would be more 
prudent in the Prussian Government to place a corps d’armée voluntarily on 
the Vistula now than to be forced hereafter to place one on the Rhine. 

Your Lordship will understand the hint intended to be conveyed,
