Inclosure in No. 364. 
Mr, Lumley to Lord Bloomfield. 


My dear Lord Bloomfield, Berlin, March 4, 1854 


‘THE fact of my having quitted St. Petersburgh forty hours after the departure 
of Sir H, Seymour will, | hope, prove sufficient excuse for addressing these lines 
to you, though my news will, I fear, be of very little interest from the length of 
my journey, consequent on the dreadful state of the Riga road. 

On the 22nd ultimo I called, by appointment, on Count Nesselrode, who 
received me with great kindness and condiality, and expressed his sincere regret 
at the circumstances attending the departure of Her Majesty's Mission. 

He had hoped, his Excellency said, that the last. propositions made by the 
Russian Mission in London would have been received in a very different 
Maier. 

| asked Count Nesselrode if he referred to Baron Brunnow's last commu- 
nication on the subject of the orders sent to the Admirals in the Black 5ea. 
He replied in the affirmative, and sad, that if Her Majesty’s Government had 


273 


taken that opportunity to declare their intention of preventing a collision 
between the Russian and Ottoman naval forces, and, while allowing Turkish 
ships to proceed from one port to another had secured the same liberty to 
Russian vessels, such a declaration, Count Nesselrode stated, would have left 
the two Governments in a very different position, the Ministers would have 
remained at their respective posts, and perhaps some means might have been 
found to employ the time thus gained in behalf of peace. 

I ventured to observe to Count Nesselrode that Baron Brunnow's commu- 
nication had not been considered so much in the light of a proposal for a naval 
armistice as in that of a demand for an explanation of the verbal communication 
which had been made to him by Sir H. Seymour, and that Lord Clarendon’s 
note to Baron Brunnow was a reply to that demand, and not to any proposition 
of the nature to which he alluded. 

T then asked Count Nesselrode if he really saw no other means of main- 
taining peace. None, his Excellency replied, unless Her Majesty's Government 
show themselves more concilitory than they have lately proved. But, I said, 
M. le Comte, | hear that proposals have been received from Vienna, since Count 
Onloff’s return; and they are reported to be of such a nature as to raise the 
expectation of a pacific solution of this question. It is true, Count Nesselrode 
replied, that we have received communication from Vienna, but its terms are 
extremely vague—it is, in fact, a proposal that we should state the preliminaries 
upon which we will treat for peace. And what can these be but those which Count 
Orloff has already proposed—terms which are based on the Vienna note and the 
declaration of Olmutz? by which we usk for nothing new, for nothing but that 
to which we are entitled, and the justice of which has been universally acknow- 
ledged. But surely, I replied, M. le Comte, the article relating to the refugees 
is a new feature, and one that raises a question which has already caused great 
embarrassment,-and which it was hoped had been set at rest. Well, Count 
Nesselrode replied, I can only say that if our propositions had been entertained, 
that article would not have stood in the way of an arrangement; its acceptance 
would not have been made a sine qua non. 

In reply to my question as to whether any answer had been sent to the 
last proposals from Vienna, Count Nesselrode answered that one was being 
prepared, and would probably be ready in two or three days. 

On the 23rd I paid a visit to General Rochow. The Chancellor, he said, he 
had just left him to read over the “projet de preliminaires '’ (drawn up by 
M. Labensky) before submitting it to the Emperor, ‘This draft was based on 
the proposals made through Count Orloff at Vienna, and the Vienna protocol of 
January 13: the objectionable Article V of the Russian propositions had been 
omitted, and it would leave St. Petersburgh on the 25th ultimo. General 
Rochow allowed that the reference backwards and forwards to Constantinople and 
St. Petersburgh would be frequent and demand a considerable time, and | could 
not but infer from his manner that this very delay was the principal object in 
view. The General said further, that Count Nesselrode had expressed great 
satisfaction at the presence of Marshal Paskiewitch at St. Petersburgh, and had 
stated that his endeavours to maintain peace had received great support from the 
very decided opinion the Marshal had given against the passage of the Danube 
by the Russian army. 

On the 24th ultimo, half-an-hour before leaving St, Petersburgh, I saw the 
Swedish Chargé d'Affaires, from whom I learnt that Count Nesselrode had sent 
for Baron Plessen, and had told him that he had reason to believe that the 
English Government intended. to recruit for Baltic pilots in Danish harbours, 
and that if such a proceeding were tolerated by the Danish Government he 
should consider it as an act of direct hostility against Russia. 

Count Piper also informed me that 4 communication, of the nature of 
which he was not aware, had also been made two days before to the Swedish 
Government; he suspects, however, that it relates to eoul, as M. de Maltzoff, 
one of the rédacteurs of the Foreign Office, had spoken on the subject, the 
night before, in a manner which lead him to suppose that a declaration would 
shortly published, or that o communication would shortly be made to the 
Swedish and Danish Governments to the effect that coal will be considered by 
the Russian Government os “ contrebande de guerre.” 

During the journey through the Baltic provinces, it was impossible not to 
be struck with the almost total absence of military.

Inclosure in No. 366. 


Préois of Intelligence from the “ Vossische Zeitung,” dated Vienna, Bucharest, 
Galatz, and the Lower Danube. 


THE Russians are preparing two pontoon bridges at Dzurdzmoo. Heavy 
artillery has arrived at ‘Giurgevo, and an unremitting fire has been opened on 
Rustchuk. The Turkish reinforcements from Shumla have arrived at Matchin, 


275 


Rustchuk, and Silistria, and an attack on their part 15 expected. The Russian 
batteries at Giurgevo, erected by the order of General Schilder, have, on the 12th 
of February, so much damag the Turkish vessels assembled in Rustchuk for 
the purpose of effecting a passage, 2 to render them unfit for service. 
Eighteen Russian batteries have been constructed between Galatz and 
Ibraila: and 100 waggons with pontoons °° assembled at the former place. 
The Turks pass over the Danube nearly every day, and sanguinary conthets 
are continually taking place. It would appear that the effects of the insurrec- 
tion of the Greeks, which is spreading, are beginning to be felt by the Curkish 
army. According to some reports, the Albanians and Arnouts demanded to be 
dismissed, or to be sent home; and Omar Pasha has been obliged to weaken 
himself by dispatching some of his regular forces against the Greeks. Others 
again say that the army of the Danube is taking no notice of the insurrectionary 
movements. 
General Schilders has left Giurgevo for Oltenitza, which has been occupied 
by the Turks from Turtukai. 
The ‘Turks have, on the 11th of February, attacked the Russian batteries 
at Braila, but could not maintain a footing on the Wallachian side of the 


river. 

In Little Wallachia the Russians are at least 50,000 strong. ‘They have 
completely surrounded Kalafat, and their nearest posts are three hours’ march 
from the ‘Turkish fortifications. The Turks having placed a post of 4,000 men 
before the village of Ciuperceni, the most easterly point of their fortifications, the 
Russians resolved to drive them back within the entrenchments. On the night 
of the 16th and 17th, two Russian columns, each of from 4,000 to 5,000 men, 
moved from both sides against Ciuperceni. One of them, missing its way in the 
dark, met the other column, and mistaking it for the enemy, opened fire upon it, 
which was immediately returned. The action continued till daybreak before the 
Russians perceived their error. The loss is said to amount to 300 men killed 
and wounded.

Inclosure in No. 307. 


Memorandum of a Conversation with the King of Prussia on the drd of 
March, 1854. 


1 SHOULD find it extremely difficult, to give even an outline of a Con- 
yersation which lasted an hour and twenty minutes, during which time the King 
spoke nearly the whole time, and pon a great variety of subjects. 

His Majesty appeared to me in great alarm as to the present aspect of 
affairs. He seems possessed with the notion of the storm which is getting up 
being likely to break upon Prussia, and is equally afraid of his Imperial brother- 
in-law and of the Emperor of the French.

He is resolved, firmly resolved, to keep to his position of neutrality, but 
conceives that even this resolution may incur the displeasure of the Emperor 
Nicholas, and lead to the attack of the east provinces of Prussia. Already His 
Majesty said there were 250,000 Russian troops in Poland, and their number 
might be easily doubled. An attack on the part of Russia would of course 
oblige him to take up arms, und he could do so effectually ; in six weeks he 
could have 470,000 men in the field, not in the Russian style on paper, but 
470,000 men well armed, and prepared to fight to the death. 

The King’s great fear, however, is that inspired by the plans which he 
imputes to the Emperor Napoleon. ‘That man, he said, is bent upon changing 
the map of Europe, and will make a sudden turn in his policy. As an ass can- 
not beeome a mule, or a mule cannot be changed into a horse, neither can the 
Emperor Napoleon change his nature, or modify the plans which he formed years 
ago, For that reason, independently of my horror of shedding blood, and of 
engaging in a cause Which is 80 indifferent to me as that of Turkey, [ must 
keep aloof, if possible, and husband the thulers and the lives of my Prussians; 
all my sympathies are with the Queen and with England; but I cannot draw 
my sword now, or sign a summons which would be equivalent to a declaration 
of war, You may call me a quaker if you please, but it will not alter my deter- 
mination: and the time may come when you will be glad to see me coming to 
your assistance with 4,000,000 or 5,000,000 men, as assuredly | would do in 
ease of teed, With respect to the importunities of France, they affect me still 
loss. I have the greatest sympathy for England. | have none for France 
nud the Emperor Napoleon, and | tell you ¢o frankly. 

I observed betore, that the King is full of anxiety and ap rehensions; these 
feara are of all kinds. He is convinced that the Emperor Nicholas is particu- 
larly excited (monté) against Prussia and against himself; that the fate of 
Turkey is already decided, and that the pnechousey forces in the Baltic and 
the Black Sea are about to be exposed to the greatest danger, The predomi- 
nating fear, and one which [in vain endeavoured to combat, is that ofa Russian 
attack, The Russians, the King 1s convinced (and Lam sure without reason), 
will leave the Danube to carry war across the Vistula, 

| used every attempt to proye to His Majesty that fortune favoured him, 
and that he had now an opportunity, suchas he never could have expected, for 
taking precautions against on avalanche which at any moment may come down 
upon his home and country 5 that sooner or later the wings of the Northern 
Eagle must be clipped, and that the occasion was most favourable ; that Russia 
was evidently entering the aggressive phasis ; that 20 first-class ships-d-hélice 
at Cronstadt, not to speak of a like number at Sevastopol, could only indicate 
an intention of being able to despateh armies at a few days’ notice ta any point ; 
to Pomerania for example; and that if Europe allowed these »reparations to be 
matured by a country of enormous military power, and without colonies or 
trade, no neighbour of Russia would hencelorward be able to pass a day in 
tranquillity. 

‘To all this the King only replied by protestations of his love of peace, and 
of affection for his Lmperial brother-in-law ; not, however, he said, but that the 
Emperor behaves extremely ill to me; the expressions about me are such, that 
my servants liave been obliged to tell him that. they cannot stay in the room if 
he persists in nsing such language, Neéanmoins je pleure, je sanglotte, quand 
je pense a lui et aux embarras qu'il s'est créé, 

Her Majesty’s Government, the King said, had no confidence in him, he 
was aware of that; but though he regretted it, he would prove that he deserved 
confidence; what he promised he would fulfil; and he would repeat that, as all 
his sympathies were with England, so might his assistance be counted upon by 
her in case of need. 

‘The King spoke of some of his plans. He proposed sending an officer to 
Russia to suggest to the Emperor to come forward with the proposal of 
evacuating the Prineipalities on the 14th of April, of declaring himself ready 
then to assemble a Congress at which his disputes with Turkey might be settled. 
« What,” he would ask, “did | think of this scheme?” I replied, that 1 was 
certain the Emperor would not listen to it, and even if he did, I doubted very 
much whether it would be entertained by the other Powers. His Majesty had 
the further intention of dispatching some trusty person in a few days to London, 


207 


whom he did not yet know, for the purpose of making known and explaining his 
resolutions to Her Majesty's Government. | 

With regard to the Conference at Vienna, His Majesty did not know how 
to act. He was willing that his Minister should continue to attend the Con- 
ference if desired, and it was perhaps better that he should do so; but His 
Majesty could not associate himself to the Acts now in preparation, and if it was 
judzed expedient, Gount Arnim could withdraw from the meeting. 

After a very long and didactic conversation, of which it is only in my power 
to note the principal points, the King dismissed me in the most gracious and 
obliging manner, repeating at the last moment that it would be to no purpose 
to attempt to make him depart from the system which he had laid down for 
himself: but that quietly, and ‘1 such a manner as would not excite the jealousy 
of Russia, he should endeavour to prepare for coming events, und that, come 
what might, Her Majesty's Government might be certain that he would not be 
found fighting on the side of Russia. 

| will only add that the King is perfectly aware of the nature of the original 
demands of Russia upon the Porte. Tout cela,’ he said more than once, 
‘n'était que mensonge et intrigue,” ano inion which | confirmed by the recital 
of various conversations which I had held with Count Nesselrode and with the 
Emperor himself. 

Nothing which escaped the King gave me (1 am sorry to observe) the idea 
of His Majesty’s being desirous of extending his dominions at the expense of 
Russia, 

Berlin, March 3, 1854. 
(Signed) G H. SEYMOUR,

GENERAL CASTELBAJAC, the late French Envoy at the Court of 
St, Petersburgh, arrived here yesterday, and left this morning for Paris. 

[ had some conversation with him on the present state of affairs. He 
seemed to be deeply imbued with the magnitude of the sone in which the 
Western Powers were shortly to be engaged against Russia, and T was somewhat 
surprised to perceive his impression of the immense resources and of the 
military power which the Emperor could command in the approaching conflict 
with England and France. : 

It is not from any participation in this conviction that I am induced to 
report these impressions of General Castelbajac. It is rather my wish that due 
account should be taken beforehand of any bins with which that General may 
seek to influence the views and opinions of the French Government, or of the 
military authorities at Paris, on grounds which can only be accounted for by 
excessive weakness or feelings of personal vanity.

(No. 108. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, March 4, 1854. 

1 REGRET to inform your Lordship that up to the present moment the King 
refuses to agree to the Convention relative to the Eastern question, which has 
been submitted to him from England, Austria, and France, and that his objec- 
tions are founded on the false impression which he has received that the 
Emperor of Russia is ready to march a large and overwhelming force against 
bins if he adopts the policy of the other Powers, and cordially unites with 

etl. 

Baron Manteuffel, who was with the King three hours yesterday, and again 
this evening, tells me he has literally sahausted every argument in his discussions 
with His Majesty, and ts at present unable to say how the matter will end, but 
nevertheless he still hopes, with a little more patience, to be able to bring His 
Majesty round; that he expects to have means of calming his fears on the 
gubject of an attack from Russia, which at one time he thought, as reported in 
my No, 93 of the Ist instant, might fortify the King in a desire to join the 
three Powers, but which unfortunately produced a contrary effect. 

His Excellency complained bitterly of the intrigues at Court, to which he 
attributed much of the present difficulty ; and I may add, in order to show 
your Lordship the painful position of the President of the Couneil, that he and 
the Minister of War had yesterday resolved to place their resignations in the 
King's hands if His Majesty did not consent to the Convention, but their inten- 
tion has been changed in consequence of His Majesty having entered on a dlis- 
cussion of the details of the Convention, which they consider a favourable 
cireumstance, and one which will open the way for its final adoption, with some 
reservations. 

Count ‘Thun called to-day on Baron Manteuffel, and requested him urgently 
to press the King to agree to the Convention, stating that the Austrian Govern- 
ment are anxiously waiting for His Majesty's decision. 

His Excellency in telling me this, said thet he had written to Vienna to 
explain the delay, and that though the King hesitated, his opinions coincided

My Lord, Berlin, March 4, 1853. 


THE Marquis de Moustier read to me this morning a despatch which he 
had just received from his Government, written in an angry tone at the delays 
of Prussia in agreeing to the Convention, and directing him to hint to Baron 
Manteuffel, if he thought it advisable, that longer hesitation would produce an 
alteration in the present good feeling of the French Government towards this 
country, and shake their confidence in the intentions of its Government, and 
that he might ask them if ‘t would be more agreeable to them to have a 
French army on the Rhine than for them to place a Prussian one on the 
Vistula. 

‘The question of Servia, and the necessity of effecting a change in the 
Government of that country, are also introduced in this despatch for the con- 
sideration of the Prussian Government. 

The Marquis.de Moustier asked my advice as to how he should act on this 
instruction, and we agreed that it would be better to delay making the contents 
of this despatch known at the present moment. I spoke to him in this sense 
under the conviction that a communication of the kind from France, in the 
present temper of the King, was more likely to do harm than good, and would 
certainly be made a handle of by the Court party, and thwart our chances of 
getting the King to sign the Convention.

(No. 293. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Paris, March 7, 1854. 

M. DROUYN DE LHUYS informs me that Count Hatzfeldt has been 
desired to enter into explanations with him respecting the determi nation of Prussia 
to maintain a complete neutrality in the Kastern question, the Prussian Govern- 
ment founding its obligation so to do on the comparatively little interest which 
Prussia has in that question, while the danger of offending Russia by active 
interference in it is great, 

Still, while holding this language of isolation, M. de Manteutfel appears 
to be anxious to ascertain what price would be offered for the adhesion of 
Prussia to the policy of the Western Powers; and he asks, with considerable 
adroitness, since Prussia could not, from her geographical position, profit by 
the dissolution of the Turkish Empire, what compensation would be given her 
nearer home. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys observed to Count Hatzfeldt that the very reason 
which Prussia had given for non-interference in the East, was that which should 
most engage her to interfere; of all the Great Powers, Prussia was the one 
most interested to prevent the partition of Turkey, precisely because she was 
the one which could not profit by it.

But Prussia evidently hoped to be indemnified nearer home, and, by 
holding aloof at present, to keep her strength unimpaired in order to assert her 
claims hereafter. Now suppose, said M. Drowyn de Lhuys, that Austria, sus- 
picious of your intentions, was to come to England and France and say that 
with the best intentions she could not cooperate with them unless they gave 
her some assurances respecting the safety of her German possessions, and that 
she was to propose to them to guarantee the present territorial distribution of 
Germany, could England and France refuse such an appeal? Let Prussia 
consider all this, and she would see that her true interests would lead her to 
contribute her aid to control the ambition of a neighbour, whose power she 
already dreaded, but which power would be increased tenfold if she was allowed 
to succeed in projects the iniquity of which Prussia had, with the other Great 
Powers of Europe, so unequivocally condemned.

Power-may be supposed to take greater interest than another, but itis whether 
the Great Powers shall quietly permit and thereby give their sanction to an 
unjust interpretation of ‘Treaties being sustained by unlawful aggression, whether 
a weak State shall be despoiled by its powerful neighbour, and whether tern- 
torial limits determined by Treaties shall be violently disturbed. The question

and your Lordship will again remark to Baron Manteuifel that the united policy 
and action of the four ae can alone shorten the duration and limit the 
extension of the war into which they are about to be forced; but we may 
reasonably expect, that as a result of that union the ambitious and encroaching 
policy of Russia will be checked, and that not only peace will be re-established 
on a solid foundation, but that Germany and the North of Europe will recover 
the independence and the freedom of action which, in consequence of Russian 
interference, they do not now possess,

The Earl of Clarendon to the Earl of Westmorland. 


(No. 108.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, March 8, 1854. 

COUNT COLLOREDO has read to me a despatch from Count Buol, 
inclosing a copy of the instructions which his Excellency has addressed to the 
Austrian Representative at Constantinople, on the affairs of Servia. 

These instructions are to the following effect : . 

Count Buol observes, that whilst the reports of Baron de Bruck represent 
the Porte as being not without anxiety as regards the dispositions of the Servian 
nation, a telegraphic communication from the Austrian Consul-General at 
Belgrade states that, if Edhem Pasha is to be believed, Servia has decided to 
declare herself against the Russians, because she neither could nor ought to 
remain neutral at the present juncture. 

The Austrian Government has always endeavoured to persuade the Servian 
Government that an attitude of strict neutrality was most in accordance with 
Servian interests, since such an attitude alone could preserve the Principality 
from the embarrassments that Servia would inevitably bring upon herself by 
taking a decided part with either of the contending parties. Austria has con- 
sidered herself the more authorised to give this advice, from the fact that as a 
bordering Power she must feel that any events that may occur in Servia must 
have a direct and most sensible influence upon Austrian provinces, 

No opportunity has been lost to hold the same language at Constantinople, 
and to represent that it is by no means the interest of the Ottoman Govern 
ment to urge Servia to pronounce herself openly in favour of the Porte, and to 
engage in hostilities against Russia. 

Baron Bruck is instructed to renew these representations, and to state, 
that although nothing can be more satisfactory to Austria than to see Servia 
persevere in the line of fidelity and devotion towards the Suzerain Power, no 
service would be rendered to the latter were Servia to assume an attitude which 
would provoke new complications, and cause & wider extension of the operations 
of war, which it is the interest of the Porte to restrict within the narrowest 
possible limits, 

In the despatch to Count Colloredo inclosing these instructions to Baron 
Bruck, Count Buol observes that it would be an illusion to imagine that the 
deeply-roated sympathies of the Servian population for the Russians have been 
weakened or are ready to give place to an unlimited devotion to the Suserain 
Power, It is more than probable that the masses of the Servian people, once 
called to arms, would only swell the ranks of the enemies af the Porte. The 
Porte would therefore do well, with a view to the true interests of Turkey, to 
abstain from exercising any pressure on Servia, in order to induce her to 
abandon the attitude of strict neutrality which she has, up to this moment, 
preserved, 

According to the Austrian Consul-General in Servia, Edhem Pasha has 
already been convinced of the justice of this view, and has considerably modified 
the ideas with which he was imbued on his arrival at Belgrade, . 

The Austrian Government hus already informed the Porte that the concen-

tration of troops on the south-east frontier had no other object than to act 
eventually with a view at once to the security of Austria and the integrity of 
the Ottoman Empire. 

Austria is the first to acknowledge, a5 8 general rule, that no Power at 
peace with Turkey has the right, without the previous consent of the Porte, to 
occupy with a military force any portion of the Ottoman territory. Cireum- 
stances, however, might occur from one moment to another of a nature to 
justify a departure from this principle, and in such a case Austria would not 
hesitate to send her troops into Servia even though there should not be sufficient 
time for obtaining the previous consent of the Porte. 

These circumstances would be: 

1. A revolutionary movement, threatening to reverse the state of things 
legally established in Servia. Care for her own security would then impose upon 
Austria the imperious duty of opposing the installation of a revolutionary power 
in the immediate proximity of her frontiers. 

® If Russian troops were seriously to menace Servia with an invasion. 
In this case military considerations of decisive weight would render it obligatory 
on Austria to anticipate the Russians and to take up a position in Servia before 
their arrival. 

In either case where delay would be productive of fatal consequences, the 
objects of Austria would be no other than to maintain the legal status quo, and 
would therefore be entirely in the interest of the Ottoman Government: in such 
an event no time will be lost in giving to Turkey, on this head, the fullest and 
most satisfactory assurances. 

I expressed to Count Colloredo my satisfaction that frank and full assurances 
upon this subject would he aiyen to the Ottoman Government, but IT said: it 
was earnestly to be hoped that the necessity for the contemplated intervention 
would not take place, as it was likely to be misinterpreted and might add to 
existing difficulties.

(No. 109.) 
My Lord, Foreign Office, March 5, 1894. 

COUNT COLLOREDO has read to me a despatch from Count Buol, 
transmitting a copy of the original project of Convention between the Four 
Powers, communicated to him by Baron de Bourqueney, and also a copy of the 
document as amended, in consequence of conversations between Count Buol and 
the French Minister. Count Buol makes the following remarks upon these 
propects ; 

With regard to the alteration in Article J, substituting for the words 
« hases indiquées dans le Protocole du 13 Janvier,” &e., “ des conditions jugées 
compatibles avec les intéréts gencraux de l'Europe,” &e., Count Buol observes 
that Russia having rejected the bases of the Protocol of the 18th January, the 
expression of a wish on the part of the Four Powers to maintain them without 
variation would be to offer as it were a premium to the obstinacy of Russia; 
since whatever might happen, even should the war be pushed to the greatest 
extremities, she would be sure to be able to end by signing a peace renewing all 
her former ‘Treaties with Turkey. Tt therefore appears to the Austrian Govern- 
ment that it would be useful to let Russia see that the disposition of the Powers 
on this subject would be susceptible of modification, if she obstinately persists 
in her present system. 

Moreover, the engagement to be made by the Powers themselves to respect 
the principle of the integrity of the Ottoman Empire would not, in Count Buel’s 
opinion, impose any obligation other than that of refraining from ‘any act of a 
nature to injure that integrity. 

If, however, despite their common wishes and exertions, the order of things 
as it actually exists in ‘Turkey should happen to be subverted by a concurrence 


285 


of circumstances independent of their will, in this cage it should be well under- 
stood that the principle of the union of the Powers should continue to exist with 
the establishment of new bases of understanding. ' iad 

The phraseology proposed by Count Buol for Article Il has in view only 
the modification of what is in his opinion too categorical in the words—* devra 
dtre opéré le plutét possible.” : : e 

The object of Article V added to the amended project 15 to establish from 
the present a closer unity between the Four Powers, and to paralyze at one blow 
the unceasing attempts of the Cabinet of St, Petersburgh to divide them. 

The Austrian Government would be ready on their part to sign the Con- 
vention as thus drawn up, without excluding changes in the wording which 
might be proposed, provided that the foundation should be kept intact—always, 
nevertheless, with the understanding that the three Powers should be unanimous 
in concluding the Act in question. According to accounts received by Count 
Buol, the Cabinet of Berlin has shown certain scruples on this subject. His 
Rycellency will however use every exertion to overcome them, and he feels 
persuaded that Her Majesty's Government, on their part, will do as much. 

Count Buol does not conceal the importance of this act. It will invest with 
a more solemn form the principles enunciated in the Protocols, it will establish 
an entire conformity of views between the Austrian Cabinet and the Cabinets of 
the maritime Powers, and will doubtless unite them in the common object of 
obtaining a solution of the Eastern question which should insure the main- 
tenance of the balance of Europe, and oppose all conquest and extension of 
influence on the part of Russia, 

The more Austria feels the importance of this act, and the more firmly 
decided frankly and loyally to follow out the end traced out by this Convention, 
the more necessary does she consider it not to allow any undue extension of its 
ecope, or any conclusions to be drawn from it which she cannot admit. Count 
Colloredo is therefore directed carefully to explain that while Austria unites in 
policy with the Western Powers, she will preserve intact her liberty of action 
as to the choice of the moment which her interests may point out to her as that 
when she should add the weight of her material forees to the measures which 
may have been agreed upon for the attainment of the common object. 

Count Buol moreover reserves to himself the right to propose in Conference 
a stipulation to the effect that the Act shall remain secret up to the moment when 
the maritime Powers shall be actually in a state of war. 

[ thanked Count Colloredo for this communication, and said that the Con- 
vention, Which had been prepared some time ago by the French Government, 
had manifestly become inapplicable to present cireumstances, but that Her 
Majesty's Government rejoiced that the necessary amendments should have been 


proposed by Austria, and upon the grounds stated in Count Buol’s despatch. 


I begged leave to add that the satisfaction of Her Majesty's Government in 
finding their views identified with those of Austria was increased by the convic- 
tion that the course now pursued by her was the one best calculated to promote 
her own interests, as a firm and decided olicy would avert the revolution which 
must have been inevitable if Austria haa unfortunately taken part with Russia 
and against the public opinion of Germany, and would lead to solid and lasting 
advantages, 

One great element of the power of Russia, | said, was the belief she had 
artfully created in her unlimited resources and in her determination to maintain 
peace and repress social disturbance throughout Europe, but more particularly in 
Germany. Tt is now appareils however, that in order to gratify her ambition, 
she is ready to plunge 
will entail ; but Russia has for many years past indirectly served the cause of 
revolution; for having acquired a right of interference with certain Governments, 
she has always exercised it to prevent the reforms and improvements that those 
Governments were disposed to grant, and that the people were entitled to expect. 

Such changes have been stigmatized as revolutionary by Russia, who has 
succeeded in averting them, but she has thereby riven Lise to just discontent 
on the part of the people, who have been constantly watching the occasion to 
rise against their Government. 

Ttussia has, however, at length created an opportunity for shaking off her 
hurtful and unjustifiable interference, and the Powers who nace now been forced 
by her to encounter the risks, the expense, and the calamities of war, would

No. 386, 
Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clurendon.—( Received March 9.) 


(No. 115. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, March 6, 1854. 


THE continued difficulties which Baron Mantenffel has had to contend 

with have been brought to a climax by a telegraphic despatch which arrived. 
yesterday from Chevalier Bunsen, ‘n which that Minister appears to have urged 
his Government to take a more decided course, and prepare at once to enter 
into hostilities with Russia; and to have stated that England would in that case 
be disposed to offer some species of guarantee to russia of her eastern 
rovinces. When this intelligence was communicated yesterday to the King, 
dis Majesty became greatly irritated, and declared that he did not comprehend 
how any of his servants could make such a proposal; that it was in. positive 
opposition to his wishes, and to the instructions which Chevalier Bunsen had 
received, and that he should be recalled from London. Baron Manteuffel at 
once felt all the inconvenience that would result from such a step, He proved 
to the King that it would be immediately interpreted into a change of the policy 
of this Government, when His Majesty beeame more calm; the matter was 
dropped, and the question of recall fell to the ground, It is, however, nearly 
settled that Count Albert Pourtales shall again wroceed to London on a special 
mission. with explanations on the subject. Aaron Manteuffel has already 
suggested this to the Wing, and His Majesty will take the proposal into 
consideration. 

The immediate effect of the communication of Chevalier Bunsen has been 
the conviction that the question of the Convention must for the present be laid 
aside; and in order not to interfere with any arrangement consequent on the 
decision which the three Powers may wish to make, Baron Manteutfel has written 
this evening to Vienna to explain the exact position of affairs here, declaring 
that the Prussian Government do not in any way depart from their approval of 
all the acts of the Conference of Vienna, and of the policy pursued by the three 
Powers on the Rusgo-Turkish question ; but are ready to support them, though 
unwilling to bind themselves to become parties to active host e operations. 

The King is extremely desirous, notwithstanding that he declines to agree 
to the Convention proposed to him by England, Austria, and France, to be a 
party to the Conference of Vienna, which he hopes will continue to act; and he 


® Not printed, 


287 


desires it to be understood that all his sympathies are with the allies, and thal 
he will gladly cooperate with them in any way short of becoming a belligerent. 

Baron Manteuffel read to me this despatch hastily this evening, and told 
me that a copy of it would be sent to Chevalicr Bunsen to-morrow for commu- 
nication to your Lordship. His Excellency told me further, that he had written 
4 confidential despatch to Count Arnim at Vienna, to the effect that he was to 
‘nform the Austrian Government that he by no means separated from their 
policy, but approved of it; and that if hereafter his material support were 
required, after the commencement of hostilities, and that if armed assistance 
were wanting to repel any attack on the Austrian territory, Prussia would be 
found ready to come forward in the case of need, 

Baron Menteutfel expressed to me his personal regret that more could not 
be done at this moment; that he had urged every argument to persuade the 
King to agree to the proposals of his allies, but that they had proved unavailing; 
and that it was painful to him to give up all present hope of obtaining any 
other result, though he was still of opinion that Prussia woul hereafter cordially 
unite with us. j

The Earl of Westmorland to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received March 4.) 


(No. 71.) 
My Lord, Vienna, March 4, 1854. 
THE messenger Blackwood having unfortunately missed the train at 
Breslau, was delayed on his journey from Berlin, and only arrived here this 
morning. immediately informed Count Buol that I desired to submit to him 
the important despatch brought by the messenger as quickly as possible, Count 
Buol being however engaged at a Cabinet Council, could not see me till 
3 o'clock, when I laid before him your Lordship’s despatch No. 86. I then 
learnt from Count Buol that he had just before received from Baron Meyendorff 
preliminaries of peace which had been drawn up at St, Petersburgh, in accord- 
ance with the suggestions made to Count Orloff for transmission to the Porte, 
and Count Buol informed me that he had in consequence called together the 
members of the Conference, and M. de Bourqueney and Count Arnim were 
already waiting to be received. Count Buol stated that he had told Baron 
Meyendorff he could in no way charge himself with the office of mediator with 
the other three parties to the Conference upon these preliminaries, and finding 
there were points of difference with the Protocol of the 13th of January, he told 
me he thought it important that these differences should be recorded in a 
protocol after being examined by the Conference. Before at once rejecting a 
document so important to the peace of the world he considered it a paramount 
duty to examine it with attention, which could not be done upon a simple 
perusal without comparing it with the propositions of Reshid Pasha, and he 
could not himself have time to examine the documents, prepare his own 
despatches, and submit it to the Emperor by to-morrow morning. He there 
fore proposed to send each of the members of the Conference a copy of the 
Russian preliminaries, and that we should meet to-morrow, after having 
examined them, to record our deliberate opinion upon them. He then proceeded 
to state the difficulty he should feel in supporting the summons from the 
Governments of England and France to evacuate the Frincipalities within a

Russia at this last moment had reached Vienna. He therefore most eurnestly 
requried Baron Bourqueney and me to delay the departure of the messenger 
to é Petersburgh till an answer can be received from your Lordship, and he 
will have his despatch in support of ape summons ready to send in case you

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.-—(Recewwed March 10.) 


(No. 118. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, March 8, 1854, 

THE state of parties here, and the intrigues at Court, are carried so far at 
this moment that it is necessary I should draw your Lordship’s attention to 
them, as they will serve to exp ain the change which appears to have come 
over the policy of this Government at a moment when we were given to expect 
that we should shortly obtain its more formal adhesion to our views with 
respect to the Russo-Turkish question. The real cause of failure is, I believe, 
attributable to the over-zealous and imprudent conduct of the Bethmann-Hollweg 
or constitutional party (to which Count Pourtales, who was lately employed on 
a special mission to London, belongs), by their having raised suspicions in 
Baron Manteuffel’s mind that they were seeking to supplant him. 

Your Lordship will recollect my having reported in my despatch No. 92 
of the 28th ultimo, that the King had issued a Cabinet order, addressed to 
Baron Manteuffel, directing that Count Pourtales should be employed in carryin 
on the correspondence of the Foreign office on Eastern affairs, and that M. 
d’Usedom was shortly to be appointed Under-Secretary of State in that depart- 
ment. ‘The above-mentioned Cabinet order lay for several days at Baron 
Manteuffel’s, and his Excellency never haying chosen to communicate it to 
Count Pourtales, the latter suspecting that some intrigue was being carried on 
against him, requested that it might be published in the official paper. Baron 

anteuffel demurred, and explained that it could not be so, for that though it 
was duly signed, His Majesty had ordered that it should not be promulgated. 
Upon hearing this, Count Pourtales naturally felt that the King’s confidence 
in him was shaken, and that it would be useless to expect to carry out the 
volicy he had recommended. He had been labouring hard to obtain His 

Jajesty's assent to the proposed Convention, had prepared several papers 
explanatory of its object, and endeavoured to show that the King would not be 
bound to take up arms if his signature were affixed to it; in fact, he exhausted 
every argument that was applicable to the sutject. The King declared that he 
had no thought of going back from the policy of neutrality and independence 
which he had all along avowed, but that he would not sign this Convention, nor 
do anything that changed his position or indicated an intention to take a step in 
advance; that he had been already led on further than he wished, and that he 
should now stop. 

‘Things were in this state when a telegraphic despatch arrived from the 
Chevalier Bunsen, stating that Her Majesty's Government expected that Prussia 
would immediately take an active part in the impending hostilities, and upon 
this the King lost all command over himself and declared that his resolution 
was definitively taken, and that nothing would induce him to change his opinion. 
Count Pourtales and M. d'Usedom, who belongs to the same party, have 
now resolved to keep aloof from the Foreign Office as long as present opinions 
prevail there. 

In the mean time, the Russian party consider that they have regained their 
lost position, and it is but too true that they have obtained an advantage of 
which it will be no easy matter to deprive them. 

M. de Bismark, the Prussian Minister at frankfurt, has arrived here, and 
his Ni has given countenance to the Russian party; he has been received 
by them and at Court with open arms, and to him in some degree is attributable 
the change which has occurred ; however, it is impossible to say who has not 
been concerned in these intrigues, for they have been curried on almost in the 
open streets. The Queen is at the head ot the movement in favour of Russia: 
she has been watching every turn which the late affairs have taken, and has 
found zealous assistants in all the officers of the Court. Letters have arrived 
from the Empress of Russia, imploring that every effort should be made ta 
prevent war from breaking out between the two countries; the King’s feelings 
ant his fears have been worked upon, his love of peace, and the hope hereafter of 
playing the part of mediator, have made His Majesty abdicate the high part in the 


ee ee ee CY ee Yh ey 


eee SS 
- = 


294 


councils of the world which he has held, and he now voluntarily seeks to 
establish for himself a position of neutrality in the important struggle for the 
maintenance of a great European principle, which is unworthy of a kingdom 
like Prussia. 

Every effort to make the King consider the responsibilities of his duties as 
one of the Great Powers has been useless, and I hear that he is under the 
conviction that, after a time, we shall all be glad to appeal to him as a neutral 
State ready and disposed to forward negotiations for peace, little thinking that 
the affairs of the world can be settled without him, and that he will have lost all 
claim to our confidence and goodwill, or to any advantage that might result 
from the war. 

I have, &e.

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.— (Received March 10.) 


(No. 119.) 
My Lord, Berlin, March 8, 1854. 

THE departure of General Count Graben for London, charged with a letter 
for Her Majesty the Queen from the King of Prussia, will take place to-morrow 
Momibe. 

Baron Manteuffel has informed me that Count Groben will probably 
remain but a very short time in London, and his Excellency did not seem to 
expect that anything would result from this mission. [told him, and I also 
told Count Graben himself, that I apprehended that his arrival in London with 
a letter from the King expatiating on the advantages of maintaining peace 
would take place very inopportunely just after the rejection by the Representatives 
of the Four Powers ut Vienna of the last Russian preliminaries ; and that I 
thought Her Majesty's Government had reason to be dissatished with Prussia, 
which, after going with us almost hand in hand the last half-year, suddenly 
stopped and refused to take upon herself the responsibility of one of the Great 
Powers and arbiters of the fate of Europe. I said that Prussia, by declining to 
accede to the proposed Convention, had forfeited all further claim to our syin- 
pathies, and had placed herself in # position which would assuredly exeite our 
suspicion. ‘That to talk of peace at the moment hostilities were about to 
commence was worse than useless, and could only lead to harm instead of good ; 
that [ was, however, sure the King’s intention in sending Count Groben to 
London was founded on the best: motives, but it was not to be expected that 
they could produce any other impression than that which I had above expressed. 

i suid ulso that the conduct of Prussia with respect to the negotiations on 
the subject of the Vienna Project of Convention had led us into @ serious Error, 
and might produce inealeulable results; but that the fatal consequence of 
Prussia's desertion of our policy was that the war which was about to commence— 
for there could no longer be a question of its being averted—would become 
general, as it could to longer he confined to the narrow limits within which we 
had hoped it might have been restricted, if Prussia had been on our side, 

Baron Manteuffel was surprised at the tone I assumed on this occasion, 
and asked me what was the part we expected Prussia to take if she had joined 
us? T replied that I knew not how far we ehould have sought her cooperation, 
and that for the moment we had only asked her to sign a Convention, which 
would not have bound her to anything in the shape of active hostilities, but 
which would have bad o moral effect which might have been of great advantage 
to the general cause, and would have proved that Prussia felt the injustice of 
the aggressions of Hussia, and proclaimed her concurrence in the motives which 
divtated our policy. 

[regret to say that Baron Manteuffel’s language gave ne encouragement 
to suppose that there was any chance of @ change in the King’s present reso- 
lution; he appeared disposed to accept the position as incapable of modification, 


295 


nnd to be himself relieved from the necessity of renewing his hitherto fruitless 
efforts to bring the King round to our views, which were too distasteful to His 
Majesty to admit any chance of success. |

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received March 10.) 


(No. 120. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Berlin, March 8, 1854. 

IT may be presumptuous in me to offer an opinion as to the language 
which Her ‘Majesty’s Government may think it right to hold to Count Groben, 
but I venture, nevertheless, to make the following observations on this 
mission. 

Count Grében is not a person of any political influence, and he is, | 
apprehend, quite ignorant of the details of the important negotiations whieh 
have lately taken place on the Eastern question. His early life and associations 
have led him to believe that the principles of the Holy Alliance are those best 
adapted to the interests of his country, He has, however, much good feeling 
and attachment to England, and Sree a grateful recollection of the kindness 
which his son, who accompanies him on his present journey, received from 
Lord Hardinge and the officers of our army in India, where he had the good 
fortune to assist at the last glorious battles in that country. He will, | am sure, 
faithfully report to the King of Prussia any impressions he may receive from 
-our Lordship’s conversation with him, and it appears to me that, when he sees 

ig mission of peace is not likely to be attended with success, he may, perhaps, 
be induced by the powerful arguments you may use, to make a last effort to 
bring his royal master again to take into his consideration the Convention 
which he has refused to sign. Should, on the other hand, no impression be 
made upon him, | would venture to say that T think it would be useless at this 
moment to hold threatening language to Prussia. Such language would, in the 
present temper of the King, only widen the difference which exists in the policy 
of the two countries, and we fave but lately seen the effect produced on the 
Prussian Cabinet by the threats of the Russian Minister. It would, therefore, 
I think be unwise at this moment, though it may become necessary hereafter, 
to follow that example, for it might immediately result in increasing Russian 
influence, in doing away with the still slender chance which exists of effecting a 
change to our advantage, and in throwing the patriotic party into the hands 
of Russia, who are now inclined to.an English alliance. ‘Ths fact of threatening 
this country would arouse the feelings of the nation and unite all parties against 
us; whereas something might occur which would leave an opening for an 
improvement in our position, and public opinion, if left to itself, cannot fail soon 
to make its way through the press and be useful to us. 

The French Minister participates in this feeling, and has written to his 
Government in the samé sense as this despatch. 

Lhave, &e.

Lord Stratford de Redelijfe to the Earl af Clarendon.—(Received March 11.) 


(No. 74.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, February 15, 1854. 


IT HAVE much satisfaction in stating that the firman, which | obtained 
about four years ago, for placing Christian evidence in matters of crimimal juris- 
prudence on the same footing as that of Mahometans, is now to be extended 
throughout the Empire, for the benefit not only of foreign Christians in Turkey, 
but for all classes of the Sultan’s tributary subjects without exception. When 
the firman was originally granted to me for the regulation of proceedings in the 
mixed criminal courts of Alexandria and Cairo, | obtained a promise that it 
should be extended, after a time, to the Rayahs of the whole Empire. Hitherto 
my repeated efforts to secure the performance of this promise failed, and the 
present appearance of success is owing to a strong appeal in writing, which | 
addressed to Reshid Pasha several weeks ago. It is altogether painful to 
observe with what unreasonable and ill-omened tenacity the professors of 
Islamism still adhere to their stupid misapplication of religious principles. In 
the present instance, however, I trust that the prejudice is practically sur- 
mounted, and that the firman, calculated as it is to remove the most crying 
injustice under which the Rayahs of the Empire have laboured for centuries, will 
shortly receive the Sultan’s sanction, in addition to the approval of the Council, 
with which it has been submitted to His Majesty.

Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.— (Received Marek 10.) 
(No. 80.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, February 24, 1864. 


THE consideration which you have shown in seeking to diminish my 
responsibility, with respect to Her Majesty’s squadron now at anchor in the 
Bosphorus, deserves. my especial acknowledgments. Though little inclined to 
shrink from tesponsibility when it ‘s imposed upon me by the interests of the 
public service, | find a welcome relief in the limitation which your Lordship has 
expressly established in the present instance. Before the receipt, indeed, of 
your Lordship's instruction of the Sth instant, I had taken a similar view of my 
duty, and acted carefully upon it in my communications with Vice-Admiral 
Dundas. I must have expressed myself ill, if T ever conveyed the idea of 
intending to do more in addressing a requisition to the Admiral than summon 
him to employ adequate means for the accomplishment of a stated object. 
Whatever latitude your Lordship’s earlier “nstructions may have left, no ordinary 
circumstances would, I conceive, have warranted an attempt on my part to 
overrule any objections rounded exclusively, by the Admiral, on strict profes- 
sional considerations. T remember, indeed, that in one of my letters to him | 
distinetly declined any responsibility on that score. 

But | question whether a clear discrimination in that respect will sutlice to 
wrevent inconvenience, oy worse, to the public service, “The command of the 

lack Sea under present circumstances 1s, 10 doubt, the principal object of 
attention. But it ts by no means the only one; and I am deeply impressed with 
4 conviction that to suceced against Russia in the more extensive struggle which 
now appears to be imminent, we shall have to cooperate with the Porte not 
only on the waters of the Euxine, but wherever the Russian forees, or the 
partizans of Russia, may obtain, or seek to obtain, a footing, Already there are 


appearances of a serious Greek insurrection in the Turkish Provinces bordering 


on Greece, seconded hy synipathisers from that kingdom and warranting a 
suspicion that the Hellenic Government is by no means unfavourable to the 
movement. It is manifestly of urgent importance to check the insurrection in 
its opening, and particularly by the employment of regular troops. The Porte is 
fully alive to its interest in these respects. Anxious to reinforee its troops in the 
disturbed Provinces, and having no steam-vessel at its disposal, it applied to the 
British and French Embassies for steam conyeyanee equal to the object in view. 
| made the application to Admiral Dundas, and the French Ambassador to 
Admiral Hamelin. A refusal was the result; and the consequence has beena 
delay of several days in consequence of the Sultan’s reinforcements to Volos and 
Prevesa: The case, without implying censure, may serve to exemplify my 
meaning, and enable your Lordship to figure others of a similar tendency, though 
differing in form and in aim. will only add, that the power of commanding 
prompt means of communication appears to be indispensable for the effective 
performance of my duties, and, that whether for the purpose of assisting the 
Porte, of cooperating with France, or of looking to our own immediate interests 
when endangered or compromised by passing occurrences, | hope not to be left 
without a degree of authority commensurate with the trust reposed in me, and 


necessary to meet the incidental exigencies of this most critical and trying state 


of things.

Paris, March 10, 1854, 


Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon—(Received Murch Id.) 
(No, 308.) 


My Bon Paris, March 11, 1854. 
YOUR Lordship's attention has, without doubt, been called to an article: 
published in the St. Petersburgh “Gazette,” of the 2nd instant, wherein 
allusion is made to certain conlidential communications which passed during the 
pertod when Lord John Russell held the Seals of the Foreign Department 
between Her sage ete Government and the Emperor of Russia, on the subject 
of the Ottoman Empire, and the course to be pursued by tha two Governments, 


should that Empire, as was the Er i ‘ Lae 
: mE 1 mperor Nicholas’ convict mene ie 
dissolution. ton, come to an early 


The object of this article could hardly be mistaken. ‘The inuendos which 


it contained respecting an understanding between Juglind and Russia, diseuised 
under the terms “confidential exchange of opinions,” “amicable SOR 
pondence,” &e., were enough to arouse the suspicions of this Government 
whose nature it unfortunately is to believe that Great Britain hus some particular 
interest at stake in the East. 1 determined, therefore, on seeing the article 
transcrilied into the French newspapers, to lay the correspondence to which it 
alluded, and of which your Lordship had furnished me with copies in the outset 
eons personal information only, at once before the French Minister for Foreign 
Affairs. e 


Accordingly, I waited this morning upon M, Drouyn de Lhuys, and, 


307 


adverting to the article, I said that it was perfectly true that confidential com- 
munications had passed between the two Governments in the spring of last 
year; that, if they had not been made public by Her Majesty's Government, it 
was from a feeling of delicacy towards the Emperor of Russia, which his Excel- 
lency would appreciate, for, as | was about to read to him the whole corres- 
pondence, he would see that, us far as Her Majesty's Government was concerned, 
there could be no object in keeping the papers seeret on any other account. 

I then read to him Sir Hamilton Seymour's despatch No. 24, Lord John 
Russell’s No. 88, and Sir Hamilton Seymour’s No. 87 und 88, of last year; 
and, having done so, I said that I left it to his Excellency to determine how far 
the assertions of the Russian Government, that they had never intended, had 
they met with an assent on the part of Her Majesty’s Government, to dispose of 
the provinces of the Turkish Empire according to their own ideas, were founded 
on fact. 

I have the satisfaction to add, that this frank communication had the 
happiest effect. M. Drouyn de Lhuys stated, that nothing could have been 
more correct than the conduct of Her Majesty's Government, both in the 
language which had been employed in replying to the overtures of the Emperor 
of Russia, and in the secrecy which they had observed until now, in respect to 
this correspondence. 

I trust that 1 may not incur your Lordship’s disapprobation for what I have 
done. ‘The effect which I wished to produce, seemed to me to depend so much 
upon immediate and spontaneous action, that I ventured to take the responsi- 
bility of the step, rather than refer to your Lordship for instructions. I have 
insisted, however, on the most rigorous silence on the part of M. Drouyn de 
Lhuys, except towards the Emperor; but I confess that I should be glad to be 
empowered to state the case fairly, in answer to the numerous questions which 
will no doubt be made to me upon the matter, 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys observed, that he was much mistaken, if he could not 
produce despatches from General Castelbajac, of about the same date as those 
of Sir Hamilton Seymour, conveying, though not in such distinct terms, offers 
of a separate understanding with France respecting the partition of Turkey. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) COWLEY,

No. 408, 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received Murch 13.) 
(No, 88.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, February 26, 1854. 


THE disorders now prevailing in the Turkish Provinces bordering on 
Greece derive, from the insurrectionary character which they have assumed, and 
from the successes attending them, a degree of importance which is enhanced 
by their probable connection with the hostile operations of Kussia against the 
Porte, to say nothing of the suspected connivance of the Hellenie Govern- 
ment. 


ee ae ie eh eo od 


=o 


308 


Her Majesty’s Consul at Prevesa has forwarded to your Lordship’s office 
such information as he possessed respecting the numbers and movements of the 
farce collected at Radovisi and directed against Arta, 

Mr, Blunt has, in all probability, transmitted to your Lordship the substance 
of his advices from Larissa ; and T cannot doubt that Mr. Wyse has been equally 

rompt in bringing to your Lordship’s knowledge whatever may best serve to 


place the proceedings of the Hellenic Goveroment and of its civil or military 


dependants in their true light, 
What I collect from these different sources, and also from the advices 


received at the Porte or from private correspondence, amounts, in general, to an 
appearance of insurrection more formidable im prospect than at present, requiride 
to be counteracted with prompt decision, and capable of being insulated an 
repressed if met at once with adequate forces. Unfortunately the Turkish 
forces are few in number, and of a bad deseription, while the Pasha of Janina is 
paralysed by an illness which unfits him for business. 

ip ri “ = ‘ _ 1 fay J 

The Porte, taken by surprise, though often warned, is called upon to apply 


its immediate attention to the means of supplying these deficiencies, and 


restraiming the Hellenic authorities from any participation, in the rebellious 


movement of its subjects. 


Communications on both these matters took place between Reshid Pasha 


and myself without loss of time. I found him disposed to act in_ perfect 
harmony with my views; to send reinforcements without delay to Prevesa, 
Janina, and Volo; to send them from the regular army; to discriminate care- 
fully between the guilty and the innecent,— punishing the former with just 
severity, protecting and encouraging the latter. 

Four battalions go by steam to Volo and Prevesa; others march by land 
on Janina. Bessim Pasha, an able and trustworthy commander, goes from 
Monastir to act as Muchir at Janina. Fuad Effendi is to follow him in the 
capacity of Imperial Commissioner. A prelate of the Greek Church is specially 
charged by the Patriarch to repair to the same district, with the view of exhorting 
the Porte’s Christian subjects to remain in peaceful and loyal submission to the 
Sultan. 

The Porte applied in the first instance to Her Majesty’s Embassy, and also 
ta the French, for steam-conveyance for the troops, having no steam-vessels of 
her own immediately within reach. Conceiving that it was most desirable to 
sive time, and also to give public evidence of our conentrents with the Turkish 
authorities, | applied to Admiral Dundas, and General Baraguay d’Hilhers 
applied to Admiral Hamelin, for means of complying with the Porte's request. 
‘The answer was a refusal, as stated in the correspondence already transmitted to 
your Lordship; and the Porte, after wailing for the return of its steamers from 
the Black Sea, and completing some necessary preparations, has finally embarked 
the four battalions; and that portion of them which is destined for Volo and 
Lurigsa starts to-day, in company with an English and French steamer, whose 
presence at their landing may be expected to produce a gootl effect. T could 
lave wished un earlier and more complete arrangement, but hope, nevertheless, 
that the troops may arrive in time to check an insurrection which cannot 
strengthen and expand without oceasioning much prejudice to the Sultan's 
interests, and, eventually, much embarrassment to His Majesty's allies. I learn 
from Mr. Saunders that Sir Henry Ward had sent one of Her Majesty's vessels 
on that station to Prevesa, 

With respect to the Hellenic Government, and its very questionable 
attitude, the first idea of Reshid Pasha, on reading the despatches from the 
Turkish Minister at Athens, was to recall that Representative, and to leave the 
post vacant. I took the liberty of advising him not to adopt so decisive a 
measure in the first instance, but to send for the Greek Representative here, and 
with due formality to require a full and clear explanation, of the circumstances 
which lave been brought to the Porte’s knowledge. An interview founded on 
this suggestion will take place to-morrow at Constantinople between Reshid 
Pasha and Count Metaxa in the presence of the Grand Vizier and the Seraskier. 
‘The conference promises to he of & serious character; and | believe it is the 
‘atention of the ‘Lurkish Ministers to make an official communication to the 
British and French Embassies of whatever may pass on the occasi 


ion; such com- 
niunication having the value ef enabling us to add our remonstrances, if 


oOt 


necessary, to those of the Porte, through the channel of our respective colleagues 
in Greece. ; 

It will afford me the liveliest satisfaction to find that, being thus called 
upon to take my line without the advantage of special instructions from your 
Lordship, I have anticipated the views of Her Majesty's Government without 
exceeding the limits of a reasonable discretion. 

I shall no doubt have occasion shortly to return to this subject, and in the 
meantime I inclose, for your Lordship’s more complete information, copies of 
the correspondence which passed between Reshid Pasha and me with respect to 
tle convevance of the Sultan’s troops to Volo and Prevesa,

Translation.) February 19, 1854. 


ALTHOUGH, in consequence of certain turbulent movements which have 
taken place first at Arta, and subsequently in the Agrafa, it 1s of urgent 
necessity to send with all speed a certain amount of regular forces to those dis- 
tricts, vet ns the Imperial steamers are at present in the Black Sea, the execution 
of this decision is delayed till their return ; and as under these circumstances a 
further loss of dime would be injurious to the state of affairs, it has become 
necessary to make an appeal for assistance to the allied Powers, who have never 
failed in any particular to display proofs of their good dispositions, your 
Excellency is requested to be so good as to use your endeavours that two steam- 
vessels of your squadron may be applied for the purpose of transporting the 
regular troops to the scene of action, The troops to be dispatched being in 
number such as the vessel is able to carry will be divided into two detachments 
one to be landed at Volo, the other at Prevesa; and this favour will he looked 
upon by the Porte as a further cause of its great obligation. ‘The same request 
has been officially made to your colleague the French Ambassador, in informing 
vou of which | avail myself, &c. : i

Wo. 409. 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to the Earl of Clarendon.—( Received March 13.) 


(No. 90.) 


My Lord, Constantinople, February 27, 1854. 


IN the despatches from Lieutenant-Colonel Neale, which I forward to 
London by this opportunity, 1 am happy to observe indications of the Porte’s 
attention to some, at least, of the suggestions which I have occasionally sub- 
mitted to its consideration, and those, in particular, which were founded on 
Colonel Du Plat's information. This is the more important, as that intelligent. 
und experienced officer confirms in later despatches the information which he 
eonveyed to your Lordship at an earlier period respecting the intended operations 
of Russia upon the Lower Danube. The works erected opposite to Ibraila, the 
additions made to the batteries at Matchin, and the collection of provisions at Silis- 
tria, appear to have in view an expected attack from the Russians in that quarter. 
[ have informed Reshid Pasha of the preparations making for the construction of 
a bridge near Galatz, and have urged nie again to hasten and extend the con- 
struction of gun-boats for service on the Danube. His Highness assures me that 
whatever information of a positive or reliable deseription I give him is forthwith 
transmitted to Omar Pasha, Among the statements in Colonel Neale’s corres- 
pondence is the advance of 10,000 men towards the Dobrudja, which, presume, 
may be taken as evidence of the just importance attached to the positions in that 
district. 

In stating the numbers which compose the Turkish army in Bulgaria, 
Colonel Neale has omitted to state whether he includes the detachment at 
Kalafat. I presume that such was his meaning; but on the return of Chekib 
Effendi in five or six days I hope to obtain an exact enumeration of the troops 
commanded by Omar Pasha, whether on the left or on the right bank of the Danube. 

Lam assured that 10,000 men have been assembled at Adrianople, 1 trust 
with the view of forming a reserve in lines to be established somewhere in that 
neighbourhood. Sir Jolin Burgoyne, who is just returned from the Dardanelles, 
will, | hope, be able to inspect that part of the country and to afford his valuable 
advice. The ‘Turkish Ministers are not yet frankly disposed to accept the 
services of European officers for the actual command of troops. Some few cases 
are quite exceptional. A French Colonel and a French Major, for instance, are 
at Kalafat in the command of troops. General Guyon, as Chef-d'Etat Major in 
Asia, may be called upon at any moment to command in person. Other otficers 
are employed upon the staff, or as instructors, but even they are far from being 
numerous. In proportion as the necessity is felt, a greater latitude will probably 
be given to the introduction of foreign officers ; but prejudice on one side, and 
ienorance of the language on the other, are serious bars to. progress. 

It is generally believed that French and English troops are likely to come 
out as auxiliaries tothe Sultan's army. However desirable and even necessary 
such a combined measure may be, it 1s well for the Turks to remain in ignorance 
of it until they have settled their defences as much as possible on their own 
resources. The relaxation which would naturally ensue on looking forward to 
foreign assistance, might have an injurious effect. ‘The additional body of men 
expected from Egypt is understood to amount to 10,000. 

| I have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFTE.

My Lord, Vienna, March 7, 1854. 
| HAVE read to Count Buol your Lordship’s despatch No. 88, which 


empowers me to sign the Conyention im its amended form. His Excellency 
expressed to me the yery great annoyance caused him by the continued hesitation 


311 


on the part of Prussia to adopt and sign the Convention, and he stated that he 
had once more written to Berlin, to urge the Prussian Government not to 
persist in its refusal. He said that it would be considered as a triumph by 
Russia, if a bond of alliance, drawn up for the Four Powers, should be signed 
only by three of them, and he added that the withdrawal of Prussia would 
produce the most unfavourable impression, especially in Germany, Count Buol 
proceeded to state that he did not withdraw from any of the engagements 
stipulated in the Convention, and he was perfectly willing to confirm them; bur 
he viewed with such grave anxiety the refusal of Prussia to sign this document 
that he would be inclined to alter its form in order to secure her cooperation. 
If. therefore, he found that the refusal on the part of the Prussian Government 
to accept the Convention rested chiefly upon its form, he should desire to 
substitute in its place a Protocol which he thought the Prussian Government 
could not refuse to adopt. 
March 8. 

Since I wrote the former part of this despatch, I have seen Count Buol, 
who had received from Count Arnim the communications which have been 
transmitted to him from his Government, upon the proposal to take part in the 
Convention in conjunction with the Governments of England, France, and 
Austria. 

Count Buol stated that these communications attested the desire of the 
Prussian Government to adhere to all the engagements they had contracted by 
the Protocols and Acts of the Conference, and therefore it was from no desire 1 
any way whatever to separate herself from that Conference, or from the policy 
by which it has been directed, but from reasons which had been transmitted to 
the English and French Governments, as well as to Austria, that she declined to 
become a party to the Convention. 

Count Buol, under these circumstances, repeated what I have already 
stated to your Lordship, that he was convineed it would have the worst eflect 
if the three Governments alone should become parties to this Convention, and 
thus separate themselves from Prussia; that the great foree of the present 
position of the allied Powers was their perfect union in face of the dangers with 
which Europe was menaced; that if that union was broken up by detaching 
from it any one of the Great Powers, it would be seized upon as an advantage 
by that numerous class of persons who had long been striving to accomplish a 
separation of interests between the Four Powers, and most particularly between 
Austria and Prussia. Count Buol therefore declared his decided opinion to be 
against the present signature of this Convention, but he su rested that when the 
answer to the summons which had been addressed to the Russian Government, 
and which had been most strongly supported by the Prussian Government, as 
well as by Austria, was received, he thought a favourable moment would offer 
for communicating that answer to the Conference, and then im a Protocol, in 
which this communication would be acknowledged, the whole of the engagements 
contained in the proposed Convention might be inserted. 

I told Count Buol that I would faithfully report his opinions to your 
Lordship, and that I eould at once assure him that his declaration that he 
withdrew from none of the engagements which were stipulated by the Convention 
would be received by your Lordship with the most entire satisfaction. 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) WESTMORLAND.

L HAVE received your Lordship’s despatch No, 85, inclosing despatches 
from M, de Fonblanque, and asking whit foundation there is for certain charges

with Russia, and adverse to the interests of the Porte. 

| cannot but think that your Lordship will concur with me in the opinion 
that the clear and decisive manner in which the Austrian Government have, 


312 


through their lighest organs, declared the identity of their policy with that of 
the Governments of England and France, most completely meets and refutes 
such charges as appear to be founded only upon the arbitrary interpretation given 
to the acts and reported language of its subordinate agents. 

I think it impossible more effectually to repel those charges than by 
referring to the language of Count Buol, reported in all my late des yatches to 
vour Lordship. At the same time it may be proper to observe that M. de 
Fonblanque himself in his last despatches which I have transmitted to your 
Lordship, appears to abandon them as eroundless. . 

Count Buol has already had to complain of the indiscreet language of some 
of his agents who had given expression to their own opinions, which had some- 
times been mistaken for those of their Government; but he remarked to me 
that now that the policy of his Government had been openly and unreservedly 
declared, it was probable that such expressions of indlividhal opinion as those to 
which he referred would no longer be indulged in, and it 1s to be hoped that the 
distorted accounts of the policy of this Government, to which they have given 
rise, will no longer be circulated.

happy to say that he rendered full justice to the moderation which had been 
used by Her Majesty's Government in the various communi¢ations that I had 
been directed to make during the course af the negotiation. He said with deep 
regret that the matter had been seriously precipitated by Chevalier Bunsen s 
despatches ; and from his Ixcelleney’s account of the way in which that Minister 
appears to have written by telegraph on the 24th instant, it would appear that
