(No. 123. Most Confidential.) 
My Lord, Rerlin, March 11, 1854. 
WITH reference to my preceding despatch, I have the honour to inform 
your Lordship that I observed to Baron Manteuffel that Her Majesty's Govern- 
ment were well aware that it was not from the want of exertion on his part thut 
the Convention had not been agreed to, but that what was now more important 
4 


—_— 


314 


than the Convention was the conviction that we could never count on the 
success of any negotiations with Prussia relating to the Bastern question ; for 
that the refusal of the King, and his announced declaration to maintain a striet 
neutrality, was not only a retrograde step, but, in my opinion, one that was 
most detrimental to the great cause in which Europe was about to embark, as 
the decision had already produced an unfavourable effect on Austria, and made 
her hesitate as to whether she would sign the Convention with England and 
France, and thus cause a separation in the position of the two German Powers ; 
and further, we must consider Prussian neutrality to be worth 200,000 men 
to Russia, as her frontiers were now guaranteed by this arrangement. She 
might now, without danger, throw all her forees against Turkey, and feel that 
she was secure to act as she pleases, for Europe was not united to support the 
opinions which had been declared in the Protocols of Vienna ; and the question, 
by this act of the Cabinet of Berlin, was no longer an European but an ‘Eastern 
one, These considerations, I said, could not fail to strike Her Majesty’s 
Government, and I was sure he must feel the altered position in which the 
affair now stood, 

His Excellency said that he deeply felt the inconvenience of what had 
vecurred ; and he added, in confidence, that he had spoken in this sense yester- 
day to the King, observing that His Majesty had made a retrovrade movement 
in his Eastern policy, and that he must beg his permission to retire from his 
service, for he could not undertake to defend it. 

Upon this the King endeayoured to explain that his opinions were 
unchanged, and that he was ready to stand by all the acts of the Conference of 
Vienna; but that he had invariably determined to maintain his neutrality as 
long as it was possible; that he wished to be on the most friendly terms with 
England; and that he certainly had no intention of entering into an alliance 
with Russia. 

We then had some conversation respecting Chevalier Bunsen’s correspond- 
ence ; and a ramour having reached me that that Minister had submitted to his 
Government some wild schemes and ambitious projects as to the future partition 
of Germany on the termination of the war with Russia, Linquired of this was true, 
His Excellency replied, that Chevalier Bunsen had really transmitted to the 
King a memoir embodying his dreams as to what was to happen hereafter, and 
had thereby greatly displeased His Majesty. He added, that Chevalier Bunsen 
must be very ignorant of His Majesty’s feclings on questions of this kind if he 
supposed that he was likely to be taken by such notions, for that His Majesty 
had invariably discountenanced all projects of aggrandisement, and was perhaps 
almost over-serupulous on the subject. 

Baron Manteutfel then said that he thought it would be essential for some 
person to be sent to London to explain what had lately taken place here; and 
that he should be glad if Count Albert Pourtales would undertake this mission, 
but that he feared he would not be disposed to do so under present circum- 
stances. 

The Government here scem to be in a sad state of contusion, Baron 
Mantenffel’s resignation is still in the King’s hands. M. de Bismark has not 
vet returned to Frankfort; and it is said that the Court party are using all their 
influence to have him placed at the Foreign Office. He is a favourite of the 
King, and not without talent, but inexperienced, and knowing little beyond the 
aifuirs of Germany. If he succeeded to Baron Manteuffel’s office he would 
probably become the mere tool of the King and the Kreux Zeitung” party; 
but it may yet be hoped that this will not be the case, 

He was at one moment this week directed to accompany Prince Charles of 
Prussia to St. Petersburgh, but he persuaded the King of the impropriety of 
cuch a mission, and the subject was dropped ; and indeed i more improper selec- 
tion than Prince Charles could not be made, for he certainly eal only have 
encouraged the Emperor Nicholas in expecting countenance at Berlin for his 
iueressive projects, and would have himself brought back from St. Petersburgh 
the most exaggerated notions of the military resources of Russia, and of the 
uecessity of making every concession to insure 4 Kussiin alliance.

ho. 426. 


Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon,—(Received March 17.) 
(No. 327.) 


My Lord, Paris, March 16, 1854. 

COUNT COLLOREDO will have made to your Lordship a communication 
similar to one made yesterday by M. de Hiibner to M. Drouyn de Lhuys, with 
the object of inducing England and France to abandon the project of a 
Quadruple Convention, and to substitute for it a Protocol of Conference, which 
should contain the same declarations that it had been proposed to consign to a 
Convention. An opportunity of signing such a Protocol would be offered if the 
English and French Governments made an official communication to the 
Conference of the answer which they were expecting from Mtussia to their 
summons to that Power to evacuate the Principalities. 

M. de Bourqueney had already communicated to M. Drouyn de Lhuys the 
‘tention of Count Buol to make this proposition, and the reasons why the 
Austrian Government were induced to put it forward; the principal being that 
since Prussia would not sign the Convention, the value of the united action of 
the Four Powers would be lost if the remaining three signed it without her, and 
the consequent triumph of Russia would be great, while the recorded schism of 
the two great German Powers would have a regrettable influence on the smaller 
States of Germany . 


321 


M. Drouyn de Lhuys is of opinion that without absolutely breaking with 
Austria by rejecting her present proposal, every effort should be made in the 
seriod which must intervene before the Russian answer to the summons al 
Prgland and France can be received, to induce her still to sign the Convention. 

With this view he has written to M. de Bourqueney and spoken to M. de 
Hiibner, in vigorous though not in unfriendly language, im the hope of proving 
to the Austrian Cabinet that the course proposed by Austria would b productive 
of the very evils which she is desirous of avoiding ; that the abandonment of a 
Convention for a Protocol, although the Four Powers might agree in signing the 
Protocol, would be a greater triumph to Russia than the isolation of Prussia, and 
the signature of the Convention by Great. Britain, France, and Austria alone; 
and that there is greater danger of exciting discord among the German people, 
whose sympathies are known to be unfavourable to Russia, by any hesitation on 
the part of the two great German Powers solemnly to record their opinions 
respecting the character of the war into which Russia was about to plunge. 
That, moreover, circumstances had occurred which had, however unfairly, 
brought the word ‘ Protocol” in connection with the Eastern question into 
disfavour, antl that the Vienna Conference would not be raised in public opinion 
by being made the vehicle of another compromise. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys proposes addressing a despatch in this sense to-night 
to Count Walewski for communication to your Lordship, but he holds himself 
free to agree to the signature of the Protocol luter, should Her Majesty's 
Government be of opinion that any advantage could result from it. 


] have, &c. 

(Signed) COWLEY,

My Lord, Constantinople, February 28, 1854, 

INTELLIGENCE from Russia reaches us very slowly. T[ have nothing 
from Odessa, Galatz, or Bucharest later than the 10th instant. 

I learn from Mr. Cunningham that the Russians have called for 32,000 
waggons in the Principalities. 

Mr, Yeames informs me that the 7th Division of Russian nfantry had 
only just reached its position between Reni and Ismail, relieving the 2nd Brigade 
of the 14th Division, now passing the Prath for Galatz. 

General Osten-Sacken had arrived at Odessa as Military Governor-General, 
expecting to be removed before long to Ismail. The Russians were moving 
forward, and the conseripts appeared in general to be mere boys. Prince 
Woronzow had obtained leave to go to Carlsbad, on the ground of ill-health. 

A letter received yesterday at the Porte from the Governor of Widin 
states that the Russians had begun to cannonade the lines at Kalafat. We are 
in daily expectation of further intelligence. 

I have, &e. ;

ALTHOUGH General Baraguay d’Hilliers has received the draft of Treaty

any full-powers, and, in consequence, feels himself unauthorised to sign the

inserted. 

Having no reason to suspect that the delay in sending his full-powers 1s 
more than an unintended oversight, I propose to adopt the expedient of a 
Protocol, and Reshid Pasha has no objection to take the same course. | 

We are to meet, all three, to-morrow at noon, and I do not despair of being 
able to forward the result of our conference to your Lordship on the 9th or 
10th instant. Meanwhile, I have informed Lord Cowley of the omission which 
retards our proceedings, and, should the requisite full-powers arrive from Paris 
in few days, the ‘Treaty will be signed and forwarded with the least practicnble 
delay, 

The day before yesterday I sent to ask the French Ambassador whether he 
was in possession of the necessary full-powers, and his answer being in the 
aflirmative, I was not prepared for the difficulty which he announced to me next 
day. No doubt there was some mistake in the delivery either of my message or 
ol his reply, =

My Lord, Berlin, March 18, 1854. 

I HAVE already had the honour to inform your Lordship by telegraph 
that a Prussian officer had been sent ta the Emperor of Austria at Munich, and 
that that officer was to proceed from thence to Vienna. Colonel Manteuffel, 
one of the King's Aides-de-camp, is the person who was selected for this duty « 
and it was with considerable surprise that I heard yesterday of his having come 
back suddenly to Berlin. : 

The reason of his unexpected return is explained by the anxiety of the 
King to hear his report of his audience of the Emperor rancis Joseph, and His 
Majesty consequently sent him a telegraphic message to Leipsig to repair to this 
place. The King saw Colonel Manteutfel immediately on his arrival, and 
despatched him again last night to Vienna, 

_ Baron Manteuffel, from whom I have endeavoured to learn the precise 
object of his cousin’s mission, has told me that he was not charged with any 
special proposals to the Austrian Government, but that he had been directed 
generally to make known to the Emperor Francis Joseph the anxious desire of 
the King for the maintenance of peace, and the intention of His Majesty in 
sending Count Grében and Prince Hohenzollern to London and Paris, “His 
Excellency said, however, that the principal object in view was to explain the 
desire of Prussia to act in concert with Austria on the Eastern question, and to 
concert with the Imperial Government as to the course which should eventually 
be followed by the two Governments. 

_ He then told me, that Colonel Mantouffel had found the Emperor inueh 
dejected at the little prospect which existed of the maintenance of peace ; that 
His Imperial Majesty was crieved to see that the conduct of Russia left no hope: 
of any accommodation of the mutters in dispute; and had said, that although 
it would be most painful to him to feel himself on the eve of a misunderstand - 
ing with the Czar, his duty to his country would be the solo interest he stiould

With regard to the former Prussia was called upon to devote her efforts to 
the maintenance of the peace of Europe, and the Government can indulge in 
the satisfactory consciousness of not having left untried any means for attaining 
that object. ‘They have not only independently exerted the influence and confi- 
dence they enjoy with foreign Governments to this end, but at the Vienna Con- 
ferences have united their strenuous efforts to those of Austria and the Western 
Powers to bring the differences between Russia and the Porte to a peaceable 
issue, The Government have not hesitated to express in the Protocols their 
honest opinion of the aflair, and to impart by their coneeslo the full weight of 
nnanimity to the steps taken by the Conference for the maintenance of peace. 
But before renouncing her liberty of decision beyond that point, and more parti- 
cularly before making engagements the direct or indirect consequences of which 
might have been a pledge for active participation in the quarrel, they believed it 
their duty scrupulously to weigh the sacrifices which they would thereby impose 
upon the country, and Prussia’s own interests which are at stake, 

The Government are determimed under all circumstances to preserve for 
Prussia her due cooperation for the maintenance of the balance of power in 
Europe, but for the present we must confess that we are not called upon in the 
same degree as other Powers are, by their geographical position and maritime 
resources, to interfere actively for the protection of the integrity of the Turkish 
Empire, in a quarrel, the extent of which is not to be foreseen, and which origi- 
nated not in the interests of our fatherland, but in the privileges and influence 
which other Powers claim in the territory of the Porte. ‘Therefore we cannot 
consider ourselves called upon to take any active part in the present struggle ; it 
is still a satisfaction to the paternal heart of His Majesty the King to be enabled 
to preserve for Prussia and her German allies the bicssings of peace longer than 
it appears desirable to those Powers more directly concerned. 

In this sense His Majesty the King has resolved only to require of the 
Prussian people those heavy sacrifices inseparable from war, when the true and 
particular interests of our country, the foremost of which are the honour and 
independence of Germany, render such a decision imperative, 

We hold now, as before, to the position taken up by the Vienna Protocols. 
For if it remains the essential object of the Vienna Conference to maintain and 
bring about peace, we shall do nothing in contradiction with it by reserving our- 
selves, as long as our particular circumstanecs permit, for fresh renewals of 
peaceful endeavours, while other States feel themselves called upon by their 
different position to appeal to arms. 

We trust our conduct will meet with fair and unprejudiced estimation, and 
consequently with the approbation of the foreign Powers; but more particularly 
our regard for our German allies, and the confidence in the good understanding 
into which we have already entered with them, and more particularly with 
Austria, have had a prominent share in guiding the decisions of the Govern- 
ment. 

In the same degree in which His Majesty is penetrated with the Royal duty 
of protecting Prussia and Germany from the miseries of war so long as the 
(dignity and welfare of either permit, he is also resolved under all circum- 
stances to do justice to the exalted mission which appertains to the position of 
Prussia as an European Power, and to stand faithfully by that ally who, by his 
geographical position, might be called upon to draw the sword sooner than 
Prussia in the defence of the interests of Germany. 

His Majesty's Government are led to hope that this independent and 
national line of policy will meet with the full concurrence of the country, and 
particularly of this House, But they cannot also conceal from themselves the faet 
that a successful execution of theirintentioas can only be attained if coupled 
with a distinet and declared determination to oppose every attempt, from what- 
ever quarter it may come, to force Prussia out of the course the decision af 
which has been her free choice, and to make the energies of this country suli- 
servienit to other interests than those which she herself recognises as incontest- 
able, with all the means whieh God has confided to the hands of the Kings of 
Prussia for the preservation of the independence of Germany. His Majesty the 
King considers he must in the present moment prove this firm resolution by 
demanding from the Chanibers the pecuniary means to enable Prussia to carry 
through with dignity and energy, in the present grave position of Europea) 
policy a part worthy of ber power and her history. 

4Q 


oat) 


I therefore submit to the House by Royal authority, which 1 will deliver 
immediately, a bill respecting @ erant of credit of 30,000,000 thalers, for the 
purpose of its boing decided upon according to the Constitution. In direct con- 
hexion with it is a proposition which las the object. of providing the means of 
paying the interest and the capital by a temporary ‘nerease of taxation in the 
possible though unwelcome case of the Government being obliged to make use of 
the grant of credit. 

His Majesty's Government openly shows you, gentlemen, the path they- 
will follow; and the greater the decision of the whole country to support 4 free 
and firm position of the Government is demonstrated by the voting of the credit 
required, the less is the probability that Prussia will be exposed to such demands 
as will necessitate the Government to raise the suins they have required ; and 
we count the more confidently on an unreserved support from the Repre- 
sentatives af the country, as we can asen's you that His Majesty’s resolutions, 
which might lead to the use of the required credit, will allow of no influence to 
considerations not strictly confined to the circle of the particular interests ot 
Prussia and her German allies. 

Gentlemen, the rulers. of Prussia, when they demanded a sacrifice and a 
pledge of confidence of their people in the name of the highest of earthly pos- 
cossions—in the name of the honour and independence of the fatherland —have 
never received other reply than the expression of @ joyful devotion of property 
and person; and you, gentlemen, will concur in our opinion that your yoice 
faithfully pourtrays the feeling of the whole eountty, if you rontidenty place in 
the hands of Mis Majesty's Government the means of protecting the inde~ 
yendence of the fatherland from every offensive attack, and if you convince 
Europe that the whole force of the country is to-day and ever ready without 
hesitation to undertake, when called upon, to transmit. that inherttance of 
honourable independence acquired by the heroism of our fathers, unsullied and 
unscathed through the storms of time. 


Berlin, March 10, 1854.

My pera Paris, Mareh 18, 1814. 
SINCE Laddressed your Lordship my despatch No, 327, M. Drouyn de 
Lhuys has received advices which convince him that the Prussian Government 
is not only ready to sign a Protocol of Conference, embodying all the stipulations 
of the proposed Quadruple Convention, but that they are willing to empower 
the Conference to discuss the measures that may become necessary to give 
effect to those stipulations. Under these circumstances, and having been 
informed by Count Walewski of the reasons why your Lordship considers that 
the wish of Austria to substitute a Protocol for a Convention should be acceded 
to, his Excellency 18 not disposed to press on the Austrian Cabinet his preference 
of a Convention, and he is willing to agree to the signature of a Protocol that 
shall contain all the points mentioned in and sanctioned by the Convention 
provided that the clause alluded to above as having been proposed by Prussia is 
added ; and that Austria binds herself beforehand to sign the Convention 
“} trois’? if Prussia declines to accept the Protocol.

The Ottoman Government appeared to be engaged in the furtherance of 
treasures to ameliorate the condition of the Sultan’s Christian subjects. 

The projected expedition to the East of British and French troops Was 
known at Constantinople, and had been reecived with lively satisfaction. 
Preparations were making to do every honour to them on their urrival, and 
supplies for their use were ordered to be collected at Adrianople, with an imten- 
tion of sending what might be wanted to Gallipoli. nee 

The Convention proposed by the French and English Governments. to 
secure the admission of French and English troops within the Turkish territory 
appears to have been well received and approved by Reshid Pasha, but it had 
not obtained the sanction of the Council of Ministers, or of the Sultan, when 
the mail of the 5th was dispatched.

Lord Cowley to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Recetwed March 20.) 


(No. 338. Confidential.) 


My Lord, Paris, Mareh 18, 1854. 
IT appears that M. Drouyn de Lhuys wrote some weeks back to the Prince 
of Servia to exhort him to maintain a strict neutrality in the struggle between 
Russia and the Porte, observing to him, that the part which France and 
England took in the contest was a guarantee that the interests of the Christian 
subjects of the Porte would not be neglected; that if the Treaties which gave to 
Russia the protectorate of Servin were destroyed by the fact of war, other 
Treaties might vest that protectorate in the hands of all the European Powers, 
and that those of the Sultan’s provinces which assisted the Christian Powers in 
their endeavour to restrict the ascendancy of Russia, would naturally find greater 
favour in the eyes of those Powers, during future negotiations, than those who 
countenanced the Czar’s proceedings. 
To this letter the Prince of Servia has replied in becoming terms, assuring 
M. Drouyn de Lhuys that he relies on the sympathy of England and France; 
and that he shall do nothing in this war which will militate against the duties he 
owes to his Sovereign the Sultan. 
Thave, &c. 
(Signed) COWLEY,

| WAS about to write to your Lordship on the subject of the sympathy 
said to have been evinced by the Pope for the Russian cause, when Mr. Lyons’ 
interesting despatch No. 14 of the 4th instant reached my hands. 

The following I helieve to be the particulars of the paltry intrigue which it 
has been attempted by Russia to get up at Rome. 

Some weeks ago the Grand Duchess Stephanie of Baden, now at Paris, 
received a letter from the Duchess of Leuelitenberg, which it was evidently 
intended should be shown to the Emperor; and in which her Imperial Highness, 
‘nm allusion to the Emperor, speaks of the sorrow with which she had seen her 
dear cousil's misunderstanding with her father, and her astonishment that the 
Sovereign of a country FO remarkable for the protection which it gaye to 
Christians in the East, ‘ould be found aiding the Turks; adding that the Pope 
himself had blessed the Russian arms, 

The Emperor, it appears, took some pains to ascertain what could have 
heen the source of such an assertion; and M, Drouyn de Liuys gave me lately 
the following explanation : 

On some occasion lately the Pope, in conversation either with @ Russian of 
Ingh rank, who was et through Rome, or with the accredited Russian 
Diplomatic Agent, spo%s® of the affairs of the Fast; and in taking leave of the 
person in question, gent some messages to the Emperor of Russia, adding, * Ido 
not forget him in ny prayers.” 

Tt seems that this phrase, although a common One ‘a the mouth of the 
Pope, when speaking of foreign Sovereigns, and ‘ntended as a prayer for their 
conversion when applied to those Prinees Who are deemed heretic by the Court 
of Reme, was magnified by the person to whom +t was addressed into a prayer 
for the Czar’s suceess in the Kast; anda letter written in the same exaggerate 
tone was immediately written by him to St. Petersburgh. “Ths produced al 
autograph letter from the Emperor Nicholas to the Pope, thanking him for his 

»rayers and good wishes, which the Pope could not understand; and His 

isines, M. Drouyn de Lhuys tells me, has written an answer in which he 
enumerated, with considerable astutentss, several complaints which it had been 
his duty to make to the Emperor of Tussin as to the treatment of the Roman 
Catholic Chureh in the Russian dominions, and supposes that these must be the 
communications to whieh His Lmperial Majesty alludes. 

I should hardly have thoult it necessary to trouble your Lordship on this 
mutter, had not ML Drouyn de Lhuys reverted more than onee to it, as if he 
wished that it should be fully explained. 

The fact of the Duchess of Leuchtenberg having written to the Grand 
Duchess Stephanie is, however, obtained from another souree 5 and | request 
your Lordship to consider this part of my communication 2s contidential.

My Lord, Paris, March 20, 1854, 

M. DROUYN DE LHUYS received yesterday 4 very interesting despatch 
from M. de Moustier, giving an account of a conyersation which that Minister 
had held with M. de Manteuffel on the subject of the attitude taken by Prussia 
on the Eastern question. 

M. de Moustier, having learnt that the King of Prussia had written to the 
‘mperor of Austria, proposing a declaration of neutrality on the part of Germany, 
appears to have caowwed to question Baron Manteuffel upon the subject; and a 
convenient opportunity having enabled M. de Mousticr to advert to the retrograde 
poliey of Prussia, M. de Manteuffel inquired to what he alluded. 

The French Minister replied by asking whether the Prussian Government 
had not some time back declined a suggestion of the Austrian Government that 
the two great German Powers should make a declaration of neutrality to the 
Diet, Truc it was that Austria had declared that she had never made any such 
suggestion, but, however that might be, the Prussian Government. had had an 
opportunity of proclaiming that they would make no declaration which would 
put their policy advisedly in opposition to that of the maritime Powers with 
whom they were united in conference. 

“"M. de Manteutlel assented to this statement. M. de Moustier then asked 
him whether it was not equally true that the Prussian Government had addressed 
a despatch to the Prussian Minister at Vienna, explaining the reasons why 
Prussia could not sign the proposed Quadruple Convention, but requesting that 
her refusal might not prevent the signature by Austria, whose interests in the 
Eastern question were very different from those of Prussia. 

Not only that, rejoined M, de Manteuffel, but we engaged, in case of any 
ert threatening Austria, In consequence of ler signature, to come to her 
vesislance. 

I must say, then, answered M, de Moustier, that, when the King now 
writes a letter. to the Emperor of Austria to recommend a contrary course, fam 
um justified in saying that your policy is retrograde. 

But how do you know that the King has so written? asked M, de 
Manteuffel, evasively. M. de Moustier replied, that it was well known, To 


his surprise M. de Manteuffel then said, that he must correct one part of 
ienne 


M. de Moustier's statement, namely, that any despatch had been sent to 

urging Austria to sign the Convention. It had been written and read to the 
aneaen Minister, Count Thun, but had not as yet been expedited from 
ferlin. 

It is to be observed, that M. de Moustier nsserts that M. de Manteuffel had 
assured him that the despatch had been transmitted to Vienna ten days ago: 
and, indeed, M. de Manteuffel does not appear to deny that he did give that 
RasUraned, 

Some discussion then ensued concerning the word “ neutrality,” M. de 
Moustier observing that a neutrality such as that proposed by the King 
amounted almost to a position of hostility towards the maritime Powers. M. de 
Manteuffel explained, that such was not its intention ; that he was about to 
make a declaration to the Chambers, in which, although M. de Moustier might 
not be satisfied with its terms, the word “ neutrality” would be carefully avoided ; 
that the King had yielded this pot, and that in general His Majesty was

coming round to his (M. de Manteuffel’s) views; but M. de Manteuftel 
vested that this might not be talked about, as noticing it would have the 
effect of throwing the King back into the arms of the Court eae 
ave, &c.

(No, 358.) 
My Lord, Paris, March 21, 1854. 

IT would appear, from a despatch received this morning by M. Drouyn de 
Lhuys from Berlin, that the Prussian Government is desirous of introducing into 
the Protocol, by which it Is intended to replace the Quadruple Convention, 
modifications of the stipulations contained im the latter instrument. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys remarked to me, with great indication of vexation, 
that this was in direct contradiction to a despatch from M. de Manteuffel to 
Count Hatzfeldt, which the latter had read to him-some days ago, and in which 
not only were the different points eontained in the Convention enumerated, and 
their introduction into a Protocol assented to, but it was proposed that the Con- 
ference should occupy itself with the measures which the signature of the 
Protocol might render necessary. 

M. Drouyn de Lhuys said that this further tergiversation on the part of 
Prussia made him regret that he had given his assent to the substitution of a 
Protocol in place of a Convention. I reminded him that his assent depended on 
certain conditions being fulfilled, and that it rested with the Austrian Goyern- 
ment, who had requested the substitution, to see that the conditions were fairly 


carried out.

(No. 108.) 
My Lord, Constantinople, March 15, 184, 


THE Tripartite Treaty concerning the reception of the allied armics destined 
for Turkey was finally agreed upon by the three Representatives at a late hour 
last night. General Baraguay 'Hilliers was prevented by the want of full- 
powers from adding his signature to those of Reshid Pasha and myself, 
waited in vain at hia request till affer the arrival of the French steam-packet 
yesterday. Reshid Pasha joined with me in urging him to sign, on the ground 
of its being clear that the absence of his full-powers was a mere necidental omis- 
sion. He persisted in declaring his inability to join with us in signing the Treaty, 
notwithstanding the importance of dispatch; and we were finally compelled to 
make the best arrangement that the view he took of his duties permitted. We 
passed the whole night at Reshid Pasha's house, avd it was not till long after 
sunrise that the arrangement agreed upon was fully executed, 

T have now the honour to inclose herewith, in copy, the formal instrument 
concluded, signed, and sealed hy the Ottoman Plenipotentiary and myself, together 
with the Supplementary Protocol, to which the Treaty is annexed, and which is 
invested with the signatures of the three Representatives. It has been the 
object of my exertions, seconded by those of Reshid Pasha, to bring the arrange- 
ments as near to a formal conclusion as the circumstances would allow, and | 
hope that what we have done, though necessarily impertvct, will meet with the 
approval of Her Majesty's Government. 

Without entertaining any unworthy suspicions, and attributing General 
Baraguay d'Hilliers’ dithculty to nothing but a mistaken scrupulousness, | 
thought it my duty to guard against the hazards which would arise out of the 
pices ofa French army in this country on formal invitation from the Porte 

efore the definitive acceptance of the ‘Treaty by France. 

: Your Lordship will observe that, although the Tyeaty has been signed in 
French, the English version transmitted officially from London has been strictly 
followed throughout, with the exception of Article IV, which is altogether ew. 
In obtaining the consent of my colleamues to that Article, amended in one part 


S04 


lee Oe 


340 


of it by the French Ambassador, I was moved by a strong sense of the importance 
of consulting the independence and efficiency of the allied armies while acting in 
this country, and of relieving them from the embarrassment of having to contend 
with misplaced pretensions on the part of the Turkish authorities. My first 
idea in framing the stipulations of that Article was to place them in the aceom- 
panying Protocol; but, finding that my colleagues preferred their insertion in 
the ‘Treaty, | acquiesced in t eir opinion, and am willing to believe that, eon- 
sidering the nature and object of the new clauses, it will appear to your Lordship 
as to me that the more solemn and stringent form is preferable. 

The closing paragraph of the Protocol was first prepared by Reshid Pasha in 
terms of a more positive character. ‘The want of instructions for so important 
an innovation determined the French Ambassador and myself to keep within the 
limits of 2 recommendation to our respective Governments. 

Should the full-epowers, which may still be expected, arrive before the 
recvipt of the ‘Treaty in Paris and London is acknowledged, 1 hope that the 
irregular course adopted from, necessity, for the moment, will be removed from 
that instrument.

Inclosure 2 in No. 454. 
Lord Stratford de Redcliffe to Mr. Wyse. 


Sir, Constantinople, March 11, 1854. 

[ HAVE the honour to transmit to you herewith copy of an official note 
addressed to me, and also to the French Ambassador, respecting the Porte’s late 
explanations with the Hellenie Envoy, antl the insurrectionary movements to 
which those explanations refer. Considering the great importance under present 
circumstances of repressing or counteracting with all possible expedition those 
expressions of sympathy and other incitements from without which appear to be 
the principal, if not the only, causes of disorder now prevailing around Arta and 
Janina, | cannot doubt your readiness, and that of your French colleague, to 
support the Turkish Charge d'Affaires in the execution of his instructions. lt 
is of the utmost consequence that the Turkish Government should place its 
relations with that of Athenson a footing of clear, unmistakeuble certainty, and 
that His Majesty the Sultan should either be enabled to rely upon the main- 
tenance of that fair and amicable policy on the part of Greece to whieh he is by 
Treaty entitled, or that he should be free to provide for the security of his 
dominions by the means which Providence has placed at his disposal. 

The first intention of the Porte, on receiving the complaints articulated by 
Neshet Bey, was to suspend diplomatic relations between the two countries. I 
was fortunate enough to prevail on the Sultan's Ministers to adopt in the first 
‘netanee a milder course, and a formal demand of explanation from M. Metaxa 
was the consequence, That demand is now transferred to the Government, of 
His Hellenie Majesty ; and it may still be hoped that a sense of justice towarils 
a neighbouring Power, which has given no ciuse of offence, and consideration 
for those Sovereigns who have pledged their honowr tm support of the Sultan 
against an unjust and violent ageression, will prevent the necessity of a resort to 
any painful alternative. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) STRATFORD DE REDCLIFFE.

whether the power and influence of Russian should be restrained within due 
limits, and whether a large portion ot Europe shoulil be released from the 
thraldem in which it was now held by Russia; and Count Griben could not 
doubt that if Russia were successful in the struggle, and were able to humiliate 
not the Porte alone but the four greatest Powers of Europe, the freedom and 
independence of Germany would be lost for ever, and that consequently the 
interest of Austria and Prussia wat even more direct than that of the maritime 
Powers in the triumph of the cause that they had undertaken together, 

[admitted that it had been right, and the bounden duty of the two German 
Powers to make every effort to maintan’ peace ; but L said that those efforts 
had been sincerely made also by England and France, and we all: knew with 
what result, England and France did not desire war—they had been compelled 
to necept it by the Emperor of Russia: and that it was utterly incomprehensible 
that the Prussian Government should now risk its most vital intercsts, its 
dignity and its position hoth abroad and at home, on account af the personal 
Character of the Emperor of Russia ; and because, if all Europe openly manitested 
what is felt by every man of courage and common sensé, the Emperor would 
only become more inflexible: while, if His Imperial Majesty still found triends 
who spoke to him the voiee of reason and truth; he would listen to thom. 

hut whut other language, | begged to ask, had his friends held to him for 
the last eight months ; and had he not been deaf to every appeal that reason and 
justice could suggest ? 

With reapect ta Count Groben's-view, that the maritiine Powers shioalil 
proceed in the first rank, and that the others should follow ma second or third,

an abdication of position, and an abandonment to all claim to influence the 
destinies of Europe, that 1 hardly thought would meet with approval or sympathy 
im the people of Prussia. ome lee

L told Count Groben 1 could not admit that the more successful the war

Prussia himself has recorded this. In conjunction with his allies he has offered 
to Russia honourable terms of peace, which have been contemptuously rejceted, 
The opinion of the world was unanimously against the course that the 
Emperor of Russia had unfortunately determined to pursue, and Leould see 
reagon to doubt the triumph of justice and reason.

Lord Bloomfield to the Earl of Clarendon.—(Received March 23.) 


(No, 144. Most Confidential.) 


My Lord, Berlin, March 21, 1854, 

THE Emperor of the French, being informed of the great interest taken by 
the King of Prussia in matters of architecture, lately forwarded to Berlin the 
drawings and plans of the improvements at the Louvre for presentation to His 
Majesty. 

The King is much gratified by this attention, and sent for the Marquis de 
Moustier to-day, in order to convey, through him, to the Emperor his thanks 
on the ocvasion. 

As it was desired that this audience should have no political character, the 
presence of Baron Manteutlel was dispensed with, 

‘The Marquis de Moustier was with His Majesty upwards of an hour, and 
he has given me the following account of his interview: 

Afier some conversation on the architectural work whieh he had received, 
M. de Moustier said that the King spoke with great emotion on the Eastern 
question, and so entively perverted the meaning of every act which had taken 
place, that he was obliged to put His Majesty right in the best way he could; 
but that he had no sooner succeeded in giving the conversation a reasonable 
turn, than His Majesty immediately sought the means of embroiling it again; 
and that in his whole life he never held so incoherent a conversation with any- 
hody, and which left the impression of so confused a mind as the King of 
Prussia’s. In the midst of endless contradictions there was, however, one fixed 
idea prevailing in the King’s mind, that he had a mission to maintain the peace 
of the world, and that all his efforts must be directed to this end. 

His allusions to the Emperor of Russian were strangely contradictory. At 
first Tis Majesty expressed his admiration of His Imperial Majesty's character 
and lovulty ; of the great position he had occupied in Europe; and of the use 
he had been in maintaining the cause of order: then, in the next moment, His 
Majesty said that his brother-in-law had latterly behaved extremely ill; that he 
had told him many untruths within the last six months; but that still he felt it 
was next to impossible to separate from him; and that he was occupied in 
writing to him (‘la lettre est éerite de mon sang" were His Majesty's words); 
and had endeavoured to call lis attention to the new laws promulgated in 
Turkey in favour of the Christians; telling him that when such things had 
taken place he could not see what cause the Emperor had to complain of the 
Turkish Government; and that he hoped he would order the evacuation of the 
Principalities, and show a better disposition to negotite peace. 

The Murquis de Moustier appears in vain to have urged on the King the 
inutility of expecting that the Emperar would give up the Greeks to the general 
Protectorate of the European Powers, for that his object was that the protection 
of the Greeks should devolve solely on himself, ‘This point appeared to make 
no impression whatever on the King, and still less the eee of regoneriting 
Turkey; infact, he expressed his hope that the Turks would be driven out of 
Europe; but he did not wish that the Greek Empire, ether, should be extended, 
for the Greeks were an abominable race; and in fact His Majesty, instead of 
throwing any light on this dark corner of the political world, seemed bent on 
making things more incomprehensible and more difficult, from his desire to 
keep aloof from them, and above all, from his unwillingness to identify his 
poliey with that of the Western Powers, though he would not go against us, 
and diecliea his reéolution to do all in his power to keep up the most friendly 
relations with France. 

His Majesty then made allusion to the naval expeditions which were being 
prepared to attack Russia; and suid that he thought England and France would 
find the task they were about to undertake one of extreme difficulty, for he 
knew Cronstadt well, and the approaches to it, and the plans of Sevastopol also 
were known to him; that any attack on these places would be useless, and only 
lead to discomfiture; and that he should grieve to hear of the loss of life that 
must ensue, and of our fine ships being sadly crippled,

No. 470. 
Lord Cowley to the Burl of Clarendon —(Received March 25.) 


(No. 377. Confidential.) 
My Lord, Paris, March 24, 1854. 

M. DE MOUSTIER has made a report received yesterday of a conversa- 
tion which he had had with the King of Prussia. M. Drouyn de Lhuys assures 
me that it is impossible (to use a homely expression) to make head or tail of 
His Majesty's observations, and that he is no wiser since he read M. de 
Moustier’s despatch than he was before. The only remark of real importance 
made by His Majesty was, that Austria and Prussia were about to make a com- 
munication to the Germanie Diet, with which His Majesty did not doubt the 
Maritime Powers would be satisfied. 

'The Emperor received by the same messenger ft letter from the King of 
Prussia in answer to one which His Imperial Majesty had addressed to His 
Prussian Majesty in sending him some plans or drawings before the mission ol 
Prince Hohenzollern, and in which His Imperial Majesty had taken an oppor- 
tunity of assuring His Prussian Majesty among other things, that if in supporting 
the policy laid down by the Conference at Vienna Prussia was attacked by Russia, 
France would be ready to assist her, , Aer ke 

The King of Prussia, in his answer, alludes to the possibility of hostilities 
with Russia, and says that if his own army was not sufficient to protect the 
interests of Prussia, he would avail himself with evatitude of the Emperor's 
aller. | 

[ have not seen the letter in question, and I believe this phrase to have been 
very loosely worded. Still it appears to have produced an impression on the 
Emperor's mind that if Austria declares against Russia, Prussia will follow. 

L have, &e. 
(Stened) COWLEY.

No, 476. 
The Barl of Westmorland to the Barl of Clarendon.—( Received March 25.) 


(No. 111.) 
My Lord, Vienna, March 22, 1854. 

LIEUTENANT-COLONEL MANTEUFFEL, one of the King of Prussia’s 
aides-de-camp, having been charged to deliver a letter from His Majesty to the 
Emperor of Austria, proceeded with it to Munich, and having executed bis 
commission there he was on his way from Munich to this place in order to 
communicate with Count Buol, when he was recalled by telegraph to Berlin, 
and he arrived here on the 19th instant from Berlin, bearing a second letter from 
the King, which he has delivered to the Emperor. 

Count Buol stated to me yesterday that His Imperial Majesty had not yet 
replied to this letter, and when T called upon him to-day at his usual hour of 
reception, he was obliged to leave me, as he was called by the Emperor to a 
council, at which the measures to be adopted with reference to. the commumnica- 
tions from Prussia would be discussed and decided upon, He merely stated 
tbat he could not object to the attitude which Prussia appeared to have assumed! 
by the speech of Baron Manteuffel, in which he maintained the entire concord- 
ance of Prussia with the acts of the Conference of Vienna, and the determination 
of the Prussian Government to-act in support of their allies for the defence of 
German interests, and to assist those Governments which, from their geographical 
position, might be called upon sooner than Prussia to assume an active part im 
the complications which might be expected to arise. Count Buol also expressed 
himself as most desirous of keeping up the action of Prussia with the Three 
Powers, and of maintaining the unity which has hitherto prevailed in the 
councils of the Conference, and with which he hoped the whole of Germany 
might be united, 

I have, &c. 
(Signed) WESTMORLAND.

Inclosure:2 in No: 477. 
Consul Michele to M, de Castillon. 


Sir, St. Petersburgh, March yg, 1894, 6 o'clock Poa. 

| WILL not attempt to conceal from you my surprise and regret at the 
intimation contained in your note of this day's date. 

Within an hour of the arrival of the British Cabinet messenger this morning, 
| placed in your hands the packet addressed to you, and forwarded to me by 
Lord Cowley, inclosing a letter from your Government to Count Nesselrode. 
1 tokl you I was in receipt of a similar communication from the Earl of 
Clarendon, and that 1 was instructed to concert with you for the sinullaneous 
delivery of the two letters to the Chancellor of the Empire. I moreover proposed 
that we should send a joint note to Count Neacetnade: informing him that we 
liad each an important communication to hand to him from our respective 
Governments, antl beeing bis: Excellency to name an hour at which it would 
cuit him fo receive us. 

Having perused the despatch I brought you, you said “you thought a 
written communication en our part, under existing circumstances, might be 
objectionable,” and you sugmested that we should proceed together to the 
Ministry for Foreign Affairs, in the hope that Count Nesselrode would receive us 
at once, Accordingly, we drove to the Chancellor's, and explained to-one of the 
chicls of the department our desire to place in Count Nesselrode’s hands the two 
notes from the French ard English Goveraments of which we were the bearers, 
‘This gentleman, after some little delay, expressed to us the Count’s regret that 
he could not see us then, and appointed 12 o'clock to-morrow for our interview 
with the Chancellor of the Empire. When 1 left you, at nearly 2 o'clock to-day, 


365 


it was arranged that I should call upon you in the morning, in order that we 
might proceed together to the Ministry for Foreign Affairs. 

{ter so positive, and, as it seemed to me, so satisfactory an arrangement, 
you may judge my surprise, on my return home at 6 o'clock this afternoon, at 
receiving your note, . . 

In that note you tell me that, “on perusing M, Drouyn de Lhuys' despatch, you 
perceived he requested you to forward the inclosure without delay, and in conse- 
quence that you were disposed to send it to M. de Nesselrode, and to tell him 
that you would not take upon yourself a delay of twenty-four hours in forwarding 
+ to him, and that you considered it your duty to apprize me of your deter- 
inination.” 

Tam sure you will give me credit for as much anxiety to acquit myself 
of the responsible duty assigned to me as you yourself displayed. 1 felt 1 was 
acting in strict accordance with my ‘nstructions in hastening to place Lord 
Clarendon’s despatch in Count Nesselrode 's hands simultaneously with the com- 
munication you were called upon to present on the part of M. Drouyn de Lhuys. 
You have now decided, as appears by your note, to transmit M. Drouyn de 
Lhuys’ despatch to Count Nesselrode by itself, and without waiting our 
appointed interview with the Chancellor. Am I to understand that you decline 
to accompany me to M. de Nesselrode at 12 o'clock to-morrow ? 

I confess that I deeply regret this circumstance, because I much fear it may 
tend to throw unjust suspicion upon that unity of action which my instructions 
enjoin, and may possibly cast a shadow of doubt upon that perfect accord which 
I feel sure continues to animate our respectiv> Governments. 

I have, &e. 
(Signed) Cc. E, GE MICHELE.
